papers.abstract: A general-purpose Vision-Language Model (VLM) has surpassed expert vision models in many domains such as object detection and video recognition. However, point correspondence is known to be challenging for VLMs since it goes beyond object-level recognition: it requires pixel-level localization of the same physical surface point across observations, even when appearance changes or the point disappears and later reappears. In this paper, we introduce AgenTAP, a VLM-based agent that directly predicts point coordinates and visibility and actively reasons over videos. Starting from its own estimate, the agent autonomously chooses what to inspect and uses the resulting evidence to verify point identity and refine its predictions. With GPT-6 Astra, it surpasses expert vision models in both point localization and visibility prediction, without correspondence-specific fine-tuning. We further use AgenTAP to re-identify physical points after disappearance and reconnect fragmented tracks, constructing EgoTAP-4D, a dataset of 3D point trajectories in long real-world egocentric videos. On sampled reappearing points, its predictions approach human agreement, and adding EgoTAP-4D to D4RT training improves average 3D tracking performance.
authors: Xuweiyi Chen, Jin Yao, Linzhan Mou, Lei Gong, Di Liu, Cheng Zhang, Ziqiao Ma, Sihan Xu, Adam W. Harley, Shengyi Qian, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Addresses VLM difficulty with pixel-level point correspondence under appearance changes and occlusions.
Predicts point coordinates and visibility, then actively selects video evidence to verify identity and refine estimates.
Outperforms expert vision models on localization and visibility without correspondence-specific fine-tuning.
Uses re-identified points to build EgoTAP-4D, a dataset of 3D trajectories from long egocentric videos.
Its reappearing-point predictions approach human agreement, and EgoTAP-4D improves D4RT’s average 3D tracking performance when used for training.

From a stereo egocentric video with camera poses and hand motion capture, we recover metric depth and camera poses, label each region as static (blue), moving (orange), or hand (green), and build 2D trajectories from the fused scene geometry, AllTracker, and MANO. When an object returns after leaving the view, AGENTAP with GPT-6 Astra locates its query points again (Fig. 9, first row). All trajectories are then lifted to 3D in one world frame.

AGENTAP’s lead over trackers grows with frame gap (c), its improvement over direct prediction is largest at strict thresholds (d), and its verification is robust (f). Agent results use GPT-6 Astra. Red: linear fit. Shading: 95% CIs. †: video input.

Figure 3 AgenTAP. (1) Initial prediction: the VLM agent inspects both views and records its own prediction. (2) Optional expert consultation: expert vision models propose candidate locations. (3) Iterative visual verification: the agent selects visual tools to test its hypothesis, revises the point’s location and visibility, and re-checks as needed.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is prohibitively expensive, making informative frame selection essential for accurate video understanding. The default uniform sampling often misses task-relevant keyframes, while recent training-free selectors instead pick frames by how well each one matches the question under an image-text alignment (ITA) score. However, we show that ITA signals correspond poorly with the MLLM's true needs: their rankings correlate weakly with downstream accuracy and are even negatively correlated on over 40% of questions, whereas the MLLM's internal yes/no judgment yields a much stronger signal. We present ProbFaS, a training- and label-free probabilistic pipeline that fuses both signals for key frame selection. ProbFaS treats dense ITA scores as cheap, biased measurements and sparse MLLM judgments as accurate, costly ones, unifying them via co-kriging, a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, to calibrate relevance across all frames. A temporal determinantal point process then selects frames capturing relevance peaks while preserving temporal coverage. Across Video-MME, MLVU and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS is the most accurate among fourteen state-of-the-art training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings (8-128 frames), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 3.1 percentage points. On MLVU and LongVideoBench, 32 ProbFaS frames match or surpass the top baseline at 128 frames and uniform sampling with up to 768 frames.
authors: Tianru Zhang, Mayank Nautiyal, Hugo Eidmann, Prashant Singh, Ekta Vats
bullets: Uniform sampling can miss keyframes, while image-text alignment rankings often poorly reflect the MLLM’s actual needs.
The training- and label-free method fuses dense ITA scores with sparse, more accurate MLLM yes/no judgments using co-kriging.
A temporal determinantal point process selects relevance peaks while maintaining temporal coverage.
Across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS leads training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings.
Using 32 frames, it matches or surpasses top-baseline performance obtained with 128 frames on MLVU and LongVideoBench.

figures.caption: Figure 4. ProbFaS pipeline. An image–text alignment model first scores every frame of a one-frame-per-second candidate grid against the question, and then the answering MLLM judges m of these frames with a label-free yes/no question. Co-kriging calibrates the low-fidelity alignment scores to these judgments on every frame, and a temporal DPP selects the k frames that the MLLM answers from.

papers.abstract: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/\rho$, and its yield stress $\sigma_Y/\rho$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.
authors: Ziyue Peng, Yanxi Hu, Junyoung Kim, Andrew Chen, Jin Yang, Chandrajit L. Bajaj, Etienne Vouga, William T. Freeman, Qixing Huang, Brandon Y. Feng
bullets: The task is to estimate density-normalized stiffness and, for plastic impacts, yield stress from how an object deforms when dropped.
Synthetic experiments misleadingly favor 3D tracklets, while real-world transfer favors short 2D optical-flow tracklets.
PhysReader learns to infer 3D deformation from video and 2D tracks by matching a teacher trained with exact simulated 3D deformation.
On 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, PhysReader was closer to reference materials than other inputs and baselines.
A scene optimizer improved accuracy slightly but required 49 minutes per video versus 12 seconds for PhysReader.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhysReader. Training in simulation (left): ❶ a teacher encodes exact 3D deformation, available only in simulation, into a feature fT , from which material heads predict E/ρ and σY /ρ (loss ℓ against the GT material). ❷ PhysReader sees only inputs that real video also provides: the RGB clip (V-JEPA 2 with LoRA), 2D optical-flow tracklets, and temporal and scale context. It maps them to f̂T and is trained to match fT (loss d) and the material through a frozen copy of the teacher’s heads (ℓ; Eq. 4). Inference in real (right): PhysReader alone predicts the material, without depth. For evaluation, the prediction re-simulates the drop with density ρ and Poisson’s ratio ν, and we report the replay loss and the parameter distance to the plausible region of reference materials (Sec. 4).

Figure 4. Simulation ranks the inputs backwards: stiffness error on synthetic validation and on real drops. Left: arrows connect each model with 2D flow tracklets to the same model with tracklets lifted to 3D (tracklets only, RGB + tracklets, and the two students). Every arrow leads to a lower error in simulation and a higher error on real videos. The feed-forward baselines (gray) are less accurate than PhysReader in both. Right: lifted tracklets, under each geometry condition of Table S7, beat 2D flow tracklets in simulation and lose to them on real videos.

Figure 3. PhysReader-Real. Left: the 16 objects, each dropped five times in different orientations. Right: for the 8 objects we cut specimens from, the reference stiffness fit jointly to the five drops (dot) and its plausible region (blue) against the measured stiffness of tensile specimens (gray).

Table 1. Inputs in simulation and on real drops. Every model uses the same RGB branch, training data, and protocol, except the “tracklets only” rows. Syn.: zE error on synthetic validation (dex). Real: distance to the plausible region, relative increases in total and deformation replay loss, and direct simulation difference (Sec. 4).

Table 3. Error budget for log10(E/ρ) (MAE, dex). Each row is one step from the row above. Synthetic rows use the 10,202 validation videos on which every row is defined; real rows use the 80 PhysReader-Real drops, scored against the reference materials. Exact geometry comes from the simulator; flow tracks from WAFT [76]; estimated depth from 4RC [51].

Table 4. Same drops, three domains: zE error (dex) of epoch-5 predictors on synthetic validation, on rendered replays of the real drops, and on real videos. The second column names the training depth and its alignment (one scale per clip or frame). “Rendered” and “LiDAR” replace the estimated depth at evaluation. Dashes: not applicable.

papers.selection_reason: Estimates material properties from video deformation dynamics; fits video understanding of physical dynamics.
papers.title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
papers.tldr: PhysReader estimates deformable-object material properties from a single real drop video using simulation-trained learning and transfers better with 2D motion cues than with explicit 3D tracks.

papers.abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv
bullets: Addresses object loss in long videos when uniform token merging accidentally coarsens fast-moving targets.
Uses velocity-shifted and block-matched mask unions, camera-compensated surprise checks, uncertainty delegation, and an all-objects-lost fallback.
On LVOS V2, improves J&F over ALGM by 2.76 points at ViT-S and 3.89 points at ViT-B, with 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs at ViT-S.
Remains close to dense-encoder accuracy on DAVIS 2017 validation, within 0.19 J&F points at ViT-S.
Reduced counted encoder FLOPs did not translate into lower startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time; latency depends on implementation and regime.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Tiers and predictions on three held-out LVOS videos (head R31c). Rows 1 and 2: the method keeps a fast-moving target that ALGM 0.98 has lost (ALGM predicts no mask in these frames). Row 3: the video where the method does worst against ALGM; ALGM keeps the target (a child), the method has lost it. These frames already run the fallback (ALGM’s own merging), so the loss happened earlier and persists through the memory. Red: high tier; orange: middle tier; white outline: the method’s predicted mask; dashed blue: ALGM 0.98’s. Frames are annotated frames where one of the two predicts no mask, whichever is more frequent in that video. Tiers replayed from the run’s own predictions through the reference implementation, whose decisions the timed run equals.

Figure 2: J&F against encoder FLOPs. (a) LVOS V2 valid, mean over three ViT-S heads; the paired difference against ALGM 0.98 with its 95% interval is given as text. (b) Short clips (the Table 5 baseline grid at ViT-S); the line marks dense.

Figure 1: The focus map. Before the encoder runs on frame t, for each tracked object we take the union of its velocity-shifted and block-matched masks on frame t (high tier). A surprise check compares frame t with frame t−1 shifted by the camera motion and promotes patches that changed without explanation. Rings sized by each object’s speed and search regions around lost objects form the middle tier, merged by the compared merger’s own rules; the rest is merged aggressively. Every decision is made before the first block, on the patch grid.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free focus-map token merging for efficient long-video object segmentation.
papers.title: Focus Only on What's Important: Training-Free Focus Maps for Frozen Vision Transformers in Long-Video Object Segmentation
papers.tldr: A training-free focus-map policy for frozen ViTs preserves high-resolution processing around likely objects, improving long-video segmentation accuracy while reducing counted encoder FLOPs, though not necessarily end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Spike cameras capture high-speed motion through an integrate-and-fire mechanism, providing fine-grained temporal observations without exposure blur. However, their binary streams encode accumulated illumination rather than instantaneous intensity, making reliable motion estimation challenging. Existing spike-based methods exploit temporal aggregation to construct motion representations, but this process may weaken fine-grained firing patterns. Meanwhile, correlation-based estimators often rely on learned matching features without explicitly characterizing the spatial distribution and ambiguity of candidate displacements. To address these challenges, we propose TIDE-Flow, a spike-based optical flow estimation framework that jointly exploits Temporal Integration Evidence (TIE) and Displacement Evidence Encoding (DEE). TIE combines raw spike patterns, multi-scale firing statistics, temporal moments, and boundary-aware interval cues, preserving complementary temporal information before spatial feature compression. DEE further integrates structured candidate-grid features with explicit displacement statistics to characterize matching geometry and competing correspondences. Both components are incorporated into a difference-correlation recurrent refinement framework, enabling effective temporal motion modeling and correspondence estimation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TIDE-Flow, with controlled ablations validating the contributions of temporal and displacement evidence modeling.
authors: Hanwen Liang, Wenxuan Liu, Wenxin Huang, Jingling Yuan, Zhaofei Yu, Xian Zhong, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Spike cameras provide blur-free temporal observations, but binary accumulated-illumination streams make motion estimation difficult.
Temporal Integration Evidence (TIE) combines raw spikes, multi-scale firing statistics, temporal moments, and boundary-aware interval cues.
Displacement Evidence Encoding (DEE) models candidate-grid structure, displacement statistics, and correspondence ambiguity.
Both components are integrated into a difference-correlation recurrent refinement framework for temporal motion modeling and flow estimation.
Experiments and controlled ablations demonstrate the effectiveness of the temporal and displacement evidence designs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. TIDE-Flow architecture. (a) Each flow update combines temporal motion evidence with local displacement evidence. (b) TIE preserves firing patterns and inter-spike interval cues before spatial compression. (c) DEE combines candidate-grid features with explicit displacement statistics.

papers.abstract: Underexposure weakens object details, and overexposure obscures boundaries. Spike cameras encode light into high-frequency binary streams. Long-window spike counts give stable appearance cues, while short observations reveal changes in firing rates from sparse measurements. We propose SPIRE, a sensor-grounded semantic-spiking framework for illumination-robust object detection from a single spike stream. SPIRE builds an appearance view from the full packet through detection-oriented illumination adaptation and constructs a sequence of cumulative views from progressively longer prefixes. Each prefix supplies a rate map, an edge map, and a rate difference that tracks changes as spikes accumulate. At selected scales, ANN features and spike-derived initialization jointly set the initial membrane potentials and firing thresholds, allowing semantic cues to shape the responses during temporal encoding. Local spike-count contrasts supervise both branches during training. The residual between measured and ANN-predicted contrasts combines with the spiking features to produce a bounded correction to the fused feature pyramid. On simulated VOC and COCO, SPIRE-D outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00-5.50 AP50 points across the four under- and overexposure settings. On real PKU-Vidar-DVS recordings, it achieves 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75. SPIRE-D also uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.
authors: Hanwen Liang, Wenxuan Liu, Wenxin Huang, Jingling Yuan, Zhaofei Yu, Xian Zhong, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses object-detail loss under underexposure and boundary loss under overexposure.
Builds an appearance view plus progressively accumulated views containing rate, edge, and rate-difference maps.
Uses ANN features and spike-derived signals to initialize membrane potentials and firing thresholds during temporal encoding.
Applies contrast supervision and a residual correction to refine the fused feature pyramid.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00–5.50 AP50 points in simulated settings, reaches 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75 on real recordings, and uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.

papers.abstract: Counting how many times something happens is among the simplest questions about a video and among the hardest for video-language models, autoregressive and diffusion alike. The difficulty lies between the frames: a model samples only a few of them, while each repetition unfolds as movement in between. Video codecs already record this movement densely as block displacements, and codec-based video models use it to shape their visual input. We are the first to show that this motion provides direct evidence for the count: a candidate count is a testable motion hypothesis, and unwinding the cycles it implies measures how strongly the observed directions support it. We present CoDiCount, a unified training-free framework that turns this test into a count potential and applies it while a frozen diffusion vision-language model (dVLM) denoises its answer. At every denoising step, structured count messages map each option letter, or each grammar-valid edit of an open integer, to the count it expresses and reweight the model's own probabilities within that set. Consistent gains over the official decoders on MotionBench, TOMATO, and SVCBench demonstrate the broad generalization of CoDiCount across diffusion models, datasets, and diverse counting tasks. With CoDiCount, a 7B dVLM outperforms GPT-5.1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro on MotionBench, surpasses GPT-4o and much larger open models on TOMATO, and matches GPT-5.4 on SVCBench.
authors: Zhuoqin Li, Jiayu Ding, Ge Li
bullets: Video counting is difficult because sparse frames miss repetitions occurring between them.
Codec motion vectors provide dense evidence about the direction and cycles of movement.
CoDiCount is a training-free framework that converts motion consistency into a count potential during diffusion denoising.
Structured count messages reweight probabilities for multiple-choice options or grammar-valid edits of open-ended integer answers.
It consistently improves official decoders across MotionBench, TOMATO, and SVCBench, with reported comparisons to leading proprietary and open models.

papers.abstract: We introduce a new model for real-time streaming captioning on a single GPU. YoloMT is a 449.8M-parameter streaming captioner that provides Pareto-frontier performance among generative vision models in its class. Distilled from a 27B teacher by SFT and GRPO, it leads every model under 1B parameters on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench and Video-MME, answered from its captions, and beats LFM2.5-VL-1.6B and SmolVLM2-2.2B. YoloMT is designed to read more frames cheaply and make them informative, encoding each frame once and caching it as 16 tokens. This allows the model to incorporate and infer from past frames without additional vision passes, making it efficient and effective. We also provide a detailed recipe for training YoloMT, with its stages and data, as well as ablations that demonstrate the contribution of each component.
authors: Nessim Ben Abbes, Duc Han Le, Sabri Mtibaa, Van-Tam Nguyen
bullets: Targets efficient real-time streaming captioning with a single GPU.
Encodes each frame once and caches it as 16 tokens, enabling inference over past frames without repeated vision passes.
Distilled from a 27B teacher using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Leads sub-1B-parameter models on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench, and Video-MME when evaluated from captions.
Provides a training recipe and ablations covering its stages, data, and components.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
authors: Cui Yakun, Tiantian Geng, Huixiang Kong, Xingqun Qi, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets the gap between offline video QA evaluation and real-time, context-dependent streaming scenarios.

Uses the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation.
Presents EviStream, a causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget.
Experiments show current VLMs remain substantially short of realistic streaming video reasoning requirements.

papers.abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Daiqi Shi, Shuang Li, Liao Zhang, Yang Cai, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sampling frames for queries requiring either holistic video understanding or fine-grained local evidence.
Uses a Determinantal Point Process to select relevant, non-redundant backbone frames spanning key moments.
Infers query needs from the backbone’s temporal distribution and allocates remaining budget to local or global context.
Local enrichment captures short-range dynamics and causal relations, while global enrichment connects isolated evidence across the video.
Shows consistently superior performance when integrated with three leading MLLMs on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU.

papers.abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.
authors: B\'ank Juh\'asz, Gerhard Widmer, Jan Schl\"uter
bullets: Targets the gap between accurate offline tracking and real-time streaming requirements.
Introduces causal architectural modifications for online beat and downbeat tracking.
Uses temporally shifted labels to predict slightly ahead of the current frame, reducing latency and improving peak-picking.
On GTZAN, F1 improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and from 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats versus BeatNet+.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised video representation learning has achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale unlabeled video data. Recent methods commonly extend Masked Image Modeling (MIM) to Masked Video Modeling (MVM), where video representations are learned by capturing semantic information from temporal contexts during masked content recovery. Unlike static images, videos exhibit inherent temporal variation, as visual objects continuously change their positions, appearances, and motion states across frames. Therefore, MVM needs to preserve semantic consistency while capturing temporal changes of corresponding regions, which raises two central challenges: 1) how to establish reliable temporal correspondence across frames, and 2) how to formulate an appropriate representation learning objective for modeling both semantic consistency and temporal variation. To address these challenges, we propose Variation-aware Temporal Correspondence for video Representation learning (VT-CoRe) framework. For challenge 1), VT-CoRe introduces a sandwich sampling strategy to construct two-sided temporal references and a Patch Registration Module (PRM) to establish reliable patch-level correspondence. For challenge 2), VT-CoRe imposes latent-space semantic alignment on registered representations through a self-distillation architecture and further proposes temporal variation modeling to constrain representation trajectories over time. Experiments on 8 downstream tasks across 16 benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of VT-CoRe across pixel-level, frame-level, video-level, and vision-based robotic learning scenarios. Complementary representation analysis shows that VT-CoRe learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware temporal correspondence learning.
authors: Yang Liu, Qianqian Xu, Peisong Wen, Siran Dai, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses unreliable temporal correspondence and the difficulty of jointly learning semantic consistency and temporal change in masked video modeling.
Uses sandwich sampling and a Patch Registration Module to establish two-sided, patch-level temporal correspondences.
Applies self-distillation for latent-space semantic alignment and constrains representation trajectories to model temporal variation.
Demonstrates effectiveness across 8 downstream tasks and 16 benchmarks, spanning pixel-, frame-, video-, and robotics-oriented learning.
Representation analysis indicates that the method learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware correspondence.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) are designed to represent the temporal structure of audio and video, yet it remains unclear how effectively they use this temporal information to relate sounds to visual events. To examine this, we probe an AV-LLM on an audio-visual synchronization task by shifting the audio so that the queried sound overlaps a different visual event. We observe that the model still favors the originally aligned event over the newly aligned one, indicating limited sensitivity to changes in audio-visual temporal alignment. To address this, we propose Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding (MSCD), a training-free decoding method that emphasizes audio-visual temporal alignment in model predictions. MSCD contrasts logits under preserved and disrupted temporal alignment to favor predictions supported by aligned audio and video. We disrupt this alignment by temporally shifting either the audio or the video, while keeping the other modality fixed. Extensive evaluations with two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MSCD for temporally grounded audio-visual understanding. In particular, MSCD improves accuracy over the base models on Daily-Omni by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively, suggesting that emphasizing temporal alignment can also benefit broader audio-visual understanding.
authors: Minyeong Jeong, Yeonju Kim, Yong Man Ro
bullets: AV-LLMs may favor originally associated visual events even when audio is shifted to overlap a different event, revealing limited temporal-alignment sensitivity.

On Daily-Omni, accuracy increases by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2\% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.
authors: Lennox Wei, Jiaqi Yao, Shixin Sun, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jianhua Han, Meng Tian, Shaohui Liu, Wangmeng Zuo

The best evaluated model reaches only 41.2% overall accuracy, while spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual understanding requires perceptual grounding, temporal understanding, and semantic inference. Multi-teacher distillation can consolidate these capabilities, but direct probability matching does not explicitly capture teacher prediction changes across audio-visual conditions. We introduce OmniMeld, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method that integrates domain expertise through modality-response-guided distribution matching. We train four teachers covering grounding and correspondence, temporal dynamics and event structure, causal and inferential reasoning, and contextual and holistic understanding. Each sample is routed to its corresponding teacher for supervision conditioned on student-generated answer prefixes. We derive transport costs from teacher prediction changes over shared candidate tokens across audio-visual conditions, using optimal transport to match student predictions to those of the teacher under complete audio-visual input. We also construct OmniMeld-20K for domain-specialized teacher training. The dataset spans four capability domains, with responses structured into evidence, reasoning, and answer sections and verified through consistency checks and media-based review. Experiments on audio-visual and general video understanding benchmarks demonstrate competitive teacher performance among similarly sized open-source models. The student improves over its base model across all evaluated benchmarks and surpasses the teachers' base model on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) requires reasoning about event progression, interactions, and the contextual conditions that distinguish abnormal behavior from common activity across diverse scenes. Although video agents enable multi-round analysis, the predefined analytical operations may not adequately satisfy these diverse reasoning demands. In this paper, we present EvoVAU, a framework that evolves a reusable tool library for a frozen video solver. Guided by task outcomes and execution trajectories, an external proposer identifies potential limitations in the library and refines it, retaining task experience as analytical operations that can be reused across questions. Specifically, Cross-Version Contrastive Feedback guides tool refinement by combining current errors with paired execution trajectories from historical corrections and regressions. Adoption-Aware Selection accepts a candidate library only when overall development-set accuracy improves and corrections outnumber regressions among questions on which the solver invokes new or modified tools. Using a small development set, EvoVAU alternates tool refinement with candidate evaluation and selection. At test time, the evolved library remains fixed, with no further involvement from the proposer. Experiments on several VAU benchmarks demonstrate strong performance and the flexibility of the evolved library across anomaly domains.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained ego-vehicle action recognition turns large-scale driving video into structured, searchable driving scenarios, providing a foundation for discovering critical maneuvers and systematically developing and evaluating autonomous driving models. However, large-scale driving videos often lack explicit ego-action labels, and existing datasets vary in action definitions, annotation granularity, and available supervision. We introduce EgoManeuver, a unified benchmark of 16 lateral and 6 longitudinal actions constructed from seven public driving datasets. Our multi-source labeling system leverages existing annotations and complementary evidence available in each source dataset, including vehicle signals, ego poses, HD-map topology, and captions, to assign labels under a unified fine-grained action taxonomy. We further standardize temporal action boundaries across datasets and validate the resulting labels through kinematic consistency checks and targeted human review. The resulting benchmark contains 86.6K segments spanning 190.8 h across 26 countries and provides a long-tail-aware evaluation protocol. We also introduce DenseEgo, a video-based baseline that combines spatially aware representations with dense per-step action supervision. On the EgoManeuver, DenseEgo achieves 82.7 lateral and 83.5 longitudinal mAP, outperforming the strongest existing video model by 1.5 and 5.0 points, respectively. Finally, we demonstrate one way to integrate DenseEgo with a language-model agent for retrieving driving videos that match user-specified actions and scenarios. All code, datasets, and model weights will be publicly released.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked which of two actions in a video happened first, given only a few sampled frames. Such frames can show that both actions occurred without showing which came first, so a reliable model should state an order only when the frames establish it. Forced-choice temporal benchmarks treat every input as answerable and reward lucky guesses, while answerability benchmarks do not separate frames that miss an action from frames that show both actions but not their order. We introduce EvOrderBench, a real-video benchmark of 579 event families. Each family fixes an episode and a question and varies only the frames: of two four-frame inputs, only one establishes the order, and two six-frame inputs extend the other one with either the frames that resolve the order or frames that do not. Every input is labeled for whether its frames establish each action and their order. Across sixteen open-weight configurations and three closed-source references, the best open models order nearly as accurately as the references when the frames establish the order, but withhold correctly on at most 83% of the inputs where they do not, against at least 90% for every reference; forced-choice accuracy cannot reveal this gap. Open models withhold mainly when the frames show neither action; once the frames show one or both, most of them commit to an order. Thinking narrows the gap, even when it is switched on within a single checkpoint, mainly by separating sufficient from insufficient evidence rather than by making models more cautious overall. Accurate ordering thus does not imply knowing when the frames fall short, and benchmarks should reward withholding alongside ordering.
authors: Xiaoqin Feng, Yuqi Li, Xinyuan Li, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Kuiye Ding, Yingli Tian
bullets: Introduces a real-video benchmark spanning 579 event families with frame sets that vary in whether they establish event order.
Labels whether each sampled input shows each action and whether it establishes which happened first.
Open models approach reference-model accuracy when order is visually established, but withhold less reliably on insufficient evidence.
Models most often withhold when neither action is shown; seeing one or both actions commonly triggers unjustified ordering.
Reasoning improves evidence sufficiency judgments, highlighting the need to reward correct withholding alongside temporal ordering.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for temporal ordering in video, relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: EvOrderBench: When do sampled frames establish event order?

papers.abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) specialize in offline video understanding; in contrast, their post-trained versions, streaming VLMs, can perform live interactions. We investigate whether streaming VLMs can replace their offline parent models on offline tasks. Such replacement could reduce deployment costs and improve efficiency. We propose Streaming Tax to systematically evaluate streaming VLMs on offline tasks. Our exploration spans three core dimensions: understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization across 15 benchmarks. Our findings reveal a critical gap between offline capability preservation and practical replaceability. This gap emerges at two stages: streaming adaptation can alter trustworthy behavior even when offline understanding is largely preserved, while the native streaming protocol can introduce further performance losses. Our analyses show that some of these losses arise from restricted access to historical visual evidence and failures to deliver usable responses. Importantly, regarding safety, streaming models often leave both harmful and legitimate requests unanswered rather than genuinely refusing unsafe ones. We then propose Stream++, a training-free plugin to improve streaming VLMs on offline tasks.
authors: Zhi Yang, Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang
bullets: Evaluates streaming VLMs on offline tasks across understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization using 15 benchmarks.
Finds two sources of performance loss: streaming adaptation can change trustworthy behavior, and the native streaming protocol can limit visual history and response usability.
Shows that safety behavior often manifests as unanswered requests—including legitimate ones—rather than appropriate refusal of harmful requests.
Introduces Stream++, a training-free plugin designed to improve streaming VLM performance on offline tasks.

papers.abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
bullets: The work proposes a fixed-length (K=16) Audio-Visual Query Transformer built on a 2.7B-parameter LLM.
Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training with entropy regularization stabilizes reinforcement-learning optimization.
The authors hypothesize “temporal alignment friction”: global audio features can disrupt visual chronology and hurt visually focused metrics.
Removing audio yields 63.0 CIDEr, below Qwen2.5-VL’s 67.4 but providing a strong sub-3B baseline.
The results suggest CIDEr on datasets such as MSR-VTT may undervalue multimodal semantic richness.

papers.abstract: A developer who reproduces a video model's error on a short clip can replay that clip after an update. How often does a correct clip answer mean the original test now passes? On 960 prespecified CG-Bench questions, we updated from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Accuracy on a 64-frame sample spanning the full video rose from 27.9% to 33.3%. Before scoring the newer model, we froze 388 clips on which the older model reproduced its exact reference error. The updated model passed the reference on 51 of 116 clip passes (44.0%, 95% Wilson interval 35.3-53.0%) and on 16 of 272 clip failures (5.9%). Closing cases on a clip pass would have declared 65 unresolved reference failures fixed. Requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of the 67 reference fixes (23.9%). In a separate 1,028-video study with different checkpoints and direct option scoring, only 15 clips passed, and the 16-frame reference confirmed one. For the generated-answer update, the short replay identified cases worth checking, while the original input remained necessary to verify individual fixes.
bullets: On 960 CG-Bench questions, accuracy rose from 27.9% to 33.3% after updating from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.
Among 388 clips reproducing the older model’s exact error, a clip pass matched a reference pass 44.0% of the time, while a clip failure still contained a reference fix 5.9% of the time.
Using clip passes to close cases would have falsely marked 65 unresolved failures as fixed; requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of 67 actual fixes.
A separate study found only one confirmed fix among 15 clip passes, reinforcing that the original input is needed for individual verification.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates short video clips for verifying fixes in video QA models, directly relevant to video understanding evaluation.
papers.title: Can a Short Video Clip Verify a Model Fix?
papers.tldr: A short video replay can flag potential model fixes, but it is not reliable enough to verify whether the original test truly passes.

papers.abstract: Understanding ultra-long videos requires retrieving sparse, query-relevant evidence from extensive video histories. Existing similarity-based retrieval methods are efficient, but they encode the question and the video content independently and thus often miss evidence whose relevance requires reasoning over both. Generative large language models (LLMs) can perform such reasoning, but they typically generate text over multiple rounds of search, which makes each query slow and costly. In this work, we introduce DeLoVi (Decision Models for Long Video), a framework that leverages pretrained decision models to retrieve evidence from ultra-long videos. Like an LLM, a decision model reads the question together with the candidate evidence, so it can reason over both. Unlike an LLM, it directly outputs a relevance score without generating text, which makes it fast and inexpensive. We first present DeLoVi-S, a simple method that generates captions for short video clips and uses a decision model to rank those captions by their relevance to a question. A generative LLM then answers the question using the top-ranked captions. Despite its simplicity, DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art performance on three ultra-long video understanding benchmarks, EgoLifeQA, EgoMemReason, and MM-Lifelong, and generalizes effectively to long-video understanding benchmarks, VideoMME-L and LVBench. However, DeLoVi-S scores every caption for every question, so its cost grows linearly with video length. To reduce this cost, we propose an automated policy evolution framework that iteratively refines the memory construction and retrieval policies around a fixed pretrained decision model. The resulting method, DeLoVi-E, maintains comparable performance while reducing input tokens by 34x on average compared with DeLoVi-S. It also runs over 3x faster than the best prior method on EgoLifeQA while achieving higher accuracy.
authors: Ce Zhang, Baiqi Li, Seongsu Ha, Gedas Bertasius
bullets: Addresses the failure of independent similarity retrieval to find evidence requiring joint reasoning over queries and video content.
DeLoVi-S ranks captions of short clips with a decision model, then uses a generative LLM to answer from the top-ranked evidence.
DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art results on three ultra-long video benchmarks and generalizes to additional long-video benchmarks.
DeLoVi-E evolves memory and retrieval policies to reduce input tokens by 34× on average while maintaining comparable performance.
On EgoLifeQA, DeLoVi-E runs over 3× faster than the best prior method while achieving higher accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DeLoVi. (a) DeLoVi-S divides the video into short clips of 10 to 30 seconds and captions every clip. A decision model scores the relevance of every clip caption to the question, and an LLM answers the question from the top-K clip captions. (b) DeLoVi-E answers the question in three steps. In Step 1, the decision model searches over a memory tree and selects the most relevant 3-minute window. The clip captions of this window are the first input of Step 3. In Step 2, keyword matching (BM25 [39]) shortlists the clip captions that share words with the question, and the decision model ranks the shortlisted captions by their relevance. Each top-ranked clip is passed to Step 3 together with its neighboring clips. In Step 3, the LLM answers the question from the clips of Step 1 and reports its confidence. If the LLM is not confident, the ranked clips of Step 2 are added in order and the LLM answers again, until it is confident.

Figure 8. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-S. The question asks for the color of the power bank that the camera wearer used last time and is asked on Day 6 of EgoLife, after 41 hours of video. The decision model assigns a relevance score to the memory entry of every clip, and the 100 clips with the highest scores are given to the LLM. We show the three top-ranked clips with their frames and memory entries. All three clips show the camera wearer handling a power bank on Day 6. The top-ranked clip is from the morning of Day 6 and does not show the power bank used last time, and the annotated evidence is ranked second. The LLM reads the retrieved memory entries in temporal order with their timestamps and answers correctly.

Figure 7. Requests to the decision model. (a) In a score request, the decision model receives the question and one memory entry and outputs a probability for each of the four levels. The relevance score is the expected level, normalized to [0, 1]. We show the instruction for EgoLifeQA, and its description of the video is adapted to each benchmark. (b) In a ranking request, the decision model receives the input fields, the instruction, and the candidates, and outputs a selection probability for each candidate.

Figure 1. Accuracy and runtime on EgoLifeQA. All methods use GPT-6 Luna as the LLM, and runtime is measured per question. DeLoVi-S achieves the highest accuracy, and DeLoVi-E is the fastest method while achieving the second-highest accuracy. Compared with MERIT [9], the strongest prior method, DeLoViE is 3.8× faster with 1.0% higher accuracy.

Figure 3. Accuracy gain of DeLoVi-S over MERIT at different time scales on MM-Lifelong. To answer a question, each method has to search an entire video, and the average video duration is 23.6, 51.9, and 105.6 hours on the day, week, and month splits, respectively. Both methods use the same LLM (GPT-6 Luna). MERIT is more accurate on the shortest video, whereas DeLoVi-S outperforms it on the longer videos.

Figure 9. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-E: answering from the first evidence window. The question asks what should be arranged in Alice’s room and is asked on Day 6, after 37 hours of video. In Step 1, the decision model selects Day 2, then the hour from 22:00 to 22:58, and lastly the 3-minute window from 22:48 to 22:51 (green), based on the summaries of these nodes. The clips of this window form the first evidence window, in which Alice describes the plans for the room. Each numbered box shows the frames and the memory entries of one evidence window. The LLM answers from this evidence window with a confidence of 0.97, so the search stops after a single LLM call.

Figure 6. Prompts for memory construction. (a) Prompt of the captioner. (b) Prompt of the free-text summaries of the initial policy and of DeLoVi-E. (c) One line of the timeline of an hour in DeLoVi-E, written from the summary of one 3-minute window. (d) One line of the index of a day in DeLoVi-E, written from the summary of one hour.

Figure 10. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-E: clip re-ranking after an answer that is not confident. The question asks which drinks the camera wearer usually does not buy at the supermarket. In Step 1, the decision model selects the hour of the supermarket visit and one of its 3-minute windows, and the LLM is not confident in its answer from this evidence window (confidence 0.62). In Step 2, BM25 shortlists 50 of the 763 clips, and the decision model re-ranks them. We show the ten top-ranked clips. Each of the first three forms a further evidence window together with its neighboring clips (boxes 2 to 4). The third and fourth evidence windows contain two statements of the camera wearer about not drinking coffee. The LLM answers after the 1st, 2nd, and 4th evidence windows, and its confidence reaches 0.91 after the 4th, so the search stops after three LLM calls.

papers.abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.
bullets: Targets cases where models identify the correct video moment but express its timestamp incorrectly.
LLM sessions inspect weights and activations to localize the source of errors, such as an MLP layer or separator token.
Edits improve grounding across TimeLens-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B, including larger gains on long videos.
Improving edits outperform same-sized random edits, and edited models run at the original speed.
Scope is limited to the reported timestamp-error cases and evaluated model/session settings.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled flexible conditional generation and editing pipelines, such as text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-guided synthesis. However, these workflows are inherently one-directional, mapping conditions to videos without providing a mechanism to invert this process. In complex media production settings, the ability to recover controllable textual conditions from a given video is highly desirable, yet remains underexplored. While inverse prompting has been studied for image generation, directly extending these approaches to video is challenging due to the need to capture temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, as well as the substantial computational cost of per-video optimization. In this work, we propose the first practical framework for efficient video inverse prompting. Specifically, we formulate inverse prompting as a meta-learning problem and introduce Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized over temporal dimensions to enable fast and effective prompt inference. Our approach amortizes the inversion process, eliminating the need for costly iterative optimization at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that MVIP recovers higher-quality inverse prompts with significantly improved reconstruction fidelity compared to image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines, while achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Code and video results are available at https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip-page/.
bullets: Addresses the lack of methods for inverting video-generation pipelines to recover controllable text conditions.
Introduces Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized across temporal dimensions.
Amortizes inversion, eliminating iterative per-video optimization at inference time.
Reports higher-quality inverse prompts, better reconstruction fidelity, and improved efficiency than image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines.
Focuses on capturing video temporal dynamics beyond static appearance.

papers.abstract: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
authors: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu
bullets: Addresses the tight coupling between utterance timing and audiovisual diarization in video captioning.
Uses a two-stage approach: synthetic-caption training on 225K clips, followed by reinforcement learning from 2.9K human-corrected clips.
Generates transcripts, utterance timestamps, speaker grouping, and visual descriptions for each utterance.
On DiaDemBench, achieves strong diarization and substantially better timestamp accuracy than Gemini 4 Argon (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME).
Maintains performance on multilingual and minute-long videos and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with similar-looking speakers. Each track shows one model’s predicted utterances over time, colored by the ground-truth speaker that its description depicts, with wrong speakers outlined in dark red.

Figure 11. A one-word turn right before another speaker (Mandarin). The young man answers with a single syllable lasting 0.3s (first frame), and the man in the gray suit continues immediately (second frame). DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E keep the short turn as a separate line with the correct speaker. Gemini 4 Argon and DiaDem merge it into the next speaker’s line, so turn A is lost. Gemini’s timestamps also miss every boundary (TIME 0), and DiaDem predicts none. This example shows that accurate timestamps and diarization are tightly coupled, as a model without precise turn boundaries tends to absorb a short turn into a longer neighboring one.

Figure 2. Overview of DiaCap. A speech recognizer Ψ transcribes the audio, and an audiovisual LLM Θ takes the transcript T together with the video and audio to predict the timestamps and speaker of every utterance. DiaCap-E2E predicts Y directly without a recognizer.

Figure 7. Failure case: off-screen speaker merged with the on-screen one. In a handheld phone video, a girl (A) asks her mother where she is going, and the mother (B) answers from off-screen. DiaCap describes a single speaker, gives the mother’s reply (“I’ll go wherever I want”) to the girl, and drops the mother’s cut-off last words. Since only the girl is ever on screen, the model does not infer that a second person is speaking.

Figure 9. Off-screen speakers in a multi-shot scene. The first and last turns are spoken while the camera shows someone else. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and describe these speakers as off-screen voices. Gemini 4 Argon gives the woman’s “Uh, Nal-what?” to the man in the blue lab coat and truncates it. DiaDem describes both men only as “man in a lab coat”, so the second man’s two turns go to the first man.

Figure 8. One speaker who goes off-screen. In this typical shot/reverse-shot conversation, a single woman speaks both lines. During the second line, the camera cuts to the listener and the speaker is off-screen. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute both lines to the same speaker. Gemini 4 Argon gives the second line to the visible listener (short reddish-brown hair). DiaDem’s description (“woman with shoulder-length brown hair”) is too generic to identify the speaker, so neither of its lines is credited.

Figure 10. A speaker seen only from behind. The last line is spoken by the man with his back to the camera. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute it to him. Gemini 4 Argon gives it to the man in the gray suit and DiaDem to the man with the mustache, the two people whose faces are visible.

Figure 12. A short interjection from a third speaker. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and place every boundary within the collar. Gemini 4 Argon merges the woman’s two turns into one line, so when scoring Gemini, we merge consecutive groundtruth utterances from the same speaker, which leaves three ground-truth turns. Gemini’s timestamps miss most boundaries (TIME 33). DiaDem describes the speaker of the final interjection only as “man’s voice”, which depicts none of the people in the scene.

Figure 13. Four speakers in one room. DiaCap, DiaCap-E2E, and Gemini 4 Argon attribute all five turns correctly. DiaDem gets three of the five turns wrong. It gives “Are you serious?” (C) and “Me too.” (D) to the young woman, and gives her own “I’m okay with that.” to a young man. Gemini’s timestamps drift by about 0.7s on the last three turns (TIME 40), whereas both DiaCap variants place every boundary within the collar (TIME 100).

We remove clips with unrelated or out-of-sync audio, deduplicate and resample the rest to balance language, speaker count, and visual scenes, and add no-speech clips with empty targets. (2) An audiovisual LLM annotates who says what, and a speech aligner timestamps each utterance. papers.abstract: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.
authors: Ce Zhang, Junyi He, Tianshi Ming, Jinxi He, Jianshu Zhang, Xiyuan Yang, Jianuo Zhu, Yicheng Tao, Xiyu Luo, Minghao Fu, Jiahui Zhu, Kehan Guo, Yunzhong Xiao, Jingyang Lin, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Katia Sycara, Yaqi Xie

papers.abstract: RGB-based video object segmentation (VOS) remains brittle under fast motion and adverse illumination. Event cameras preserve signal under blur and challenging exposure, but provide little evidence when motion slows. Interaction can restore object state for subsequent propagation, yet promptable event methods merely address single windows. We formalize event-based Promptable Video Segmentation (ePVS), where prompts at arbitrary windows initialize, correct, or introduce objects and predictions. We present Event Memory-As-Prompt Segmentation (E-MAPS), which transfers a pretrained promptable segmenter to event streams and learns propagation and correction. Event-to-Token (E2T) aligns recurrent event features with pretrained representations while preserving prompt-conditioning priors. Memory-Aware Prompting (MAP) converts object-conditioned history into sparse prompts, allowing memory and user inputs to share one decoder pathway efficiently. We construct Event-View Masklets (EViM) from 206K aligned RGB-event pairs and 620K masks for two-stage representation transfer and native event-video learning, and establish three training-disjoint benchmarks. E-MAPS leads prompt-once and interactive ePVS across all three benchmarks while being more efficient. It further demonstrates strong performance on zero-shot object tracking benchmarks. Uses Event-to-Token to align recurrent event features with pretrained promptable-segmentation representations.
Uses Memory-Aware Prompting to turn object-conditioned history into sparse prompts shared with user inputs through one decoder.
Trains with Event-View Masklets from 206K aligned RGB-event pairs and 620K masks, evaluated on three training-disjoint benchmarks.
Reports leading prompt-once and interactive ePVS performance across all benchmarks, with improved efficiency and strong zero-shot tracking results.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video question answering enables blind and low-vision (BLV) users to query their immediate surroundings through natural language. However, existing benchmarks and models primarily optimize for semantic agreement with reference answers, reducing visual assistance to a purely factual matching task. In real-world scenarios, a factually correct response remains practically unhelpful if it lacks the spatial orientation, actionable detail, or conciseness required by the immediate task of the user. Drawing upon real BLV egocentric videos and authentic user queries from EgoBlind, we construct the PA-EgoQA, a preference-aligned dataset that reconstructs reference answers according to empirical BLV communication criteria. Based on this dataset, we introduce Preference-Aligned Visual Egocentric Learning (PAVE), a unified learning and inference framework that couples structured answer-policy fine-tuning with deterministic question-conditioned routing to adapt response formulation directly to the surface form of the query at inference time. We further align the model via Filter-GRPO, which pairs a hierarchical correctness-quality reward with contrast-based candidate-group filtering to extract learning signals from both factual accuracy contrasts and fine-grained quality variations among correct answers. Extensive experiments across three vision-language backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in factual accuracy alongside substantial gains in assistive response quality. These results establish a concrete paradigm for translating human-centered response requirements into egocentric supervision, generation policies, and post-training objectives. Code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/PAVE.
authors: Nan Li, Shaofeng Liang, Shiyun Zhao, Keni Shi, Zhencheng Huang, Bowen Tian, Jiemin Wu, Wenshuo Chen, Kaishen Yuan, Runwei Guan, Yutao Yue

Uses Filter-GRPO to learn from correctness contrasts and quality differences among correct answers.

papers.abstract: In text-to-video retrieval, MLLM-based embedding models do well when the text describes the scene (general retrieval), but poorly when it describes actions and their direction (time-sensitive retrieval). TARA, a pioneering work, fine-tunes such a model on text triplets with temporal hard negatives; it improves time-sensitive retrieval but lowers general retrieval (mean R@1 over six benchmarks in our rerun on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B: 58.4->44.8), and its released model keeps general retrieval only when ensembled with Qwen3-VL-Embedding. Our goal is strong general and time-sensitive retrieval with one model and one vector per clip. Three findings lead to three simple components. Keep loss: general retrieval follows how far the output embeddings drift from the base model, not how far the weights move; we therefore keep them near the base model, which keeps most general retrieval even without general-domain data. Pair loss: the text embeddings of an action description and its reversed-direction version are well separated, but the video embeddings of a clip and its reversed copy are close; we therefore widen the gap between the video embeddings of each clip and its reversed copy, in the direction of the difference between their two text embeddings. Middle-layer LoRA: frames are combined in the middle layers, and temporal information peaks in or just after them; we therefore train LoRA only on these layers, which nearly matches training all weights on most time-sensitive benchmarks with 0.15% of the parameters and keeps general retrieval better. General R@1 stays at 58.4, while R@1 with each clip's reversed copy in the gallery rises from 55.5 to 63.2; the gains carry over to unseen benchmarks and InternVL2-8B-RA. The keep loss is also a remedy for the TARA recipe (general R@1: 44.8->57.8), and ensembling TARA with Ours gives the highest scores on RTime and unseen CiA among the compared models.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in harness-based recursive self-improvement (RSI) have improved video understanding by evolving executable agent workflows without updating foundation model parameters. However, extending this paradigm to omnimodal understanding remains challenging, as the heterogeneous and interdependent nature of multimodal perception and reasoning creates a complex evolution space, making targeted harness optimization difficult. To address these challenges, we propose OmniHarness-RSI, a modality-aware framework for evolving agent harnesses. Specifically, we factorize the evolution space into three capability dimensions: modality routing and collaboration, modality-aware evidence localization, and modality-specific perception. Based on this factorization, we construct a Factorized-Harness Agent integrating specialized perception experts and audio-video retrieval tools. We further introduce modality-guided harness evolution, which identifies deficiencies through structured modality-capability attribution and refines corresponding harness strategies through interactive code revisions and execution feedback. Validation-guided selection and held-out evaluation assess generalization within and across datasets. Experiments on WorldSense, Daily-Omni, and OmniVideoBench demonstrate test accuracy improvements of 8.86, 8.13, and 6.23 percentage points, respectively, consistently outperforming modality-agnostic RSI. The evolved harnesses also demonstrate cross-dataset transfer without adaptation, while reducing planner calls and viewed frames.

papers.abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
authors: Ayush Barik, Fan Lai, Francis Y. Yan
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of selecting and compressing video evidence without modeling the value of additional tokens.

Improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points at comparable compute, and by up to 1.5 points with 1.7–17.3× fewer TFLOPs in multi-turn understanding.

papers.abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy
authors: Divya Joshi, Ruize Yang, Colleen Peyton, R. James Cotton
bullets: Addresses the time and expertise required for observational assessments such as GMA and BabyOSCAR.
BB3D estimates 3D joint-angle trajectories from single-camera infant video rather than relying on 2D keypoint motion.
A transformer trained on BB3D trajectories predicted BabyOSCAR items and totals on held-out recordings.
The predicted BabyOSCAR total separated infants with and without cerebral palsy better than a replicated 2D-feature classifier, but worse than expert ratings.
Predictions also reflected functional ability and body distribution, though less strongly than clinician scores.
