papers.abstract: High-resolution video matting requires accurate recovery of continuous alpha values, including fine hair, soft boundaries, and motion blur, yet dense alpha supervision remains scarce. Pretrained text-to-video diffusion transformers (DiTs) offer rich spatio-temporal priors, whereas existing generative video matting approaches typically route alpha predictions through RGB-trained VAE latents, which can attenuate fine details and introduce additional decoding overhead. We present TokenMatte, which adapts a pretrained video DiT into a single-pass, auxiliary-free RGB-to-alpha predictor with a pixel-native output interface. At its core is a single shared linear readout that maps each spatio-temporal token directly to its corresponding ($t \times p \times p$) block of alpha pixels, predicting spatial details and temporal variations within the same local video block. Tiling these blocks produces the full-resolution alpha sequence without a convolutional decoder or learned upsampling. The predicted alpha is supervised directly in pixel space, while the ground-truth alpha never enters the VAE, eliminating target-side alpha encoding and output-side VAE decoding. Leveraging the pretrained video prior, TokenMatte is trained using only existing public matting datasets, without additional data curation or auxiliary inputs at inference. Compared with a matched latent-output baseline, our pixel-native interface improves matting accuracy while achieving a 1.51$\times$ inference speedup. TokenMatte establishes a new auxiliary-free state of the art on VideoMatte, YouTubeMatte, and V-HIM60.
authors: Zanyi Wang, Dengyang Jiang, Fengfei Yu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Addresses scarce dense alpha supervision and detail loss from routing predictions through RGB-trained VAE latents.
Uses one shared linear readout to map each spatio-temporal token directly to a local block of alpha pixels.
Supervises alpha directly in pixel space, avoiding alpha VAE encoding, convolutional decoding, and learned upsampling.
Outperforms a matched latent-output baseline in accuracy and achieves a 1.51× inference speedup.
Reports auxiliary-free state-of-the-art results on VideoMatte, YouTubeMatte, and V-HIM60.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method Overview. From an RGB video, a frozen VAE encoder produces latent tokens and a pretrained T2V backbone runs one deterministic pass (τ = τ0, ϵ=0) to yield a spatio-temporal token field (Sec. 3.1). A shared linear head unfolds each token into its local block of alpha pixels (Sec. 3.2), supervised in pixel space with no alpha encoding or VAE decoding (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison with auxiliary-free and mask-guided methods. We compare TokenMatte with auxiliary-free RVM and GVM, and with mask-guided MatAnyone2 and VideoMaMa using SAM2 guidance. The SAM2 mask sequence is shown for reference, and colored boxes indicate the magnified regions on the right. While all methods recover the main foreground, RVM produces diffuse hair boundaries and the other baselines tend to smooth some thin strands. TokenMatte preserves finer and more separated hair structures without auxiliary mask guidance.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison with auxiliary-free methods. We compare TokenMatte with RVM and latent-based GVM across three video frames. The blue and orange boxes indicate regions magnified on the right. RVM produces diffuse alpha boundaries, while GVM exhibits over-smoothed predictions that blur fine structures and merge neighboring details. In contrast, TokenMatte preserves sharper boundaries and finer, more separated alpha structures without auxiliary inputs.

Figure 1. Latent-based vs. our native pixel-based training. (a) Latent supervision encodes the GT matte through a frozen VAE and supervises in latent space; the alpha target must survive a VAE round-trip, and the pixel objective only reaches the model through the decoder. (b) We never encode the alpha target: a readout module unfolds each token directly into pixels, supervised in pixel space. (c) Quality bottleneck—the GT matte incurs reconstruction error after a VAE round-trip, revealing an empirical ceiling for alpha reconstruction, especially on detail-heavy data (VideoMatte 3.50, V-HIM60 1.22, YouTubeMatte 0.54, MAD). (d) Speed bottleneck—removing the VAE-decode stage cuts per-clip latency from 576ms to 382ms, a 1.51× saving at equal depth.
Figure 6. Translucent fabric. TokenMatte preserves thin fabric layers and spatially varying opacity across the sequence.
Figure 7. Fast water spray. TokenMatte captures rapidly changing water structures and fine spray details from RGB input alone.

Figure 4. Generalization to non-human foregrounds. TokenMatte produces detailed alpha mattes across diverse animal categories, preserving fine whiskers, fur, and irregular boundary structures beyond the predominantly human-centered evaluation domain. Ground-truth mattes are shown for reference.
Figure 11. Complex foreground interaction. TokenMatte preserves the articulated foreground together with thin structures such as hair, ropes, and the moving weapon across temporally separated frames.
Figure 8. Transparent soap bubbles. TokenMatte recovers transparent bubbles with clear boundaries and varying opacity over time.
Figure 10. Soft emissive boundaries. TokenMatte captures the foreground together with soft, spatially varying alpha transitions around the glowing hand across frames.
Figure 9. Translucent tentacles. TokenMatte preserves thin tentacles and translucent structures across separated frames.

papers.title: TokenMatte: Unlocking T2V Diffusion Priors for Pixel-Native Video Matting

papers.abstract: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.
authors: Xiao Ma, Lin Li, Shiqing Wu, Wang Gao, Chuanbo Liu, Jianquan Liu
bullets: Targets real-time sign-to-gloss, sign-to-text, and sign-to-gloss-to-text streaming tasks.
Freezes the pretrained offline model and trains a boundary adapter supervised by CTC alignments, avoiding human boundary annotations.
Uses prefix voting with an adaptive Wait-K output policy to control when outputs are committed.
Evaluated across four offline methods on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily.
Adds less than 0.1% trainable parameters per offline method and achieves a strong quality–latency trade-off for S2T, while remaining competitive on S2G and S2G2T.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overall framework of BCP for online sign language recognition and translation. The framework consists of a boundary prediction module and a boundary-controlled Wait-K output policy incorporating LCP-based prefix voting.

papers.selection_reason: Online sign language recognition/translation is a video-language understanding task; the lightweight streaming adaptation framework is transferable to video understanding.
papers.title: BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
papers.tldr: BCP efficiently converts pretrained offline sign-language models into online recognizers and translators using a lightweight, annotation-free boundary-control module.

papers.abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.
authors: Chenrui Fan, Qiyang Hu, Luca Scharr, Paolo Favaro
bullets: Generated videos often contain subtle deformations and sliding that undermine 3D reconstruction and are difficult to label manually.
The method pairs real clips with keyframe-conditioned re-creations, then measures each pixel’s deviation from rigid-scene behavior along the generated camera path.
The released dataset contains 871 real-generated video twins, with construction code and an official benchmark test split.
NRG-PD predicts per-pixel rigidity-violation angles from RGB alone and achieves 0.85 AUROC, outperforming seven existing consistency or motion-segmentation methods.
Its predictions improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction for videos containing generated content.

papers.abstract: Temporal localization in long videos is challenging because brief, question-relevant events are dispersed among extensive redundant content. Limited visual budgets increase the risk of omitting these events or their temporal context, undermining reliable reasoning. Existing frame selection methods emphasize semantic relevance or temporal coverage, often overlooking the complementary evidence needed to locate related events and establish their temporal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TESS, a training-free framework for query-guided temporal event-structured frame selection. TESS selects frames that jointly show the reference event and the event asked about, in the required temporal order. Leveraging frozen vision-language representations, TESS integrates soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and within-role redundancy suppression to preserve complementary event evidence. Extensive experiments across four long-video understanding benchmarks and three multimodal backbones demonstrate that TESS consistently outperforms the strongest compared baseline by 4.0-5.5 percentage points under a fixed frame budget. Further analyses reveal greater improvements on longer videos and robust performance under tighter visual budgets, while independent evidence annotations confirm enhanced event and temporal-relation coverage. These findings establish explicit temporal evidence organization as an effective training-free strategy for preserving event relationships and supporting efficient temporal reasoning over long videos. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TESS_code.
authors: Qi Lu, Shiyan Tong, Shujie Li, Sen Li, Likun shi, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Yao Hu
bullets: Targets the omission of brief, related events and their temporal context in long videos.

Selects complementary frames showing both the reference event and the queried event in the required order.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.0–5.5 percentage points across four benchmarks and three multimodal backbones.
Shows larger gains on longer videos and under tighter frame budgets, with improved event and temporal-relation coverage.

papers.abstract: In streaming video understanding, the evidence needed to answer a question may have already left the recent-frame window. Keeping all frames does not scale with video length, while dropping older frames limits the model's ability to reason about the past. We propose Visual-State Graph (VSG), a training-free memory that stores the state of a stream rather than the raw sequence of frames. VSG represents the stream as a graph of objects and their relations, together with a log of events; similar to a dynamically evolving scene graph. An object observed repeatedly is represented by one persistent node, with a timestamped history of how its state changes. To determine whether a newly mentioned object already exists in the graph, we compare the relations it takes part in with those of stored objects. We build this memory as the video arrives, before the questions are known. When a question arrives, we retrieve relevant objects and events alongside recent frames under a fixed input budget. Our evaluation spans four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models ranging from 7B to 32B parameters. Under matched input budgets, VSG improves reasoning about the past while preserving real-time understanding.
authors: Ailar Mahdizadeh, Pritam Sarkar, Xiangteng He, Leonid Sigal
bullets: Addresses the loss of long-term evidence when streaming systems retain only recent frames.
Builds a dynamically updated graph of persistent objects, their relations, and timestamped state histories, plus an event log.
Matches newly observed objects to existing graph nodes using their relational context.
Constructs memory online before questions are known, then retrieves relevant objects and events with recent frames.
Evaluated on four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models; improves past reasoning while preserving real-time understanding under matched budgets.

papers.abstract: In fitness and sports training, timely action quality assessment (AQA) is essential for learners to identify and correct technical errors during movement execution. However, most AQA methods assess completed performances, limiting their ability to provide timely feedback. Streaming methods alleviate this latency, but limited reasoning hinders their use of subtle movement cues and sport-specific knowledge. Moreover, their fragmented feedback focuses on one body part at a time, overlooking movement details of other body parts and transitions between action phases. To address these limitations, we propose StreamCoach, a streaming AQA framework under the OnCueCoaching paradigm that couples continuous chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with proactive, evidence-gated coaching. Technique-Aware Reasoning tracks body-part movements and action-phase transitions against sport-specific criteria, while Holistic Coaching integrates accumulated evidence to deliver timely, comprehensive feedback on strengths and technical errors. To support training and benchmarking, we construct EE4D-Stream from 1,213 sports video sequences in Ego-Exo4D through LLM-assisted reannotation and manual review of selected claims, pairing dense CoT annotations with evidence-gated speech content. Building on this dataset, we train StreamCoach using Temporal-Semantic Alignment Reinforcement Learning to jointly optimize feedback timing and content. We benchmark 11 offline and streaming baselines on EE4D-Stream, including three proprietary models. StreamCoach achieves state-of-the-art results across intervention timing, action assessment, and coaching quality, surpassing both GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5.

papers.abstract: Existing clip-based soccer commentary models often produce delayed, repeated, or poorly synchronized narration on untrimmed full-match videos. Recent streaming video-language models make low-latency full-match narration feasible, but they often favor general descriptions rather than professional, event-grounded soccer commentary. They may describe nearby actions while failing to mention key events such as goals, cards, substitutions, and offsides correctly and on time. In this paper, we present SoccerNarrate to bridge low-latency streaming narration with event-grounded professional soccer commentary across data, training, and evaluation. First, we construct SoccerNarrate-Data, a large-scale time-anchored dataset with word-level ASR alignment, quality filtering, and entity calibration. Second, we perform macro-window preference alignment (MWPA), which aligns the model with complete event-level commentary semantics by comparing causal multi-step rollouts from the same streaming prefix while keeping second-level inference unchanged. We further use event-mismatched human commentaries as counterfactual negatives to emphasize event semantics over commentary style. Third, we introduce SoccerNarrate-Eval, an event-centric benchmark based on temporally constrained event entailment. Full-match experiments show that SoccerNarrate improves event coverage and event-aligned precision over strong offline and streaming baselines. Code and models are released at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/SoccerNarrate.
authors: Zihan Jia, Zhilin Dai, Zhengming Zhang, Min Yang, Zhenpeng Huang, Jiaqi Li, Caixia Sun, Xi Chen, Liang Li, Junlan Feng, Gangshan Wu, Limin Wang

Uses macro-window preference alignment to compare multi-step streaming rollouts and emphasize complete event-level semantics.
Adds event-mismatched human commentaries as counterfactual negatives and proposes the event-centric SoccerNarrate-Eval benchmark.
Full-match experiments show improved event coverage and event-aligned precision over strong offline and streaming baselines.

Figure 5: Overview of Macro-window Preference Alignment (MWPA) and counterfactual hard-negative construction. Given the same streaming prefix and video window, MWPA compares two human commentary trajectories from the same match. The preferred trajectory Y + k matches the target event, while the rejected trajectory Y − k is sampled from a type-mismatched event as a counterfactual hard negative. This provides event-level preference supervision while preserving micro-step streaming inference.

papers.abstract: In embedding-based video anomaly detection (VAD), normal clips can have high similarity to anomalous descriptions, an anomaly bias that leads to false positives. Methods such as PRISM mitigate this bias by measuring deviations from a normality reference along anomaly directions. Both the normality reference and the anomaly directions are derived from text and shared across videos, although normal activity and the appearance of anomalies vary across scenes. The resulting scores are also sensitive to prompt selection. To address these limitations, we propose Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation (VIDE), a training-free framework that adapts text-derived scoring to each test video using frozen clip embeddings. VIDE estimates normal scene content from clips with low initial anomaly scores and uses this estimate to partially correct the textual reference. It then rescales category responses, penalizes clips with strong responses across categories, and refines the anomaly directions using high-scoring clips. VIDE averages scores across prompt views to reduce sensitivity to prompt selection and fuses scores from two frozen encoders. With both encoders, VIDE improves AUC over the best PRISM result by $1.5$, $1.9$, and $3.5$ points on UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, respectively, and AP by $6.5$ points on XD-Violence and $9.3$ points on MSAD. VIDE yields the highest AUC among the compared training-free methods on all three benchmarks and the highest reported AUC among all compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD. Our code is included in the supplementary material and will be made publicly available.
authors: Kevin D. Nguetche, Atif Belal, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli

Improves over PRISM across UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, achieving the best reported AUC among compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD.

papers.abstract: Promptable video trackers such as SAM2 achieve accurate and robust performance through strong temporal consistency, making them important foundations for downstream video understanding and tracking applications. As their use continues to expand, understanding their robustness to adversarial perturbations becomes increasingly important. Existing attacks on SAM2 largely focus on local mask degradation and short-term temporal feature disruption, leaving its longer-term dynamics and competing object interferences (Distractors) insufficiently explored. We observe that SAM2 itself exposes useful distractor cues when tracking becomes uncertain. Based on these observations, we propose DistractAttack, a white-box attack that uses background distractors to disrupt target tracking persistently. Its core procedure, Counterfactual Distractor Search (CDS), propagates clean and attacked trajectories in parallel to discover plausible competing regions and identify those that become increasingly effective under perturbation. The discovered evidence is accumulated over time to weaken target support and promote recurrent alternatives or disappearance predictions. Extensive experiments under video-level and one-shot perturbations across Visual Object Tracking and Video Object Segmentation demonstrate strong attack effectiveness, raising DRE to $4.4\times$ and NRE to $7.3\times$ their nearest baselines under video perturbation, while transferring effectively across model scales and tracker variants in black-box settings. authors: Adonay Demewez Gebremedhin, Mohamad Alansari, Wessam Shehieb, Muzammal Naseer

Across tracking and segmentation tasks, reaches up to 4.4× higher DRE and 7.3× higher NRE than nearest baselines under video perturbations.
Transfers effectively across model scales and tracker variants in black-box settings.

papers.abstract: Advancing surgical automation requires a comprehensive spatio-temporal understanding of how instruments act on tissue throughout an action. Existing surgical benchmarks, however, largely define supervision through task-specific targets, leaving the relationships between action semantics, instrument motion, and tissue interaction incompletely specified. To address this limitation, we introduce TACTUS (Tool, Action, Contact and Trajectory Understanding in Surgery), a new dataset and benchmark that establishes a unified annotation framework for complete surgical actions. The framework jointly specifies tool and action identities, nested action and interaction windows, instrument-specific landmark trajectories, and tissue-region tracks. To construct these annotations at scale, we develop a two-tier pipeline combining human annotation, point tracking, and model-generated spatial prompts. Using this pipeline, we re-annotate 141 videos from five public sources, producing 22,995 action clips spanning 2.9 million frames. The dataset comprises 15,668 Gold clips with human spatial prompts followed by review and re-checking, and 7,327 Silver clips combining human semantic and temporal annotations with model-generated spatial prompts. We further introduce TactusNet, the companion reference network, to benchmark semantic, temporal, and spatial prediction from shared video features. Across TactusNet and 13 published baselines, tool-action accuracy reaches 95.8% with per-head encoder fine-tuning, while the best temporal recall and contact Dice reach 46.6% at temporal IoU 0.7 and 0.351, respectively. Moreover, adding Silver improves the default TactusNet's pair accuracy from 93.8% to 95.5%. Together, these contributions establish a foundation for learning and evaluating the instrument-tissue interactions underlying future surgical automation.

papers.abstract: Training capable omni video agents requires more than diverse question-answer pairs: agents must learn to reliably find, connect, and correct task-relevant evidence in omni-setting. However, we argue that existing data pipelines provide limited control over task-relevant evidence and weak supervision for these capabilities. In this work, we present Open OmniCoach, a new framework for evidence-seeking omni video agents. It contains a high-quality dataset, OmniCoach-240K, and a new agentic reinforcement learning (RL) method, Step-Level Evidence-Guided Policy Optimization (SEPO). For the former, OmniCoach-240K comprises 248.2K interaction trajectories, including 230.7K multi-span trajectories and 17.4K reflection trajectories. We design a three-stage data pipeline by leveraging both fine-grained omni-evidence and the agent's own errors. Meanwhile, compared with other RL baselines, SEPO provides turn-level credit based on improvements in evidence coverage and temporal localization. Applying both trajectory data and the SEPO method, we obtain Open OmniAgent models. The resulting models outperform the baselines across multiple video and audio-visual understanding tasks by significant margins, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Open OmniCoach framework. In particular, Open OmniAgent-30B improves average accuracy over Qwen3-Omni by 6.3 percentage points across nine benchmarks, with gains of 12.2 and 13.3 points on LVOmniBench and LVBench, respectively.

papers.abstract: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.
authors: Luoyuan Zhang, Xuanyu Zheng, Yancheng Long, Haoyang Xu, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao

papers.abstract: As live video streams grow longer, repeatedly encoding and processing their full histories becomes increasingly costly. Answering questions as they arrive therefore calls for visual memory built in one pass before future questions are known. Existing methods mainly keep tokens that differ from earlier ones or match surrogate queries fixed in advance. Without modeling world dynamics, these criteria struggle to tell subtle surprising details from expected change. We introduce Dreamcatcher, a training-free framework and, to our knowledge, the first to use predictive signals from an independently pretrained, frozen video world model for online memory formation in streaming video question answering. Conditioned on recent history, the world model predicts incoming features using learned world priors. Its normalized prediction errors yield temporal and spatial surprisal signals that guide online segmentation and the retention of a frozen Video-LLM's native visual tokens, balancing surprising details with broad visual coverage under budgets that decay with segment age. At query time, an evidence gate admits a segment from a similarity-based shortlist only when the Video-LLM judges that it adds evidence for the question beyond the current view. We evaluate Dreamcatcher on three streaming and three offline long-video benchmarks. On OVO-Bench, Dreamcatcher achieves the highest overall accuracy among the compared training-free methods for each of four frozen Video-LLMs, reaching 78.9% with Qwen3.8-27B. With the three Qwen Video-LLMs, it also reduces average input tokens for answer generation by more than 80% relative to their base models at 1 fps.

Uses an evidence gate to admit shortlisted segments only when they add question-relevant evidence.
Achieves the best accuracy among compared training-free methods on OVO-Bench and cuts answer-generation input tokens by over 80% for three Qwen Video-LLMs.

papers.abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Existing benchmarks can be largely solved by timing alone: a video-blind timer surpasses published mistake-detection results on Ego-MC-Bench, while published per-step systems and tested zero-shot models remain within the timing-based frontier.
Evidence-Contrastive Training pairs examples from the same recording at the same elapsed time, preventing models from using time as a shortcut.
A 2B model trained with ECT crossed the video-blind frontier on both benchmarks across all four seeds, using 209 QICD videos and about 15 GPU-hours.
Without adaptation, the model confirmed 59% of mistake-free steps on Ego-MC-Bench, compared with 30% for a published comparable-backbone model.

Its decisions reflect video content: it distinguished finished from unfinished steps in 90–92% of equal-time pairs, while time-based instruction statistics reached 65%; performance degraded substantially when recordings were swapped.

papers.abstract: Identifying subtle errors in generated videos is an important step toward automated video generation, where errors must be detected to assess and refine generated clips. Recent work shows that pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) can localise such errors, but their effectiveness depends strongly on the workflow used: choices about which frames to inspect, which tools and model calls to make, and how to combine predictions can lead to substantially different results. We study VLM harnesses for video error localisation. Instead of relying on manually designed harnesses, we propose Harness Search and Merge (HSM), an algorithm that automatically constructs them by searching over executable evaluation programs. An LLM orchestrator refines candidate harnesses independently on random training subsets, records findings in a memory, and constructively merges complementary candidates. We evaluate HSM on Spotlight, a recently proposed benchmark for localising errors in generated videos. HSM achieves 0.234 +- 0.012 F1, exceeding the strongest benchmark strategy (0.173 +- 0.016), and retains its lead on an unseen video generator (0.213 +- 0.008 versus 0.140 +- 0.003). On IPV-Bench, it achieves strong localisation performance with lower false-alarm rates than existing optimisation baselines. Together, these results show that searching over complete VLM harnesses can outperform existing evaluation strategies, transfer to an unseen video generator, and reduce false alarms on real videos.
authors: Ankit Yadav, Nikhil Cherian Kurian, Arpit Garg, Lingqiao Liu
bullets: VLM error-localisation performance depends heavily on frame selection, tool/model calls, and prediction aggregation.
HSM searches over executable evaluation programs rather than using manually designed harnesses.
An LLM orchestrator refines candidate harnesses on training subsets, stores findings in memory, and merges complementary solutions.
On Spotlight, HSM reaches 0.234 ± 0.012 F1 versus 0.173 ± 0.016 for the strongest benchmark strategy.
It retains an advantage on an unseen video generator and achieves strong IPV-Bench localisation with lower false-alarm rates than optimisation baselines.

papers.abstract: Video polyp segmentation (VPS) is essential for computer-aided colonoscopy, as it localizes and tracks polyps frame by frame. However, VPS remains challenging because polyps resemble the mucosa and change quickly in scale, which calls for history beyond a short clip, and because blur, specular highlights, and occlusion often degrade only part of a frame. Existing methods keep history as whole frames, so their cost grows with the history length, and a partly degraded frame carries its degraded content to later predictions. To address these issues, we propose STREAM, a streaming framework for VPS that extends the causal multi-scale aggregation (CMA) of our conference work from a fixed clip to an online stream. STREAM introduces a Recursive Slot Memory (RSM) that summarizes multi-scale features and soft foreground and background cues into a constant number of slots, which the current features read and pass to CMA, supplying long-range history at a constant cost. Furthermore, we design Reliability-Aware Slot Writing (RASW), which estimates a pixel-level quality map from the current frame, supervised by its local error, and uses it to control which locations are written into RSM and how much each slot is updated. Experiments on SUN-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB demonstrate that STREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving the Dice of the conference model from 81.3% to 85.7% on the hardest subset while running at 48 FPS with a constant state of 0.32 MB. Code will be released at https://github.com/wangtong627/STREAM.
authors: Tong Wang, Wenbo Peng, Yaolei Qi, Yuting He, Yutong Xie, Guanyu Yang
bullets: Addresses long-range temporal history, scale changes, blur, highlights, and occlusion in causal video polyp segmentation.
Uses Recursive Slot Memory to summarize multi-scale features and foreground/background cues into a constant number of slots.
Uses Reliability-Aware Slot Writing to estimate pixel quality and control which information updates memory.
Evaluated on SUN-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB, achieving 85.7% Dice on the hardest subset, 48 FPS, and a constant 0.32 MB state.
Scope: designed for online causal video polyp segmentation; code is planned for release.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can process hour-long videos, but the large number of input frames incurs substantial inference overhead. Existing approaches to efficient long-video understanding largely overlook video decoding, which can take longer than LLM prefill. We propose RAPID (Reference- and Access-Point-Informed Decoding), a codec-aware framework that exploits information embedded in compressed bitstreams to reduce both frame decoding and selection costs. RAPID consists of two components. RAPID-Dec exploits reference-frame information and random access points to skip unnecessary frames and decode the retained frames in parallel while preserving exact reconstruction of the target frames. It achieves up to a 3.7x decoding speedup over the fastest baseline on H.264/AVC videos. RAPID-Sel uses keyframes as coarse representatives of video segments, avoiding the dense candidate decoding and scoring required by existing frame selection methods. It achieves comparable accuracy with up to a 3.0x preprocessing speedup. Together, RAPID achieves a 4.9x time to first token (TTFT) speedup on hour-long videos over a state-of-the-art frame selection method using the fastest baseline decoder.
bullets: Targets the substantial video-decoding and frame-selection overhead in hour-long VLM inputs.
RAPID-Dec uses reference-frame dependencies and random access points to skip unnecessary frames and decode retained frames in parallel with exact reconstruction.
RAPID-Sel uses keyframes as coarse segment representatives, avoiding dense candidate decoding and scoring.
Reports up to 3.7× decoding speedup and up to 3.0× preprocessing speedup, while maintaining comparable selection accuracy.
Scope: results are reported for H.264/AVC videos and hour-long video workloads.

The retained groups are then distributed across threads for parallel decoding. RAPIDSel decodes and scores only the keyframes against the query and selects target frames by combining uniform frames with relevant frames allocated to groups by relevance.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires models to interpret unfolding events, respond timely, and retrieve relevant historical evidence. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce SVUBench, a comprehensive proactive streaming video benchmark comprising 12,131 questions and 62,881 answer points across ten proactive tasks spanning Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning. Constructed through model-assisted annotation and human verification, SVUBench introduces two complementary interaction modes. Basic evaluates sustained proactive responses from video onset, while Trajectory requires historical recovery and continuous response updates following task activation during streaming. A Duration-Scaled Challenge further evaluates these capabilities across four video duration tiers. We develop the Proactive Response Score (PRS) with task-adaptive answer windows to jointly assess answer correctness, response timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality. Extensive experiments and analysis reveal the strengths and limitations of existing models, highlighting directions for advancing proactive streaming video understanding.
authors: Yuxuan Liang, Bohan Zhang, Haiyang Yu, Bocheng Hu, Ke Niu, Xu Li, Zhengtao Yao, Yan Wen, Haotian Chen, Xiaolei Chen, Jiacong Wang, Zhe Liu, Jingqun Tang, Benlei Cui, Fan Shi, Xiangyang Xue
bullets: Covers 12,131 questions and 62,881 answer points across 10 tasks in Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning.
Tests two interaction modes: continuous responses from video onset and trajectory-based updates after task activation.
Includes four video-duration tiers through a Duration-Scaled Challenge.
Introduces Proactive Response Score (PRS), measuring correctness, timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality.
Experiments expose strengths and limitations of existing models and suggest directions for future research.

papers.abstract: Point supervised temporal action localization is becoming the need of time in this era of ever growing and non-stop video data. Existing method mainly rely on snippet level action response to generate pseudo labels. However, these labels often suffer from boundary ambiguity, over extended proposals, and weak temporal structure. To address these issues, we propose STAR, a structure-aware Temporal Action Recovery framework for point supervised temporal action localization. STAR works by enhancing the base S model with temporal difference interaction with attention module to capture forward and backward snippet changes, and introduces the learning of start, core, and end roles to model the internal temporal structure of actions. In addition, STAR further improves the pseudo label generation through All point proposal ranking and Rolebank based structural re-ranking, which suppress neighbor crossing and structurally inconsistent proposals. Finally, temporal action detector to STAR feedback supervision transfers high quality detector prediction back to the STAR model through soft start, core, end, action, and background targets. This helps to further refine the pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks shows the effectiveness of STAR. By using I3D features, STAR achieves 67.2% at AVG@0.1:0.7 on THUMOS'14, 58.1% on GTEA, 74.6% on BEOID, and 31.7% at AVG@0.5:0.95 on ActivityNet-1.3, outperforming previous point supervised methods across multiple benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses ambiguous boundaries, overextended proposals, and weak temporal structure in point-supervised localization.
Models forward/backward snippet changes with temporal-difference attention and represents actions through start, core, and end roles.
Refines pseudo-labels using all-point proposal ranking and Rolebank-based structural re-ranking to reduce neighbor crossing and inconsistency.
Uses detector feedback with soft structural targets to iteratively improve pseudo-label quality.
Reports strong results across THUMOS’14, GTEA, BEOID, and ActivityNet-1.3, outperforming prior point-supervised methods in the reported comparisons.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overall architecture of the proposed STAR framework. STAR calculates the attention based temporal difference interations using the I3D snippets. The enhanced features are then forwarded to the S model for class activation sequence scores and action seeds. Using those seeds, STAR constructs soft Gaussian target for temporal role learning. St, C, Ed, and Bkg represents Start, Core, End, and Background roles, respectively. Once candidate proposals are generated using the snippet level action responses those are refined through All point ranking and Rolebank re-ranking schemes to select the high quality action proposals. The selected action proposals are then converted to pseudo labels for the training of temporal action detector. Detector prediction are fed back to the STAR model as soft supervision for start, core, end, action, and background targets for further refinement of pseudo labels

Fig. 5. Qualitative analysis of progressive improvements by the proposed STAR method. GT with blue bars depict the ground truth action intervals, Seed Proposals with green bars denote coarse seed proposals generated by the basic S model of HRPro, Before Feedback with yellow bars shows the improvement caused by the STAR method, and After Feedback with orange bars shows the further refined localized action instances after learning the information from feedback. Video names are written instead of pasting images from video for copyright issues

Fig. 1. STAR at a glance: Structure-aware temporal action recovery (STAR). For snippet video features with point annotations, STAR model calculates temporal difference interaction between neighboring snippets. This enhance feature information is then forwarded to estimate CAS of action and background snippets. To recover the action structure from point supervision, STAR learns role aware representations for start, core, and end regions of action and background. Candidate action proposals are refined by All point ranking, which rejects action proposal that crosses neighboring point annotations. Action proposals are re-ranked with Rolebank re-ranking that penalizes action proposals whose structure is not similar to the action structure. Pseudo labels are then created and TAD is trained. Finally, TAD prediction are fed back to STAR to refine the role aware learning.

papers.abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to categorize unlabeled data from both known and unknown classes using labeled data from only the known classes. While recent GCD methods have shown promise on static images, their performance degrades in videos due to temporal dynamics, larger intra-class variation, and the lack of temporal consistency in existing approaches. We introduce VideoGCD, a framework tailored for video action recognition under the GCD setting. Our method integrates (i) a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module that encourages specialization for known and novel categories, (ii) a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes, and (iii) a temporal optimal transport loss that promotes consistent routing across frames. Experiments on three video benchmarks demonstrate that VideoGCD significantly improves performance over existing GCD methods, particularly on novel categories. Our findings highlight the importance of combining temporal modeling and expert specialization for video GCD.
bullets: Addresses video GCD, where temporal dynamics, greater intra-class variation, and weak temporal consistency hurt recognition.
Uses a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module to specialize processing for known and novel categories.
Introduces a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes.
Applies temporal optimal transport to encourage consistent expert routing across video frames.
Experiments on three video benchmarks show improved performance over existing GCD methods, especially for novel categories.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed VideoGCD framework for Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) in video action recognition. Frameglobal representations (g1, gt, gT ) are obtained via temporal pooling and routed through the MoE module, which consists of known and novel experts. The router predicts expert assignment probabilities, and each expert applies low-rank adapters (Ue, Ve) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Three auxiliary losses are used: (i) Balancing Loss promotes uniform expert usage, (ii) Novel-Class Balancing Loss ensures sufficient learning signal for novel-class experts, and (iii) Temporal OT Loss enforces consistent expert assignments across frames. The updated representations are integrated back into the transformer backbone. For simplicity, LoRA fine-tuning on the multi-head attention modules is not shown.

Figure 1. Average clustering accuracy on three benchmark datasets (UCF-101, HMDB-51, and Something-Something-V2) compared to the state-of-the-art method SPTNet. VideoGCD achieves significant improvements in overall performance, particularly on the Novel subset, demonstrating its strong generalization ability for the GCD task.

papers.abstract: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.
authors: Dankai Liao, YuFeng Wu, Ziyue Wang, Guanxi Liu, Tianyi Zhang, Zeyu Liu, Linghan Cai, Yueming Jin
bullets: The work addresses the gap between pathology AI and pathologists’ trajectory-based, multi-region, multi-magnification diagnostic workflow.
Five pathologists’ viewing trajectories across 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images and ten organs support PathStreamBench, covering response timing, morphology, session-level findings, and diagnosis.
PathStream jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis, using a diagnosis-attention loss to focus on relevant accumulated visual and textual evidence.
It outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines; its trajectory WSI Relevance score is 77.87 versus 62.76 for the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline.
Without additional training, the model generalizes to educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

papers.abstract: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to identify the temporal segment in an untrimmed video that corresponds to a natural language query. Existing approaches commonly refine temporal predictions within the localization pathway, without explicitly verifying candidate-level semantic consistency. Moreover, directly reusing semantic scores as feedback can cause over-correction when the verification signal is unreliable. To address these issues, we propose Bi-Refine, a semantic verification-guided progressive refinement framework that formulates MR as a closed-loop verification-and-refinement process. A Heuristic Localization Branch first generates candidate moments, while a Semantic Verification Branch evaluates their query consistency in a semantically enriched latent space. Query supervision further trains the verifier with the same candidate moment but different queries, encouraging it to distinguish the matched query from semantically similar mismatched queries. The resulting verification features are incorporated into a Progressive Refinement Loop that updates both query representations and multimodal features. To suppress potentially harmful updates, a lightweight reliability estimator gates query updates and reweights candidate contributions in feature feedback. A convergence-based adaptive stopping strategy additionally terminates unnecessary refinement during inference. Experiments on three standard MR benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and state-of-the-art performance of our method.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Jiaxuan Lin, Yuxuan Wu, Gang Hua
bullets: Targets semantic inconsistency in temporal candidates and the risk of over-correction from unreliable verification signals.
Uses a Heuristic Localization Branch to generate candidate moments and a Semantic Verification Branch to assess query consistency.
Trains verification to distinguish matched queries from semantically similar mismatched queries for the same candidate moment.
Employs reliability-gated progressive refinement, adaptive candidate reweighting, and convergence-based early stopping.
Shows effectiveness and state-of-the-art performance on three standard moment-retrieval benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of Bi-Refine. HLB generates candidate moments and proposal features, and SVB estimates their query-conditioned semantic relevance. A reliability estimator predicts R(i) from semantic relevance, localization confidence, and boundary variation; R(i) gates query feedback and weights candidate contributions in feature feedback within PRL. Query supervision is used only during training, whereas convergence-based adaptive stopping is enabled only during inference.

Figure 1: Motivation of Bi-Refine. (a) Existing retrieval frameworks mainly refine predictions within the localization process, without explicit semantic verification feedback for subsequent refinement. (b) Bi-Refine establishes a closed-loop semantic refinement process, where semantic consistency signals are iteratively fed back to progressively improve candidate moments.

papers.abstract: Moment Retrieval (MR) aims to localize the temporal segment in a video that corresponds to a given textual description. However, a textual query often provides only a sparse semantic description of the target event, whereas the video contains rich and fine-grained visual variations. This mismatch creates an inherent gap between textual semantics and visual content, making a single textual input insufficient for precise cross-modal alignment. As a result, when multiple temporally adjacent or semantically similar segments exist, the model may struggle to distinguish the target moment from confusing candidates. To address this challenge, we propose a Multi-Perspective Auxiliary Representation (MPAR) framework, which aims to bridge this alignment gap by enriching a single textual input with complementary visual cues from multiple perspectives. Specifically, MPAR consists of three key components: (1) Auxiliary Representation Initialization (ARI) constructs multiple learnable representation slots from the original query, preserving the query intent while preparing flexible carriers for subsequent visual cue injection; (2) Visual-Induced Semantic Structuring (VISS) injects target-specific visual attributes into each representation while preserving semantic coherence with the original query; and (3) Multi-Perspective Semantic Aligner (MPSA) aligns each auxiliary representation with corresponding video regions to enhance discriminative localization. By constructing multi-perspective auxiliary representations and guiding the model to attend to relevant visual regions across these representations, our model achieves more accurate moment localization. Extensive experiments on MR benchmarks demonstrate that our MPAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods, validating the effectiveness of MPAR.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Jiaxuan Lin, Gang Hua, Le Wang
bullets: Addresses the semantic gap between sparse text queries and fine-grained visual content, especially among adjacent or similar candidate moments.
ARI creates multiple learnable representation slots while preserving the original query’s intent.
VISS injects target-specific visual attributes into the representations while maintaining semantic coherence.
MPSA aligns each auxiliary representation with relevant video regions to improve discriminative localization.
Experiments on moment-retrieval benchmarks show MPAR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

papers.abstract: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.
authors: Xinyu Yan, Yurong Hao, Zherui Li, Yebo Wu, Tiantong Wu, Jiaming Zhang, Zihao Zeng, Zheng Lin, Zijie Wang, Pengpeng Qiao, Yang Cao, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
bullets: Targets overconfident errors, false alarms, and difficult threshold calibration when future deepfake generators are unavailable.
Fuses four visual experts using authentic videos as shared calibration references, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes.
Provides finite-sample false-alarm control when scoring is fixed before calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable.
Uses a tool-using multimodal investigator for cases near the calibrated threshold, trained with held-out-generator and counterfactual evidence.
Across six protocols, reports an 88.3% mean benchmark score and gains over evaluated MLLM, conventional-detector, and ARGUS baselines.

papers.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR) requires finding the video and time interval that match a text query in a corpus of videos. We present RELAY, a training-free framework for VCMR that shares memory across queries. RELAY processes a batch of queries in three stages: search with a query bank, ranking with video notes, and localization with video prompt caching. In the search stage, an embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank penalizes videos that score highly for many other queries in the batch. In the ranking stage, a vision-language model (VLM) writes notes on each candidate video's scenes, people, objects, and actions once. Then, a large language model (LLM) reranks the candidates from these notes. In the localization stage, a VLM predicts the time interval of the moment in the top-ranked video. When multiple queries select the same video, prompt caching lets the VLM reuse its frames. On the three VERIFIED benchmarks, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 without training. Without any labeled moment, its predicted intervals are shorter than the annotated ones. In VCMR, it achieves similar performance to VideoSearch-R1 on one benchmark and trails it at IoU 0.5 on the other two. Human annotators also mark shorter moments than the original annotations of the benchmarks. A single margin, calibrated on a few labeled queries, widens the predicted interval to the annotation convention of the benchmarks. With it, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in VCMR at IoU 0.5.
authors: Chenwei Xu, Shang Wu, Zhenyu Pan, Jianshu Zhang, Pranav Maneriker, Lie Lu, Fan Du, Manling Li, Han Liu
bullets: Processes query batches through search, candidate ranking, and temporal localization.
Uses a query bank to reduce cross-query confusion and video notes for LLM-based reranking.
Caches video prompts and frames when multiple queries target the same video.
Outperforms trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 on three VERIFIED benchmarks.
Predicted intervals are initially shorter than annotations; a single calibrated margin improves VCMR at IoU 0.5.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline of RELAY. The top row follows one query of a batch through the three stages. The bottom row is the memory that the queries of the batch share. 1⃝ Search: the embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank subtracts a bias from each score. The bias is larger for a video that matches more queries. 2⃝ Ranking: a VLM writes notes on each candidate video once. An LLM orders the candidates from their notes. Reciprocal rank fusion merges this order with the embedding-based ranking. 3⃝ Localization: the VLM predicts the start and end of the moment in the top-ranked video. Queries for the same video share a prompt prefix containing its timestamped frames. Each request adds the current query.

Figure 5. Qualitative Example. (a) Success. The search ranks the annotated video 6th, the query bank raises it to 3rd, and RELAY ranks it first. Its notes name the bathroom, the red hooded sweatshirt and the dark gray pants of the query. They also record that the woman enters carrying a mug at 2.7–4.8 s. The predicted interval, 2.6–4.6 s, lies within the moment of the human annotator, 1.4–5.8 s. The annotation, 0.4–9.2 s, adds seconds on both sides. The margin widens the predicted interval to 0.6–6.6 s, closer to the annotation. (b) Failure. The search and the query bank rank the annotated Video 1 first. Its notes describe a man opening the door and taking out clothes, but they call the machine a washing machine. The notes of Video 2 describe a woman opening the door of a dryer, so RELAY ranks Video 2 first. Bars: dataset annotation, human annotation, the predicted interval, and the interval with the 2 s margin. Human annotation is from Otani et al. [30].

Figure 3. Margin around the predicted interval: VCMR R@1 (%) at IoU 0.5 on the three test splits when the predicted interval is widened by w seconds on each side, or shrunk for w < 0. Gray dashed lines: w = 0 and w = 2 s. Embedding only: our baseline that uses only Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, the embedding model of RELAY and VideoSearch-R1 [20], to retrieve the video and predict the moment. Its moment grows from the best-matching frame of its top-ranked video while the frames score above the midpoint of the video’s scores. VideoSearch-R1: its released predictions on Charades-FIG, widened the same way. Numbers: R@1 at w = 0 and w = 2 s. RELAY outperforms the embedding-only baseline at every w ≥ 0 on all three benchmarks. The 2 s margin raises RELAY and lowers VideoSearch-R1.

Figure 1. Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR). Given a text query and a corpus of videos, VCMR retrieves the video that contains the moment the query describes. papers.abstract: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.
authors: Lang Lin, Tianyu Chen, Yi Gu, Yang Zhao, Xinran Song, Xinyang Liu, Jianpeng Cheng, Mingyuan Zhou
bullets: Evaluates 33 open models—12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs—on 51,060 questions across 94 image, video, and audio tasks plus 102 closed-loop games.
On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM on images and is nearly tied on video and audio.
Decision-focused post-training mainly improves probability calibration; on video, System-1 models generally achieve lower Brier scores than their MLLM counterparts.
Extended MLLM reasoning provides only slight accuracy gains and often worsens Brier scores.
In closed-loop games, System-1 models achieve markedly higher progression and tolerate up to 1.1-second decision latency without measurable loss in real-time play.

One point per model; a gray arrow goes from each base MLLM to the System-1 model post-trained from it. Static: the 32 video tasks that every model takes. (a) The four models with the highest static accuracy (65.8–66.9%) reach 7.0–33.3% progression in BALROG. We show four frames spread evenly over the window, draw the outline thicker than in the input so that it stays visible at this size, and shorten the state text. An open MLLM gets the same request as a prompt (Appendix A).

papers.abstract: AI-generated video of politicians can pass for real footage, and once such fakes are common, real footage can be dismissed as fake. Platforms address both problems with detectors, but whoever uploads a clip controls its pixels. Existing datasets of political video are small, show real politicians, and test no attacks. We introduce CivicBench, with 10,800 generated clips of invented politicians from eight open generators and 2,632 public-domain or openly licensed real clips. Each clip can be attacked, to hide a fake or to frame real footage. Published detectors trained on a general benchmark reach at most .781 AUC on CivicBench. Adversarial changes of 1 gray level per pixel hide nearly every generated clip from the detectors not built to resist attacks. An attack's reach is how far it can move a clip's score. A clip keeps its label when its margin from the threshold exceeds this reach, and we find that the reach grows almost linearly with the budget. On this basis, we propose Tau-Anchor, which fine-tunes an encoder pretrained on attacked images. It attacks real and generated clips during training and adds a margin term at its deployed threshold. It reaches .941 AUC on CivicBench. It also keeps .668 of generated clips flagged at 2 gray levels, against at most .289 for published detectors. When real clips are framed at the same 2 gray levels, Tau-Anchor's false alarms rise only from 8% to 14%, whereas four published detectors flag nearly every framed real clip at just 1 gray level. External political footage and two general benchmarks show the same pattern under attack. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/CivicBench.
authors: Mert Onur Cakiroglu, Elham Buxton, Mehmet Dalkilic, Hasan Kurban
bullets: The benchmark contains 10,800 generated clips of invented politicians and 2,632 real clips, all attackable to hide fakes or frame real footage.
Published general-purpose detectors achieve at most .781 AUC, while near-imperceptible 1-gray-level changes evade detectors not trained against attacks.
Tau-Anchor fine-tunes an encoder on attacked real and generated clips and adds a deployment-threshold margin objective.
Tau-Anchor reaches .941 AUC and flags .668 of generated clips under 2-gray-level attacks, while limiting false alarms on framed real clips to 14%.
Similar robustness patterns appear on external political footage and two general benchmarks; code and data are released.

papers.tldr: CivicBench evaluates political deepfake detectors under adversarial pixel attacks and introduces Tau-Anchor, which is substantially more robust than published detectors.

papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.
authors: Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang, Gang Zhou
bullets: Different sampling pipelines can make teacher reasoning depend on evidence unavailable to the student, creating a Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap.
The framework first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior, then optimizes its execution across multiple observations.
Execution-Aware Reference Regularization preserves the prior when executable and permits adaptive changes when observations differ.
Across multiple backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks, the approach outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, including on held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our acquisition-to-execution framework. Stage II computes GRPO losses separately for multiple temporal observations of the same video and aggregates them to update a shared student policy. Reference regularization uses a larger KL weight when the frozen Stage-I model answers correctly under the current observation and a smaller weight otherwise.

papers.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes visual media, such as video, accessible to blind or low-vision (BLV) audiences, but the high cost of professional production limits coverage. Due to recent advances in AI, numerous approaches to automatically generate intermediate AD scripts and/or final AD audios have been proposed. We present an expert evaluation of AI-generated AD scripts for movies in Italian and German that compares two AI systems, a GPT-4o- and a Qwen-based pipeline, against human-authored descriptions. Professional audio describers rated description quality and annotated errors using a detailed error taxonomy that includes content, character, fluency and coherence errors. The results show that while GPT-4o outperforms the Qwen models, both AI systems still fall short of human professional quality: the generated descriptions show substantially higher error rates and lower quality ratings. Based on the error annotations, we identify two key areas that require improvement: 1) character references, which includes both issues with identification and coherent naming, and 2) content errors and hallucinations, where the AD misrepresents or invents events. These error types are particularly critical, as they directly affect the viewer's ability to follow the narrative.
authors: Annette Rios, Lukas Fischer, Sarah Ebling
bullets: Professional audio describers evaluated movie AD scripts from two AI pipelines against human-authored descriptions.
Evaluation covered description quality and errors in content, character references, fluency, and coherence.
GPT-4o performed better than the Qwen-based systems, but both produced more errors and received lower quality ratings than human work.
The most critical issues were incorrect or inconsistent character references and content errors or hallucinations.
The study focuses on Italian- and German-language movie descriptions and does not establish human-level quality.

papers.abstract: When two musicians in an ensemble play the same instrument, they sound alike and their instruments look alike. Audio-only separators, and audio-visual separators that rely on appearance, cannot tell them apart. What still differs is how each player moves, and when. We study same-instrument per-player separation: a user clicks one musician in a video and receives that musician's sound alone, even when other players in the video play the same instrument. Our model follows the clicked player and describes them with high level video features and the velocities of body and hand keypoints. A pretrained music separator attends to these tokens through cross-attention. Earlier motion-based separators were scored only on synthetic mixtures of solo videos. We give the first per-player evaluation of same-instrument separation on real ensemble recordings. On 58 players in URMP, each sharing an instrument with at least one other player in the piece, our model reaches a median SDR of 5.3 dB, while four released separators, audio-only and audio-visual, stay at or below 0.3 dB. The gap is wider on same-instrument duets, and our model also beats the audio-visual baselines on their own MUSIC benchmark. Tests show that the gain comes from movement: replacing the video with a still frame removes it, and so does shifting the video by a fraction of a second against the audio.
authors: Abhinaba Roy, Ambuj Mehrish, Sebastiano Vascon, Dorien Herremans
bullets: Targets per-player separation when appearance and audio cues cannot distinguish musicians playing the same instrument.
Uses high-level visual features and body/hand keypoint velocities from the clicked player.
Feeds these motion-aware tokens via cross-attention into a pretrained music separator.
On 58 same-instrument players in URMP, it achieves a median SDR of 5.3 dB versus at most 0.3 dB for four released baselines.
Ablations show the improvement depends on synchronized movement, not static appearance; it also outperforms audio-visual baselines on MUSIC.

papers.abstract: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.
authors: Kewei Wei, XueXiang Wen, Bocheng Hu, Weili Xu, Haiyang Yu, Kaiyue Zhou, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Separates per-video observation from cross-video judgment to avoid one controller accumulating all observations.
Each LocalAgent plans observations for its own video and maintains a private history.
A GlobalAgent directs LocalAgents and combines their reports through joint reasoning.
Across CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, it improves average scores over single-pass and prior-agent baselines, while running 1.8–2.7× faster than comparable prior agents.
The framework is training-free and evaluated with multiple Qwen3.5 model sizes and GPT-6-sol.
