papers.abstract: Purpose: Analyzing clinicians' visual attention from exocentric camera views can support surgical scene understanding without requiring wearable eye trackers. However, existing gaze-following research in the operating room (OR) estimates only 2D gaze locations without identifying attended scene entities or localizing gaze targets in 3D space. In this work, we investigate gaze graphs as a scene-level representation of visual attention that connects clinicians to attended scene entities, and evaluate their utility for fine-grained surgical action recognition and semantic scene graph (SSG) generation. Methods: We extend the public EgoExOR dataset with gaze annotations to create EgoExOR-Gaze, the first benchmark for multi-view gaze graph generation in the OR. We propose a novel architecture that jointly estimates 3D gaze targets and predicts attended entities using only exocentric camera views. Specifically, our approach exploits 3D gaze geometry to sample local visual features across multiple views for attended entity prediction. We further utilize predicted gaze graphs for fine-grained surgical action recognition and SSG generation. Results: For gaze graph generation, our model outperforms both exocentric-only and combined exocentric-egocentric baselines. For surgical action recognition, our model incorporating predicted gaze graphs outperforms both exocentric and egocentric baselines across all evaluated metrics, with particularly strong gains in temporal metrics. For SSG generation, incorporating gaze graphs improves macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 compared to exocentric inputs alone, although performance remains below that achieved with egocentric inputs. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate the value of gaze graphs for surgical action recognition and SSG generation, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling scene-level visual attention even when egocentric views are unavailable.
authors: S\'eraphin Baributsa, Keqi Chen, Vinkle Srivastav, Nicolas Padoy
bullets: Introduces EgoExOR-Gaze, a multi-view operating-room benchmark with gaze annotations.
Proposes a model that jointly predicts 3D gaze targets and attended entities using multi-view exocentric features.
Predicted gaze graphs outperform exocentric-only and combined exocentric–egocentric baselines for gaze graph generation and action recognition.
Gaze graphs improve semantic scene graph macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 over exocentric inputs alone.
Semantic scene graph performance remains below that achieved using egocentric inputs.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the gaze graph generation architecture. A frozen DINOv3 backbone extracts raw and text-aligned visual features. The initial 3D gaze point is computed from the estimated gaze direction and depth. The role prediction module estimates each clinician’s role, and the corresponding role embedding is added to the initial appearance query. Decoder layers iteratively refine the 3D gaze point and appearance query through projective attention. Finally, the appearance query is compared with ‘dino.txt’ vocabulary embeddings using cosine similarity to identify attended entities.

papers.abstract: Learning-based optical flow estimation approaches generally rely on both inter-frame correspondence evidence and intra-frame contextual guidance, yet features from general-purpose image encoders may not fully support these roles. Strongly activated but weakly discriminative channels can outweigh more informative ones when computing inter-frame feature similarity, while context feature affinities can be low within motion-coherent regions yet high across motion boundaries. To address these mismatches, this study proposes TO-Flow, a task-oriented feature adaptation framework that aligns matching and context features with their respective requirements through dedicated channel modulation and spatial reorganization approaches. An affinity-based soft partition distinguishes motion-region interiors from boundary-adjacent regions to guide both processes. Channel modulation uses simulated flow refinement to assess whether each channel assigns higher similarity to estimated correspondences than to nearby competing candidates. The resulting similarity differences are aggregated within each region type and averaged across iterations to derive channel weights that emphasize informative channels and suppress ambiguous ones. Spatial reorganization combines affinity-guided feature attraction and repulsion from coarse to fine to simultaneously improve consistency within motion-coherent regions and distinctiveness across motion boundaries, with feature resampling mitigating boundary blurring during cross-scale fusion. Extensive experiments on the MPI Sintel, KITTI 2015, Spring, and LayeredFlow datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and general applicability of TO-Flow across diverse iterative refinement architectures as well as supervised and unsupervised training paradigms. The source code will be publicly available at https://mias.group/TO-Flow upon publication.
authors: Mengtan Zhang, Dazhong Wang, Haoran Zhang, Hongbo Zhao, Yuhang Ming, Weihao Yuan, Wei Ye, Hanli Wang, Rui Fan
bullets: General-purpose features can overemphasize weak channels and confuse motion interiors with boundaries.

Coarse-to-fine spatial reorganization improves within-region consistency and cross-boundary distinctiveness while reducing boundary blur.
Experiments on MPI Sintel, KITTI 2015, Spring, and LayeredFlow show effectiveness across iterative, supervised, and unsupervised flow systems.

papers.abstract: Long video question answering requires finding relevant evidence before reasoning over it. With a limited frame budget, single-pass frame selection can miss critical evidence, while adaptive search often relies on repeated text generation to decide where to look. We introduce LoopSeek, a framework that decouples evidence search from answer generation through a division of labor between a non-thinking System I and a generative System II. Our key insight is that search can be expressed as a sequence of small, typed decisions, allowing System I to find the evidence that System II needs. Four System I role agents navigate a tree of video windows and coordinate through probability outputs to select frames, assess evidence, and revise the search without generating text. To align search with System II, System I learns from annotated evidence on questions that System II answers correctly only from that evidence, and the verifier's evidence estimates steer the search without calling System II, which stays frozen and answers once from the selected frames. On five long-video benchmarks, with a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B reading 32 frames, LoopSeek improves average accuracy from 53.5 to 63.9 over the uniform baseline and takes 32--80\% less GPU time per question than agentic methods.
authors: Chengzhong Wang, Lang Lin, Xinyang Liu, YueQin Yin, Mingyuan Zhou, Shengwei An
bullets: Addresses missed evidence under limited frame budgets and the cost of repeated text-based search.
Uses four non-generative System I agents to navigate video-window trees, select frames, assess evidence, and revise searches.
Trains search using annotated evidence from questions that a frozen System II answers correctly from that evidence.
On five long-video benchmarks, accuracy rises from 53.5 to 63.9 with 32 frames, while using 32–80% less GPU time than agentic methods.

papers.abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.
authors: Kaili Zheng, Wei Ding, Yuchen Ding, Kaiwen Wang, Xun Zhu, Chenyi Guo, Yudong Zhang, Ji Wu

Converts heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format while preserving assessment guidelines and scoring rules.
Fine-tunes Qwen3.5-9B and evaluates it with X-AQA-Bench on in-distribution and four held-out out-of-distribution datasets.
Reports stronger performance than evaluated open-source MLLMs, competitive performance with proprietary MLLMs, and improved OOD generalization from joint training and explicit criteria prompts.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI-generated content (AIGC) video generation and editing technologies has raised growing societal concerns about the authenticity and reliability of digital videos. Existing video detection methods primarily exploit temporal inconsistencies through holistic frame-level representations, whereas manipulation localization methods focus on artifacts within individual spatial regions. However, holistic representations may obscure localized artifacts through global feature aggregation, while region-centric approaches may overlook disagreements between individual regions and their surrounding spatiotemporal context. To address these limitations, we propose VIdeo Contextual Agreement (VICA), a unified framework that masks individual video regions and leverages a frozen V-JEPA model to predict their representations from the surrounding spatiotemporal context. Complementary masking ensures complete regional coverage, while context-conditioned predictions establish references for assessing regional agreement with the broader video context. By comparing predicted and observed representations, VICA derives spatial residuals that characterize intra-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals that capture inconsistencies across preceding and subsequent frames. These residuals characterize contextual disagreements, providing a shared forensic representation for both tasks and shifting the focus from identifying isolated manipulation artifacts to assessing regional agreement with expectations inferred from the broader video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VICA achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks across multiple benchmarks, with strong generalization to unseen video generators and editing methods.
authors: Runheng Lin, Jialiang Shen, Jiyang Zheng, Ruiqi Liu, Zonglin He, Yu Yao, Huajie Chen, Chris Russell, Runqi Lin
bullets: Addresses limitations of frame-level holistic features and isolated region-artifact analysis.
Masks video regions and uses a frozen V-JEPA model to predict each region from surrounding context.
Computes spatial residuals for within-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals for cross-frame inconsistencies.
Provides a shared forensic representation for both AIGC video detection and manipulation localization.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks with strong generalization to unseen generators and editing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VICA. Given an input video clip, the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 target encoder extracts observed features Y , while the frozen context encoder and predictor generate context-conditioned predictions from two complementary masked views. The resulting predictions are combined into P̂ , providing a predicted representation for every spatiotemporal token. Spatial residuals S are computed between predicted and observed features at the same time step, whereas bidirectional temporal residuals F and B capture discrepancies across paired time steps. Finally, a shared readout integrates [S, F,B] to support both video-level detection and region-level localization.

Figure 2. The video is generated by Vidu and sourced from AIGVDBench, which does not provide localization annotations. P̂t and Yt denote the predicted and observed regional features at temporal step t, respectively. The three rows show the spatial residual P̂1 − Y1 and the bidirectional temporal residuals P̂2 − Y1 and P̂1 − Y2. The columns display the input frame, channel-wise signed residual sums, and ℓ2 norms, with and without overlays on the input frame. The right boxer’s glove appears malformed, while the spatial residual P̂1 − Y1 produces a localized response around the fist. In comparison, the bidirectional temporal residuals P̂2−Y1 and P̂1−Y2 exhibit stronger and more extensive ℓ2 responses along the moving arms and gloves, highlighting motion-dependent discrepancies that are less apparent in the spatial residual. This visualization illustrates how spatial and bidirectional temporal residuals reveal complementary patterns of contextual disagreement in AI-generated videos.

papers.abstract: Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.
bullets: Endpoint-matched negatives expose failures in composing event-level evidence into internal states, even when the start appears visibly wrong.
Writing reasoning before answering raises performance substantially when all events are disclosed, but not when the event must first be found in natural video.
Verifier rankings change with the negative examples used for evaluation; event-denial negatives may not reflect generator-like detail errors.
Verifier evaluation should match the errors it will encounter in deployment.
Low direct scores and reasoning gains should not be interpreted as intrinsic model properties without controlling the test protocol.

papers.abstract: Surgical triplet recognition requires identifying which instrument performs which action on which anatomical target, and following these interactions as they unfold over time. The task is challenging because several triplets can occur at once, their components span very different durations, and the evidence for an interaction is rarely complete in a single frame. We introduce STRIDE, a post-hoc temporal readout that adds temporal context to any trained recogniser. It averages the recogniser's features and logits over a few fixed temporal windows and combines them with the current frame through ridge regression, solved in closed form on a CPU. Applied as a plug-and-play readout to nine existing methods, STRIDE improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method-dataset pairs, by up to 7.4 points. Moreover, we propose a simple pipeline consisting of an adapted foundation vision encoder with a linear classifier and STRIDE. Across thirteen encoders, STRIDE improves 37 of 39 encoder-dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points. STRIDE reduces false alarms by 41%, at the cost of a slower response at interaction boundaries. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Lemar Abdi, Amaan Valiuddin, Fida Mohammad Thoker, Karen Sanchez, Bernard Ghanem, Fons van der Sommen
bullets: Addresses overlapping surgical interactions whose instrument, action, and target components unfold over different durations.
Averages features and logits over fixed temporal windows, then combines them with the current frame using CPU-solvable ridge regression.
Improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method–dataset pairs by up to 7.4 points when added to nine existing recognisers.
With a foundation vision encoder and linear classifier, improves 37 of 39 encoder–dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points.
Reduces false alarms by 41%, but responds more slowly at interaction boundaries.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, Yale Song
bullets: Addresses video VLMs’ growing key-value memory and the capability gap of small models.

papers.abstract: Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and fixed retrieval pipelines, which restrict how the agent can search. We propose VideoJSON, a minimal harness for ultra-long video understanding that keeps the memory simple and lets a coding agent write its own search programs. During indexing, a vision-language model turns each minute of video into a single JSON record containing a dense caption and structured fields such as events, entities, places, and speech transcripts. At query time, the agent writes Python or Bash programs in a sandboxed container to filter, link, and read these records over multiple steps, without task-specific training or raw video access. On four ultra-long video benchmarks, VideoJSON with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outperforms MAGIC-Video by 7.0, 20.0, and 24.75 points on EgoLifeQA, Ego-R1-Bench, and MM-Lifelong Week, and beats the best prior EgoMemReason score by 12.6 points. Across four policy models of increasing capability, VideoJSON's average score rises by up to 11.58 points over the weakest model, compared with at most 5.50 points for MAGIC-Video. Ablations show that both agentic code search and the structured JSON records drive these gains, while adding hourly summaries, extra tools, or video access changes the average score by less than 1.5 points. In addition, fine-tuning Qwen-3.5-Flash on 64 VideoJSON trajectories from an unrelated 100-hour livestream improves its MM-Lifelong scores by up to 8.25 points. Code will be open-sourced after publication.
authors: Wenqi Marshall Guo, Kuan-Hao Huang, Junda Chen, Hao Zhang

Ablations attribute gains mainly to agentic code search and structured records; fine-tuning on 64 unrelated trajectories further improves one benchmark by up to 8.25 points.

papers.abstract: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.
authors: Vu Nhat Minh Pham, Cong Khanh Nguyen, Minh Tuan Le, Van Thong Huynh
bullets: SCR improves over the retrained backbone by 0.87 UAR points in ABVnet on DFEW under one protocol, but this gain reverses under the development protocol.
A parameter-matched pooled comparison and plan-replacement interventions are needed to separate module effects from transport-plan effects.
Replacing the learned plan with a uniform plan or its marginal-product approximation reduces UAR, indicating inference-time reliance on frame-specific routing.
Row permutation is less damaging than uniform replacement, but the corresponding comparisons are unresolved under wider fold-dependence intervals.
Results cover MMA-DFER and ABVnet across DFEW, MAFW, and CREMA-D, with one training run per configuration.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains video agents to locate sparse evidence for long-video question answering through structured memory retrieval and temporal re-observation. This training, however, faces a long-tail modality distribution in the data. In our source pool, text-heavy questions account for 58% of samples, compared with 15% graph-heavy, 17% visual-heavy, and 10% time-range questions. Fixed-distribution RL therefore allocates fewer rollouts to underperforming question types. Reweighting these types could increase their sampling frequency but repeatedly reuses the same finite banks of original questions. To solve this problem, we introduce VideoGym, a curriculum-based RL environment that jointly constructs video-grounded training tasks and allocates rollouts among them. Within the environment, a memory-augmented VideoAgent is trained to coordinate retrieval from text, graph, and visual memories with temporal re-observation. Across episodes, VideoGym adapts VideoAgent's training distribution online: it casts per-period sample selection as an adversarial bandit over (modality, mode) arms and applies the EXP3 update to shift sampling toward arms with low answer accuracy. To supply the augmented-mode arms, a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline produces harder variants of existing questions that remain answerable within the same video. Across five long-video benchmarks, VideoGym lifts RL accuracy from 60.4% to 64.8% on average and by up to 10.5 pp on underrepresented graph-heavy questions with 3.3x sample efficiency. Together, these results show that task expansion and adaptive allocation can improve video agent learning from limited, imbalanced training data.
authors: Jing Wang, Yi Ke Yun, Yifeng Yao, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao, Tao Wang
bullets: Addresses imbalanced training data, where text-heavy questions dominate and graph-, visual-, and time-range questions are less frequent.
Uses a curriculum-based RL environment with a memory-augmented VideoAgent for text, graph, and visual retrieval plus temporal re-observation.
Models task selection as an adversarial bandit over modality and task-mode arms, using EXP3 to favor low-accuracy areas.
Generates harder but answerable question variants through a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline.
Across five benchmarks, average RL accuracy rises from 60.4% to 64.8%; graph-heavy questions improve by up to 10.5 percentage points with 3.3× sample efficiency.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.
authors: Jiaye Luan, Chaoning Zhang, Pengcheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Sheng Zheng, Ping Guo, Caiyan Qin, Yang Du, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets failures on motion attributes such as speeding up or slowing down, which models may otherwise solve using static visual cues.
Constructs order-necessary supervision through time-reversal pairs, matched spatial extent, and uniform interval coverage.
Uses six procedural motion primitives, low-rank adaptation, answer-level training, and self-distillation replay on real videos.
Training on 4,000 synthetic clips improves mean accuracy across four motion benchmarks by 7.6, 4.9, and 5.1 points for three video LLMs.
Shuffled-frame training yields less than one point of change, supporting the importance of order-dependent supervision.

papers.abstract: Long videos spanning tens of minutes to hours far exceed the context window of today's vision-language models, and the standard remedy of sparse uniform frame sampling discards exactly the fine-grained evidence that specific questions depend on. Existing video agents explore on demand but re-explore from scratch for every question and discard their exploration state once an answer is produced, so per-question cost scales with video length. Hierarchical-memory methods instead fix the scope of each depth in advance and deepen along a pre-committed pyramid rather than toward the question. We observe that a video's coarse structure (where its scenes and topics begin and end) is question-independent, whereas which part a question must zoom into, and how deep, is question-dependent. We propose VTree, which builds a coarse hierarchical memory tree over a video once and then, for each question, grows branches only where that question needs depth. The growth is globally routed so any part of the timeline is reachable, sufficiency-gated so drilling stops when the evidence suffices, and query-conditioned so a branch unfolds into the sub-intervals that answer \emph{this} question. Crucially, every expansion is written back into the video memory, allowing later questions to reuse previously discovered structure and evidence without repeating the corresponding expansion process. Across five long-video understanding benchmarks, VTree consistently improves the accuracy of diverse vision-language backbones while substantially reducing the context length and execution time required for each question.
authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Lianyu Hu, Zixuan Hu, Zhizhen Wu, Zeqin Liao, Shengqian Qin, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling and agents that re-explore long videos independently for every question.
Separates question-independent coarse video structure from question-dependent evidence and required zoom depth.
Uses globally routed, sufficiency-gated, query-conditioned branch growth to locate relevant fine-grained content.
Writes each expansion back to memory so later questions can reuse discovered structure and evidence.
Improves accuracy across five long-video benchmarks while reducing per-question context length and execution time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VTree. (1) Build phase: a question-independent level-1 event skeleton is constructed once per video. (2) Growth phase: for each question, the controller routes over the updated level-1 nodes, reuses stored descendants, and expands an unexplored leaf only when finer evidence is needed. Newly acquired information is propagated bottom-up. (3) Persistent memory: the refined hierarchy is retained across questions for subsequent reuse.
Figure 3: Qualitative examples of the Route–Check–Expand process. VTree routes to a relevant branch, checks evidence sufficiency, and expands the branch only when finer detail is required.

Figure 1: VTree raises accuracy while sharply cutting perquestion cost. papers.abstract: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.
authors: Yuzhe Hao, Ikuro Sato, Rei Kawakami, Koichi Shinoda
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-objective pre-training, which can underuse differences between video and inertial modalities.
Uses frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers to provide dense modality-specific targets.
Trains a multimodal student from temporally sparse inputs through dual representation reconstruction.
On EvIs-Kitchen, improves noun/verb F1-macro over supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at 4 frames and 1.21/1.82 points at 32 frames.
Reports larger gains under sparse video observation settings within the evaluated unified-backbone setup.

papers.abstract: Violence in films and streaming media remains a concern for audience protection and creates substantial workload for manual content classification. Existing violence-detection methods often rely on limited modalities or short video clips, making it difficult to capture complementary evidence and localise violent events in long, untrimmed videos. In this study, we develop a framework for multimodal video understanding that classifies violence severity, predicts multiple violence types, and locates violent events in time. We combine temporally aligned visual and audio features extracted using pretrained encoders through attention-based adaptive fusion, followed by Transformer-based temporal modelling. Our framework supports three complementary tasks: video-level violence-severity classification, multi-label violence-type prediction, and temporal localisation of violent events. We evaluate the framework on the XD-Violence benchmark and examine its cross-domain performance using AIRTLab. On XD-Violence, our multimodal model achieves 93.27\% severity-classification accuracy and a micro-F1 score of 88.60\% for multi-label violence-type prediction, outperforming the corresponding unimodal configurations. We achieve a mean temporal intersection-over-union (tIoU) of 0.5075 for temporal localisation. Our cross-domain experiments reveal performance degradation under different recording conditions, while our movie case studies demonstrate the framework's potential to retrieve potentially violent scenes for further review. Our results highlight the practical value of multimodal intelligent systems in supporting human reviewers with the identification, classification, and temporal retrieval of violent content in films and streaming media.

Cross-domain performance degrades under different recording conditions; movie case studies indicate practical retrieval potential.

papers.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval asks a system to find, in a large collection of untrimmed videos with subtitles, the video and the time interval that a natural-language query describes. We find that most top-ranked errors of a strong corpus-level scorer come from choosing the wrong video, not from imprecise boundaries, and that re-weighting the evidence the scorer already uses does not fix them. We present DiTraR, which addresses video selection from two complementary directions. A witness-interval scorer decomposes the query into probes and scores every candidate interval of every corpus video exactly; a multi-scorer energy ensemble averages the energies of independently trained scorers before one exhaustive search; and a transcript verifier, a frozen language model that reads the time-stamped dialogue of the highest-ranked videos, re-orders the moments without changing their boundaries. With all settings frozen on development data and a single evaluation, DiTraR reaches 24.36 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 0.7 on the TVR validation split. The ensemble improves queries about visual content, the verifier improves queries about dialogue, and their gains largely add up.
authors: Mohammad Alijanpour Shalmani, Alale Rezvani Boroujeni, Ali Amini
bullets: Most top-ranked errors arise from selecting the wrong video rather than inaccurate temporal boundaries.
A witness-interval scorer evaluates query probes against every candidate interval across the corpus.
A multi-scorer energy ensemble combines independently trained scorers before exhaustive search.
A frozen language-model transcript verifier re-ranks top moments using time-stamped dialogue without changing boundaries.
On TVR validation, DiTraR achieves 24.36 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.7; visual and dialogue-query gains are complementary.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of DiTraR. K independently trained witness-interval scorers, which differ in query decomposition or random seed, assign an energy to every lattice interval of every corpus video. One exact search over the averaged energy returns the 100 best moments. A frozen language model reads the time-stamped transcripts of the highest-ranked videos, and its confidence that the moment occurs in each video re-orders the moments without changing their boundaries.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/roverx12345/MoHA.
authors: Jianghan Chao, Wenhui Tan, Hang Su, Qiuyu Tian, Tanxiao Li, Bingzi Zhang, Zequn Liu, Ruihua Song, Yingce Xia

papers.abstract: Echocardiography assesses the structure and function of the heart. Cardiologists read each study across several standard views and report the findings visible in those views by cardiac structure. AI foundation models can learn to analyze these studies from clinical reports, reducing annotation burden and supporting clinical interpretation. However, existing models are trained by pairing each video with the full clinical report, including structures and findings its view does not show. This mismatch lets a model associate a finding with incidental or spurious signals rather than its visual evidence, which limits accuracy, anatomical grounding and clinical trust. Here we introduce EchoAlign, a vision-language foundation model developed on 2.87 million echocardiographic videos and images from 159 clinical centers. EchoAlign aligns each cardiac structure, video and study with its report text, and a visibility matrix restricts supervision to the views that actually depict each structure. We compare it with five public foundation models on 0.47 million test videos across ten unseen external datasets from more than 25 clinical centers. EchoAlign achieves the highest mean AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.881 to 0.897) for classification and the highest mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.530 (95% CI, 0.511 to 0.544) for severity grading. Across 62 clinical findings, EchoAlign provides one model that detects findings, grades their severity, estimates measurements and segments cardiac structures.
authors: Ahmed Aly, Darya Taratynova, Lotfi Abdelkrim Mecharbat, Roman A. Sandler, Joseph Z. Sokol, Joshua Penn, Klaus H. Maier-Hein, Numan Saeed, Mohammad Yaqub

papers.abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking
authors: Davide Gardenal, Mingxuan Liu, Flavio Vella, Quentin Guimard, Elisa Ricci
bullets: Introduces TTU, which requires continuous tracking through object transformations and maintenance of semantic state graphs.
Proposes TIPO, a training-free generate–evaluate–judge framework for detecting and labeling split and merge events.
Uses mask components, overlap-based proposal scoring, and MLLM verification for transformation understanding.
Introduces VISTA, a benchmark with 50 sequences, 124 assembly events, 132 disassembly events, and over 26,000 frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA and runs 6×–15× faster than prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TIPO. At each frame It, the tracker provides the set of per-object masks. The pipeline operates in four stages (1–4): (1) extraction of the disjoint components and mask sampling, (2) generation of all possible assembly and disassembly states, (3) evaluation of the state proposals based on mask overlap metrics, (4) validation of the highest-scoring proposal by the MLLM Judge and semantic labeling. Lastly, the state graph and the tracker are updated with the validated state.

Figure 9. Overview of the VISTA Annotation Tool. Our custom interface couples automated object tracking with expert human verification to construct high-fidelity state graphs. (Top) The landing page features an interactive video player, central tracker controls, and lateral panels for object and graph management. (1) Add Object: The annotator registers a new distinct entity ID in the system. (2) Segment and Track: By clicking on the object within the video frame, the annotator prompts the segmentation model to extract the spatial mask and initiates temporal tracking. (3) Log Transformation: At the exact frame of a physical state change, the expert opens a dialog box to explicitly link the pre- and post-transformation object tracks and assign a semantic action label (e.g., “Unscrew”). (4) Transformation Logged: The validated event is immediately committed to the state graph and displayed in the right-hand panel for continuous review.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.
authors: Changin Choi, Jungwon Park, Jungmin Ko, Jimyeong Kim, Wonjong Rhee

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VMSA. The skill libraries are updated accordingly and periodically consolidated to reduce redundancy while preserving procedural knowledge. (c) At inference time, the video agent receives the target query, retrieved memory skills, and entity-aware episode memory as input context. The agent then gathers and verifies evidence through tool calls to generate its answer.

papers.abstract: General-purpose point tracking requires large-scale training data with diverse dynamics, yet existing datasets struggle to combine rich dynamic content, accurate scene geometry, and sufficient scale. We introduce TrajRealm, the first public synthetic point-tracking dataset to reach the ten-million-frame scale, constructed from games and embodied simulations. TrajRealm uses the rich environments and motion systems of modern games to capture diverse targets, activities, and interactions across diverse worlds, while embodied simulations add robot manipulation and indoor navigation data. The dataset provides RGB observations, depth, camera parameters, and persistent 2D and 3D point trajectories. These annotations provide precise, geometrically consistent supervision across foreground objects and static environmental surfaces. We also build TrajRealm-Bench with eight subcategories under Interaction and Locomotion to evaluate tracking across diverse scenes. Benchmark evaluations reveal the strengths and limitations of existing trackers in handling complex motion and maintaining long-term point correspondences. Training on TrajRealm improves the performance of existing tracking methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
authors: Ni Yang, Weiguang Zhao, Jiafei Cao, Yankai Jiang, Haoyu Guo, Tao Yang, Chunhua Shen, Junting Dong
bullets: Combines game environments with embodied simulations to cover varied targets, interactions, robot manipulation, and indoor navigation.

Benchmark results expose strengths and limitations of existing trackers, especially for complex motion and long-term correspondences.
Training on TrajRealm improves existing trackers on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

papers.abstract: LLM-generated descriptions enrich zero-shot skeleton-based action recognition but repeat cues shared by confusable actions. Their contextual semantics also lack explicit links to skeleton features. To address these challenges, we propose CRAFT, which couples Concept Refinement and Feature-grounded Tokens. Hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring identify concepts that distinguish each action from its closest rivals. Unique-QDPP selects complementary descriptions within each semantic slot and prevents their reuse across slots. This bank supervises learnable concept tokens that read motion and context cues from each skeleton. On fixed NTU-60 and NTU-120 splits, CRAFT improves five baselines spanning four recognition paradigms. ZSL accuracy and GZSL harmonic mean increase on every baseline-split pair, by 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on average. Random-split experiments extend these gains to three datasets, including PKU-MMD. Code will be released after acceptance.
authors: Siyu Zhu, Feng Ding, Zixiao Jin, Kaizhi Li, Xin Dong, Haisheng Fu, Yuchen Zou, Guohe Zhang, Jie Liang
bullets: Targets redundant LLM-generated descriptions and weak links between semantics and skeleton motion.
Uses hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring to find concepts that distinguish confusable actions.
Selects complementary descriptions with Unique-QDPP and assigns them to separate semantic slots.
Learns concept tokens that extract motion and contextual cues from skeletons.
Improves ZSL and GZSL performance across five baselines and multiple splits, with average gains of 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on fixed NTU splits.

papers.abstract: Many questions about videos ask for a number, such as how tall a person is, how far a cart travels, or how fast a ball leaves a ramp. We study this task, quantitative physical reasoning from video, where the inputs are a video, a question, and a prior of known facts such as object sizes, speeds, and distances from the camera to named objects. End-to-end video-language models lack an explicit metric scale and physical consistency, and their errors cannot be inspected. We present SceneRuler, which instead recovers a measurable physical scene and answers with that scene as evidence. Its central principle, Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction, builds, for each question, only the smallest scene that suffices to measure the asked quantity, and tests sufficiency on measurements rather than assuming it. The scene is written as a program whose structure a vision-language model writes and whose magnitudes are left to measurement. Physics-guided Fitting measures them through physical motion laws, so that gravity itself can anchor the metric scale, and marks every parameter, and the read-out of the asked quantity, as determined or undetermined. Each question receives a read-out and an answer. The read-out is the asked quantity evaluated on the scene, and it is empty when the scene does not fix that quantity. The answer is always given by a model that takes the scene as evidence. We evaluate on QuantiPhy and also apply the method to 27 in-the-wild videos that we collected, which have no ground-truth answers. On its validation split, the final answer reaches a mean relative accuracy of 0.709 against 0.624 for the strongest baseline, and the reconstruction determines the asked quantity on 47 of 158 questions, where the final answer reaches 0.781. Because every intermediate quantity is explicit, each answer can be traced to the objects, scale, and motion behind it.
authors: Yumeng He, Gezheng Kang, Fanlian Zeng, Yin Yang, Chenfanfu Jiang
bullets: Targets questions requiring physical quantities such as height, distance, and speed from video plus known prior facts.
Uses Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction to build the smallest question-specific scene that can determine the requested measurement.
Represents scene structure as a program, estimates magnitudes with physics-guided fitting, and can use gravity to establish metric scale.
Marks parameters and outputs as determined or undetermined; answers are generated with the reconstructed scene as evidence.
On QuantiPhy validation, achieves 0.709 mean relative accuracy versus 0.624 for the strongest baseline; fully determined cases reach 0.781 on 47 of 158 questions.

papers.selection_reason: Quantitative physical/spatial reasoning from video via scene reconstruction, fitting spatial intelligence and video understanding.
papers.title: SceneRuler: Measuring Physical Quantities in Video via Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction
papers.tldr: SceneRuler answers quantitative video questions by reconstructing only the physical scene needed for measurement, making scale, uncertainty, and evidence explicit.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.
authors: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui, Jinli Ou, Yuhua Zheng, Jianqiang Huang
bullets: Introduces Cognitive Inertia and Perceptual Inertia as two opposing failure modes of multimodal integration.
Presents TheaterBench, a benchmark featuring counter-intuitive videos that violate physical laws or common sense.
Finds severe Modal Polarization across current state-of-the-art video understanding models.
Reports that existing de-hallucination methods often shift the balance between the two inertias rather than resolve the conflict.
Positions perceptual-cognitive equilibrium as an important direction for future model evaluation and improvement.

papers.abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/
authors: Jingchen Sun, Jiaxing Zhang, Qingqiao Hu, Dingqiang Ye, Yuqi Jia, Yijun Liang, Di Fu, Yunjie Tian, Dongdi Zhao, Changyou Chen
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of annotated or externally supervised video foresight training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation over past–future video pairs as a natural self-supervised signal.
Introduces a foresight score and contrastive privilege advantage to emphasize informative future content over irrelevant context.
Optimizes a tractable lower-bound surrogate combining true-versus-random future comparison with teacher–student distillation.
Improves base models by up to 14.2 points on open-ended prediction and 15.9 points on closed-ended planning, without harming general video understanding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Future-OPSD and comparison with other training paradigms. (a) SFT learns annotated future descriptions y⋆ from past observations x using cross-entropy. (b) Naive OPSD uses a frozen future-aware teacher π0 to score the student’s own response ŷ, converting the teacher–student log-probability gap into token advantages for PPO. (c) Future-OPSD (ours) has a frozen teacher score the same response under the true future z (blue) and a reference future z̃ from another video (orange). The contrastive privilege advantage ℓzt −ℓz̃t compares the two futures, and the teacher–student distillation advantage ℓzt −ℓSt compares the true-future teacher with the past-only student. Their interpolation at down-weights context tokens supported by both futures (next / chop / the) while keeping content tokens specific to the true future (cilantro), helping the student focus on the most valuable future information. The advantages are clipped and centered into At for PPO, and inference uses only the student.

Figure 4. Case study: why Future-OPSD improves video foresight reasoning. On an EgoPlan-IT example with Qwen3-VL-8B, we compare the initial token advantages and trained predictions of Naive OPSD and Future-OPSD. A frozen teacher scores the same initial rollout under the paired future z and a reference future z̃ from another video, giving token log-probabilities ℓzt and ℓz̃t ; ℓSt is the past-only student’s log-probability. The context and content components are Ct = ℓz̃t − ℓSt and It = ℓzt − ℓz̃t . Before clipping and centering, Naive OPSD uses at = It + Ct, while Future-OPSD uses at = It + (1 − λ)Ct with λ = 0.75. Plotted values are initial advantages, with Ct and It below each token. Future-OPSD suppresses context information and amplifies decision-relevant content information, yielding the correct next-action prediction.

Figure 1. Not all of the future is equally important. To answer what will I do next? from what is seen now, only a small part of the future clip carries content information (rinse the knife); most of it is context information (tap, dish rack, sink, sponge) that neither answers the question nor reflects the expected action and trajectory of the ongoing event.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
authors: Zirui Zhao, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong
bullets: Long-video token pruning and merging can lose accuracy because sparse frames may span unrelated scenes, causing 3D patch tokenizers to blend them before token selection.
The method analyzes frame similarity and tokenizer behavior across 16 open models to guide budget allocation.
A closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and tokenizer class to choose token grids and the reduction dimension before encoding.
Across five accelerators and three video LLMs, ESSENCE is more accurate in 58 of 60 matched-TTFT comparisons.
Using 80% of tokens, it matches full Qwen-model accuracy with 1.6× faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it improves accuracy by up to 3.4 points.

papers.abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.
authors: Mohammed El Amine Mokhtari, Matei Mancas, Virginie Vandenbulcke
bullets: Compared fixed perception agents and a common reasoning model using agent messages, a tool-explored evidence graph, flat text, or a single audio-visual model.
On 799 XD-Violence clips, flat text nearly matched the single model (F1 0.967 vs. 0.968), while graph and message interfaces were less accurate.
Sound events improved F1, consistent with annotators relying on sound or speech for most violent clips.
Stored-observation citations were generally faithful, but graphs did not improve faithfulness over flat text; the agent pipeline used about 3× the GPU time.
Results were broadly robust to prompt rewording and a larger reasoning model, though model scale changed the relative ranking of message passing and graph use.

papers.abstract: Surgical video analysis requires video object segmentation (VOS), yet existing methods are commonly based on pretrained model fine-tuning using a large number of expert labels. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers the promise of bypassing this high cost by segmenting a target video using a few annotated references, which are the sole source of surgical knowledge for a frozen model. However, existing ICS methods tend to draw such references at random, which concentrate on a few views that dominate a surgical video and can miss other objects of interest (e.g., transient instruments and small structures). To address these challenges, we propose INCISE, a training-free ICS framework for surgical videos. INCISE selects unlabeled frames from multiple surgical videos that jointly cover the local appearances of a target video, and then segments the target video using these references. With only 1.7% of training frames selected and annotated as references and no target video frame labeled, INCISE obtains 67.2% mean mIoU and outperforms the best SOTA fine-tuned method by 9.2 points. We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.
authors: Yifan Xu, Bofang Zheng, Guangyu Meng, Nishchal Sapkota, Xianshi Ma, Xu Cao, Tianjiao Yu, Danny Z Chen
bullets: Addresses the high expert-labeling cost of fine-tuning-based video object segmentation.
Selects unlabeled frames across multiple surgical videos to cover the target video's local appearances.
Uses the selected frames as the sole references for a frozen model, with no target-frame annotations.
Using annotations for only 1.7% of training frames, achieves 67.2% mean mIoU.
Outperforms the best fine-tuned baseline by 9.2 percentage points, according to the abstract.

(3)–(4) Only these B frames are labeled by experts to form a fixed reference set R. papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP have shown great success in image tasks, however, applying CLIP to open-vocabulary video recognition poses challenges. Due to the limited text information, directly fine-tuning CLIP on video recognition datasets may lead to overfitting and hinder its generalizability. A prevalent method is to enrich text information by generating prompts using Large Language Models (LLMs). However, limited efforts have been made to explore how to generate higher-quality prompts that can contribute to classify unseen categories, and how to further enhance vision-text alignment based on these prompts. In this paper, we propose P2CLIP (Prompt-guided CLIP), which aims to bridge this gap by exploring the impact of prompts across three aspects: category, video, and frame. At the category level, we argue that LLM-generated prompts under simple instructions may suffer from semantic overgeneralization, which can blur the category boundaries and hinder the performance of the model. To address this issue, we design Generic-Discriminative Prompt using LLMs to obtain discriminative category embeddings with rich semantic information. At the video and frame levels, we first use VLM and LLM to generate frame and video descriptions for enhancing vision-text alignment. Then we propose a Knowledge-Guided Temporal Aggregation mechanism, which leverages the expert knowledge derived from LLMs to guide the temporal modeling of videos and encourage a better construction of the joint visual-textual feature space. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, including zero-shot and few-shot settings, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
bullets: Addresses CLIP’s overfitting and limited text-information challenges when adapting to open-vocabulary video recognition.
Generates Generic-Discriminative Prompts to reduce semantic overgeneralization and sharpen category boundaries.
Uses VLMs and LLMs to produce video- and frame-level descriptions for richer visual–textual alignment.
Introduces Knowledge-Guided Temporal Aggregation, using LLM-derived expert knowledge to guide video temporal modeling.
Experiments on multiple benchmarks in zero-shot and few-shot settings demonstrate the method’s effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.
authors: Changli Tang, Jie Yang, Tianyi Wang, Lei Li, Daoze Zhang, Zijie Xin, Zhan Liu, Li Li, Jinchang Xu, Fengyun Rao, Chao Zhang, Jing Lyu
bullets: Supports unified text, image, audio, and video processing in both fast instruct and explicit reasoning modes.
Offers 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants trained with progressive pre-training and multi-stage post-training.
The flagship 35B-A3B achieves a reported open-source state of the art on omni-modal video evaluations.
The 9B model reportedly surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on these evaluations.
The model family, evaluation suite, and reproduction pipeline are publicly released for research.

papers.abstract: Tracking objects through transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. Recent work has extended traditional object tracking to detect state changes. However, existing methods require an initial object prompt and detect only its decompositions, missing assembly events, which begin with multiple objects rather than one. We therefore introduce a prompt-free formulation of this task, where the goal is to recover all object tracks and detect both decomposition and assembly events given only a video. Our key insight is that assembly is decomposition in reverse. Building on this insight, we present Atlas, a zero-shot system that constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions to recover object tracks and their transformations. We further introduce OmniST, a benchmark with dense annotations of objects and both transformation types. On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing benchmarks that only evaluate decomposition.
authors: Cheryl Lam, Yihong Sun, Bharath Hariharan
bullets: Addresses prompt-dependent tracking methods that miss assembly events involving multiple objects.
Introduces a prompt-free task: recover object tracks and both types of transformations from video alone.
Atlas is a zero-shot system that jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions.
Introduces OmniST, a densely annotated benchmark for objects, assemblies, and decompositions.
On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on decomposition-only benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Video-language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on video-text retrieval and are increasingly used for egocentric video understanding. Yet, despite gains in zero-shot retrieval, they have shown limitations in compositional understanding, and it remains unclear whether they understand compositional relationships between verbs and nouns. In this work, we introduce Ego-ExBind, a compositional diagnostic protocol for analyzing pretraining exposure and verb-noun binding in egocentric video-text retrieval. Ego-ExBind consists of an Exposure Ledger built from the EgoClip pretraining corpus used by EgoVLPv2, which defines Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits for EPIC-KITCHENS-100 multi-instance retrieval (MIR). We further probe noun and verb binding channels through controlled noun-swap and verb-swap negatives. We find that zero-shot retrieval is positively associated with pair exposure within seen compositions, even after controlling for the marginal frequencies of verbs and nouns. However, higher pair exposure is associated with larger noun-swap margins and slightly smaller verb-swap margins. This asymmetry motivates us to test whether exposure reweighting can improve retrieval with little change in the measured swap margins. To isolate the effect of exposure input, we keep the trained checkpoint fixed and replace only the exposure input at inference. We demonstrate that this exposure reweighting can improve video-text retrieval without stronger verb-noun compositional understanding, and that the gain depends on the correct sample-level exposure correspondence. By separating exposure-driven retrieval gains from verb-noun binding, Ego-ExBind provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating whether future improvements in egocentric MIR reflect compositional understanding rather than pretraining familiarity.
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic protocol for separating pretraining familiarity from compositional binding in video-text retrieval.
Builds exposure-based Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits from the EgoClip corpus, with controlled noun- and verb-swap negatives.
Pair exposure correlates with zero-shot retrieval performance even after accounting for separate verb and noun frequencies.
Inference-time exposure reweighting improves retrieval while leaving measured binding largely unchanged, and requires correct sample-level exposure correspondence.
The framework helps assess whether future retrieval gains reflect genuine compositional understanding or pretraining exposure.

papers.title: Better Retrieval, Not Better Binding: Pretraining Exposure in Egocentric Video Retrieval
papers.tldr: Ego-ExBind shows that improved egocentric video retrieval can come from greater pretraining exposure rather than stronger verb–noun compositional understanding.

papers.abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated videos has raised growing concerns about misinformation, fraud, and potential societal risks, creating an urgent need for detection. Reconstruction-error-based methods have shown strong empirical performance for AI-generated image detection by exploiting discrepancies between an input and its reconstructed version. Their extension to video detection, however, faces two challenges: (i) a fixed reconstructor is not optimized for the detection objective and may yield weak discriminative signals; and (ii) an additional raw-video feature stream is often introduced to model temporal dependencies, increasing architectural overhead. To address these challenges, we develop a detector that learns and exploits reconstruction errors as a unified source of spatiotemporal evidence. First, we jointly optimize a reconstructor and the downstream classifier to produce reconstruction errors that are more informative for detecting AI-generated videos. Second, we show that consecutive reconstruction errors alone carry temporal evidence, and thus a 3D convolution over them captures spatiotemporal evidence without a raw-video stream. Extensive experiments on over 30 existing AI-video generators demonstrate competitive performance against baselines.
authors: Jiahua Jiang, Jinglai Li, Jianru Zhang, Jin Zhu
bullets: Addresses weak detection signals from fixed reconstructors and the overhead of parallel raw-video streams.
Jointly optimizes the reconstructor and classifier for more discriminative reconstruction errors.
Uses consecutive reconstruction errors with 3D convolution to model spatiotemporal evidence.
Evaluated across more than 30 AI-video generators, achieving competitive performance against baselines.

papers.abstract: Long-form video understanding, as a fundamental yet crucial vision task, is being revolutionized by multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based video agents. However, the retrieval-driven nature inherent to these agents creates a significant bottleneck, forcing them to reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan. To address this, we present ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that transforms long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. Rather than blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations, and continuously refines its search based on emerging evidence, where failed expectations serve as informative signals for principled backtracking. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training framework that equips MLLMs with foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. Extensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks demonstrate that ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning, achieving competitive or superior accuracy while observing $2.5$--$4.4\times$ fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. Code is available at https://github.com/harry0021/ForeSeek
authors: Yuchen Sun, Siyuan Cheng, Shi-Zhe Chen, Yixin Qin, Jinwen Luo, Zheng Wei
bullets: Addresses the lack of global temporal planning in retrieval-driven long-video agents.
Builds visually grounded expectations about unseen regions, verifies them with targeted observations, and backtracks when expectations fail.
Uses a two-stage training framework for foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision-making.
Across five long-video benchmarks, achieves competitive or better accuracy while observing 2.5–4.4× fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent.
