papers.tldr: ForeSeek enables MLLM video agents to reason through long videos by predicting and verifying relevant future regions instead of reactively retrieving clips.

papers.abstract: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD
authors: Andrii Yermakov, Jan Cech, Mario Fritz, Jiri Matas
bullets: Existing detectors perform well on blending fakes but struggle on entire face synthesis (EFS), where blending traces are absent.
TwinD uses reconstruction twins to target neural decoder traces and blob twins to target blending artifacts, without requiring a generator or face-shaped mask.
Across 19 datasets, TwinD achieves 96.3% mean AUROC: 98.1% on blending datasets and 95.6% on EFS datasets.
Training on twins alone still achieves 94.3% mean AUROC across three seeds.
Code, trained models, and training data are publicly released.

Both get the same augmentation, so they differ only by the manipulation. TwinD is a frozen PEcoreL with LoRA, trained on batches of such pairs. papers.selection_reason: Addresses the generalization gap in deepfake detection by training on 'twins' (reconstruction and blob twins) to handle entire face synthesis, a task within video understanding and manipulation detection.
papers.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis
papers.tldr: TwinD improves deepfake detection on unseen entire-face synthesis by training on two generator-free synthetic “twin” manipulations that capture decoder traces and blending artifacts.

papers.abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.
authors: Yutong Guan, Meixing Shi, Haoran Sun, Bing Sun, Yuxiang Cai, Yankai Jiang
bullets: Builds a hierarchical, time-indexed memory that aligns diverse evidence along a unified video timeline.
Uses temporal cues from retrieved evidence to constrain and guide subsequent memory access.
Introduces retrieval skills that adapt search targets, memory operations, temporal ranges, and stopping decisions based on the current evidence state.
Evolves skills through reward-guided policy improvement, accepting useful policy patches without updating model parameters.
Across four benchmarks, achieves 60.1% average accuracy and an 8.6-point average gain over prior best methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall pipeline of EvoMem: hierarchical time-indexed memory construction, skill-guided retrieval over textual, interval, and visual evidence, and reward-guided active skill bank updates without modifying model parameters.

Figure 1: Motivating example of EvoMem. (a) Base VLMs suffer from redundant frames and limited context. (b) HippoMM’s textcentric semantic memory may miss fine-grained visual evidence. (c) WorldMM lacks explicit temporal control for maintaining evidence chains. (d) Skill-free retrieval lacks guidance on what to seek, where to search, and when to stop. (e) EvoMem uses self-evolving skills for time-aware memory retrieval and coherent long-video reasoning.

papers.title: EvoMem: Self-Evolving Skills for Time-Aware Long Video Memory Agents
papers.tldr: EvoMem improves long-video question answering by using time-aware memory retrieval and self-evolving skills to maintain coherent evidence chains.

papers.abstract: Temporal action localization (TAL) detectors must identify actions and estimate their temporal boundaries, but localization remains a major source of detection errors. While understanding what determines boundary placement requires faithful attribution of temporal evidence, existing attribution methods have not sufficiently addressed the temporal structure of TAL or the need to tailor attribution to boundary localization. We introduce a structure-aware attribution framework that averages contributions across random evidence-restoration orders following the Shapley-Shubik principle. We make it tractable by using the detector's receptive field to limit which time steps are ordered individually, and by approximating each order with a soft gradient path. For boundary predictions, we further introduce cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references that selectively remove adjacent evidence. We also adapt faithfulness evaluation to assess the joint effects of contiguous temporal evidence and the direction of boundary displacement. Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer demonstrate improved attribution faithfulness over existing methods. Attribution analysis and controlled interventions further reveal that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement, providing input-level evidence that classification relies on content less informative about boundary placement. Code and evaluation artifacts will be publicly released.
authors: Ruoshan Lan, Zongru Shao, Chieh Tsai, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the lack of faithful, boundary-specific explanations for temporal action localization errors.
Averages contributions over Shapley–Shubik-inspired evidence-restoration orders, restricted by the detector’s receptive field and approximated with soft gradient paths.
Uses cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references to model adjacent evidence and boundary displacement.
Introduces faithfulness evaluation for contiguous temporal evidence and directional boundary shifts.
Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer show improved attribution faithfulness; analyses indicate class scores do not reliably reflect boundary placement.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses temporal action localization with a structure-aware attribution framework, contributing to the understanding of temporal dynamics in video.
papers.title: What Places an Action Boundary? Structure-Aware Attribution for Temporal Action Localization
papers.tldr: A structure-aware attribution framework explains which temporal evidence drives action-boundary placement in temporal action localization.

papers.abstract: Human proficiency estimation is challenging because skill is a high-level and often subjective property that is not captured by action identity alone. Existing approaches leverage multimodal observations such as ego-exo video, gaze, pose, and inertial signals, but the gap between sensor-level evidence and abstract proficiency labels remains difficult to bridge. We present SkillLens, a proficiency estimation framework that uses atomic action descriptions as temporal guidance, rather than direct semantic supervision, to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction. Each window is summarized into an action-dynamics feature and scored by a high-low prototype margin against higher- and lower-proficiency executions from the same activity-action category. Fusing these ego/exo PDM cues with a global ego-exo-gaze baseline through CORAL ordinal calibration, our method achieves 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D. Our project page is available at https://skill-lens.net/
authors: Deokhyun Ahn, Hyukjin Kim, Jae-Ho Han, Bumsub Ham, Heeseung Choi, Ig-Jae Kim, Haksub Kim
bullets: Targets the gap between multimodal sensor observations and abstract proficiency labels.
Uses temporal action guidance to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction.
Scores window features via margins between higher- and lower-proficiency executions within the same activity-action category.
Fuses ego/exo visual-dynamics cues with global ego-exo-gaze features using CORAL ordinal calibration.
Reports 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D; the abstract does not specify limitations beyond the task’s inherent subjectivity.

We concatenate both signals and use a CORAL ordinal head to predict the final proficiency level.

papers.title: SkillLens: Action-Guided Dense Visual Dynamics for Proficiency Estimation
papers.tldr: SkillLens estimates human proficiency by using atomic action descriptions to identify skill-relevant video windows and compare their dynamics against high- and low-proficiency prototypes.

papers.abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.
authors: Amit Feldman, Ilan Shimshoni, Rotem Dror
bullets: Addresses the need to identify and assess procedural mistakes before recovery is no longer possible.
Uses observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions to recognize completed steps, localize them temporally, and classify execution errors.
Compares separate modular components with a joint model that predicts step identity, timing, and correctness together.
The joint model improves binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 from 80.7% to 84.1%, with the largest gain for slips.
The dataset split is revised to include erroneous videos across all splits; omitted steps are identified only after the video ends.

papers.abstract: Sign language translation and recognition have been shown to benefit from various pretraining approaches. We propose a novel two-stage pretraining approach for the motion encoder, which first learns to reconstruct masked motion, followed by joint masked prediction of pseudo-gloss units and motion. Pseudo-glosses serve as an intermediate structured representation of natural language text and are obtained from the captions by a large language model. We curate a corpus of about 1,100 hours of American Sign Language from five public datasets, estimate 2D pose for all clips and define an evaluation protocol. We then reproduce state-of-the-art translation methods and evaluate them using the same train and test splits. We propose a translation model built on our pretraining strategy, and this model outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods Uni-Sign and SHuBERT, as well as the YouTube-ASL baseline, on the How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki and OpenASL datasets. Furthermore, the gain from the joint pretraining using motion and pseudo-gloss grows as translation data shrinks. A classifier built on the same encoder also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ASL Citizen isolated sign recognition and outperforms our reproduction of Uni-Sign on WLASL2000.
bullets: Uses a two-stage motion-encoder pretraining strategy: masked-motion reconstruction, then joint masked prediction of motion and LLM-derived pseudo-gloss units.
Curates approximately 1,100 hours of ASL video from five public datasets, estimates 2D poses, and defines a common evaluation protocol.
The resulting translation model outperforms prior methods and the YouTube-ASL baseline on How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki, and OpenASL.
Joint motion–pseudo-gloss pretraining is especially beneficial when less translation data is available.
The shared encoder achieves state-of-the-art isolated-sign recognition on ASL Citizen and surpasses a Uni-Sign reproduction on WLASL2000.

papers.abstract: Tracking a hidden object through a video is effortless for humans, yet it remains a bottleneck for vision language models (VLMs). In the shell game, where a ball is hidden under one of several identical cups that are then swapped, VLMs that answer directly stay near chance, thinking models fail on long games, and fine-tuning learns only the lengths it has seen. We argue that the limit is serial computation: each swap must be composed with the last result, and a VLM of fixed depth has only a fixed number of state transitions for it. To address this, we propose RecurrentVLM, which makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time by computing the keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output. With a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench and 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. We also observe several interesting phenomena: length generalization emerges suddenly at an aha moment; without recurrence, each swap costs an attention layer; the ball's state forms in the first four attention layers; and recurrence keeps the latest state at the cost of details of earlier moments. These results suggest that recurrent VLMs are a potential solution for tracking the states of unobserved objects in video. Code will be released.
authors: Dingqiang Ye, Jiacong Xu, Wen Zhang, Yiqun Mei, Vishal M. Patel
bullets: VLMs struggle with shell-game tracking because each swap requires composing a new state with the previous one.
RecurrentVLM applies every attention layer recurrently, recomputing keys and values from completed frame groups while using a single answer token.
It achieves 100% on VET-Bench, 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps.
Length generalization appears abruptly, while recurrence preserves the latest state but loses details from earlier moments.
The findings suggest recurrence can support tracking unobserved object states in video.

(c) Each query reads keys and values of earlier tokens’ inputs in (a), but of earlier frame groups’ outputs in (b).

papers.abstract: JEPA-based video encoders learn strong representations for video and image understanding through prediction in latent space. However, their standard pretraining predicts features within individual images or video clips, without explicitly exploiting paired camera views of the same object or moment. Consequently, the learned representations may not reliably support matching across different camera viewpoints. To solve this problem, we introduce multi-view predictive post-training to strengthen cross-view instance and temporal correspondence while retaining independent single-view inference. A shared encoder processes masked context views independently, and a training-time predictor jointly predicts latent tokens for masked context regions and a fully held-out view. We alternate cross-view prediction with single-view masked prediction on general image and video data to help retain the encoder's pretrained capabilities. After only 9,000 post-training updates on a single GPU, MV-JEPA improves cross-view instance retrieval and coarse cross-camera moment retrieval on various datasets, with further gains in zero-shot action-phase retrieval and frozen-feature classification on AE2. Frozen-probe evaluations further indicate that post-training largely preserves motion recognition, image recognition, and dense semantic segmentation performance on the evaluated benchmarks. Together, these results demonstrate that multi-view predictive post-training can strengthen instance and coarse temporal correspondence in JEPA video encoders without modifying the encoder architecture or single-view inference interface.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Addresses weak cross-view instance and temporal correspondence in standard JEPA pretraining.
Uses a shared encoder with a joint predictor for masked context views and a fully held-out view.
Alternates multi-view and single-view masked prediction to retain pretrained image and video abilities.
With 9,000 post-training updates on one GPU, improves cross-view instance retrieval, coarse cross-camera moment retrieval, and some zero-shot and frozen-feature tasks.
Evaluations suggest motion recognition, image recognition, and dense segmentation are largely preserved; scope is limited to evaluated benchmarks and coarse temporal matching.

papers.abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.
authors: Hongyu Wang, Chuhan Li, Congjin Xu, Xuandong Zhao, Hua Shen

The strongest model recognizes object motion in 91.37% of comparisons but identifies passage-constraint changes in only 66.50%.
Models often select entities that move but do not physically conflict with or constrain the wearer’s passage.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised video encoders are commonly trained to either reconstruct pixels or predict latent features, yet it remains unclear how these objectives shape representations for downstream dynamics. We present a capacity-matched study isolating this choice: two identical video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck are trained under autoencoding and V-JEPA objectives on a continuous control environment. We introduce a simple asymmetric discretization scheme to apply the same bottleneck to the predictive model. The resulting representations exhibit a clear trade-off: the autoencoder preserves substantially more physical state information and achieves slightly better one-step latent prediction, while the predictive encoder accumulates less error under autoregressive rollout. Structural probes suggest that this advantage is associated with greater robustness to low-level visual perturbations and stronger dependence on temporal context. These results indicate that predictive and reconstructive objectives induce distinct representations of dynamics, trading state fidelity for properties that may benefit long-horizon prediction.
bullets: Studies reconstruction versus latent-prediction objectives using capacity-matched video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck.
Introduces asymmetric discretization to apply the same discrete bottleneck to the predictive V-JEPA model.
Autoencoding retains substantially more physical state information and performs slightly better on one-step latent prediction.
Predictive representations accumulate less error during autoregressive rollout, with benefits linked to robustness to visual perturbations and stronger temporal-context dependence.
The objectives create a trade-off between state fidelity and properties useful for long-horizon dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. Code and dataset: https://github.com/austincbaker/A3Bench.
authors: Austin C Baker, Raiyaan Abdullah, Daniel Zeev Yoffe, Shruti Vyas, Yogesh S Rawat

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.

papers.abstract: Generalizable AI-generated video detection remains challenging because natural motion and content variations can resemble synthesis artifacts, making isolated video discrepancies unreliable indicators of authenticity. To address this challenge, we propose Spatial and Contextual Reference-informed Detection (SCRiD), a framework that interprets video variations through complementary spatial and contextual references. Specifically, we introduce Matched-Coordinate Residual Response (MCR) to characterize temporal residual associations under motion and coordinate references with matched subpixel sampling conditions. We further develop Real-Conditioned Score Adaptation (RCSA), which learns a content-conditioned denoising reference from authentic videos and probes its responses across multiple noise scales and quality views to guide feature adaptation. To integrate these complementary sources of evidence, we design Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) to enable information exchange through reversible symplectic updates. We train SCRiD using synthetic videos from only 4 generators and evaluate it across 88 generator or task subsets spanning 6 benchmarks. Our method achieves average ACC and AP of 72.72% and 74.23%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.24 and 0.81 percentage points.Ablation and robustness experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and the stability of SCRiD under common post-processing operations.
authors: Hao Tan, Zekai Zuo, Boyang Chen, Jinghui Qin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of distinguishing synthesis artifacts from natural motion and content variation.

Combines evidence through Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) with reversible symplectic updates.
Trained on videos from 4 generators and evaluated across 88 subsets and 6 benchmarks, achieving 72.72% average ACC and 74.23% AP; robustness tests support stability under common post-processing.

papers.abstract: Streaming video models must answer questions about a live video under strict memory and latency limits. Feeding only the latest few frames keeps present perception sharp, whereas adding past frames dilutes attention on the current scene and triggers hallucinations. Recent cascade methods retrieve past frames when uncertain, but they still fail when current frames are blurry or when decisive future clues have not appeared yet. We introduce ActiveForager, a streaming video agent that maintains a clean short working window and gathers extra evidence only on demand. For each query, the agent either answers directly, zooms into high-resolution recent frames, recalls past events from memory, or waits for upcoming frames. When recalling history, a shared-weight sub-agent verifies candidate clips in isolation and returns a compact evidence summary. A stream-decoupled attention mask then keeps historical evidence from interfering with present visual tokens. We train this policy using counterfactual information gain, which rewards a tool call only when the gathered evidence makes the true answer more likely and prevents tool collapse across all actions. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on OVO-Bench, ActiveForager improves real-time perception, historical recall, and proactive response at once, lifting overall accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B from 47.6% to 65.9%. It also doubles zero-shot accuracy on the multi-hop Video-Holmes benchmark while adding minimal visual tokens per query.
authors: Pengyu Li, Zhitao Gao, Lingling Zhang, Wenxuan Huang, YiCheng Xiao, Chen Zheng, Jun Liu
bullets: Maintains a clean short-term frame window to preserve current-scene perception and reduce hallucinations.

Uses an isolated verification sub-agent and stream-decoupled attention to integrate recalled evidence without disrupting present visual tokens.
Trains tool-use decisions with counterfactual information gain to encourage evidence-gathering only when useful.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B accuracy on OVO-Bench from 47.6% to 65.9% and doubles zero-shot accuracy on Video-Holmes with minimal added visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

Without extra training, LookAway nearly matches full-video accuracy at 0.12–0.13× the modeled decode cost.
With fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model withdraws after a median of 66–68 tokens and reads 27–35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy across three held-out benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.
authors: Yiyang Zhu, Guangyuan Liu, Jingdi Lei, Li Wei, Chau Yuen
bullets: Static pooled embeddings can collapse distinct physical executions under identical conditions into the same representation.
Theoretical analysis shows that longer temporal pooling converges toward the stationary recording condition, making twin events indistinguishable from pooled features alone.
Physical events are identified by an “event gap”: instantaneous, synchronized changes across modalities that accumulate along unpooled trajectories.
CounterPoint removes each modality’s temporal mean and scores frame-level cross-modal agreement.
Integrated into four multimodal aligners, it consistently outperforms existing temporal alignment methods, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.

Evaluates single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use with feedback across five models, revealing varied evidence-acquisition behaviors.

papers.abstract: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) for video-related tasks, automatic rough-cut remains underexplored, without a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation or mature workflows for producing executable cut plans. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce RoughCut-Bench, which covers two practical settings: (1) a visually driven setting over video cases, covering highlight detection and selection, source-video ordering, and adherence to user requirements when provided; and (2) a speech-driven setting over automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, covering filler removal, expression deduplication, and low-value content trimming. Across these settings, the benchmark contains 101 visually driven cases, including 831 raw videos with 1,476 highlight annotations. It also includes 84 speech-driven cases, each consisting of an ASR transcript with annotated cleanup spans. The evaluation compares cut plans with these annotations in both settings and additionally uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator to assess rendered-cut quality in the visual setting. To apply LVLMs to automatic rough-cut, we further propose agentic workflows that guide them to produce structured cut plans from input materials. Experiments show that current LVLMs remain limited in producing expert-aligned cut plans. Our benchmark, code, and prompts are released at https://whalesong-zrs.github.io/RoughCut-Bench-Project-Page.

Compares generated cut plans with annotations and uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator for rendered visual cuts.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) have significantly improved video understanding capabilities, yet processing long videos remains challenging due to the substantial computational cost of extensive visual inputs. Frame selection offers an efficient alternative, but many existing region-based methods rely on fixed or predefined temporal partitions, which may result in suboptimal temporal regions, compromising subsequent budget allocation and frame selection. In this work, we propose Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection (APS), a training-free framework that adapts temporal partitions to local variations in query-frame relevance. Specifically, APS formulates temporal partitioning as a complexity-regularized fitting problem, jointly optimizing partition boundaries and local models through dynamic programming. The resulting adaptive temporal partitions guide frame budget allocation based on query relevance and temporal extent, enabling informative frame selection under limited visual budgets. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that APS consistently improves performance across diverse LVLM backbones, achieving the highest average gains over uniform sampling among competing methods. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of adaptive partitioning and demonstrate its generalizability across model scales, similarity encoders, and advanced LVLMs.
authors: Junxiang Wen, Yinxi Zhao, Jiawei Chen, Jingying Hu, Lijun Wang, Zhen Qin, Shuiguang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of processing long videos with LVLMs.
Uses a training-free, complexity-regularized fitting objective with dynamic programming to jointly optimize temporal boundaries and local relevance models.
Allocates frame budgets according to local query relevance and temporal extent.
Improves performance over uniform sampling across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench and diverse LVLM backbones.
Generalizes across model scales, similarity encoders, and advanced LVLMs.

papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of AI-generated videos (AIGVs) has raised critical concerns about content authenticity. Existing benchmarks suffer from a fundamental limitation: real and fake videos are often collected or generated from different semantic distributions. As a result, detectors may rely on spurious correlations involving objects, scenes, or actions rather than intrinsic artifacts introduced by generative models. To this end, we introduce SAVGE, a large-scale semantically aligned AIGV detection dataset comprising 2,369,822 videos, including 424,115 real videos and 1,945,707 generated videos. SAVGE organizes samples into real-fake semantic groups by using captions paired with real videos as prompts for text-to-video generation, thereby providing both group-level correspondence and textual semantic anchors. Based on SAVGE, we further propose Explicit Disentangling and Semantic-aware Contrasting (EDSC), a model-agnostic training framework for learning artifact-focused representations with reduced semantic interference. EDSC first extracts and aligns visual semantic features with textual representations, and then explicitly suppresses semantic information in the artifact branch while contrasting real and fake samples within each semantic group. By integrating caption-guided semantic supervision with intra-group contrastive learning in a two-phase optimization strategy, EDSC encourages detectors to capture generation-related cues under matched semantic conditions. Extensive experiments on SAVGE and GenVideo demonstrate that EDSC improves most evaluated backbone-metric combinations, enhances robustness under challenging evaluation settings, and strengthens cross-dataset generalization. These results highlight the importance of semantic alignment in AIGV detection and validate explicit semantic-artifact disentanglement as an effective strategy for robust detector learning.
authors: Jiaquan Yu, Jingyi Xie, Zeyu Zhang, Yunhang Qian, Xiaobin Hu, Jiawei Liu
bullets: SAVGE addresses benchmark bias by grouping real and generated videos with matched semantics and textual anchors.
The dataset contains 2,369,822 videos, including 424,115 real and 1,945,707 generated videos.

The approach focuses on generation-related artifacts under semantically matched conditions, rather than object, scene, or action correlations.

papers.abstract: Proactive video understanding requires vision-language models (VLMs) to decide not only what to answer as a video unfolds, but also when newly arrived evidence warrants a response and when to remain silent. Although modern VLMs excel at offline long-video understanding, they struggle in proactive streaming settings, leading prior work to introduce task-specific reinforcement learning or auxiliary triggering modules. We find that explicit reporting rules and structured streaming context substantially improve a frozen VLM's proactive response performance. We exploit this observation to build SIMPLEPRO, a training-free baseline for proactive video understanding. At each decision step, the model combines recent high-resolution frames, bounded historical observations, and prior answer records to determine whether new information warrants a response and, when needed, generate a concise answer. The system then filters consecutive duplicate answers while retaining the raw outputs as context for subsequent decisions. Without any parameter updates or auxiliary triggers, SIMPLEPRO with a 4B backbone consistently outperforms specialized proactive systems across OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, and ProactiveVideoQA. SIMPLEPRO shows overall performance gains as backbone size increases from 2B to 32B. We hope this simple yet effective method will serve as a strong baseline for proactive video understanding, and we will release our code and inference pipeline to support future research.
authors: Yilin Wang, Xiangxi Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Linjie Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Alex Jinpeng Wang

papers.abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.
authors: Yu Yuan, Ruizhou Ding, Shaoheng Fang, Stanley H. Chan, Zhuo Chen

Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, it improves motion evaluation, generalizes to unseen defects, and benefits motion generation and data selection; the abstract reports top dynamics scores among 21 tested models.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates can cause irreversible evidence loss. In this paper, we study this problem from the perspective of assessing the spatiotemporal distribution of query-specific evidence and propose a novel and training-free approach termed NULLTOK. For every patch across all frames, we construct an empirical-null distribution from 64 group-matched irrelevant control queries, capturing the scores expected in the absence of target-specific evidence. Target affinities are calibrated against these same-position references into right-tail Monte Carlo p-values, which are discrete super-uniform under a conditional exchangeability assumption. Calibrated screening and a high-recall semantic guard produce candidate tokens for deterministic visual deduplication and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation. To validate NullTok, we apply it to two representative MLLMs and conduct extensive experiments on a set of video benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness under a bounded visual token budget. For example, it achieves 65.81% and 68.85% on Video-MME using frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones, respectively, at a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents (FFE), without subtitles or audio. These results outperform all evaluated baselines on Video-MME under the same budget for both backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/potato-kitty/NullTok.

papers.abstract: An anatomical pose provides interpretable joint structure, but no fixed set of physical landmarks can fully specify a person's movement. We introduce PRISM, a complementary representation that characterizes repetitive movement using tracked masks and dense optical flow. Torso-relative flow measures intensity, frame-wise mask variation measures spatial extent, signed-flow recurrence estimates frequency, and persistent sliding-window geometry describes the rhythmicity of the movement. Across 1,890 synthetic conditions, the measurements recover controlled speed, amplitude, and frequency while exposing observation limits. An idealized hand-motion experiment demonstrates variation omitted by identical exact COCO-17 trajectories; controlled corruption experiments separately examine measurement sensitivity. Audits of two pose methods on the same data cohort and 36,930 external skeleton clips document incomplete observation and dependence on processing choices. In 1,404 annotated complex stereotypical motor movement bouts from six autistic participants, total flow converges with pose motion, while matched-coordinate examples and repeated-session profiles show differences in intensity, extent, frequency, and rhythmicity within behavior labels. A separate VLM comparison evaluates quantitative frequency estimation, and a profile-conditioned decoder links the measurements to illustrative skeletal movements. PRISM connects numerical profiles to visible examples, providing an interpretable way to compare how the same behavior is expressed beyond its label or event count.
authors: Austin A. MBaye, Savik Kinger, Matthew S. Goodwin
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed anatomical landmarks and behavior labels for representing individual movement styles.
Combines torso-relative optical flow, mask variation, flow recurrence, and sliding-window geometry into quantitative movement profiles.
Synthetic and controlled experiments show the measures recover speed, amplitude, and frequency while revealing observation and processing limits.
Analyses of autistic participants show that people with the same movement label can differ in intensity, spatial extent, frequency, and rhythmicity.
Links numerical profiles to illustrative skeletal movements for interpretable comparison beyond pose trajectories or event counts.

papers.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.
authors: Mohammad Eslami, Mousa Moradi, Negin Ghamsarian, Nazlee Zebardast, Jennifer L Lindsey, Sophia Y. Wang, Lucia Sobrin, Rishi P Singh, Tobias Elze
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of searching large surgical video archives for similar operations, complications, and workflow events.
Combines eight public datasets spanning four surgical domains, six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips.
Provides Scene retrieval of operative states and Workflow retrieval of phase transitions or deviations, with safeguards against timing and labeling shortcuts.
Evaluates generic and surgical foundation models, retrieval methods, and benchmark-trained contrastive heads under within- and cross-dataset settings.
Frozen representations barely beat timing-only baselines, transition retrieval is near chance, and trained heads degrade substantially across datasets.

papers.abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of symbolic recognizers and methods requiring hard-to-transfer dynamics models.
Learns a trajectory prior and runs a warm-started denoising process for each candidate goal.
Steers samples toward observed motion using a closed-form likelihood gradient, then applies Bayes’ rule to estimate goal posteriors.
Evaluated on simulated robots, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories with four metrics covering distinct failure modes.
Preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs during ambiguous trajectory prefixes, unlike filter- and classifier-based observers that may collapse or become overconfident.

Colour identifies the method; marker shape identifies the domain (legend below). WORD points carry a thicker outline. The desirable corner is bottom-right in every panel; panel (d) reverses the x-axis so lower Brier still points right.

Figure 2: WORD online inference on a 2-goal synthetic scenario. An agent (green) starts at the bottom of a 10× 10 world and must reach one of two goals separated by a circular obstacle; WORD maintains one denoising chain per candidate goal and updates a posterior as observations arrive. (a) Prior. Before any observation, the score network ϵθ shapes Gaussian noise into two obstacle-aware trajectory clusters, one towards each waypoint, and the goal prior is uniform. (b) Ambiguity. The agent has skirted the lower edge of the obstacle but its heading is still consistent with both goals; both clusters survive and the posterior remains nearly balanced. A filtering baseline would already have collapsed onto one mode here. (c) Observation guidance. Once the agent commits left of the obstacle, the score-guidance term ∇τ log p(Z | τ ) (orange) pins each chain to the observed path; the right cluster must arc awkwardly over the obstacle to remain reachable, and posterior mass shifts toward w1. (d) Commitment. As the agent approaches w1, the surviving chain dominates and the posterior collapses. Pseudocode is in algorithm 1.

papers.abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.
authors: Chengqian Ma, Yuanze Zeng, Hongyu Wang, Mingfeng Lin, YiCheng Xiao, Yu Chen, Pengyu Li, WenHao Wang, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
bullets: Addresses spatial dilution of small moving objects and temporal loss of motion direction, speed, and event order.
Uses Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning to select anchors, while Patch Diffs encode changes between neighboring frames.
Dual-Road Change Memory, active motion ROIs, and Entity State Chains form dynamic, temporally ordered representations.
With only 0.22% trainable parameters on a frozen 27B backbone, VIVID-Small outperforms eleven baselines overall across 8,083 questions.
VIVID-Large achieves the strongest results on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass; the method is evaluated under limited-data settings.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.
authors: Bingjun Luo, Jialin Guo, Siqi Li
bullets: Uniform frame budgets overlook variation in how much visual evidence different questions require.
The authors find that question subsets favor different frozen frame-sampling policies, and more frames do not consistently improve every metric.
FrameRouter is a training-free test-time framework with an evidence-demand router, budget-constrained allocation, and frozen sampling-policy bank.
It keeps the average visual budget equal to a uniform reference while reallocating frames selectively across questions.
Experiments on Video-MME-v2 and other long-video benchmarks show improved QA performance without changing the underlying samplers.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.
authors: Tianci Xie, Li Chen, Pinxue Guo, Rui Zheng
bullets: Targets counting actions, ordering events, and locating state changes scattered across long videos.
SightForge verifies tasks by reconstructing answers from densely reacquired evidence and checking for counterexamples.
SightLine contains 310 verified tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated with the multiscale SightLoop harness.
The strongest model scores 54.52% unaided versus 79.35% with annotated evidence, revealing a substantial search gap.
With fewer than 6K examples, Sight-35B improves interactive accuracy from 21.29% to 42.26% and gains over 8 points on two external benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Detailed video captioning requires comprehensive and faithful descriptions of objects, actions, and temporal events. Fixed-frame sampling, however, can miss brief motions, small objects, and other fine-grained evidence, motivating captioning agents that actively seek relevant moments and inspect local regions. Training such behavior is challenging because, unlike video question answering, generic captioning instructions do not specify what visual evidence should be acquired. We propose Perception-Question On-Policy Distillation (PQ-OPD), which uses training-only Perception Questions (PQs) to guide active video perception. PQs specify what should be inspected without revealing the corresponding answers, encouraging the teacher to explore the video more comprehensively and focus on relevant visual evidence. Along trajectories generated by the student, on-policy distillation transfers this guidance to the student's reasoning, tool calls, and captions; no PQs are required at inference. Across three detailed-captioning and two caption-to-QA benchmarks, PQ-OPD consistently improves the corresponding untrained agents across teacher-student scales and input-frame budgets. Under our evaluation protocol, PQ-OPD achieves the strongest primary-metric results among the compared open-source models on DREAM-1K, CaReBench, ShortVidBench, MotionBench, and VidCapBench-AE. Our ablations, together with analysis of temporal coverage and answer leakage, further indicates that the student internalizes the training-time guidance as a more effective video exploration policy.
authors: Yifan Xu, Ruopeng Gao, Zhixiao Wang, Jiafu Tang, Yichun Yang, Zihao Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Limin Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed-frame sampling, which can miss brief actions, small objects, and fine-grained temporal evidence.
Uses training-only Perception Questions to specify what to inspect without revealing answers, encouraging comprehensive and relevant video exploration.
Applies on-policy distillation along student-generated trajectories to transfer guidance into reasoning, tool use, and captions; no perception questions are needed at inference.
Improves corresponding untrained agents across multiple teacher–student scales, frame budgets, and five detailed-captioning or caption-to-QA benchmarks.
Ablations and analyses suggest the method improves temporal coverage and helps students internalize a more effective video-exploration policy.

papers.title: Teaching What to Look For: Privileged Perception Questions for Agentic On-Policy Distillation in Video Captioning

papers.abstract: Modern video moment retrieval systems often propose windows that overlap the target event, yet still select the wrong one. We study this scorer bottleneck on QVHighlights with a fixed QD-DETR-derived temporal expert: the parent-aware temporal expert reaches 64.71 R1@0.5, while diagnostic oracles over the same candidate family reach 75.68 R1@0.5 within the parent-reranked pool and 94.97 R1@0.5 over the full 100-candidate evidence pool. We introduce OVET-Consensus, a rank-preserving counterfactual event verification layer that keeps the temporal expert's ranked list as the default and permits only high-confidence rank-1 overrides from a policy calibrated on held-out training videos. The verifier uses parent-aware interval evidence, structured Qwen3-VL event judgments, VideoLLaMA3 pairwise temporal signals, and dense temporal evidence, but never lets those signals freely reorder the top-K list. On QVHighlights validation, OVET-Consensus improves the parent-aware temporal expert from 64.71 to 65.35 R1@0.5 with a positive paired-bootstrap interval, while mAP is largely unchanged, from 42.67 to 42.74; it makes 20 overrides, with 15 helpful corrections and 3 harmful corrections. The results point to a practical constraint on verifier design: semantic compatibility is useful evidence, but temporal grounding still requires deciding where the event starts, changes, and ends inside a visually compatible scene.
bullets: Targets the scorer bottleneck: systems often retrieve windows overlapping the event but select the wrong one.
Combines parent-aware interval evidence, structured vision-language judgments, pairwise temporal signals, and dense temporal evidence.
Preserves the temporal expert’s ranking by default; only high-confidence rank-1 counterfactual overrides are permitted.
On QVHighlights validation, R1@0.5 rises from 64.71 to 65.35, while mAP remains nearly unchanged (42.67 to 42.74).
Among 20 overrides, 15 were helpful and 3 harmful, highlighting the need for precise temporal boundary grounding.

papers.abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.
authors: Li Li, Xiangbo Gao, Bo Ni, Samyadeep Basu, Viet Dac Lai, Jing Shi, Seunghyun Yoon, Gang Wu, Yu Wang, Thien Huu Nguyen, Tyler Derr, Franck Dernoncourt, Zhengzhong Tu, Yue Zhao
bullets: The study identifies “motion collapse,” where reward models prefer motion-suppressed edits; the baseline does so in 97% of VE-Bench cases.
Learned video rewards, a VLM judge, latent optimization, and reward-guided fine-tuning all show vulnerability to motion suppression.
The proposed model adds an RGB frame-difference stream and trains on motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives, with a human-quality distillation anchor.

It selects motion-suppressed candidates in 0% of motion-ladder cases, reaches 0.57 Spearman correlation with human ratings, detects unseen suppression variants, and preserves motion during fine-tuning.
Scope: the method is evaluated on VE-Bench and two editing pipelines.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Chang Sun, Yijun Tian, Zhenwei Tang, Yuchen Deng, Yifan Simon Liu, Chenxu Wang, Wei Wang
bullets: Targets hallucinations caused when irrelevant or misleading audio, video, or text cues distort another modality’s prediction.
Uses Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration when unimodal branches disagree, selecting task-relevant evidence and alternative answers.
Uses Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery when branches agree, checking layer-wise evidence consistency and strength to detect false consensus.
Evaluated on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across hallucination mitigation and audio-visual reasoning tasks.
Reports up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding and 7.7% average improvement over the best baseline, as stated in the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free decoding to mitigate cross-modal hallucinations in Omni-LLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning and video-language understanding.
papers.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: PACD is a training-free decoding framework that reduces cross-modal hallucinations in omnimodal LLMs by using modality evidence provenance to arbitrate disagreement and correct erroneous consensus.

papers.abstract: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting. Sign spottings already locate words in time at corpus scale, but training subtitle alignment jointly on subtitle and word spans remains underexplored. We present SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator that maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval. It is first trained jointly on subtitle spans and word spans from sign spottings, then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples. On the subtitle test set of the British Broadcasting Corporation-Oxford British Sign Language (BOBSL) corpus, the refined model reaches 66.68 F1@0.50 (F1 with a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of one half), the best among compared systems without external sign-video resources. This overlap-reward refinement outperforms cross-entropy continuation from the same jointly trained model. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment in a pair of our generators matched in code, labels and maximum update budget. The advantage remains after both models of the pair are refined with overlap rewards. For word queries, the refined model follows the queried word, not a fixed position in the video: when the word's sign lies away from the video centre, it is far more accurate than predictions that use position alone. Together, these findings support one shared span generator refined with overlap rewards, aligning subtitles and producing word spans for human review.
authors: Jongbhin Woo, Youngjoon Jang, Joon Son Chung
bullets: Targets two granularities: subtitle spans for alignment and word spans for sign spotting.
Uses a prompt-conditioned visual-language generator to predict start/end frames for sentence or word queries.
Trains jointly on subtitle and sign-spotting word spans, retaining word examples during refinement.
Achieves 66.68 F1@0.50 on the BOBSL subtitle test set, best among compared systems without external sign-video resources.
Word-query predictions follow the queried sign rather than relying on fixed video position; scope is evaluated on BOBSL and matched comparison systems.

papers.abstract: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra generation cost in text-based communication between multimodal language models.
Provider models observe complementary video frames and transfer projected, aligned visual KV states to a carrier model via gated residual updates.
The injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while adding provider and communication-module computation.
Experiments on MLVU and Video-MME report modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower latency than the evaluated text-based baseline.
More provider-side frame coverage helps selected tasks, but some categories are unchanged or worse; computation budgets remain an open consideration.

papers.title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments
papers.tldr: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection enables multimodal LLMs to communicate complementary video information through aligned visual KV states, yielding modest task-dependent gains and lower latency than text communication.

papers.abstract: Short-video platforms are now a common way for the public to follow unfolding events. Their rapid, visually persuasive format also makes fake news easier to spread. Unlike text-image posts, short-video news interleaves multiple modalities and changing scenes, making it difficult to identify which frames verify a claim. Existing detectors either pool sampled frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity. Both overlook that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim, whereas less dominant context may challenge it. We present CEVA (Complementary Evidence Verification Approach), to our knowledge the first short-video fake news detection framework to explicitly organize frames by their evidential roles before multimodal fusion. Its Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames, and cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization operates on the reorganized evidence. On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among the compared methods. Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors. Together, these results establish pre-fusion evidence organization as an effective and transferable component of short-video fake news detection.
authors: Wenshen Yang, Junfeng Hao, Jing Li, Decheng Liu, Yangkunfei, Shuyu Jiang, Haizhou Wang
bullets: Short videos combine changing visual scenes and multiple modalities, making relevant verification frames difficult to identify.
CEVA’s DBCR module separates explicitly aligned frames from potentially complementary context frames.
Bidirectional contrastive regularization is applied during cross-modal fusion of the reorganized evidence.
CEVA achieves the best overall results among compared methods on FakeSV and FakeTT.
Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based frame selection across two detector architectures.
