papers.abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.
bullets: The study tests whether answers depend on the regions models cite in their reasoning chains.
It blacks out cited boxes and compares answer flips with same-sized control boxes elsewhere in the frames; the difference is the cite gap.
On CLEVRER, the cite gap was 0.089, with cited-box masking flipping 2.2× as many correct answers as controls.
On NExT-QA, the cite gap was 0.003 and cited-box masking caused only 1.1× as many flips; cited entities remained visible across most frames.
Grounding checks alone miss this distinction: citations can be verifiable and relevant without being causally necessary for the answer.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline and tests. Chains are generated exactly for CLEVRER and pseudo-labelled for NExT-QA (real frames with the evidence boxes of one chain), and a 2–3B model learns to emit them. Both tests start from the regions the trained model cited: the self-citation test masks the cited boxes or the same boxes moved elsewhere; the entity-track test does the same for the named entity on every frame.

Figure 1. The self-citation test on two items from the same model. Left: the frame with the regions the mixed chain SFT model cited (orange). Middle: those regions blacked out. Right: boxes of the same size at random positions (illustrative placement). On CLEVRER (top) masking the citations flips the answer and masking elsewhere does not; on NExT-QA (bottom) the citations sit on the named entities and the answer survives either mask.

Figure 3. Cite gaps on CLEVRER and NExT-QA (95% question-clustered bootstrap intervals). papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual intervention test for grounded reasoning chains in video-language models, directly relevant to video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
papers.tldr: A citation can be correctly grounded yet irrelevant to a model’s answer, so grounded reasoning should be tested by removing what the chain names—not just where it points.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.
authors: Pradip Gupta, Shubham Mandloi, Ravi Kumar Satzoda, Sujeeth Bharadwaj, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth
bullets: Deepfake detectors often lose accuracy across datasets because they rely on generator-specific artifacts.
The method uses V-JEPA 2.1 with a frozen encoder, a rank-16 LoRA-adapted predictor, and a Latent Consistency Head to analyze prediction residual magnitude and direction.
It tests standard versus reversed consistency-margin objectives; the reversed direction produces a larger cross-dataset generalization gap.
Trained only on FF++, the model reaches 90.5 AUC on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well on other cross-dataset benchmarks.
Ablations support separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using low-rank projection; the model adds 8.25M trainable parameters.

Real and forged samples largely overlap before LCH, while the learned representations show clearer class separation after LCH.

papers.abstract: Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.
authors: Haiyu Yang, Heidi Lesscher, Enhong Liu, Miel Hostens
bullets: Covers four week-long camera deployments across research and commercial farms in the Netherlands.
Includes 1,173 video files spanning 651 hours of group-housed calf recordings.
Trained observers annotated eight days using an 18-item ethogram, including play and other behaviours.
Provides 1.1 million decoded frames, camera-clock timestamps, per-calf segmentation tracks, and frame-level play labels.
Supports behavioural welfare research and development or evaluation of automated recognition systems.

papers.abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.
authors: Renhe Sun, Yueying Feng, Bohan Yu, Tong Niu, Yunqi Liu, Zitong Wang, Haolin He, Kexin Shi, Hualei Wang, Qiuqiang Kong, Chang Yao, Yuge Huang, Weiqiang Wang, Jingyuan Chen, Jian Liu
bullets: Covers social reasoning in first-person video and interactive service tasks involving dialogue, tools, and closed-loop execution.
Evaluates emotional and social cues, grounded reference resolution, request interpretation, and state-changing actions.
Track 1 uses a multi-stage pipeline for MCQ, chain-of-thought, quality grading, and video filtering.
Combines answer accuracy with process- and outcome-based measures; top reported results were 0.9263 Track 1 accuracy and 0.844 joint success/0.916 micro accuracy in Track 2.
Participant solutions emphasize explicit evidence verification, robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.
bullets: Addresses missed brief or localized artifacts and the rigidity of fixed multi-agent inspection workflows.
Uses an investigator agent to select artifact types, inspection windows, and stopping points.
Applies dual-timescale policy optimization to jointly improve investigation decisions and forensic inspectors.
Introduces ForenCue-30K with role-specific annotations and interaction trajectories for inspection and coordination training.
Reports 95.2% average accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain, and agentic benchmarks, with localized evidence grounding.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of WeVisForensics. Top: the investigator πθ repeatedly calls an inspector st on a temporal scope ut, reads its report zt, and issues a verdict with the evidence chain. Middle: DTPO updates the investigator on every batch, while the trainable inspectors self-evolve on a slower timescale. Bottom: accuracy on the four evaluation benchmarks against representative detectors.

Figure 4 Overview of ForenCue-30K. Curated videos are annotated with role-specific artifact evidence and converted into sub-agent records and interaction trajectories, and an RL pool supports DTPO. Examples show artifacts targeted by each sub-agent.
Figure 1 Overview of WeVisForensics’s role-specific forensic evidence across appearance, physics, common sense, on-screen text, and audio.

Figure 3 WeVisForensics and its training strategy, DTPO. The investigator rolls out with a fixed FSL snapshot and is updated on every batch with outcome rewards and CLUE. Grounded calls (DOPD) queue by role in the interaction pool, from which the slow process distills privileged EMA teachers into students, revises skill cards, and refreshes the FSL every H steps.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is a fundamental and safety-critical task in computer vision. Recent generative approaches detect anomalies from a distributional perspective, but remain limited by local anomaly modes. Meanwhile, video anomaly anticipation (VAA), as a proactive extension beyond post-hoc detection, introduces additional challenges. In particular, the contrastive inference paradigm in VAD, which relies on ground-truth frames, is not applicable to VAA, hindering its development. To address these challenges, we propose a unified score-driven framework, termed Uni-DSM, based on denoising score matching (DSM), which models anomaly patterns through likelihood estimation and score functions over the learned data distribution. Within this unified framework, we adopt a shared noise-conditioned score transformer backbone with scene-dependent embeddings and motion-aware weighting for distribution-level modeling. Instead of introducing separate architectures, Uni-DSM unifies VAD and VAA through different inference and supervision paradigms built upon the same score-based formulation. For VAD, we instantiate an autoregressive denoising score matching (ADSM) mechanism, which progressively accumulates anomalous evidence via autoregressive denoising, enabling enhanced perception of local modes beyond visual cues. For VAA, we extend the same architecture by incorporating a lightweight auxiliary decoder and a novel self-distilled denoising score matching (SDSM) mechanism. By constructing supervision from output discrepancies instead of relying on unavailable future ground truth, our method achieves efficient training suitable or early anomaly anticipation. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both VAD and VAA while maintaining high efficiency, establishing a unified and scalable pipeline from anomaly detection to anticipation.
bullets: Addresses local anomaly-mode limitations in generative VAD and the lack of future ground truth in VAA.

Applies self-distilled DSM with a lightweight decoder for efficient early anomaly anticipation without future labels.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.

papers.abstract: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.

papers.abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

Separately measures Task Fulfillment and Artifact Performance across content, organization, visuals, and delivery.

Evaluates nine model-harness configurations, whose overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52.

papers.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

papers.abstract: While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation. We will publicly release the benchmark dataset and open-source the evaluation code.

papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming intelligent transportation systems by connecting roadside cameras, edge computing units, vehicles, and traffic infrastructure into a shared sensing and decision-making ecosystem. However, transmitting raw traffic video over vehicle-to-everything (V2X) links is bandwidth-intensive, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is often impractical. To address these limitations, this article proposes VISTA (Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness), a multimodal vision-language edge-intelligence framework that combines predictive video representation learning with lightweight language-based reasoning to provide communication-efficient traffic situational awareness. In the proposed architecture, roadside surveillance units employ the Video Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) and an attentive-pooler module to convert traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings. These embeddings are transmitted through V2X links to vehicle-mounted systems, where a TinyLlama small language model, enhanced with a custom visual adapter, interprets the embeddings alongside natural-language (NL) traffic queries. VISTA enables vehicles to obtain interpretable traffic information, reason about upcoming scene dynamics, and identify potential collision risks without receiving raw video streams. Experimental results in a digital-twin urban traffic environment show that VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing the communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video transmission. These results demonstrate the feasibility of embedding-based multimodal intelligence for low-latency, communication-efficient, and safety-oriented IoT-enabled transportation systems.

papers.abstract: Video creative plagiarism refers to the unauthorized reproduction of creative ideas across videos despite substantial differences in visual appearance, posing a new challenge to video copyright protection. However, existing video copy detection methods primarily focus on visual content similarity, struggling to capture abstract creative that are entangled with specific visual realizations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel task, named Video Creative Plagiarism Detection (VCPD), and propose an iterative creative evidence tracing framework, termed CreaTrace, to verify creative similarity and accurately localize the corresponding evidence segments. Specifically, we design a Multimodal Semantic Event Segmentation strategy to divide similar long videos into coherent narrative events, facilitating event-level dataset construction and retrieving similar segments. Based on these events, CreaTrace employs Coarse Creative Matching to identify candidate event pairs through narrative semantics and camera language. Then CreaTrace presents Creative Decoupling to disentangle abstract creative patterns from specific visual realizations. Meanwhile, Creative Swap Contrastive Learning is devised to enhance creative consistency through cross-realization feature swapping. Benefiting from the above designs, our CreaTrace enables accurate creative similarity detection and temporal localization, while providing interpretable evidence report. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CreaTrace across diverse creative plagiarism scenarios.

Separates abstract creative patterns from their visual realizations and applies creative-swap contrastive learning for consistency.

papers.abstract: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360{\deg} field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.

Works with four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining or changes to detection boxes or the underlying tracker.
On held-out QuadTrack and zero-shot DualPano-MOT sequences, it reduces identity switches by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, with IDF1 gains up to 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points.
Reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% versus continuous Full-HR acquisition under the stated offline JPEG-based acquisition model.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Surgical training benefits from explicit comparison between cases: in patient condition, in technique and in skill proficiency. Surgical vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising and flexible interface for this purpose. Yet current VLMs typically see one video at a time, and they often fall short when asked to compare videos. Methods: We propose EndoComparer, a VLM for comparative surgical video question answering with two components. (a) A Pseudo-Siamese Visual LoRA (PSVL) gives each video slot its own low-rank adapter over a shared frozen vision encoder, separating the two videos in the visual pathway at the cost of a single encoder pass. (b) A Perceive-then-Compare chain of thought (PtC-CoT) trains the model to first state what each video shows, then derive the answer from these statements. We further curate EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice questions on video-pair over cholecystectomy and gastric bypass procedures, covering anatomy, tool, action and skill. Results: EndoComparer outperforms strong generalist and surgical VLMs on detecting and specifying difference between videos. Ablations show that two proposed components contribute complimentarily, and the model remains more robust under a video-swap control that exposes confusion between the two videos. Conclusion: Providing a dedicated visual reasoning path through PSVL and PtC-CoT makes cross-case comparison of surgical videos more robust for VLMs. EndoDiffVQA and EndoComparer provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for this task. Project page: https://camma-public.github.io/endocomparer
authors: Shi Li, Lalith Sharan, Jo\"el L. Lavanchy, Kun Yuan, Lorenzo Arboit, Nabani Banik, Elif Yazici, Maria Vannucci, Vinkle Srivastav, Pietro Mascagni, Nicolas Padoy
bullets: Addresses the limitation that most surgical VLMs process one video at a time and struggle to compare cases.

Uses Perceive-then-Compare chain-of-thought reasoning to describe each video before deriving a comparison answer.
Introduces EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice video-pair questions spanning cholecystectomy and gastric bypass.
Outperforms generalist and surgical VLMs on identifying and specifying video differences, with improved robustness to video swapping.

papers.abstract: Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.
bullets: Evaluates cross-dataset fall detection across nine datasets, holding out each target in turn.
Compares three vision-language models and three visual baselines under zero-target transfer and local target-site personalization.
Source training improves frozen-model mean AUROC for Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL from 0.821→0.912, 0.883→0.947, and 0.939→0.962, respectively.
With five labeled examples per class, source initialization benefits Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN over Target-only training.
Benefits are model- and label-budget-dependent; VLMs also show threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly in image and video understanding, yet their ability to reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos remains poorly understood. Such video poses a harder test than standard RGB video QA: targets are often small, evidence may appear only briefly, viewpoints change with the platform, and useful cues may appear in only one stream. We introduce RAVEN-Bench (Reasoning over Aerial Videos with EO-IR aligNment), a paired EO-IR video QA benchmark for low-altitude aerial multimodal understanding. RAVEN-Bench contains 100 temporally aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 human-authored four-way multiple-choice questions, each independently audited for answer keys, modality requirements, evidence intervals, and group validity. It supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation, and uses hierarchical capability levels and structured question groups to diagnose paired-input gain beyond the stronger unimodal condition, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence. We evaluate frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs, showing that aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning. RAVEN-Bench provides controlled modality conditions and group-level diagnostics for auditing whether progress on RGB video benchmarks transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yuhu990424/RAVEN-Bench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/TerraSenseAnalytics/RAVEN-Bench.

Supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation under hierarchical capabilities and structured question groups.
Diagnoses paired-input gains, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence.
Evaluations show aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported cross-spectral reasoning; code and data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Surgical workflow assistance is inherently anticipatory: systems must reason about how procedures evolve, not just recognize the current frame. However, many prior approaches perform prediction in pixel space by synthesizing future frames, which primarily focuses on appearance fidelity rather than the semantic representations required for downstream reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose a feature-space semantic forecasting framework that models temporal dynamics directly within the representations of a frozen Vision Foundation Model (VFM). Specifically, we build a hierarchical target representation from multi-layer VFM features, replace future-frame feature tokens with learnable \texttt{[MASK]} tokens, and train a masked transformer to forecast the corresponding future latent features from observed context, thereby formulating procedural evolution as masked future feature prediction. Experiments on public laparoscopic benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in phase anticipation, multi-label tool presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based forecasting baselines, while enabling a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream heads.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of pixel-space prediction, which emphasizes visual fidelity over task-relevant semantic reasoning.
Builds hierarchical multi-layer features from a frozen Vision Foundation Model and masks future feature tokens.
Uses a masked transformer to forecast future latent features from observed procedural context.
On public laparoscopic benchmarks, improves phase anticipation, tool-presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based baselines.
Provides a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream prediction heads.

papers.abstract: Long-video reasoning requires a system to localize sparse evidence over extended temporal sequences, preserve temporal structure, and generate answers despite substantial multimodal distractors. Existing video retrieval-augmented generation methods typically build indexes from uniformly sampled video segments. In long-video settings, this design readily introduces irrelevant context and is unreliable for questions with explicit temporal constraints. We propose VTG-RAG, a framework for long-video question answering that combines query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling with temporal graph retrieval. First, a two-stage sampling strategy selects core segments with high mean query relevance or high intra-segment relevance variance. The framework then integrates subtitles, speech transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations from these segments into a temporally ordered multimodal graph. Finally, it performs temporally filtered, two-pass retrieval and reasoning across frame, text, and graph evidence spaces. A lot of experiments have proven the effectiveness of the VTG-RAG. Specifically, we evaluate the framework on Video-MME and LongVideoBench. On LongVideoBench, the reported Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B results improve from 48.16% to 50.56% and from 52.13% to 53.32%, respectively, with 24 answer-input frames. These correspond to gains of 2.40 and 1.19 percentage points. The ablation experiments of VTG-RAG further support that the contributions of each component are very important.
authors: Yao Lu, Yunhao Wang, Yaxin Gao, Feifei Teng, Chenxiao Liu, Zhe Tang, Jiaheng Wei, Zhaowei Zhu, Shanqing Yu, Qi Xuan
bullets: Addresses irrelevant context and weak handling of temporal constraints in uniformly sampled video retrieval.
Uses query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling based on segment relevance and intra-segment relevance variation.
Builds a temporally ordered graph combining subtitles, transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations.
Performs temporally filtered, two-pass reasoning over frame, text, and graph evidence.
On LongVideoBench, improves reported Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B results by 2.40 and 1.19 percentage points, respectively, using 24 answer-input frames.

papers.abstract: Recognizing individual events does not guarantee correct execution of compositional instructions in streaming video. For example, given the request "Notify me when the pot boils after someone turns on the stove and leaves the kitchen", existing models may recognize the individual events yet notify too early or miss the intended moment, failing to track how their temporal conditions are satisfied over time. To evaluate this gap, we introduce CoTriggerBench, which composes annotated video events into temporally constrained instructions and verifies notification timing and silence through executable event plans and source-event replay. To address this challenge, we propose a real-time VLM agent, TEMPI. TEMPI decomposes instructions into atomic event queries and temporal constraints, and uses Scenario Memory to continuously maintain task progress as event evidence arrives, allowing earlier observations to support subsequent decisions beyond the detector's visual window. Even when no notification is required, relevant events continue to update the scenario state. On CoTriggerBench, TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, outperforming the strongest closed-source and fine-tuned open-source VLM baselines by 15.6 (Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash-Realtime) and 18.1 (MOSS-VL-Realtime) percentage points, respectively. To support efficient on-device streaming inference, we further optimize the streaming inference pipeline by overlapping partial visual encoding and LLM prefix prefill with frame arrival. On an 8 GB RTX 5060, our optimized detector implementation achieves a 4.90$\times$ speedup.
authors: Yehua Huang, Penglei Sun, Xiang Li, Jinhao Zhou, Jiawen Wen, Qingqing Xiao, Zihan Yang, Wenqi Wang, Haolan Chen, Yu Xu, Xiaowen Chu

Scenario Memory preserves earlier evidence beyond the detector’s visual window and updates state even when no notification should be issued.
TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, exceeding the reported baselines by 15.6 and 18.1 percentage points.
An optimized streaming pipeline overlaps visual encoding and LLM prefix prefill, yielding a reported 4.90× detector speedup on an 8 GB RTX 5060.

papers.abstract: Computer vision methods for video understanding, such as object detection and tracking, inherit the way videos are captured and displayed: as successive frames processed sequentially. However, a video is an inhomogeneous 2D+time volume of pixels, named voxels, and frames are only one family of cuts through it. In this frame-based representation, static backgrounds introduce computational redundancy, and motion can only be understood across several frames. In this position paper, we study another family of cuts: spacetime images (STIs), obtained by sampling any set of pixels other than frames, for instance a line of pixels followed over time. Such images are familiar in narrow forms, from line-scan inspection and kymographs to spatiotemporal slices for motion analysis, but have received little attention as a general input representation for computer vision and are often limited to (x,t) or (y,t) cuts. We define new cuts leading to STIs in their general form, explain how to read their content, and show that a family of cuts tiles the video so that existing dense annotations transfer at no cost. We also detail how motion appears in an STI, spatially and in the frequency domain, and discuss applications such as walking pedestrians, deposited objects, and dynamic scenes. Two pilot experiments illustrate the representation. The first trains a segmentation network entirely in the spacetime domain, on transferred annotations, and performs background subtraction on CDnet 2014 close to supervised frame-based methods, without explicit temporal modeling. The second recovers the pan speed of a camera as a moving cut, identified by a simple criterion on the frequency spectrum of the resulting image, turning a temporal estimation problem into the choice of a cut. Our position is not that STIs should replace frames, but that slicing the video volume is a design variable worth studying in its own right.
authors: Jade Lambert, S\'ebastien Pi\'erard, Anthony Cioppa, Marc Van Droogenbroeck
bullets: Problem: Frame-by-frame processing is redundant for static backgrounds and requires multiple frames to understand motion.
Method: Sample arbitrary sets of pixels over time to create STIs, including cuts beyond conventional (x,t) or (y,t) slices.
Contribution: Define general STI cuts, explain their spatial and frequency-domain content, and show that a family of cuts can tile videos while transferring dense annotations at no cost.
Results: Pilot studies perform background subtraction with a spacetime-trained segmentation network and estimate camera pan speed from STI frequency spectra.
Scope: STIs are proposed as a complementary design choice, not a replacement for conventional frames.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces spacetime images (STIs) as an alternative representation for video understanding, offering a novel perspective on temporal data processing.
papers.title: Thinking from Another Side of the Box: Spacetime Images for Computer Vision
papers.tldr: Spacetime images (STIs) offer a general alternative to frame-based video representation by slicing the video volume along arbitrary pixel paths, enabling motion analysis and vision tasks directly in the spacetime domain.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is wasteful and lossy when a multimodal model must re-encode the same video for every query: context limits force sparse sampling or truncation, and no reusable representation remains for later questions. We present VidEngram, an agentic video QA system that builds a persistent hierarchical memory once at ingest and answers later questions from that memory. VidEngram captions video and audio jointly with Qwen2.5-Omni, consolidates segment memories into episode and entity layers, and uses a text-only agentic planner with specialized retrieval tools to produce grounded answers. The web interface makes this process inspectable: users can watch memory formation, inspect retrieval traces, verify cited evidence in the video player, and explore entity relationships. On the full OmniVideoBench, VidEngram with a GPT-5-mini planner outperforms a strong single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline (37.0% vs. 32.3%), with gains concentrated on longer videos where single-pass coverage becomes sparse. Because perception is paid once, subsequent queries use low-cost text-only planning.
authors: Zinuo Cheng, Yueqian Lin, Zhongxi Wang, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: Addresses repeated video re-encoding, context limits, and information loss in long-video question answering.
Jointly captions video and audio, then organizes memories into segment, episode, and entity layers.
Uses specialized retrieval tools and a text-only planner to generate grounded answers with inspectable evidence traces.
On OmniVideoBench, achieves 37.0% versus 32.3% for a single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline, with larger gains on longer videos.
Subsequent queries avoid repeated perception, reducing them to low-cost text-only planning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: VidEngram architecture. Offline (build once): each video is segmented, captioned by Qwen2.5-Omni into eleven structured fields, and consolidated into a three-layer memory (segment → episode → entity) in the memory manager. Online (answer many): a ReAct agent answers each question from memory through specialized retrieval tools and timestamp citations, so users can inspect how an answer was produced without re-encoding the full video.

Figure 3: ReAct retrieval workflow. The planner selects among six tools; the memory manager returns evidence, and the agent iterates until it has enough support to answer with a timestamp citation.

papers.selection_reason: Targets long-video understanding with persistent hierarchical memory and agentic retrieval.
papers.title: VidEngram: Agentic Long-Term Video Understanding via Structured Hierarchical Memory
papers.tldr: VidEngram enables efficient long-video QA by building a persistent hierarchical memory once and using an agentic text-only planner for later grounded queries.

papers.abstract: Narrative video understanding requires more than recognizing visible events: models must extract evidence from dialogue, bind it to speakers, and use it to infer narrative meaning. Existing video benchmarks evaluate aspects of this problem, including video question answering, audio-visual reasoning, and temporal grounding, but rarely test whether these abilities form a coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chain within the same clips. We introduce \textbf{CineMME}, a human-verified benchmark designed to diagnose dialogue-grounded plot understanding, supported by approximately $1,600$ expert person-hours of annotation. CineMME contains $975$ curated short narrative video clips and two linked tracks: \textit{CineMME-Grounding}, with $13,554$ timestamped speech segments and $33,083$ speaker face boxes for temporal dialogue localization, transcription, and active-speaker grounding; and \textit{CineMME-Reasoning}, with $1,600$ multiple-choice and $316$ open-ended questions spanning perception, audio, narrative, social, and scene-presentation understanding. Our main evaluation compares $20$ MLLMs on reasoning and $9$ omni-modal models on grounding. The results reveal a pronounced who-what-when decoupling: Gemini-3 Pro localizes dialogue in time ($68.34\%$ tIoU) and transcribes it with a WER of $28.99\%$, yet achieves only $7.74\%$ vIoU for active-speaker grounding while achieving $67.66\%$ MCQ accuracy on questions with extractable answers. Modality ablations further show that vision is not uniformly beneficial: it improves performance on perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning. CineMME provides a compact diagnostic testbed for evaluating how multimodal video models connect dialogue, speakers, visual evidence, and narrative meaning.
bullets: Targets a missing evaluation link: coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chains within the same narrative clips.
Includes 975 human-verified clips with grounding and reasoning tracks covering speech localization, transcription, active-speaker grounding, and narrative questions.
Evaluates 20 multimodal LLMs for reasoning and 9 omni-modal models for grounding.
Finds strong time localization and transcription but weak active-speaker grounding, revealing a who–what–when gap.
Vision helps perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning.

papers.abstract: Weakly Supervised Video Semantic Segmentation (WS-VSS) aims to learn temporally consistent semantic object masks in videos using only video-level labels. While fully supervised models successfully learn temporal relationships by means of cross-attention, training these temporal weights under weak supervision is unstable and even pushes the model below its single-frame baseline. Therefore, existing WS-VSS methods exploit temporal consistency by relying on external priors, such as optical flow. Unfortunately these cues are non-semantic, computationally expensive and noisy, degrading the supervisory signal. Instead of supervising attention weights directly or using external priors, we propose MemCAM, a WS-VSS transformer framework that learns temporal cross-attention directly through feature-space self-supervision. MemCAM introduces a CAM Propagation Algorithm that synthesizes a supervisory signal by propagating past CAMs according to patch-level feature similarities in the latent space. Specifically, we constrain their induced CAMs through a consistency objective between predicted and propagated maps, stabilizing temporal attention learning. Experiments on the YouTube-Objects v2.2 and WS$^2$ datasets demonstrate that MemCAM consistently outperforms the temporal localization and segmentation performance of WS-VSS alternatives, showing that cross-attention can be effectively trained in label-scarce video settings through internal self-supervision.
authors: Andrea Marelli, Alessandro Ardenghi, Giacomo Boracchi, Luca Magri
bullets: Targets temporally consistent object masks from only video-level labels.
Propagates past CAMs using patch-level feature similarities in latent space to create self-supervision.
Trains temporal attention with a consistency objective between predicted and propagated CAMs.
Experiments on YouTube-Objects v2.2 and WS² show improved temporal localization and segmentation over existing WS-VSS methods.
The approach is evaluated in label-scarce settings and avoids reliance on computationally expensive, noisy optical flow.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MemCAM architecture. Inputs (left) are encoded by the multi-class transformer backbone into class tokens V t cls (a1) and patch tokens V t p (b1). V t cls are pooled and fed to the classification head (a2) producing Lcls. V t p are refined via the MAM, (c) using context retrieved from the Memory Bank’s patch queue Qp. The memory-refined patch embeddings V t p ′ (b2) are reshaped (b3) and passed through the Patch-Level Supervision branch (PLS) to produce per-patch activations V t M and the patch-level loss Lp. Class-aware CAMs V t M ′ are obtained after attention-based refinement and stored in the CAM queue QM of the Memory Bank (d). CAMPA consumes the CAMs stored in QM to produce a propagated pseudo-CAM M̂ t, which is used to compute the consistency loss LM.

Figure 3. CAMPA overview: The current frame’s patch embeddings V t p and the memory queues from past frames patch queue Qp and CAM queue QM as input (section Setting). (a) A Similarity Matrix S is computed by comparing the current frame’s patch embeddings against all embeddings stored in the Qp queue. (b) We convert S into a Probability Matrix P, by keeping only the top K entries per row (and so per current patch) and then applying a per-row softmax. In this way, we can see P as a matching likelihood between current and past patches. (c) The final propagated CAM M̂ t is computed as a weighted aggregation of past CAMs (from QM ), using the probabilities from matrix P to weight the activation values. M̂ t will be used as pseudo-label to supervise the CAM of the current frame t. A step-by-step pseudo-code is given in Alg. 1 in Section B the Supp. Mat.

Figure 4. Detailed architecture of the MAM. Starting from the backbone patch embeddings V t p , the module refines representations through three stages, each equipped with a residual connection. Self-attention (left): current-frame tokens act as queries, keys, and values. The arrows entering the yellow block indicate that the attention matrix Aself t is learned from the input; its output Attn(qself ,kself ,vself) is added back to the backbone features, producing the self-attended representation V t,self

papers.selection_reason: Weakly supervised video semantic segmentation with temporal cross-attention learning fits video understanding.
papers.title: Unlocking Cross-Attention in Label-Scarce Regimes: A Weakly Supervised Approach for Video Semantic Segmentation
papers.tldr: MemCAM enables weakly supervised video semantic segmentation to learn stable temporal cross-attention using internally propagated class activation maps instead of optical flow or other external priors.

papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
authors: Keuntae Kim, Dongjun Kim, Yong Suk Choi
bullets: V-JEPA retains shared representations of dynamics such as direction, speed, order, and state, but standard caption-based training largely leaves them unused.

V-JEPA-LM models from 1B to 8B lead their size classes across eleven video benchmarks; the 4B model scores 72.1.
Controlled studies find counterfactual supervision improves average performance by 4.5 points and speed-question performance by 38 points on natural benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of assistants that respond only after user prompts.
Introduces Model-Initiated Conversation, Stream-Aware Tool Calling, and Interactive Visual Grounding.
Adds Long-Horizon Interaction Memory for continuity across extended video streams.
Uses a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and three-stage training scheme to integrate these behaviors.
Reports leading performance among open-source streaming models on public benchmarks and releases model weights and inference code.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the AURA 2.0 streaming interaction framework. Tool results are incorporated into the context to support subsequent responses. Dashed outlines indicate historical messages beyond the active visual window.

Figure 3. Data construction pipeline for AURA 2.0. The pipeline transforms collected videos into a verified streaming training mixture through three stages: (1) Video collection and preparation standardizes videos into clips and generates clip-level descriptions. (2) Task-specific data synthesis uses the clips and descriptions to construct General QA, MIC, SATC, and IVG trajectories. (3) Streaming assembly and quality assessment aligns the trajectories to video chunks and filters invalid or low-quality samples.

(b) Stage-wise sample and token allocations and silent/response decision proportions. (c) Task-wise sample counts and shares aggregated across stages. Together, these distributions characterize the task coverage and supervision balance of the training mixture.

papers.abstract: Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate-diagnose-repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience-augmented In-context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair-Website/.
bullets: Addresses failures that emerge after video generation without requiring full regeneration.
Uses Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints to identify the first invalid state and affected downstream states.
Applies localized, adaptive regeneration while preserving unaffected content.
Combines repair context with prior repair experiences through in-context learning.
Improves physical plausibility across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism on Physics-IQ Verified.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PhysRepair. Starting from an initially generated video, a Physics Repair Agent diagnoses the realized physical failure and performs localized counterfactual repair. Spatiotemporal causal constraints determine what may change and what must remain fixed, while experience-augmented in-context learning retrieves relevant repair experience to adapt how to repair. The resulting counterfactual physical state guides video regeneration, followed by physicsand-preservation verification and experience distillation for subsequent repair.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on multi-object spatiotemporal interactions. Top: fan–garment interaction; bottom: wrench–box interaction. Baselines exhibit incorrect contact timing, inconsistent motion, or object artifacts, whereas PhysRepair preserves object identity and coherent contact–response dynamics.
Figure 5: Analysis of PhysRepair. Memory efficiency and user-perceived physical consistency of PhysRepair.

Figure 1: Comparison of physics-grounded video generation paradigms. (a) Plan and Prompt Refine iteratively updates generation plans or physics-aware prompts, while (b) Simulator Program Refine iteratively updates physical programs or simulator configurations; both impose physical guidance before synthesis and may require repeated regeneration. (c) PhysRepair instead follows a generate–diagnose–repair paradigm: it diagnoses physical failures from the generated video (what to repair?) and performs localized, causally constrained repair, while leveraging prior repair experience to adapt the intervention and preserve generated already-valid content (how to repair?).

Table 1: Quantitative results on Physics-IQ Verified. SP, ST, and WS denote Spatial IoU, Spatiotemporal IoU, and Weighted Spatial IoU, respectively. The best, second-best, and third-best results for each metric are marked in bold, single underline, and double underline, respectively.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual models improve egocentric action recognition by exploiting complementary cues, yet typically assume that both streams remain available at inference. Existing missing-modality methods operate on trimmed, single-event clips in which a stream is entirely present or absent, whereas real sensors fail and recover within long, untrimmed observations. We redefine egocentric modality missingness as temporally localized sensor outages within untrimmed, multi-event observations, with whole-clip absence as the limiting case. We introduce \textbf{MacJEPA}, a missing-modality-robust \textbf{Ma}sked-\textbf{c}ontext query \textbf{JEPA} that recognizes visual actions and acoustic events from supplied interval queries over audio-visual context. Window-local modality dropout simulates these sensor outages during training. MacJEPA further repurposes masking in JEPA from a self-supervised pretext into a supervised robustness objective, aligning masked and clean latent representations of both multimodal content tokens and the task-conditioned queries. All objectives are optimized jointly with recognition in a single stage, requiring no test-time adaptation. Across Epic-Kitchens-100 and Epic-Sounds, a single checkpoint remains competitive under complete input and consistently surpasses published missing-modality baselines when either the dominant or auxiliary stream is removed. MacJEPA thus unifies strong full-input recognition with temporal missing-modality robustness in a single model operating on untrimmed multi-event videos.
bullets: Reframes missing modality as within-video, time-localized outages, including full-clip absence as a special case.
Uses a masked-context query JEPA to predict visual actions and acoustic events from interval queries over audio-visual context.
Trains with window-local modality dropout and aligns masked and clean representations for content tokens and task-conditioned queries.
Jointly optimizes robustness and recognition in one stage, without test-time adaptation.
On Epic-Kitchens-100 and Epic-Sounds, one checkpoint remains competitive with full input and outperforms published missing-modality baselines when either stream is removed.

papers.abstract: The proliferation of user-generated video content has made accurate and robust no-reference video quality assessment (NR-VQA) a highly important challenge. Existing research increasingly relies on architecturally complex multi-branch pipelines or computationally intensive fine-tuning of single-branch backbones. In this paper, we investigate whether a single frozen video foundation model can serve as an effective NR-VQA backbone, and propose HiVE-VQA, the first framework (to our knowledge) to apply a JEPA-based video encoder to this task. HiVE-VQA extracts token grids from multiple depths of a pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and stacks them into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume, which a compact 3D convolutional head fuses across its layer, spatial, and temporal axes, combining low-level distortion cues from shallow layers with the semantic and temporal context captured at greater depths. The encoder remains frozen throughout, so only the head is trained: 5.2M parameters (5.7\% of the total), with no auxiliary multi-modal models and an inference cost that is invariant to video resolution. Trained solely on LSVQ and evaluated without any fine-tuning, HiVE-VQA outperforms 17 state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in SROCC and PLCC on both intra-dataset (LSVQ-test, LSVQ-1080p) and cross-dataset (KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC) benchmarks. These results indicate that hierarchical, depth-wise fusion of features from a single frozen video foundation model provides a more effective and efficient basis for NR-VQA than task-specific multi-network fusion. Code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RobHam99/HiVE-VQA.
authors: Robbie Hamilton, Fan Zhang, David Bull
bullets: Targets robust NR-VQA without complex multi-branch pipelines or backbone fine-tuning.
Stacks token grids from multiple encoder depths into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume.
A 3D convolutional head fuses layer, spatial, and temporal information while the encoder remains frozen.
Trains only 5.2M head parameters, with inference cost invariant to video resolution.
Trained on LSVQ and outperforms 17 SOTA methods across intra- and cross-dataset SROCC and PLCC benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io
authors: Gabriel Manalu, Minh Son Hoang, Hyeontaek Hwang, Jaesung Lee, Hyojin Choi, Tran Tuan Phong, Seon Kwon Kim, Saad Wazir, Daeyoung Kim

Models often miss or misjudge dangerous events and hallucinate agents or actions in their explanations.
The benchmark includes an evaluation toolkit and diagnosis of model limitations; code and data will be released.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) reason effectively about video content, but whether they perceive its event boundaries in a manner consistent with humans remains unclear. We first investigate this through Generic Event Boundary Detection (GEBD), which identifies event boundaries naturally perceived by humans in continuous video, without relying on predefined event categories. On Kinetics-GEBD dataset, LVLMs miss many boundaries when predicting directly from frames, but effectively refine candidates proposed by an unsupervised discovery method, achieving state-of-the-art unsupervised GEBD performance. We extend this discovery-refinement approach to hour-long egocentric video, where boundary discovery requires a broader semantic scale and whole-video LVLM refinement becomes impractical. We address these challenges through coarse-to-fine temporal discovery and localized LVLM accept/reject judgments. Human evaluation shows that the LVLM's agreement with group consensus falls within the range observed among human annotators, with disagreements concentrated on low-consensus cases. Using this pipeline, we construct EgoBoundary, a benchmark for event boundary detection in hour-scale egocentric video. Representative supervised and unsupervised methods degrade substantially on EgoBoundary, highlighting the challenge of long-horizon event boundary detection.

Human evaluation finds LVLM–consensus agreement within the range of human annotator agreement, with disagreements concentrated on low-consensus cases.

papers.abstract: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.

papers.abstract: An assistant watching a worker can prepare for an emerging need before the worker is ready to receive help.As the need evolves, the assistant must maintain preparation until a response is due, or withdraw it if the need disappears. Video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks leave this interval between early evidence and response largely unmeasured. We introduce FuGIBench (Future-Grounded Interaction), a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation, and response given a causal video prefix and a task contract. The benchmark contains 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity, and cancelled-need tracks. One primary score credits sustained preparation, incorporates response-interval alignment, and penalizes activity when the reference prescribes waiting. On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment, while similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios. Together with cancellation analyses, these results show why evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable, or disappear.

Uses a score that rewards sustained, well-timed preparation and penalizes unnecessary activity when waiting is prescribed.
Analyses show that longer preparation leads do not necessarily improve response alignment, and cancellation behavior is important to evaluation.

papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation requires precise alignment and controlled handling of rigid, deformable, and flexible components. Yet, the benefits of pretrained visuomotor policies remain underexplored in settings where limited access to specialized hardware, components, and fixtures constrains demonstration collection and evaluation. Understanding task-specific data requirements is important for assessing their scalability across diverse processes on the factory floor. We investigate whether video pretraining can support reliable industrial manipulation with limited action data. We propose FLUX-mimic, a video-action model, motivated by the potential of video pretraining to capture motion and interaction patterns that enable sample-efficient training. FLUX-mimic is built on a backbone pretrained on large-scale web and industrial task data, and an action expert to generate robot trajectories. We train our policy by joint video-action training. Across four automotive manufacturing benchmark tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, FLUX-mimic outperforms all considered baselines on the dexterous robot platform and matches pi_{0.5}'s average success rate on the gripper-based robot platform. On a deformable part kitting task, FLUX-mimic reaches 77.5% success with as little as two hours of task-specific action-labeled demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.
authors: Yuzhe Chen, Muxi Diao, Lele Yang, Wenbin Xu, Xuyang Liu, Qile Su, Changyi Liu, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Jiale Cao

Agents handle basic staging and camera work but struggle with challenging requests and rarely correct errors after inspecting renders.
Results motivate stronger spatial/camera reasoning, explicit checks, and item-by-item render verification.

papers.abstract: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.
