Performance is strongest on action recognition (80.27%) and causal reasoning (77.22%), and weakest on gesture recognition (54.70%) and event OCR (34.57%).
Post-hoc analysis identifies poorly tightened crops that reduce OCR resolution and a bias toward the first two answer choices in detailed understanding.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding aims to continuously process incoming visual observations, making the retention and retrieval of relevant information increasingly important as the video history grows. Although existing benchmarks include memory-related questions, question-answering accuracy alone does not reliably measure memory capabilities. Incorrect predictions may arise from failures in visual understanding rather than forgetting, whereas correct predictions may rely on linguistic priors or recent observations without requiring historical memory. To address these ambiguities, we introduce MemInStream, a benchmark dedicated to evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding. We develop an evidence-controlled validation protocol that associates each question with temporally localized evidence intervals. The protocol validates evidence solvability and memory necessity by retaining questions that models can answer from the annotated evidence but cannot resolve using recent observations, post-evidence observations, or textual input alone. This helps disentangle memory limitations from understanding failures while reducing memory-independent shortcuts. MemInStream provides a systematic evaluation of memory capabilities through four major categories, covering Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking \& Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory across diverse video scenarios. Overall, \textsc{MemInStream} provides a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for systematically evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.
authors: Zhenqi He, Dunyuan Xu, Yang Bo, Kien T. Pham, Yanghao Wang, Shuhan Li, Xintong Guo, Yuyang He, Fang Liu, Huankang Guan, Jingyan Chen, Rui Liu, Long Chen

It evaluates four capabilities: Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking & Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory.
The benchmark targets diverse streaming-video scenarios and aims to disentangle memory limitations from other sources of failure.

papers.abstract: Short videos have become a dominant online medium, where harmful content is increasingly conveyed in implicit and fragmented forms. Prior work largely focuses on explicit categories, such as violence and hate speech, and often fails to detect videos that subtly promote misleading values through narrative context, emotional framing, or cross-modal cues, partly due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks for implicit harm. To bridge this gap, we construct DeepHarm-7K, a large-scale harmful short-video dataset comprising 7,110 samples annotated according to a fine-grained harmful-content taxonomy. The dataset systematically covers implicitly harmful videos across diverse real-world scenarios and is constructed through a rigorous multi-stage quality-control process. Building on this dataset, we propose DeepHarm-VL, a multimodal detection framework that integrates visual, audio, and cross-modal reasoning. The framework employs a two-round reasoning strategy to progressively identify surface-level evidence and infer latent harmful implications. Experimental results show consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods across multiple open-source video-language models, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting both explicit and implicit harmful short videos.
authors: Chenyang Li, Qifan Yu, Saihui Hou, Zhaofeng He
bullets: Implicit harm is conveyed through narrative context, emotional framing, and cross-modal cues, which existing explicit-harm detectors often miss.

DeepHarm-VL combines visual, audio, and cross-modal reasoning in two rounds: identifying surface evidence, then inferring latent harmful implications.
Experiments report consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods across multiple open-source video-language models.
The study focuses on harmful-content detection in short videos; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.
authors: Shunming Liu, Jianyi Peng, Cheng Li, Lu Hou, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu

papers.abstract: Expert review of surgical videos is essential for surgical training but labor-intensive, motivating AI-assisted skill assessment to provide feedback at scale. Although surgical assessment rubrics may use different language to describe similar skills, existing automated methods commonly predict predefined skill levels or numerical scores tied to fixed rubrics, limiting their ability to transfer across semantically equivalent assessment criteria. We propose Predictive Rubric Alignment (PRA), a joint embedding prediction approach that scores surgical videos using natural-language descriptions of skill levels. Rather than matching level probabilities, PRA predicts a rater-weighted combination of skill-level description embeddings. Adjacent description features define a score-parameterized path, and the predicted embedding is projected onto this path to read the score. We introduce two variants: \textit{PRA-item}, which uses learned queries for predefined assessment items, and \textit{PRA-cond}, which generates queries from textual item names to enable assessment of unseen items without retraining. On AIxSuture, a dataset of expert-rated suturing videos, PRA outperforms published baselines in skill classification. We further evaluate zero-shot transfer to the smaller surgical skill assessment benchmark JIGSAWS. Trained on only two AIxSuture rubric items, PRA-cond assesses unseen JIGSAWS items without further training, yielding positive score correlations and greater Grad-CAM overlap with instruments and suture than a description-matching baseline. These results support predictive rubric alignment as a promising direction for flexible and explainable automated surgical skill assessment.
authors: Jiajun Cheng, Haidar M. Abdul-Muhsin, Juha Choi, Shan Lin

Zero-shot transfer to JIGSAWS yields positive score correlations and better visual alignment with instruments and sutures than description matching.

papers.abstract: Agentic video-reasoning frameworks iteratively explore a video, choosing what to observe based on the query and evidence gathered so far. Existing methods are typically evaluated with different backbones, preprocessing pipelines, and computational budgets, making it difficult to determine which components actually drive performance, how much they cost, and whether agentic inference is preferable to native video reasoning in the first place. We conduct a controlled evaluation of a diverse set of recent agentic video-reasoning systems across two strong contemporary backbones, with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting. Across Gemini 3 Flash and Gemma 4, most existing agentic frameworks fail to consistently improve over native video inference and often increase computational cost. We investigate two primary questions: (1) How much agentic framework complexity is necessary for effective video reasoning? (2) When, if at all, is agentic video reasoning preferable to just using the backbone directly? To answer the first question, we introduce a deliberately minimal Active Exploration Baseline and show that it remains competitive with substantially more elaborate agents. We then propose targeted extensions to this baseline, yielding SAVE (Simple Agentic Video Explorer). SAVE outperforms all evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone-benchmark settings. Turning to the second question, our results indicate that the advantage of agentic exploration grows when dense processing would otherwise represent answer-relevant events too sparsely, particularly for long videos and temporally concentrated evidence. Overall, our results suggest that agentic video reasoning should favor simple frameworks over increasingly elaborate pipelines and focus primarily on long-form video, where selective evidence acquisition offers the clearest advantage over native inference.
authors: Tymoteusz Wilk, Sergey Prokudin, Xi Wang
bullets: Existing agentic video-reasoning systems often add computational cost without consistently improving over direct native video inference.
The study provides a controlled comparison across two contemporary backbones with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting.
A minimal Active Exploration Baseline remains competitive with substantially more elaborate agents.
SAVE extends this baseline and outperforms evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone–benchmark settings.
Agentic exploration is most beneficial when dense processing sparsely represents answer-relevant events, particularly in long videos.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Example of both Gemini 3 Flash Native and SAVE answering a question from Minerva (question #34). No timestamp is given in the question, so both methods first have to find the relevant moment in the video. SAVE employs a multi-step search strategy: First, it queries the whole video at low granularity, subsequently isolates the crucial segment from the rest of the video and answers the question correctly. Gemini’s native video processing instead passes the whole video into the model at a higher granularity than SAVE, but nonetheless fails to answer the question correctly, as fine, crucial details get lost in the large amount of irrelevant context passed into the model.

Figure 1: SAVE exploring Minerva video. A video-wide query locates Game 4 (five of 15 sampled frames shown). A focused query distinguishes Ian’s opening EKE from Mack’s response AXE, which the transcript also confirms. SAVE stops with the correct answer.

Neither timestamp is given in the question. SAVE employs a multi-step search strategy: First, it queries the whole video at low granularity and subsequently isolates the first crucial segment from the rest of the video. After having correctly interpreted the first relevant segment, it proceeds to search for the second relevant segment later in the video. After 6 iterations, the second relevant moment is found and SAVE answers the question correctly. Gemini’s native video processing instead passes the whole video into the model, manages to correctly identify the first moment, but the second moment is lost among the large amount of irrelevant visual context presented to the model.

papers.tldr: SAVE shows that simple, selective video exploration can outperform complex agentic frameworks, especially for long videos with temporally concentrated evidence.

papers.abstract: AI-manipulated video detectors are typically evaluated on clean, curated datasets. In deployment, however, videos have usually passed through repost compression on social-media platforms and sometimes were captured by imperfect hardware. To measure detection under these conditions, we introduce Reality Perception Gap (RPG), a benchmark of 10,000 videos from frontier generators and partially synthetic edits, processed with cross-platform repost compression and paired with real footage that carries camera-side optical artifacts. RPG also includes socially fragile content, such as crime and wartime footage, where fabricated videos can cause severe social harm. Across 18 detectors, none catches more than 15% of fakes at a 1% false-positive rate. A positive control and a re-encoding sweep separate two sources of failure: generator and content shift degrades detectors before any compression, and repost compression erases the low-level traces that the artifact-based detectors relies on. Existing detectors therefore struggle when deployment conditions strip away the generation artifacts they rely on. These complementary failures suggest that robust detection requires training under deployment conditions and combining low-level, temporal, and semantic evidence, where passive detection may have reached its limits.
authors: Xiangrui Liu, Xinmiao Luan, Xinyuan Wang, Zhiyuan Fang, Chi-Yao Huang, Douglas C. Montgomery, Yanjie Fu, Felix Juefei-Xu, YeZhou Yang
bullets: Introduces Reality Perception Gap (RPG), a 10,000-video benchmark covering frontier-generated videos, partially synthetic edits, repost compression, camera artifacts, and socially fragile content.
Evaluates 18 detectors under deployment-like conditions; none detects more than 15% of fakes at a 1% false-positive rate.
Generator and content shifts already degrade performance, while social-media re-encoding further removes the low-level artifacts detectors rely on.
The findings point toward training under deployment conditions and combining low-level, temporal, and semantic evidence.
The study suggests passive detection alone may be approaching its practical limits.

papers.abstract: Cross-domain video deepfake detection increasingly uses frozen foundation-model experts, combined by calibrated score averaging, a per-video router picking one expert, or a learned head over concatenated features. Expressive routing and feature fusion are often reported to beat plain averaging. Across a 22-dataset frozen-expert testbed, we find those gains are largely evaluation artifacts. A corner theorem locates the gap routing aims to close: because AUC depends only on score ordering, the best any score-space router can do is an oracle reading the test label to pick each video's expert, a ceiling no realisable, label-blind router reaches. The theorem does not order real routers against a calibrated global average; the case against routing is empirical, and no router we test beats that average. Feature fusion reads raw features, falls outside the theorem, and is audited empirically. Reported gains trace to leakage: holding out one dataset leaks siblings sharing identities and reals (over-crediting routing), while holding out one manipulation keeps that dataset's reals in training (over-crediting feature fusion). A $2\times 2$ over fold and evaluation granularity pins the $+2.6$pp feature-fusion "win" to the fold alone: 12/12 significant under leaky folds vs. 0/12 under honest family-held-out folds, where both gains vanish. Fusion still pays off in the tail of hard videos and families: as experts are added, videos every expert misclassifies drop from 15.2% to 2.3%, and global calibrated fusion (InvB) beats the best single expert on worst-family AUC, selective risk (AURC), and low-false-positive recall, stably across protocols. Practitioners should calibrate and combine globally, hold out whole dataset families, and measure tail performance. For score-space routing under ranking metrics, honest evaluation and expert diversity matter more than combiner complexity.
authors: Luke Collins, Chang-Tsun Li, Duc Thanh Nguyen
bullets: Leakage from dataset-family splits can falsely credit routing and feature fusion.
A theorem shows score-space routers have an unattainable label-aware oracle ceiling under AUC; it does not prove they beat averaging.
Across 22 datasets, no tested router beats calibrated global averaging.
The reported +2.6 percentage-point fusion advantage disappears with honest family-held-out folds.
Adding experts reduces videos missed by all experts from 15.2% to 2.3%; calibrated fusion improves worst-family AUC, selective risk, and low-false-positive recall.

papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of video generation has narrowed the perceptual gap between authentic and synthetic videos, making generalizable AI-generated video detection increasingly challenging. Existing detectors predominantly rely on visual representations, leaving caption-derived textual semantics underexplored. Meanwhile, temporal regularity in fine-grained visual representations has received limited attention. We find that caption-derived textual representations provide complementary discriminative cues to global visual representations. Our analysis further reveals that AI-generated videos exhibit stronger temporal persistence and lower temporal variability, a pattern we term temporal over-regularity (TOR). Based on these findings, we propose MTOR with a multimodal branch and a TOR component. The multimodal branch integrates global visual and caption-derived textual representations, while the TOR component models temporal over-regularity at three levels: coarse inter-frame continuity, fine-grained token correspondence, and frame-to-video stability. Extensive evaluations on five benchmarks covering 46 generator variants demonstrate state-of-the-art overall performance against 16 representative baselines, while robustness experiments confirm strong resilience to twelve real-world video perturbations. Code and models will be released at https://github.com/hwang-cs-ime/MTOR.
bullets: AI-generated videos show stronger temporal persistence and lower temporal variability than authentic videos, termed temporal over-regularity (TOR).
The multimodal branch combines global visual features with caption-derived textual representations for complementary detection cues.
The TOR component models coarse frame continuity, fine-grained token correspondence, and frame-to-video stability.
Evaluations across five benchmarks and 46 generator variants report state-of-the-art overall performance against 16 baselines.
Robustness experiments show resilience to 12 real-world video perturbations.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional gait analysis guides rehabilitation after spinal cord injury but depends on marker-based motion capture and force plates, which few clinics have. Monocular markerless pipelines have been established in fewer healthy adult cohorts but not in neurological cohorts. We present the SCAI SCI Gait dataset, comprising 239 adult individuals with spinal cord injury with synchronized video, motion capture, and force-plate measurements, we fitted a parametric body mesh to a single sagittal-view video, driving an anthropometrically scaled OpenSim model via virtual markers. Markerless lower-body kinematics showed state-of-the-art agreement with motion-capture measurements (r = 0.68-0.90, p < 0.001, and RMSE = 4.18-6.49 degrees), and accurate kinematics-based predicted ground-reaction forces closely matched those measured by force plates (r = 0.85-0.87, p < 0.001, and RMSE = 2.13-2.19 Newton per kg). Furthermore, conditional-dependence graph analysis with Markov blankets revealed that waveform components were conditionally associated with functional independence, and speed-stratified clustering revealed distinct mechanical strategies among individuals walking at similar speeds. These findings establish the use of monocular video as a scalable approach for clinically meaningful biomechanical assessment and data-driven phenotyping in patients with spinal cord injury. Github: https://github.com/SCAI-Lab/SCAI-SCI-Gait-Dataset
bullets: Addresses the limited clinical availability of marker-based motion capture and force plates for spinal cord injury gait assessment.
Introduces the SCAI SCI Gait dataset of 239 adults with spinal cord injury with synchronized video, motion-capture, and force-plate data.
Fits a parametric body mesh to video and drives an anthropometrically scaled OpenSim model through virtual markers.
Markerless kinematics and video-based ground-reaction-force estimates showed strong agreement with reference measurements.
Graph-based and speed-stratified analyses linked gait waveform components to functional independence and identified distinct mechanical strategies.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Figure 3. Markerless IK agreement with marker-based motion capture (Pose2Sim model). Markerless kinematics: monocular-video SMPL meshes → SMPL virtual markers → IK in OpenSim 4.5. Marker-based kinematics: physical MoCap markers processed with the same musculoskeletal model and joint definitions. The recordings were trimmed (first/last 10%) and segmented into gait cycles using extrema-based events (hip minima; knee/ankle maxima), and only matched cycles were retained (Cycles, panel a). Cycles were time-normalized, mean-centered, and DTW-aligned. Panel (a) reports similarity/error metrics (Pearson r/p; RMSE/MAE; offset mean ± SD; MSM/nMSM; DTW distance/z/effort). Panel (b) shows DTW-aligned ensemble-averaged sagittal flexion waveforms (bilateral hip/knee/ankle). SPM with Cohen’s d identifies significant gait-cycle regions and effect magnitude.

Figure 1. Monocular markerless gait analysis workflow and downstream clinical inference used in this study. (1) Synchronized monocular sagittal-plane video and force-plate GRF acquisition. (2) Video preprocessing with 2D pose estimation and body segmentation. (3) Monocular 3D human-mesh recovery (HMR) with body-model constraints for robust occlusion. (4) Extraction of virtual markers from the 3D mesh (head, shoulders, ASIS, hip, knee, ankle, heel, and toe). (5) Participant-specific OpenSim model scaling/alignment to enable kinematics and GRF prediction. (6) Inverse kinematics (IK) yields joint-angle waveforms; kinematics-based prediction of vertical GRFs (pGRFs) provides kinetic estimates; performance is summarized by IK accuracy (correlation with MB) and pGRF error (RMSE, N/kg). (7) Graph-based conditional-dependence analysis links principal components of kinematic/GRF features to clinical outcomes (SCIM, AIS, injury category/subcategory, and etiology), with Markov blankets highlighting conditionally relevant associations. (8) Two-stage unsupervised clustering: speed stratification (slow/medium/fast) followed by within-stratum mechanics subclustering to identify coordination/compensatory strategies. (9) Results dashboard for clinicians (kinematic waveforms, predicted GRFs, summary metrics, and clustering/graph insights) to support interpretation and rehabilitation planning. (10) Patient-facing visual feedback and a personalized rehabilitation plan close the loop between quantitative gait assessment, clinician guidance, and rehabilitation planning.

papers.abstract: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. Object state readout provides this information by describing a target object's states and transitions across video frames. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate detailed visual descriptions, these descriptions may leave the attributes needed to distinguish successive states insufficiently specified. In this paper, we propose look-ahead state readout (LASER), an anticipation-guided agent for object state readout that uses possible next-step changes to determine which attributes to inspect in the present. Given temporally ordered frames and a target object, LASER converts anticipated changes into targeted visual questions and inspects the current frame to establish attribute values. It then checks state readouts and forecasts against independent observations of subsequent frames, refining a state record used to generate the final description. Reusable textual observation skills guide this process and are refined by tracing discrepancies with reference captions to the responsible instructions. Candidate revisions are selected on separate videos based on improved caption quality without increased contradictions with reference facts. Model parameters remain frozen throughout adaptation and inference, and the revised skills remain fixed during evaluation. Experiment results and further analysis on OSCaR and PLM RCap show consistent improvements of LASER over strong baselines and existing approaches, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.
bullets: Addresses underspecified attributes in multimodal language-model descriptions of changing object states.
Uses anticipated changes to generate targeted visual questions about the current frame.
Validates readouts and forecasts against later frames, then refines a state record for final descriptions.
Adapts reusable textual observation skills by tracing caption discrepancies, without updating model parameters.
Shows consistent improvements over strong baselines on OSCaR and PLM RCap, according to the abstract.

(3) Sequential visual correction checks the readout and hypotheses against the next observation, obtained independently of the hypotheses. Corrected history and local guidance support subsequent inspection; the accumulated state record supports the final description. (4) Feedback-guided skill revision uses source-video traces and reference captions to propose edits, then selects edits on separate selection videos when caption quality improves without increasing reference contradictions. Solid arrows indicate information flow; orange dashed arrows indicate source-trace transfer and skill-library updates for adaptation. The MLLM remains frozen, and the skill library is fixed during evaluation.

Each case shows the input frames and target region, an anticipated change, later visual evidence, the model caption, and the reference. Case 1 links an anticipated forward lean to a visual inspection criterion. Case 2 rejects a standing forecast and preserves the observed transition to sitting. Green contours identify the target.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a new paradigm in wildfire management for detecting both visible and obscured fire using Deep Learning (DL). The essence of our method is the joint spatial and temporal analysis of RGB videos, embracing the fact that temporal patterns of smoke motions in consecutive video frames can indicate obscured fire flames. This perspective contrasts the traditional approach of independently analyzing images and individual video frames. To this end, we propose a frame-wise transformer architecture that applies an attention mechanism between the consecutive frames while preserving spatial information within frames as opposed to regular attention mechanisms like the non-local block, which combines spatial and temporal information into a single vector. We also optimize the temporal pattern lengths under different spatial resolutions to achieve the highest performance while reducing the computational cost. To investigate the applicability of our method in aerial image processing, we applied it to a curated version of the FLAME2 dataset that includes dual-mode RGB/IR videos. The IR video feed is used to extract ground truth, while the model is trained only on RGB videos to maintain applicability to lowcost commercial drones (which are equipped only with regular cameras) and facilitate processing existing RGB-only datasets. Our proposed method achieves a Segmentation Foreground Dice score of 92.61%, an Object Detection Precision and Recall rate of 93.21% and 91.73%, and clip-level classification accuracy of 98.02%, respectively. We also investigated the efficacy and generalizability of our method through ablation study
authors: Uma Meleti, Abolfazl Razi, Fatemeh Afghah

Reports 92.61% foreground Dice, 93.21% detection precision, 91.73% recall, and 98.02% clip-level accuracy. [Abstract also mentions ablation and generalizability studies.]

papers.abstract: Under a fixed frame budget, video understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) depends on whether the sampled frames provide sufficient evidence for the question. Sufficient frame evidence supports direct answering, whereas less informative observations may benefit from reasoning that connects the available cues. We introduce EVAThink, which enhances video understanding through evidence sufficiency-guided training for adaptive thinking. First, Recoverable Evidence Gap Mining constructs evidence-dense and evidence-sparse video views that share the same question and answer under an identical frame budget. It retains pairs where sparse views yield lower direct-answer accuracy than dense views but benefit from explicit reasoning, providing supervision for response-mode selection. Second, Evidence-Guided Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning uses stage-specific rewards to guide training with evidence-based mode preferences and then refine response efficiency, while first-token advantage regularization mitigates mode collapse. Trained on only 6.7K curated samples, EVAThink consistently improves upon the base model across video understanding benchmarks under both 32- and 64-frame budgets, while outperforming strong baselines on average. The code, model, and datasets are available at \href{https://github.com/ChangtiWu/EVAThink}{EVAThink}.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Predicate-State Video Reasoning Segmentation (PS-VRS), where a query defines a dynamic predicate $P(o,t)$ over objects and time rather than a fixed object identity. Existing methods typically treat the target as permanently active once identified, leading to over-emission of masks during vacant intervals and failure to handle target switching. To address this, we construct PS-Bench, a large-scale benchmark with 2,077 videos and 16,250 queries annotated with explicit active/vacant predicate states, temporal intervals, and pixel masks. We further propose Predicate-State Grounding (PSG), a State-Bind-Emit pipeline that: (1) predicts [ACTIVE]/[VACANT] state tokens; (2) aligns them to video frames via dense cross-modal similarity; and (3) emits masks via SAM2 only for active states. Experiments show that PSG outperforms existing baselines by +9.32 J&F on PS-Bench and significantly reduces false-positive mask emissions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit predicate-state modeling for video reasoning segmentation with dynamic visual witnesses.
authors: Yuhuan Hong, Yiming Ren, Zhiqiang Lin, Feize Wu, Xingyun Liu, Yitong Xie, Lei Zhou, Lisheng Wu, Junjie Wang, Yujiu Yang
bullets: Problem: Existing methods assume a target remains active, causing masks during vacant intervals and failing when the target switches.
Method: PSG predicts ACTIVE/VACANT states, aligns them to video frames using cross-modal similarity, and uses SAM2 to emit masks only for active states.
Benchmark: PS-Bench contains 2,077 videos and 16,250 queries with annotated predicate states, temporal intervals, and pixel masks.
Result: PSG improves J&F by 9.32 points over existing baselines and reduces false-positive mask emissions.
Scope: The approach targets video reasoning segmentation with dynamic visual witnesses and time-varying predicate states.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the Predicate-State Grounding (PSG) Segmentation architecture. PSG decouples semantic validity from mask generation via a strict State-Bind-Emit pipeline. (1) State: A Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) infers the dynamic predicate states by generating discrete structural reasoning tokens ([ACTIVE], [VACANT], and [SEG]). (2) Bind: The Span-Frame Projecting module performs dense cross-modal alignment, binding these abstract state tokens to continuous video frames to establish frame-level temporal boundaries. (3) Emit: The [SEG] token acts as a semantic prompt for SAM to decode masks exclusively during active spans. Mask decoding is bypassed during predicted vacant intervals, substantially reducing invalid mask emission.

Figure 4: Explicit baseline prompt. System prompt used to adapt generalist MLLMs to predicate-state temporal segmentation with explicit active/vacant states, target-set transitions, and bounding-box localization.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on dynamic predicate-state transitions. For the query about the cleaning implement currently being used, the valid visual witness changes over time and is absent in the initial frames. PSG suppresses mask emission during the vacant state and rebinds the active state to the query-valid witness when the used implement changes. In contrast, existing baselines often segment visually plausible but query-invalid objects, or continue emitting masks across invalid states.

Figure 1: Task formulation comparison. Referring Video Object Segmentation segments explicitly referred targets, while Video Reasoning Segmentation introduces implicit reasoning queries but typically lacks explicit target switching and temporal predicate-state boundaries. PS-VRS treats the query as a predicate over objects and time, requiring reasoning, target switching, active/vacant temporal grounding, and pixel-level masks for active segments.

papers.abstract: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. Empirical results across ten T2V models show that physical commonsense remains far from solved, and that PhyRubric-Judge correlates more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges while matching the frontier proprietary Gemini 4 Argon. Further analysis provides actionable insights for T2V models.
authors: Huiyi Chen, Weitai Kang, Shicheng Fan, Xinshuo Wang, Zhixiang Shen, Yan Yan, Philip S. Yu, Baoxin Li
bullets: Addresses subjective single-score evaluations that do not identify which physical principles are violated.
Builds a caption-specific rubric before viewing the video, decomposing it into semantic and physical items with timestamped evidence.
Introduces PhyRubric-Bench across 34 categories and five physical domains, plus PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos.
PhyRubric-Judge’s evaluations correlate more closely with human judgments than existing open-source judges and match the reported performance of Gemini 4 Argon.
Evaluation across ten T2V models indicates that physical commonsense remains far from solved and yields actionable diagnostic insights.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhyRubric. papers.abstract: Traffic cameras continuously record urban road-user behavior, providing proactive safety evidence beyond crash reports. Yet safety-critical events - conflicts, near misses, unsafe turns, sudden braking, and crosswalk interactions - are rare and brief, buried in hours of routine footage. Existing traffic-video pipelines extract detections, trajectories, and risk scores but process footage uniformly, without adapting to an analyst's query. Vision-language methods improve scene understanding but often lack traffic-specific verification of participant-level conflicts. We introduce AgenticConflictLens, an agentic, query-conditioned framework for efficient, auditable conflict extraction from long fixed-camera traffic videos. Given a natural-language safety query, a Traffic-Aware Controller combines structured traffic memory with specialized conflict-analysis tools to choose where to search, which road users to examine, and which evidence to verify or reject. A coarse-to-fine search retrieves candidate intervals and applies detailed verification selectively. The framework produces conflict records with refined time intervals, participant pairs, semantic regions, trajectories, motion evidence, uncertainty, rejection reasons, and supporting clips. On 96 annotated hours from Bellevue and NYC DOT, AgenticConflictLens achieves the highest conflict-existence F1 and temporal IoU on both datasets: 0.84 F1/0.77 tIoU on Bellevue and 0.80 F1/0.73 tIoU on NYC DOT, while inspecting only 8.7% and 11.9% of video, respectively. These results support scalable, evidence-grounded urban traffic-safety analysis.
authors: Boshra Khalili, Sonia Moshfeghi, Jinwoo Jang, Andrew W Smyth

papers.abstract: Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.
authors: Xiang Fang, Wanlong Fang, Junhao Dong, Daizong Liu
bullets: Addresses temporal quantization errors and rankings that favor semantic similarity over localization precision.
Smooths predicted temporal score distributions with Gaussian kernel convolution.
Uses 2-Wasserstein optimal transport and Sinkhorn iterations for boundary refinement.
Reranks candidates using a composite score combining localization quality and semantic relevance.
Reports consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds, including 0.7, across Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models has transformed computer vision, yet their adaptation to medical imaging, particularly purpose built foundation models for spatio temporal echocardiography videos, remains limited. In this work, we explore the feasibility of fine tuning a pretrained foundation model for video (TimeSformer) for automated diagnosis of reduced ejection fraction heart failure (HFrEF) from apical four chamber videos. The model is finetuned on the publicly available RVENet A4C dataset with a phase aware clip generation strategy that captures complementary systolic and diastolic dynamics. We employ divided space time attention, layer wise learning rate decay, and multi clip inference to enhance robustness under limited data. Experimental results show that full fine tuning of the proposed model outperforms classifier only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline. These findings highlight the potential of leveraging foundation video models for echocardiography based heart failure diagnosis and motivates further domain adaptation studies in medical imaging.
authors: Mahyar Bolhassani, Tijana Geroski, Narayana S. Singam, Amir Amini
bullets: Addresses limited adaptation of video foundation models to spatiotemporal echocardiography.
Uses apical four-chamber videos from the publicly available RVENet A4C dataset.
Combines phase-aware systolic/diastolic clip generation, divided space-time attention, layer-wise learning-rate decay, and multi-clip inference.
Full fine-tuning outperformed classifier-only tuning and a 3D CNN baseline.
The study supports further domain-adaptation research for medical video imaging.

papers.abstract: Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is commonly trained on large banks of pre-extracted frame features, but storing and replaying those features becomes a practical bottleneck for long-form video, especially in incremental TAS where past-task data must remain available to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Recent TAS replay and condensation methods reduce this burden, but they rely on dense frame-wise annotations and allocate storage through fixed segment-level structures, limiting their flexibility for long procedural videos whose frame complexity varies substantially over time. We introduce Adaptive Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (ARQ-VAE), a compact and label-free memory representation for TAS features that learns a discrete residual quantization of frame-level video features and then adaptively truncates the residual chain on a per-frame basis, retaining only the residual prefix that best reconstructs each frame feature. This yields a practical compact feature memory that does not depend on frame-wise labels and can therefore support multiple TAS settings with the same stored representation, while a lightweight fine-tuning stage further improves reconstruction quality for the truncated codes that are actually retained. Across standard TAS benchmarks, ARQ-VAE achieves a substantially improved storage-performance trade-off over prior replay and condensation baselines. On Breakfast, our final representation reduces training-set storage from 28 GB for the original I3D feature bank to 10 MB while retaining strong downstream segmentation performance; with ASFormer, it achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in the supervised setting. We further show that the same label-free memory remains effective for incremental and unsupervised TAS. We position ARQ-VAE as a practical memory representation for TAS and a promising direction for broader dataset condensation applications.
authors: Gerard Donahue, Guven Gergerli, Ayush Gupta, Reza Ghoddoosian, Enna Sachdeva, Faizan Siddiqui
bullets: Addresses the storage and replay bottleneck of large frame-feature banks, especially for incremental TAS and long procedural videos.
Uses discrete residual quantization with per-frame adaptive truncation, retaining only the code prefix needed to reconstruct each feature.
Requires no frame-wise labels, enabling one shared memory representation across multiple TAS settings.
A lightweight fine-tuning stage improves reconstruction of the truncated codes that are actually stored.
On Breakfast, storage drops from 28 GB to 10 MB while ASFormer achieves 71.5 Edit and 51.2 F1@50 in supervised TAS; the abstract reports improved storage-performance trade-offs over prior baselines.

papers.abstract: Children's earliest years are a period of intense social learning, during which meaning is built through gaze, gesture, and physical contact. Yet, this critical aspect of social interaction remains under-evaluated in multimodal video understanding, as existing benchmarks prioritize the conversation-driven interactions of adults. We address this gap with \bench ($\textbf{N}$aturalistic $\textbf{E}$arly-childhood $\textbf{S}$ocial in$\textbf{T}$eractions), the first child-centric benchmark for nonverbal social reasoning. \bench comprises \totalvids manually annotated clips ($\sim$12s) curated for diversity across naturalistic settings, cultural contexts, and developmental stages. Beyond a lack of data, targeted model improvement in this domain is hindered by coarse evaluation schemas that conflate basic perception with higher-order reasoning. To resolve this, \bench introduces a compositional schema that builds atomic interaction cues into progressive levels of social reasoning: contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended descriptions. Extensive analysis of state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reveals a stark performance collapse: despite strong contextual recognition, models exhibit substantial gaps in decoding precise behavioral and interpersonal cues. We trace these failures to specific biases, including poor consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity. Finally, we ground \bench in real-world applications by evaluating VLMs using domain adaptation strategies. Ultimately, \bench provides a rigorous testbed for advancing socially grounded artificial intelligence in early childhood. Project page: https://laubravo.github.io/nest_website/.
authors: Marie Amale Huynh, Laura Bravo-S\'anchez, Lauren Klein, Nick Haber, Philip Fisher, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Targets an under-evaluated setting: early-childhood interactions conveyed through gaze, gesture, and physical contact rather than adult conversation.
Provides manually annotated, ~12-second clips spanning diverse naturalistic settings, cultures, and developmental stages.
Uses a compositional evaluation schema covering contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended social reasoning.
Analysis finds performance drops sharply on precise behavioral and interpersonal cues, linked to weak consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity.
Also evaluates domain-adaptation strategies to connect benchmark performance with real-world applications.

papers.abstract: Multimodal humor detection requires interpreting language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior jointly. Expressive fusion must also regulate how interactions of different orders enter the final judgment. We propose M\"obius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), which learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. Private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction construct supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors. Their uniform aggregate is exactly a M\"obius-domain filter with a geometrically decreasing interaction-order response. This formulation retains higher-order representations while regulating their contribution to prediction. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders. The induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62-2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments achieve 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods on these detection metrics. CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations establish applicability to sentiment prediction, and cross-seed analyses show more stable estimates on all three datasets. MoIF connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF.
bullets: Targets unreliable high-order interactions in joint language, vocal, and visual reasoning.
Uses private temporal encoders, balanced reciprocal interactions, and unimodal/bimodal/trimodal predictors.
Applies a uniform aggregate as a Möbius-domain filter with geometrically decreasing emphasis on interaction order.
Perturbation studies show a 1.62–2.79× improvement in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio over a co-trained trimodal predictor.
Reports 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, with applicability and more stable estimates on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI.

papers.abstract: Generalizable deepfake video detection remains challenging because forgery artifacts vary substantially across manipulation types and often combine diverse spatial and temporal inconsistencies. Existing parameter-efficient adaptation methods typically rely on a single shared representation, rendering them prone to manipulation-specific bias and limiting transfer to unseen forgeries. To address this challenge, we propose Mixture Of Spatio-Temporal Experts (MoSTE), an adaptation framework that enables conditional specialization of forensic representations. Instead of forcing one adapter to model all forgery patterns, MoSTE decomposes adaptation into parallel spatial and temporal expert pools and dynamically routes tokens to the most relevant experts through an unsupervised token-level routing mechanism. This allows experts to naturally specialize in complementary forgery cues without requiring explicit manipulation labels or multi-stage training, while effectively transferring representations from CLIP to the video domain. Extensive experiments across cross-dataset and cross-manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that MoSTE sets a new state of the art in average generalization while preserving strong performance across diverse manipulation families. Additional analysis of expert routing and attention behavior reveals the emergence of expert diversity, suggesting that MoSTE learns complementary spatio-temporal forensic features. Code is available at https://github.com/charbelyah/MoSTE
bullets: Deepfake artifacts vary across manipulation types and involve both spatial and temporal inconsistencies, making transfer to unseen forgeries difficult.
MoSTE uses parallel spatial and temporal expert pools with unsupervised, token-level dynamic routing.
The framework adapts CLIP representations to video without explicit manipulation labels or multi-stage training.
Experiments on cross-dataset and cross-manipulation benchmarks report state-of-the-art average generalization and strong performance across manipulation families.
Routing and attention analyses indicate that experts learn complementary forensic features.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the MoSTE architecture. MoSTE adapters are inserted into a frozen CLIP-ViT backbone and operate in the adapter bottleneck space. Tokens are routed to independent spatial and temporal expert pools. The selected expert outputs are masked, weighted, fused, and projected back through a residual adapter update.

Figure 3. Expert routing load. Each cell shows the percentage of tokens routed to each of the four experts (E1–E4), with separate heatmaps for spatial and temporal attention. A perfectly balanced distribution corresponds to 25% per expert. The middle layers (4- 12) exhibit near-uniform routing, while the early (0-2) and late (18-23) layers show stronger specialization.

papers.abstract: Traversability prediction is a core component of autonomous navigation, yet most vision-based methods operate frame-wise and produce temporally inconsistent predictions. We present SAM-VTP (Video Traversability Prediction), which fine-tunes SAM2's video memory pathway for dense, prompt-free traversability segmentation, conditioning each frame on a persistent memory of prior observations. Rather than inferring terrain geometry from appearance, we measure it: slope, roughness and height are computed from depth and fused into the image features. We also introduce an offline continuous supervision pipeline that generates dense per-pixel traversability targets in [0,1] from depth-derived geometry and semantic priors, requiring no robot deployment and no per-pixel annotation, capturing conditional feasibility that binary labels cannot represent. On TartanGround, a large-scale synthetic ground-robot dataset, SAM-VTP improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924 and binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886 over SAM-TP, a frame-wise SAM2 baseline, against a seed-to-seed spread below 0.001, and cuts frame-to-frame flicker by 31%. In closed-loop trials at two field sites, driving the same planner and controller, the baseline's dropouts leave the planner without a feasible path 3.3x more often on a paved course and 6.9x on rough ground, while SAM-VTP runs at 21.4 FPS on the Orin Nano the robot carries.
bullets: Addresses frame-wise vision models that produce inconsistent traversability predictions for autonomous navigation.
Fine-tunes SAM2’s video-memory pathway and fuses depth-derived slope, roughness, and height with image features.
Generates dense continuous traversability targets without robot deployment or per-pixel annotation.
On TartanGround, improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924, binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886, and reduces flicker by 31% versus SAM-TP.
In closed-loop field trials, reduces planner dropouts and runs at 21.4 FPS on an Orin Nano.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose CM3AE 2.0, a unified RGB Frame and Event-Voxel/-Frame pre-training framework. By jointly learning multimodal spatiotemporal representations and exploiting latent cross-modal dependencies through cross-modal generation, the framework enhances multimodal information interaction and collaborative modeling capabilities. Specifically, we first propose an Event-aware Spatiotemporal Masked Reconstruction (ESMR) strategy to learn unified multimodal spatiotemporal representations. It leverages event responses to guide masking toward dynamically salient regions. Through spatiotemporal masked reconstruction, it learns spatial structures and their temporal variations from continuous RGB-Event observations. In addition, it incorporates multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning to facilitate the modeling of cross-modal complementary information and the learning of shared representations. Building upon this, we further propose a Hierarchical Cross-modal Generation (HCG) strategy to learn latent cross-modal dependencies through visual and language generation. At the visual level, Event-conditioned RGB generation is performed using a pre-trained diffusion model to capture visual associations between the two modalities. At the language level, video-level text description generation based on joint RGB-Event representations establishes connections between multimodal visual features and linguistic semantics, further enriching the learning of cross-modal dependencies. Extensive experiments on four diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that CM3AE 2.0 consistently improves performance, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability of the proposed pre-training framework.
bullets: Uses event responses to mask dynamically salient regions for spatiotemporal masked reconstruction of RGB–event observations.
Combines multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning to capture complementary and shared information.
Learns latent cross-modal dependencies through event-conditioned RGB generation and video-level text description generation.
Experiments across four diverse downstream tasks show consistent performance improvements and support the framework’s generalization.
Scope: the abstract does not specify datasets, quantitative gains, or task-specific limitations.

papers.abstract: Video reasoning hinges on a small number of visually decisive tokens embedded in otherwise largely language-driven chains of thought. Yet prevailing post-training methods such as GRPO overlook this structure, assigning coarse trajectory-level rewards while requiring multiple rollouts and often costly external judges. We introduce Visually-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (VIOS), a post-training framework that identifies where a model under-utilizes visual evidence and concentrates learning at those positions. Our key insight is that a model can audit its own visual reliance: the divergence between its next-token distributions with and without the video reveals how strongly each prediction depends on the visual input. Measuring this reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged teacher exposes a per-token reliance gap, identifying positions where the teacher exploits visual evidence that the student overlooks. VIOS translates this signal into dense, targeted supervision through three complementary components: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher that co-evolves with the student, a contrastive objective that encourages predictions to depend on the video, and a reliance-gap gate that focuses learning on visually under-utilized tokens. Crucially, VIOS requires only a single on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers. Across 12 benchmarks spanning general, temporal, spatial, knowledge-intensive, and long-video understanding, VIOS consistently improves three model backbones and outperforms contemporary video-reasoning systems, while training in over 9x fewer steps, 60x fewer FLOPs, and 111x fewer generated tokens. Project page: https://vision.cs.utexas.edu/projects/VIOS/
bullets: Targets a limitation of GRPO-style post-training: coarse trajectory rewards, multiple rollouts, and costly external evaluation overlook token-level visual reliance.
Measures how predictions change with versus without video to estimate visual reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged EMA teacher.
Uses a contrastive visual-dependence objective and a reliance-gap gate to focus supervision on visually under-utilized tokens.
Requires one on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers.
Across 12 benchmarks and three backbones, it consistently improves performance while using over 9× fewer steps, 60× fewer FLOPs, and 111× fewer generated tokens than contemporary approaches.

papers.abstract: Attention heads in video Transformers vary greatly in functional importance. Understanding their contributions requires examining not only which heads are important, but also how they participate in collective computation within the network. We study this collective computation from two perspectives: the downstream use of head outputs and the composition of interactions across layers. Ablation analyses of four video Transformers show that high-importance heads identified on a single task also support other video understanding tasks and help preserve the representational structure that distinguishes different videos. Representational responses to head ablation correlate weakly with head importance after the attention module, but more strongly after the MLP in the same block. Adapting this downstream processing through MLP-only fine-tuning further improves the use of lower-importance head outputs. Meanwhile, through composition across layers, sets of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances support stronger perturbation responses at distant tokens than sets with longer distances. Their joint ablation causes even greater performance loss than ablating equally sized sets of high-importance heads, revealing collective contributions not fully captured by individual importance rankings. These findings highlight collective computation as a key perspective for understanding attention head function: functional contributions depend on both how head outputs are used downstream and how local interactions compose across layers.

papers.abstract: Optical flow requires reliable matching from sufficient visual context and precise motion at every pixel. Existing methods such as WAFT match and estimate flow on the same coarse grids, then recover dense flow through learned upsampling, without explicitly linking visual support for matching to dense flow reconstruction. Our key insight is that dense pixel-level flow does not require equally dense matching. We decouple correspondence scale from flow resolution by adapting the size and shape of spatial supports to image structure for reliable matching, while reusing these supports for precise dense flow reconstruction. We realize this in Flow from Adaptive Token Estimation (FATE), whose token supports expand within coherent regions and contract near motion boundaries. Shared pixel-to-token associations pool features for matching and reconstruct pixel flow from token motions. Flow supervision jointly trains pixel grouping, token matching, and flow estimation without grouping labels, allowing FATE to anticipate which pixels are likely to move together from appearance alone. Trained on FlyingChairs/FlyingThings3D, FATE achieves the highest zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI, a critical setting given scarce real-world flow labels. For visible pixels, FATE improves accuracy within coherent regions, and more near motion boundaries. Its largest gains occur where direct matches are unavailable: Occluded or out-of-frame pixels account for roughly 10% of valid pixels but 50% of WAFT's total error. Experiments show that adaptive correspondence through pixel-to-token grouping enables reliable matching and precise pixel-level flow, improving generalization to unseen real scenes.
bullets: Decouples correspondence density from flow resolution, avoiding uniformly dense matching.
Adapts token supports to image structure: larger in coherent regions and smaller near motion boundaries.
Shares pixel-to-token associations for feature pooling, token matching, and dense flow reconstruction.
Joint flow supervision learns pixel grouping without grouping labels and helps infer shared motion from appearance.
Trained only on synthetic data, FATE achieves the best zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI, with notable gains near boundaries and for occluded or out-of-frame pixels.

The same associations combine estimated token motions into dense pixel flow (bottom), allowing each pixel to draw on multiple tokens. Image 2 (lighter branch) has its own associations but shares network weights with Image 1. Dashed arrows indicate ground-truth flow supervision (Fig. 4).

Figure 4: Matching in token space estimates flow in pixel space through shared associations and flow supervision. Matching operates in coarse token space (top), while dense flow is formed in pixel space (bottom), across both the image features (left) and flow predictions (right). Features from Image 1 and Image 2 are pooled into adaptive tokens and matched across images (blue links). On the right, predicted token flow Fq is combined into pixel flow Fx, while ground-truth pixel flow F gt x is pooled into pseudo-ground-truth token flow F gt q . The probabilistic predictions Fq include token flow Fq and its uncertainty. We learn token matching and pixel-to-token associations using only ground-truth pixel flow, through three complementary losses: Ltoken(Fq | Pq) trains token-flow prediction against pooled ground truth, holding Pq fixed in constructing the pseudo-ground truth; Lassign(Px | Fq) trains associations to favor tokens that confidently explain pixel motion, holding token-flow predictions fixed; and Lrecon(Pq, Px | F gt x ) trains flow-preserving grouping by pooling and reconstructing fixed ground-truth flow, independently of matching. papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles use pedestrian crossing intention prediction (PCIP) to participate safely in traffic. Existing models are largely trained under favourable daytime conditions with sufficient daylight. Little is known about the robustness of these models under night-time and low-light conditions, due to the lack of datasets containing night-time footage. This paper investigates how a dataset, named NightSteps, can be constructed and evaluated as a baseline benchmark. The dataset is based on nighttime dashcam footage collected from six different cities around the world, capturing a wide variety of road conditions. The dataset consists of dashcam-recorded point-of-view footage, raw data of pedestrians' locations with corresponding 'track ids' and ground-truth labels containing accurate information about pedestrian crossing behaviour, resulting in a diverse dataset. Gemini, ChatGPT, and human assessment are used to demonstrate the usability of the dataset by predicting crossings in clips from the dataset and comparing the results with the initial ground-truth labels. These results show that human input achieves an accuracy of 88.17% and an F1-score of 80.21%. Predictions from Gemini and ChatGPT perform lower, with accuracies of 60% and 79.13% respectively, and F1-scores of 42.50% and 63.64%. The evaluation demonstrates that the NightSteps dataset can be used for future model evaluation to test the performance of PCIP, with the aim of improving road safety at night.
bullets: Addresses the lack of nighttime data for robust pedestrian crossing intention prediction.
Uses dashcam footage from six cities with varied road conditions, pedestrian locations, track IDs, and crossing labels.
Evaluates dataset usability with human assessment, Gemini, and ChatGPT predictions against ground truth.
Humans achieved 88.17% accuracy and an 80.21% F1-score; Gemini and ChatGPT performed lower.
Supports future evaluation and improvement of nighttime PCIP systems for road safety.

papers.abstract: As long-video understanding gains increasing attention, augmented reality (AR) devices are emerging as a compelling deployment platform. However, egocentric videos exhibit significant temporal redundancy, imposing substantial memory and computational burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware. To address this challenge, we introduce UTOPI, a plug-and-play pre-compression module designed specifically for egocentric long videos on AR platforms. First, we leverage user motion signals to estimate inter-frame overlap and propose a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm. Second, we exploit eye-tracking sensors to identify user fixations, enabling the separation of attended foreground content from background and its preferential retention via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism. Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance. Code and project page are available at https://sai-lab-nyu.github.io/utopi/.
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of temporally redundant egocentric videos on resource-constrained AR hardware.
Uses user motion to estimate inter-frame overlap and perform viewpoint-shift-invariant token pruning.
Uses eye tracking to distinguish attended foreground content from background and preferentially retain it.
Works as a plug-and-play pre-compression module across multiple benchmarks and model backbones.
Achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for video action recognition typically conflate spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map. We propose a perturbation-based framework that disentangles these contributions into a spatial appearance mask ($M_a$) and a temporal motion mask ($M_m$). The two masks are jointly optimized against a frozen action recognition model through factored perturbation architecture, with nearest frame replacement to identify important temporal dynamics. A separation penalty discourages the appearance mask from spending budget on frames that the motion mask has already discarded. A ReLU-based area constraint penalizes explanations larger than an assigned budget. To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+, and Something-Something V2, our method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.
bullets: Addresses the conflation of spatial appearance and temporal dynamics in existing video explanations.
Jointly learns an appearance mask and a motion mask against a frozen recognition model.
Uses nearest-frame replacement, separation penalties, and area constraints to isolate temporal and spatial importance.
Introduces a protocol that independently sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames to evaluate explanations.
Across three video datasets, achieves the lowest deletion AUC among compared baselines with masks about five times sparser.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer adapts frozen image foundation models to video via lightweight trainable adapters. Existing methods insert the same adapter at every transformer layer, implicitly assuming all layers require equal temporal modeling. A layer-wise sensitivity analysis across four video-native model families and two pretraining paradigms reveals that this assumption is wrong: temporal sensitivity increases with depth, and the pretraining paradigm determines its growth profile. Vision-only models exhibit a gradual rise, while vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery. This finding motivates STRAP, a training-free adapter placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model. Spatial adapters are assigned before this boundary and temporal adapters after it, without modifying the adapter architecture itself. On four fine-grained action recognition benchmarks, STRAP improves accuracy by up to 11.8% over uniform placement, reduces trainable parameters by 29 to 48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%. On standard benchmarks, it matches accuracy with fewer parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/th-nesh/STRAP.
bullets: Temporal sensitivity generally increases with transformer depth, but its pattern depends on the model’s pretraining paradigm.
Vision-only models show a gradual sensitivity increase; vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery.
STRAP is a training-free placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model.
Across four fine-grained action-recognition benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 11.8%, reduces trainable parameters by 29–48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%.
On standard benchmarks, STRAP matches accuracy with fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Surgical procedures are inherently partially observable, requiring surgeons to continuously infer evolving anatomical dynamics and future surgical states beyond the current observation. However, existing self-supervised learning methods primarily learn from observed surgical videos through masked reconstruction or predicting representations within the camera's current field of view, lacking the capability to explicitly model the out-of-sight surgical dynamics. Inspired by latent predictive world models, we introduce SurgWorld, a video-native, self-supervised framework for surgical representation learning, which treats a specified spatial or temporal shift as a pseudo-action and learns to predict the target latent representation from a partial observation. Specifically, we propose Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling (OSDM) as the pretraining objective for predicting representations conditioned on relative spatio-temporal shifts. We further regularize the learned latent dynamics from OSDM with a Geometric Visual Similarity (GVS) objective by aligning patch-level relational structures between predicted and target representations, preserving spatial geometry and local visual coherence for dense perception. These two objectives are integrated through an agglomerative training framework that consolidates complementary supervisory signals from multiple teachers to learn a unified latent representation of surgical dynamics and visual geometry. Extensive transfer learning experiments on 17 surgical benchmarks show that SurgWorld consistently outperforms existing vision foundation models across surgical workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense visual perception. We further conduct tailored qualitative and quantitative analyses, demonstrating that SurgWorld effectively captures surgical dynamics beyond the directly observed context through latent prediction.
bullets: Addresses the partial observability of surgery, which limits methods focused only on visible content.
Uses spatial or temporal shifts as pseudo-actions and introduces Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling to predict target latent representations.
Adds Geometric Visual Similarity regularization to preserve patch-level spatial relationships and local visual coherence.
Combines complementary supervisory signals through an agglomerative training framework for unified dynamics and geometry representations.
Transfers effectively across 17 surgical benchmarks spanning workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense perception.

papers.abstract: Compressing continuous human motion into a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens is now the first stage of many motion understanding and generation pipelines. Vector quantization partitions a latent space into Voronoi cells around a finite codebook, but the geometry of that latent space is inherited from the input pose encoding, and it is unclear which encoding admits an efficient discretization. We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding. Encodings of the same pose family can thus yield effective vocabularies differing by an order of magnitude, a difference that reconstruction loss alone does not reveal, which points to input geometry as a first-order design choice in motion tokenization.
bullets: Compares four pose geometries: joint heatmaps, root-relative positions, local rotations, and full kinematic features.
Trains VQ-VAE tokenizers while varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension.
Evaluates reconstruction alongside codebook utilization and entropy-based effective vocabulary size.
Rotation and position encodings continue benefiting from larger codebooks; full kinematic features saturate at a few hundred effective cells, while heatmaps remain below 60.
Small code dimensions generally maximize utilization, and temporal-stride effects depend on the encoding.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of pose encodings for discrete motion vocabulary learning, relevant to motion representation and understanding.
papers.title: Does Pose Encoding Matter? Analyzing Geometric Representations for Discrete Motion Vocabulary Learning
papers.tldr: Pose encoding strongly determines how efficiently continuous motion can be converted into discrete tokens, with rotation and position representations supporting much larger effective vocabularies than heatmaps or redundant kinematic encodings.

papers.abstract: Video understanding evaluations are intended to measure a model's proficiency in video perception and task solving. However, current VideoQA benchmarks struggle to isolate these capabilities due to their reliance on multiple-choice (MC) answer guidance, language priors, and fragile scoring pipelines. Disentangling these confounding factors reveals how much of a model's score is supplied by the evaluation context rather than earned through faithful perception. Across six VideoQA benchmarks of varying length, we find that accuracy is significantly above chance without any visual input. This is caused by shortcutting and option-prior reliance. We express these effects in the language of faithfulness: option-exploitation and answer-conditioned reasoning traces are unfaithful even when they are correct. Together, our results show that a VideoQA score is jointly determined by language priors, option timing, and how outputs and labels are converted into correctness. We produce a novel Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) mechanism that discloses options at controlled stages of an open-ended (OE) trajectory, to obtain objective MC scores from faithful option-free inference. Our work demonstrates that agentic methods with ODR and faithful inference can match option-exploiting performance. Finally, we formalize our diagnostic collection and ODR as a reproducible evaluation protocol, and we release a human-relabelled edition of LVBench (correcting $20.5\%$ of keys) to remove annotation noise as a confounding variable.
bullets: Across six VideoQA benchmarks, models perform above chance even without visual input, indicating reliance on language priors and answer-option exploitation.
The study identifies option timing, answer-conditioned reasoning, and scoring/label conversion as major confounds in VideoQA evaluation.
Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) reveals answer choices at controlled points during an otherwise open-ended, option-free inference process.
Agentic methods using ODR and faithful inference can match performance achieved through option exploitation.
The authors release a reproducible diagnostic protocol and a human-relabelled LVBench edition correcting 20.5% of answer keys.

Each column withholds or perturbs a single input while holding all other settings fixed relative to MC (full). Chance and Heuristic use no model at all (Appendix F). The two OE columns report the mean judge rating (0–100) followed in parentheses by the binarised accuracy (the percentage of items rated ≥ 80, corresponding to “mostly correct” in Box 3); all MC−OE differences in the paper use this binarised accuracy (see Table 8 for alternative thresholds). This equals the full split everywhere except LVBench open-ended (1,477 of 1,549 items) and the two QBench-Video Author-AVP replay conditions (622 of 868 items), where differences are taken over the shared subset. The two OE columns take the difference against the judge binarised at ≥ 80 (§G.7), not against the mean rating, so both sides of every entry are per-item correctness on one scale; the bracketed figures in Table 1 are these binarised scores.
