papers.abstract: Surgical video understanding is an important foundation for intelligent assistance in robot-assisted surgery. Similar surgical views can reflect different actions or procedural stages. Interpreting these views requires access to earlier observations, yet frame-centric prompting leaves this history unavailable. We introduce MemSurg, a framework that remembers surgical observations before reasoning over them. Its structured memory graph stores timestamped entity categories, locations, motion cues, and interaction summaries. Chronological links preserve recent context, while entity-associated links connect recurring observations across the procedure. Task-adaptive retrieval then supplies evidence-grounded prompts for scene and workflow reasoning, supporting both frozen inference and memory-conditioned supervised fine-tuning. Evaluation on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two complementary surgical benchmarks shows a 10.43-percentage-point gain over SurgRAW with GPT-4o. Memory conditioning adds 6.52 points under matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and an inference-time plug-in adds 7.04 points to EndoChat. These results support structured memory as a reusable source of procedural evidence for surgical video understanding. Our code will be publicly released.
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of similar surgical views that correspond to different actions or procedural stages.
Builds a memory graph containing timestamped entities, locations, motion cues, interaction summaries, and chronological or entity-linked context.
Uses task-adaptive retrieval to generate evidence-grounded prompts for frozen inference or memory-conditioned fine-tuning.
Improves performance by 10.43 points over SurgRAW with GPT-4o, by 6.52 points with matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and by 7.04 points as an EndoChat plug-in.
Evaluated on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two additional surgical benchmarks; code is planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Video fusion aims to integrate complementary cues from heterogeneous sources, producing visually informative videos with coherent spatio-temporal structures. Jointly learning cross-modal complementarity and temporal dependencies typically relies on large-scale, high-quality video datasets, whose storage and repeated use during optimization incur substantial costs, making data-efficient learning highly desirable. To address this challenge, we rethink video fusion from the perspective of dataset condensation and propose STAR-VF, the first framework that condenses spatio-temporal representations for data-efficient video fusion. STAR-VF condenses the original training set into a compact set of learnable spatio-temporal representations, which are decoded into synthetic video clips and optimized using feature-level supervision provided by a frozen proxy model. The resulting condensed data preserves fusion-relevant spatial and temporal cues without requiring ground-truth fused videos as supervision. To adapt fusion learning to condensed representations, we equip the final fusion model with flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation, enabling direct temporal interaction and adaptive selection of fusion-relevant information in representation space. Extensive experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-VF, trained with only approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training set, achieves fusion quality comparable to methods trained on the full data. Further analyses validate the contributions of learned condensation and flow-free temporal modeling, and demonstrate the robustness of the condensed supervision across different proxy encoders and downstream fusion models. Project page: https://zju-xyc.github.io/STAR-VF-Project-Page/.
bullets: Targets the storage and optimization costs of large video-fusion training datasets.
Learns compact spatio-temporal representations, decodes them into synthetic clips, and optimizes them with feature-level supervision from a frozen proxy model.
Uses flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation for fusion directly in representation space.
Supports infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion without requiring ground-truth fused videos.
Using approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training data, it achieves fusion quality comparable to full-data training; robustness is shown across proxy encoders and downstream fusion models.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed STAR-VF framework. In Stage I, learnable compact spatio-temporal canvases and the canvas decoder𝑈 are jointly optimized under feature-level supervision from a frozen proxy feature extractor, yielding the learned condensed set 𝑆∗ and decoder 𝑈 ∗. In Stage II, the learned condensed set is decoded into synthetic temporal samples to train the final fusion model 𝐹𝜃 with flow-free temporal alignment and query-driven intra-frame aggregation. During inference, only the trained fusion model is used, without the condensed set or proxy model.

Figure 1: Comparison of temporal alignment paradigms under video fusion dataset condensation. Conventional flowbased alignment is not naturally suited to condensed synthetic clips , whereas our method models order-aware temporal dependency in compact representation space.

At the same time, a larger 𝜌 weakens the compression effect by making the condensed source more flexible. The default setting 4 × 4 in STAR-VF is selected as a balanced operating point under this trade-off.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic diagnosis unfolds over native video, where a single positive finding during traversal of the gastrointestinal tract sets off a multi-minute chain of reasoning over location, morphology, severity and intervention. Existing endoscopy multimodal benchmarks test only static images or single-disease videos, which miss the temporal and clinical reasoning that real-world reporting demands. We introduce EndoSCOP-V, a video-grounded multi-turn evaluation framework for structured endoscopy reporting and clinical reasoning. It contains 1,307 real-world endoscopy and colonoscopy videos (63.2 h; 97% 1080p) averaging about 174 s. Its 20,274 question-answer turns are instantiated deterministically from clinician-filled structured endoscopy-reporting EHRs, so no per-case annotation is synthetic or LLM-rephrased. They come from 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates, about 18 per disease, that span a clinically aligned 9-task x 30-sub-task reporting taxonomy over 54 World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) MST 3.0 diseases. 22% of procedures carry co-existing pathologies, up to six per case. A Markovian context-pruned oracle-forcing protocol evaluates the dialogue turn by turn, injecting the gold answer before each subsequent turn so that per-turn reasoning is isolated from cascading dialogue errors. A panel of 15 board-certified endoscopists sets a 78% strict-accuracy baseline on 1,500 questions. Across 14 open-weight LMMs, the best 27B-class model reaches 59.8% strict accuracy, falling to 53.4% once format-trivial disease-rejection items are excluded. On a between-subjects spot-check, the best of 3 frontier proprietary models trails the clinician panel by 23 pp on strict NDR accuracy. Sub-task analysis reveals consistent gaps in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading and intervention reasoning on long-horizon video. Data: Hugging Face (EndoSCOP-V). Code: GitHub (abhi25t/EndoSCOP-V).
bullets: Addresses the limits of static-image and single-disease benchmarks for temporal, multi-finding endoscopy reasoning.
Includes 1,307 real-world videos, 20,274 deterministic question-answer turns, 54 diseases, and a 9-task, 30-subtask reporting taxonomy.
Uses clinician-derived EHR templates and context-pruned oracle forcing to isolate turn-level reasoning from cascading dialogue errors.
The best 27B open-weight model achieves 59.8% strict accuracy versus 78% for 15 board-certified endoscopists; performance drops to 53.4% after excluding format-trivial items.
Models show persistent weaknesses in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading, and intervention reasoning over long videos.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.
bullets: Addresses privacy risks from continuous egocentric video capture, where sensitive content varies by user and context.
Converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations for reasoning.
Combines a privacy reasoner with explicit user-specific memory to support personalization and continual adaptation.
Evaluated on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users using a cross-user chronological protocol.
Reports 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming the described baseline systems.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires models to answer user queries over continuously evolving video streams. Unlike offline video QA, SVU must handle queries whose evidence may lie in the past, appear in the current scene, or emerge only after future observations. Existing streaming video systems often rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which can lose fine-grained details and fail to adapt the answering process to the temporal intent of each query. In this paper, we propose TimeTraveler, a streaming VQA framework that performs temporal strategy planning with a Time Dictionary. Inspired by the need to search across different temporal regions of a stream, TimeTraveler stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption and uses this dictionary as an explicit source of queryable evidence. Given a query, TimeTraveler determines whether to recall past evidence, read the present context, or wait for future observations, and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process. Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show that TimeTraveler improves streaming question answering by preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the appropriate temporal strategy for each query. The project page is available at https://geppa.github.io/TimeTraveler.
bullets: Addresses streaming video queries whose evidence may occur before, during, or after the current scene.
Stores observed moments as timestamp-indexed structured captions for fine-grained, queryable temporal evidence.
Selects a query-specific strategy: retrieve past evidence, read present context, or defer answering for future observations.
Experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show improved question answering through temporal evidence preservation and strategy selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TimeTraveler. Incoming video frames are encoded into structured captions and stored in a timestamp-indexed Time Dictionary. Given a query, a Temporal Strategy Planner acquires evidence following temporal intent: past queries retrieve relevant captions through similaritybased lookback, current queries access local captions, and future queries continue observation until evidence appears. Then, the retrieved evidence is used to produce the final answer.

Figure 1: Conceptual comparison between prior memory-based SVU and TimeTraveler. Prior methods preserve streaming history as agentic memory [19], pruned tokens [22], or KV-memory recall [24], but rely on a single evidence-access path and do not ensure that retained evidence remains query-recoverable. In contrast, TimeTraveler plans whether each query should be grounded in the past, current scene, or future, and accesses a structured Time Dictionary accordingly.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming video QA with temporal strategy planning and timestamp-indexed evidence; directly targets video-language temporal understanding.
papers.title: TimeTraveler: Temporal Strategy Planning with Time Dictionary for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: TimeTraveler improves streaming video QA by planning whether to recall the past, inspect the present, or wait for the future using a timestamped Time Dictionary.

papers.abstract: Deepfake videos generated by advanced generative models pose serious threats to digital security, misinformation control, and media forensics. Although numerous detection methods have been proposed, their reported performances are often based on heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, inconsistent data splits, and model-specific training protocols, hindering fair architectural comparison. This work presents a controlled and reproducible comparative study of convolutional neural networks (ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0) and a transformer-based architecture (ViT-B/16) within a unified, face-centric deepfake detection framework. All models are trained using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization settings, and data splits on Celeb-DF v2 and FaceForensics++, and results are validated across three independent random seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals. Experimental results show that while CNN-based models perform competitively at the frame level, their performance degrades after video-level aggregation. In contrast, ViT-B/16 demonstrates more stable video-level performance, achieving 92.8\% [95\% CI: 91.7--94.0] video-level accuracy and an AUC of 0.950 [95\% CI: 0.934--0.964] on Celeb-DF v2 (3-seed bootstrapped). Cross-dataset evaluation across the same three random seeds reveals a large, asymmetric generalization gap (AUC 0.79 FF++$\rightarrow$Celeb-DF vs. 0.64 Celeb-DF$\rightarrow$FF++), indicating that in-domain video-level stability does not transfer to unseen manipulation domains. These findings indicate that global self-attention improves robustness and video-level stability for deepfake detection within a given data domain, while highlighting the need for further work on cross-domain generalization.
bullets: CNNs perform competitively at the frame level but degrade after video-level aggregation.
ViT-B/16 achieves 92.8% video-level accuracy and 0.950 AUC on Celeb-DF v2, with bootstrapped confidence intervals across three seeds.
The study uses a unified face-centric pipeline with identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization, splits, and evaluation across ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, and ViT-B/16.
Cross-dataset performance shows an asymmetric generalization gap: AUC 0.79 from FaceForensics++ to Celeb-DF versus 0.64 in the reverse direction.
Results support improved in-domain stability from global self-attention, while emphasizing limited cross-domain robustness.

papers.abstract: Computer vision (CV) for policing has centred on recognising objects such as seized weapons, while body-worn video (BWV) is still reviewed by people, with existing AI tools using only its audio. Multimodal video AI could make BWV review faster and cheaper. At the object level, we present the KnifeHunter dataset, developed with UK law enforcement, with over 25,000 images of 543 knife classes and a protocol reflecting investigative conditions, and KHNet, a retrieval architecture fusing local and global features, which with about 125,000 distractor images attains 85.7% and 63.4% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the medium and hard protocols. At the event level, we present an evaluation protocol for video understanding pipelines, which describe a video as events and a transcript, that scores transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation and unsupported events. Whether each event is supported by the recording is labelled by a judge validated against blinded human labels. We apply it to complete pipelines, three 2026 omni-modal models and our hybrid NarrativeBridge-PAL-GPT-5 pipeline, on UKBWV-27, a pilot stress-test set of 27 publicly released UK BWV recordings (118 minutes). On this set the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures, yet it leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances, and every pipeline degrades on recordings from edited releases, long recordings and noisy audio. We propose readiness levels separating assistive tasks from those requiring verification of every output.
bullets: Introduces KnifeHunter, a law-enforcement-developed dataset with over 25,000 images across 543 knife classes and investigative evaluation protocols.
Presents KHNet, which fuses local and global visual features for knife retrieval, achieving 85.7% mAP on the medium protocol and 63.4% on the hard protocol.
Proposes an event-level evaluation framework covering transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation, and evidential support.
On 27 UK body-worn-video recordings, the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures but produces 13.6% unsupported events and misattributes 27.7% of utterances.
Performance declines for edited releases, long recordings, and noisy audio; the paper recommends readiness levels distinguishing assistive uses from outputs requiring verification.

papers.abstract: Benchmark scores license claims about the capabilities being evaluated. We audit the inference licensed by an evaluation protocol, rather than the predictive model alone. Using procedural action anticipation as a controlled case study, we study a broader evaluation-validity failure mode: a protocol can remain temporally causal and free of classical target leakage while still supplying a privileged intermediate representation. The failure is not merely optimistic accuracy, but a mismatch between the capability claimed and the construct actually measured. On Breakfast, matched recognizer-history and GT-history regimes score 30.3% and 62.3% (Delta_PH(R_BA) = +32.0, 95% Student-t interval [+24.1, +39.8]). A fixed-checkpoint 2 x 2 intervention isolates a +14.6-point test-time oracle contrast; a matched no-video provenance probe yields a +26.8-point gap; and a boundary-independent query/history control retains a +19.4-point gap. We refer to this discrepancy as a privileged-information gap, defined relative to a specified non-oracle recovery pipeline, and propose a reusable four-condition audit. Across five evaluation settings the gap is heterogeneous; a standard 50 Salads long-term-anticipation re-implementation provides cautious support beyond the audit-specific next-action construction.
bullets: Audits the validity of evaluation protocols, not just predictive models.
In Breakfast, ground-truth history scores 62.3% versus 30.3% for recognizer history, a 32.0-point privileged-information gap.
Controlled interventions show the gap persists without video and under boundary-independent history controls.
Proposes a reusable four-condition audit and finds heterogeneous gaps across five evaluation settings.
Evidence beyond the audit-specific setup is cautiously supported by a 50 Salads re-implementation.

papers.tldr: Evaluation protocols for action anticipation can appear causal yet overstate capability by giving models privileged intermediate information.

papers.abstract: 3D spatial reasoning from video remains challenging for VLMs because videos provide sequential, view-local observations rather than persistent metric scene records. Many questions must be answered in a query-specified perspective rather than the observed camera viewpoint, and prompting with a fixed set of RGB views may miss sparse or occluded visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce BEV3SR, a training-free and backbone-agnostic framework for RGB-D videos with camera parameters. BEV3SR turns video observations into queryable metric bird's-eye-view (BEV) scene memory and formalizes each query into an evidence-aware spatial task. The Spatial Task Formalizer specifies the query's reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and evidence requirement. The evidence requirement determines the appropriate reasoning pathway. A query treated as requiring geometric evidence is handled by the Geometric Reasoner, which deterministically computes the answer using the metric BEV records in the query-specified reference frame. Otherwise, a query treated as requiring visual evidence is passed to the Visual Evidence Aligner, which uses BEV-indexed object records and their associated supporting views to retrieve object-consistent and scene-context RGB frames for VLM grounding. Within a standard 16-frame budget, BEV3SR consistently improves different VLM backbones across multiple 3D scene QA benchmarks, delivering large gains on spatially intensive questions and significant improvements on open-ended scene QA. These results demonstrate that BEV3SR offers an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for explicit 3D spatial reasoning from video.
bullets: Addresses view-local, sequential video observations, query-specific viewpoints, and sparse or occluded evidence.
Formalizes each query’s reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and required evidence.
Computes geometry-based answers deterministically from metric BEV records in the requested reference frame.
Retrieves object-consistent and contextual RGB frames for VLM grounding when visual evidence is needed.
Improves multiple VLM backbones across 3D scene QA benchmarks, especially spatially intensive and open-ended questions, within a 16-frame budget.

papers.abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .
authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Jingyu Xiao, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 124 real-world webpages across 7 domains and 33 animation types, paired with reference videos and original static assets.
Provides a two-dimensional evaluation protocol measuring static appearance fidelity and animation fidelity across aligned frames.
Finds that webpage animation reconstruction is harder than reproducing static visual appearance.
Shows that explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve coding-agent reconstruction quality.
Reports that rapid, continuous motion is more difficult to reproduce than discrete state transitions.

papers.abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.
authors: Xiangqun Zhang, Likai Wang, Zekun Qian, Rui Zhou, Ruize Han, Wei Feng
bullets: Formulates cross-view dense video object captioning (CVDVOC), combining synchronized multi-camera evidence instead of processing views independently.
Constructs CRTrack-Cap with 425 global trajectories, 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, and canonical captions for 335 identities.
Introduces CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate cross-view tracking and caption quality.
The reference framework uses VECA for cross-camera association and CEG to integrate reliable, non-conflicting caption evidence.
It reports CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 in-domain and 33.48 cross-domain on scene-disjoint tests.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Reference framework for cross-view DVOC. The local tracker exports tracklets, Re-ID descriptors e, and trajectory queries q. VECA forms global identity groups; CEG combines member evidence with reliability and conflict estimates to produce a prompt residual ∆Pn. papers.abstract: We address geometric video alignment for the same scene captured by multiple freely moving cameras. Existing methods, which are based on image stitching or video stabilization, are typically limited to two cameras or must assume the restrictive setting of a fixed linear ordering of the cameras. We propose MViS, a lightweight test-time optimization framework for joint multi-view alignment with temporal consistency. MViS uses a spatial-transformer-inspired net to jointly process frames from all views within a short temporal window and predict per-view, per-time homographies. Optimization proceeds in two stages: geometry-guided alignment followed by appearance-based refinement, with both stages enforcing multi-view and temporal consistency across the sequence. The method requires no scene-specific hyperparameter tuning, handles arbitrary and time-varying view-intersection graphs, and remains robust under rapid camera motion. On a standard two-view video benchmark, MViS matches or surpasses the state of the art. To facilitate evaluation in more complex scenarios, we introduce an annotated dataset with more than two freely moving cameras and establish the first benchmark for this setting. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/MViS-project/ .
authors: Shira Ifergane, Roy Amoyal, Shahar Benishay, Oren Freifeld
bullets: Addresses multi-view video alignment beyond two cameras and fixed camera orderings.

Supports arbitrary, time-varying view-intersection graphs without scene-specific tuning and remains robust to rapid motion.
Matches or surpasses state of the art on a standard two-view benchmark and introduces a multi-camera dataset and benchmark.

papers.abstract: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of detecting anomalies from video-level supervision, where existing methods rely mainly on frame-feature magnitudes.
Uses textual prompts and an LLM to provide task-specific prior knowledge, then normalizes and compresses it through dictionary learning.
Improves consistency among textual descriptions of similar frames using LLMs and auxiliary information.
Integrates prior knowledge with cross-modal attention to learn relationships across modalities and build more reliable representations.
Experiments report that the method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches, though no specific datasets or metrics are provided.

papers.abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
authors: Dian Jiao, Yuqian Yuan, Jiaqi Zhu, Mingjian Gao, Siwen Tan, Yunqi Cao, Jinhui Li, Sijing Li, Zhenxuan Fan, Haoyang Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Siliang Tang
bullets: Addresses MLLMs’ difficulty composing precise temporal and spatial evidence into coherent multi-step reasoning.
Represents videos as Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives grounded reasoning chains from validated evidence paths.
Introduces a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark with grounded chain-of-thought annotations.
Finds that MLLMs often localize relevant evidence but struggle to compose it correctly, a weakness hidden by answer-only evaluation.
Fine-tuning with V-STORM improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
bullets: Recasts long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem under a fixed budget.
Plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to refine candidate evidence segments into compact memory.
Combines sparse low-resolution global frames with dense high-resolution local frames from refined memory.
Outperforms budget-matched uniform sampling and frame-selection/agentic methods on LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
authors: Mingjia Huo, Yao Fu, Bo Chang, Yaqing Wang, Dawei Zhu, Dylan Zhang, Xinyang Yi, Lichan Hong, Ed H. Chi, Hao Zhang, Jiaxi Tang
bullets: Benchmarks VLMs on 20 Atari 2600 games using high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams.
Separates in-game dynamics from inference speed to test spatiotemporal perception, reasoning, and action grounding.
Finds failures in tracking object motion and direction, brittle sequential decisions, and over-reliance on textual history over new visual feedback.
Analyzes which game scores reliably reflect competence and examines the effects of memory design and prompting.
Highlights a persistent gap between passive visual understanding and active decision-making in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to temporally localize abnormal events in videos. Most existing approaches rely on dataset-specific training and curated annotations, limiting generalization in open-set scenarios. Recent zero-shot methods based on Large Vision- Language Models (LVLMs) alleviate this dependency but often lack temporal continuity and structured reasoning. We propose Cog-VADU, a fully training-free framework that reformulates VAD as a sequential cognitive reasoning task. Cog-VADU introduces Chain-of- Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP), which unrolls an LVLM into a recurrent reasoning chain across video segments. By propagating structured rationales over time, the model maintains implicit temporal memory, enabling robust discrimination between com- plex anomalies and high-motion normal activities. To improve reliability, we further design a cross-modal re-ranking stage that aligns textual rationales with visual embeddings, enforcing semantic consistency and temporal coherence for refined and stable predictions. Extensive experiments on multiple public VAD benchmarks demonstrate that Cog-VADU achieves competitive zero-shot performance. Moreover, cross-model evaluations show that CoADTP consistently enhances reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic manner, pro- viding interpretable and generalizable anomaly understanding for real-world applications.
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization and weak temporal reasoning of dataset-specific and existing zero-shot VAD methods.
Uses Chain-of-Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP) to propagate structured rationales across video segments as implicit temporal memory.
Applies cross-modal re-ranking to align textual rationales with visual embeddings, improving semantic consistency and temporal coherence.
Reports competitive zero-shot performance across multiple public VAD benchmarks.
Cross-model evaluations indicate that CoADTP improves reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic way.

papers.abstract: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning six action-video tasks. With only narrow-domain data, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.
bullets: Addresses the lack of native metric-3D human-action representations in modern video models.
Supports action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation.
Uses a role-adaptive action renderer and cross-stream action-video coupling to align motion with visual dynamics.
Covers six action-video tasks and generalizes from narrow-domain data to unseen scenes and interactions.
Provides effective action control and visual quality while preserving pretrained visual knowledge.

papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is a long-established problem that aims to detect defects in industrial products during manufacturing for quality control. Most existing studies focus on static visual patterns as the basis for detection. However, in real manufacturing environments, many anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that cannot be perceived from static cues alone. We observe that even recent Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based approaches fall short in identifying such dynamic anomalies due to limited temporal modeling capability. To address this, we introduce MUSTARD: MUltimodal SpatioTemporal Anomaly Reasoning and Detection, a framework that equips MLLMs with fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting and reasoning about dynamics-based defects. MUSTARD introduces optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to capture critical motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. Its normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline requires only a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates. This enables efficient adaptation across various products and provides high decision interpretability. MUSTARD is the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based IAD. Experiments demonstrate its superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and providing plausible explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/racercode/Mustard
bullets: Targets dynamics-based industrial anomalies, such as irregular movements, that static visual methods may miss.
Uses optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to model local motion patterns and global temporal evolution.
Employs normal-pattern reasoning without model updates, supporting efficient adaptation across products.
Experiments show strong detection of spatiotemporal anomalies and plausible explanations.
Scope: designed for motion-related defects; the abstract does not quantify performance or specify datasets.

(2) Normal Pattern Extraction: Extracts multi-faceted normal patterns from a small set of reference videos. (3) Pattern Reasoning (Inference): Compares the test video’s description with the extracted normal patterns to detect deviations, producing a final anomaly judgment and explanation.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal models can answer questions about video, but their predictions rarely show which participant, event, or interval supports an answer. Moreover, answer-level supervision alone does not teach a model to interpret structured video evidence. To systematically mitigate this issue, we present THG-Omni, a human-centric graph-supervision framework that links Segment Anything Model~3 participant tracks with temporally grounded Qwen3-VL annotations. Candidate semantic claims are checked against the source video and available audio before they are used to construct training questions, while track geometry provides explicit spatial and temporal supervision. The resulting questions teach an omni-modal reasoning model to interpret participant attributes, actions, affect, interactions, and their timing from a structured graph. At inference, THG-Omni uses a predicted graph constructed from the evaluation video. Experiments on IntentBench show consistent improvements over the unadapted backbone across social reasoning, emotion understanding, and deception perception. On NExT-QA, THG-Omni achieves 89.54\% accuracy with the matched graph, compared with 85.10\% without graph input. Further validation experiments show that compact graph input achieves 78.22\% accuracy, compared with 78.02\% using the full graph and 77.58\% without graph input. A complementary diagnostic demonstrates that the predicted graph preserves evidence useful for answering questions even without the source video and audio. Together, these findings show that THG-Omni improves human-centric video reasoning while grounding its evidence in identifiable participants and events. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-n94hhfcwp5666/
bullets: Addresses the lack of evidence traceability and limitations of answer-only supervision in omni-modal video models.
Builds structured graphs from participant tracks and temporally grounded annotations, with claims checked against video and audio.
Trains models to reason about participant attributes, actions, emotions, interactions, and timing.
Improves over the unadapted backbone on IntentBench; on NExT-QA, matched graph input reaches 89.54% versus 85.10% without graph input.

papers.abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.
bullets: Addresses short, ambiguous questions whose visual referents cannot be uniquely identified.

papers.abstract: Action recognition, and more specifically egocentric action recognition, is a core task in computer vision, with applications such as monitoring the daily life activities of elderly people and task assistance. Recent methods rely on visual modalities such as RGB video or depth. However, in egocentric video, an action is largely defined by its objects, which these methods rarely model. We propose a method that combines a frozen SlowFast video expert with an attention-based object expert by late fusion. Each object is represented with its affordances, that is, what can be done with it, generated zero-shot by a vision-language model. Since datasets such as MECCANO annotate only the objects involved in each action, evaluating with these boxes tells the model which objects are active. We therefore train on annotated boxes and evaluate the method with detections from the official active-object detector, and with annotated boxes as an upper bound. Without affordances, our fusion reaches 68.4% Top-1 with annotated boxes but 49.0% with detections. About half of this drop comes from non-active detections. To remove them, the same vision-language model generates an interaction affordance that decides whether a hand is manipulating each detected object. On MECCANO, objects raise the Top-1 of the video expert from 44.9% to 49.0%, and the two affordances raise it to 49.9%, above SlowFast and object-aware RGB baselines. Code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Egocentric actions are strongly defined by the objects being manipulated, which standard RGB/depth methods often underuse.
The method late-fuses a frozen SlowFast video expert with an attention-based object expert.
A vision-language model generates object affordances and an interaction affordance to filter detections that are not actively manipulated.
On MECCANO, objects improve SlowFast from 44.9% to 49.0% Top-1, while both affordances reach 49.9%.
Performance is substantially higher with annotated object boxes than with detector outputs, highlighting sensitivity to non-active detections.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the method at test time. A frozen SlowFast expert gives the video probabilities pv . An object detector finds the objects in the candidate frames of the segment. For each detection, a VLM answers whether a hand is manipulating the object, and the interaction filter removes the detections answered with no (red, dashed). Then K frames are selected, and each remaining object becomes a token of crop, class name, position, and affordance features. The affordance is generated by a separate prompt to the same VLM. The object expert applies self-attention to the tokens, averages them, and an MLP gives the probabilities po. Finally, late fusion combines both experts with the weight α. During training, the annotated boxes replace the detector, and the filter is not used.

papers.abstract: We study action-conditioned monitoring of autonomous-vehicle behavior in semantically unusual driving scenes. The target is whether the executed ego action is appropriate for the scene: the same scene can admit both normal and anomalous behavior, so visual unusualness alone does not determine the monitoring label. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) first predicts the scene-required action from an outcome-hidden video window; the monitor then compares that expectation with the realized ego-motion trajectory under an explicit compatibility rule. To study this monitoring task, we contribute a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios spanning both failure polarities (42 derived from documented incidents), a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories, and an exploratory two-stage monitor on that corpus. On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, the two-stage protocol with a fixed T-2.5 s window obtains 83.0% accuracy and anomaly recall 0.773, versus 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage video-only baseline; specificity is 0.880 versus 0.928.
bullets: Targets whether the ego action is appropriate for the scene, not merely whether the scene looks unusual.
Uses a two-stage process: predict the required action from an outcome-hidden video window, then compare it with the realized trajectory using an explicit compatibility rule.
Introduces a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios, including 42 derived from documented incidents, plus a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories.
On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, achieves 83.0% accuracy and 0.773 anomaly recall, compared with 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage baseline.
Specificity is lower than the baseline: 0.880 versus 0.928; evaluation uses a fixed 2.5-second observation window.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is usually studied as frame selection: which few frames should a vision-language model see? We introduce VideoRouteAudit, a controlled audit that separates this choice from two alternatives, injecting non-visual evidence and routing to another answering model. It holds the backbone, frame budget, decoding, prompt and grader fixed while varying one decision at a time. On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling. The largest selection-only estimate is +1.9 pt (95% CI [-1.2,+5.0]) and our cascade is +1.2 pt [-1.7,+4.1]; all are equivalent to uniform within +/-5 pt. The same contrasts are unstable at the n=200 subset scale commonly used: three of four are up to 3.8x larger, one reverses sign, and resampled 200-item subsets reverse the full-bucket effect's sign in 35.8% of draws. The audit also corrects our own first results. The anomaly-domain "+ASR" arms injected no text, so the pooled +4.7 pt gain was selection plus a development prefix. With transcripts, ASR lowers XD-Violence accuracy by 10.0 pt when appended after the question and not at all when placed before it, and lowers UCF-Crime by 13.0 pt either way; on Video-MME, placing it first adds about 4 pt (7 on Qwen2-VL) to uniform sampling and to the cascade alike (post hoc, unadjusted). Swapping the answering model gives the largest contrast (+15.1 pt on MUSIC-AVQA, +33.3 pt on its worst type), but the same audio-visual expert with its soundtrack silenced keeps 92% of the gain (69% with a mismatched soundtrack), so the contrast is mostly a model swap. Code, per-item predictions and scripts that recompute every statistic are available at https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/long-video-qa-audit.
bullets: On all 900 long-bucket Video-MME items, no tested frame selector significantly beats uniform sampling; estimated gains remain within ±5 points.
Results from 200-item subsets are unstable: effects can grow by up to 3.8×, reverse sign, and disagree with the full-bucket effect in 35.8% of resamples.
A claimed anomaly-domain “+ASR” gain was partly caused by a development prefix; transcript placement also changes performance substantially and inconsistently across datasets.
Routing to another answering model produces the largest contrast, but most of its gain persists when the soundtrack is silenced, indicating a model-swap effect rather than selection.
The audit releases code, per-item predictions, and scripts for reproducing all statistics.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach for improving video generation, but its success depends heavily on reliable reward models. Existing methods either map videos directly to opaque scalar scores or generate free-form rationales that are not explicitly optimized as the basis of the final judgment. We propose ArtiVidRM, a verifiable, artifact-as-rubrics video reward model that follows an observe-then-score paradigm. It first identifies visible generation artifacts and organizes them into a structured artifact list, then uses these artifacts as explicit rubrics for quality assessment. This intermediate representation grounds each score in concrete video-level evidence, making the reward more interpretable and informative for optimization. We further introduce a multi-reward reinforcement learning strategy to jointly optimize artifact prediction and quality assessment. The reward decomposes into complementary objectives that evaluate artifact prediction quality, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency, together with a pairwise preference objective that supervises quality ranking through score differences. By jointly optimizing the intermediate artifact representation and the downstream preference prediction, the model learns to produce informative artifact lists while improving the accuracy of video quality assessment. Experiments show that ArtiVidRM achieves state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks, provides effective signals for video diffusion optimization, and enables artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.
bullets: Addresses opaque scalar rewards and ungrounded free-form rationales in video-generation reinforcement learning.
Uses an observe-then-score pipeline: predict a structured list of visible artifacts, then assess quality based on those artifacts.
Jointly optimizes artifact prediction and pairwise quality ranking through multiple reward objectives, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks and useful signals for video diffusion optimization.
Supports artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.

papers.abstract: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Introduces a dual-timeline benchmark for localized manipulations in open-scene, long-form audio-visual videos.
Includes 16,650 pristine–manipulated twin pairs spanning 998 hours and 27 editing configurations.
Zero-shot AV-LLM prompting performs near chance for detection and poorly for temporal localization.
NFSR uses separate audio and visual temporal decoders over frozen AV-LLM features, achieving the best localization in-domain and across three out-of-distribution settings.
The benchmark exposes errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation and is intended for public release with code and model weights.

papers.title: AV-FABLE: Audio-Visual Manipulation Forensics in Long-Form Videos

papers.abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark, comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.
bullets: Targets CoM localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies where visual geometry and tracking are unreliable.
Adapts pretrained V-JEPA features with a temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories.
Introduces HiddenMass Benchmark: 50K simulated MuJoCo trajectories and 63 real-world sequences with calibrated CoM ground truth.
Reduces normalized simulation CoM error from 41.7% to 25.2% and improves real-world physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%.
Zero-shot transfer remains challenging: phase-aware supervision moves predictions toward hidden offsets but can cause overshoot, while phase-agnostic targets may collapse toward centroids.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Qualitative Kinematic Trajectories. A comparison of 2D predicted paths during multiaxis tumbling within a static observation window. (Left) Spatial models (e.g., DINOv2) suffer from visual-kinematic aliasing, tracking high-contrast surface distractors instead of momentum. (Right) STATERA-50K-Crescent successfully isolates the smooth Newtonian parabolic arc of the hidden mass, directionally aligning with the verified Ground Truth despite a Euclidean vector overshoot.

Figure 2: STATERA Architecture. A 16-frame video sequence is processed via a partially-frozen V-JEPA 2.1 backbone. Temporal tubelets are mixed using a 1D Convolution before passing through the Spatial Preservation Decoder. The network bifurcates to output a continuous spatial heatmap (Head A) and a regularizing 1D Z-Depth scalar (Head B).

Figure 6: The Vector Overshoot Artifact. (Left) An architecturally complete model (1K-Anchor) correctly learns to bound the hidden mass phase within realistic 3D physical constraints. (Right) Ablating the absolute 1D Z-Depth regularizer (1K-No-Z-Depth) causes the 2D spatial extractions to lose physical scale constraints, leading to a severe, unregularized Euclidean explosion far beyond the physical boundaries of the rigid body.

Figure 1: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematic Tracking. (Left) The HiddenMass-50K training environment featuring procedurally generated asymmetric masses. (Right) Zero-shot inference on real-world video sequences. While spatial baselines collapse to the visual centroid, STATERA successfully identifies the directional phase of the offset Center of Mass. The prediction pulls away from the visual center along the true kinematic vector (noting an empirical Euclidean overshoot inherent to the 2.5D spatial projection).

Figure 4: Curriculum Label Smoothing. Target probability distributions across training epochs. By mathematical design, at Epoch 0 (κ = 0), both targets initialize as identical broad Gaussian rings (σ = 12.5). Over the curriculum, the phase-agnostic baseline (Sigma) decays into an isotropic impulse (σ = 3.0), omitting phase data. Conversely, the phase-aware SOTA (Crescent) scales its Von Mises angular mask (κ → 50.0), forcing the network to continuously optimize for rotational torque direction.

Figure 5: Visual-Kinematic Aliasing (Bimodal Split). During high-torque rotations where groundtruth phase is highly ambiguous, models trained on static phase-aware targets output high-variance, bimodal probability heatmaps. The network essentially “hedges its bets” between two physically plausible mass locations, resulting in expectation collapse and severe temporal jitter.

Figure 7: HiddenMass Benchmark Profile. The Unified HiddenMass Score (HMS, orange) is calculated as a weighted composite: 25% Kinematic Accuracy, 25% Tracking Stability, and 50% Physics Disentanglement, explicitly penalizing statistical reward-hacking. Low Disentanglement (teal) reveals that DINOv2 and STATERA-50K-Sigma are deceived by visual and heuristic aliasing, defaulting closer to the geometric centroid. STATERA-50K-Crescent actively breaks this heuristic, achieving substantial positive physical disentanglement and securing the highest overall HMS (59.6).

Table 2: Zero-Shot Real-World Transfer (N=63). STATERA-50K-Sigma achieves the lowest spatial and jitter errors. However, unclamped Disentanglement analysis reveals DINOv2 and STATERA50K-Sigma struggle to fully disentangle the offset. STATERA-50K-Crescent remains the only architecture to achieve substantial positive disentanglement toward the hidden mass. Point trackers were evaluated via an idealized Dynamic Surface Centroid Proxy (initializing a uniform point grid around the object’s initial bounding center and gracefully falling back to the geometric center upon track death).
Table 1: In-Domain Simulation Performance (10,000 Sequences). Evaluated on the held-out MuJoCo validation set. Lower is better for all metrics.
Table 3: Temperature Pareto Sweep. The impact of the Soft-Argmax temperature (τ ) on physical capture versus Euclidean error. Evaluated on STATERA-50K-Crescent.

papers.selection_reason: Video representation learning for physical property estimation from motion, fitting video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: STATERA: Hidden Mass Estimation via Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematics using Frozen Temporal Tubelets
papers.tldr: STATERA uses mostly frozen video representations plus a lightweight temporal mixer to estimate hidden centers of mass from monocular motion, achieving strong simulation performance and meaningful zero-shot transfer to real objects.

papers.abstract: Scene Graph Anticipation (SGA) predicts object relationships in future video frames. Continuous-time SGA models evolve each subject-object pair with an independent Neural ODE, so relationships sharing an entity cannot influence one another during integration, and nothing prevents mutually exclusive predictions, such as "sitting on" and "standing on", for the same pair. We introduce CoupledSGA, which links such relationships through a Relationship Interaction Graph with graph attention inside the ODE vector field, and adds a Structural Consistency Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{SC}$) based on a matrix of mutually exclusive predicates. Developing CoupledSGA revealed a limitation of the evaluation protocol. With-Constraint evaluation keeps one predicate per group for each subject-object pair, so its R@K and mR@K cannot capture the within-group violations targeted by $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$: we prove they are unchanged whenever each group's winning predicate and its score are held fixed. We further show that the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ depends on predicate scores rather than ground-truth labels: for two-predicate rules it amplifies the ordering the model already holds, and when all scores in a group are equal it suppresses predicates in more exclusion rules more strongly, explaining why the penalty can lower recall while improving consistency. On Action Genome, activating $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ after two warm-up epochs reduces R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% while lowering the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07% (matched-budget R@20: 40.48% CoupledSGA vs. 44.78% SceneSayerODE). CoupledSGA is a testbed, not a state-of-the-art claim: With-Constraint recall captures the cost of enforcing structural consistency but not the improvement. We recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate for methods that constrain predicate co-activation.
authors: Zeno Nongmaithem, Anushttha Srivastava, Anshit Sinha, Apoorv Sisodia, Suman Chowdhury, Prerana Mukherjee, Rajesh P. Barnwal
bullets: Independent Neural ODEs in continuous-time SGA cannot model interactions among relationships sharing an entity and may produce mutually exclusive predicates together.
CoupledSGA adds graph-attention coupling through a Relationship Interaction Graph and a Structural Consistency Loss based on mutually exclusive predicates.
The authors prove With-Constraint R@K and mR@K cannot reflect within-group violations when each group’s winning predicate and score remain fixed.
On Action Genome, the consistency loss reduces contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07%, but R@20 falls from 42.21% to 35.18%; matched-budget R@20 is 40.48% versus 44.78% for SceneSayerODE.
The paper recommends reporting No-Constraint results with contradiction rates; CoupledSGA is presented as a testbed rather than a state-of-the-art method.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Illustration of the target failure mode; the scores shown are illustrative and are not model outputs. Left: an uncoupled ODE evolves each relationship alone, and nothing in it prevents high scores on mutually exclusive predicates such as sitting on and standing on. papers.selection_reason: Scene graph anticipation for video understanding; introduces structural consistency loss and evaluation critique.
papers.title: Coupled Scene Graph Anticipation: When With-Constraint Recall Hides Structural Inconsistency
papers.tldr: CoupledSGA enforces structurally consistent future scene-graph predictions, sharply reducing predicate contradictions while revealing that standard With-Constraint recall can hide this trade-off.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
authors: Shuai Dong, Kanghui Tian, Linghan Chen, Wenqi Shao, Hongrui Wu, Haowen Hou, Yongfu Zhu, Xuehui Wang, Ziyue Wang, Wenpu Liu, Weichu Xie, Yuqi Xu, Congcong Wang, Kaiwen Tuo, Caoyuan Ma, Taiqiang Wu, Ji Zhao, Wenzheng Chang, Dianyi Wang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei, Yu Qiao, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Streaming video models must repeatedly choose whether to respond or keep observing, but trajectory-level credit can reinforce redundancy or suppress useful follow-ups.
TurnWise computes turn-level group-relative advantages from silence-completed prefix scores and each decision’s remaining return.
Turn-mean policy optimization gives response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of token output length.
The framework requires neither a learned critic nor additional rollouts.
Experiments report improved performance over prior RL methods for streaming video understanding.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overview of TurnWise. Given streaming video input x, user queries, dialogue history, and an observation plan, the policy samples a group of trajectories {τi}Gi=1. TurnWise converts trajectory rewards Ri into group-relative remaining-return advantages Âi,t through silence-completed prefix scoring. Turn-mean aggregation then gives every response-or-wait decision equal weight in the trajectory loss Li.

Fig. 1 Shared advantages can reinforce redundant replies. GRPO assigns one trajectory-level advantage to all turns, so later repetitions may inherit positive credit from earlier successes. TurnWise subtracts group-relative accrued reward before each decision, allowing later turns to receive credit according to their remaining return. The dialogue is illustrative. The advantage plot uses recorded TurnWise advantages and the corresponding GRPO counterfactual.

Fig. 4 Turn-level credit assigns negative advantages to 59.83% of repetitive replies with positive global advantages (432 of 722). Both allocations use the same sampled groups from Qwen2.5-VL-3B training, using complete trajectories with full credit correction at α = 1. Panel a shows advantage density over 84,184 decisions. Turn advantages are clipped to ±5 as in training. The dashed diagonal marks unchanged allocation. Panel b shows advantage signs for all 2,972 Judge-labeled repetitive replies in this cohort.

Fig. 3 TurnWise achieves higher late-stage reward with fewer redundant replies relative to creditonly optimization. Panel a shows reward, panel b shows reply-normalized repetition penalty magnitude, and panel c shows non-silent decision fraction. Faint traces are batch means. Solid curves are trailing 20-update averages. Gray shading marks credit warmup.

papers.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
papers.tldr: TurnWise improves streaming video RL by assigning credit to each response-or-wait decision instead of sharing one advantage across the entire trajectory.

papers.abstract: Online reasoning video segmentation (Online RVS) requires a model to segment query-referred objects as a video streams in, using only the frames observed so far. Existing formulations largely assume a fixed target set throughout the video, overlooking a fundamental property of streaming reasoning: as new events occur, the objects that satisfy a query may change over time. To address this, we propose a new task, Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation (GRVS), where the target set depends on query-relevant events accumulated over the observed video history. As new evidence accumulates, the target set can evolve from empty to one or multiple objects, requiring a model to continuously maintain target validity while localizing the valid objects currently in view. To evaluate GRVS, we build Isekai, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 videos and 197 queries across 11 temporal query families, with 12,569 scoring points whose target sets are causally annotated over time. We further propose Sekai, an online framework with two complementary components: an Event Memory Reasoner (EMR) that maintains query-relevant events and evolving target states in structured memory, and a Memory-Grounded Decoder (MGD) that identifies valid targets from this memory and localizes them in the current frame. Experiments show that Sekai significantly outperforms existing online RVS methods, achieving 50.33 J&F and improving over the strongest baseline by 3.2 points. Code, example annotations, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zenastangbi/Sekai.
authors: Zhengtao Liu, Jinrong Xu, Shiu-Hong Kao, Huixin Sun, Yicong Li
bullets: Problem: Existing online video segmentation assumes a fixed target set, while streaming events can change which objects satisfy a query.
Method: The Event Memory Reasoner maintains query-relevant events and target states; the Memory-Grounded Decoder selects and segments valid objects in each current frame.
Benchmark: Isekai contains 60 videos, 197 queries, 11 temporal query families, and causally annotated target states across 12,569 scoring points.
Result: Sekai achieves 50.33 J&F, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.2 points.
Scope: The task focuses on online, causal reasoning where target sets may evolve from empty to one or multiple objects.

papers.abstract: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.
authors: Yunhao Huang, Kaushik Bhargav Sivangi, Tianyi Yu, Fani Deligianni
bullets: Targets the trade-off among pose localisation, temporal motion quality, and energy use in non-event-driven video.
Uses a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder for spatial evidence and MAM to estimate joint motion, align past heatmaps, and fuse them adaptively with current predictions.
Evaluated on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset using localisation, motion-error, and estimated arithmetic-energy metrics.
Compared with an architecture-matched ANN using MAM, it reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% with a 1.12-point PCK_HB(0.5) decrease.
Adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46%, respectively, with minimal computational and parameter overhead.
