papers.title: SpikePose: Lightweight Video Human Pose Estimation
papers.tldr: SpikePose delivers energy-efficient video pose estimation by combining a lightweight spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory, retaining near-ANN accuracy while improving motion quality.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained action understanding requires vision-language models to ground what an agent does, how it acts, and why it acts in spatio-temporal evidence. However, richer supervision can backfire: fine-tuned models may generate detailed action descriptions grounded in static scenes and salient objects rather than motion, a failure we call Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH). To mitigate EGAH, we propose Staged Attention Rectification and Reinforcement (STARR), an action-centric video-text alignment framework that breaks scene-action shortcuts through Action-Environment Dissociation and reinforces action-focused grounding with an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization. We further construct FineActionR&R, combining temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points over its base model and achieves 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench. Qualitative comparisons further indicate more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.
authors: Zhiliang Zhu, Jiazheng Huang, Dawei Zhao
bullets: Fine-grained vision-language models can hallucinate actions from static scenes and salient objects, termed Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH).
STARR uses Action-Environment Dissociation to break scene-action shortcuts and an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization to reinforce action-focused grounding.
FineActionR&R combines temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data.
Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points and reaches 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench.
Qualitative results suggest more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Staged Attention Rectification and Reinforcement method for fine-grained action understanding. (a) Attention Rectification: SFT is used to train on distractor videos that combine an action clip with irrelevant backgrounds, forcing the model to focus on true action regions. (b) Attention Consistency Reinforcement: GRPO optimizes a reward encouraging stable attention on key action-relevant visual tokens throughout generation.

Figure 1: Illustration of Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination. (a) VLM often generate accurate environment descriptions but incorrect action ones. During SFT, the model develops a strong tendency to anchor action predictions on easily perceived static backgrounds rather than true spatio-temporal evidence, leading to systematically incorrect action descriptions even when its environment descriptions remain accurate. papers.abstract: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points. NER thus enables partial transfer from text to video, while more reliable grounding will likely require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.
authors: Divyanshu Mishra, Sabine Sternig, Rakshith Shetty, Erhan Gundogdu
bullets: Motivation: avoid costly paired video-text data and precise temporal annotations by training solely on textual video descriptions.
Method: adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on 134K time-indexed text sequences using CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, then provide video only at inference.
LLM2CLIP transfers better than CLIP, achieving 61.54 vs. 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid.
Nearest Entity Replacement maps each frame to nearby text-entity embeddings, improving mtIoU to 14.45 on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights.
Scope: transfer remains partial, indicating that better-aligned text and visual encoders are needed for reliable grounding.

papers.abstract: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.
authors: Yifan Wang, Junyu Lu, Shun Zhang, Chaozhuo Li, Fanliang Bu, Rong Yin, Lingbin Bu, Changrong Min, Peng Chen
bullets: MechScam contains 6,614 scam and similar non-scam videos spanning diverse scam mechanisms and categories.
It includes video-supported explanations, scam-element/context annotations, and misleading arguments based on genuine evidence.
ScamCourt uses prosecution and defense debaters plus a citation-verifying judge to evaluate competing claims.
Experiments find that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle with scam-versus-advertisement discrimination, while ScamCourt reduces false positives and resists misleading arguments.
The work targets more reliable and interpretable web scam video detection; its scope is defined by the benchmark’s annotated mechanisms and categories.

papers.abstract: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, with progress driven largely by scaling model size and omni training data. We ask whether a model needs to hear the audio directly at all, and present SleuthVLM, an agent harness built on a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech will be transcribed into text, and the VLM will sleuth the video on its own without any predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, SleuthVLM achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it also tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8%}; with an open-source 27B VLM, it beats all open-source omni models. We draw three findings: SleuthVLM beats a model that glances; hearing is not the bottleneck, agentic ability is; omni understanding needs better agentic ability, not just more omni data for modality alignment. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding. Omni understanding needs better agents, not just bigger models that hear.
authors: Peiran Wu, Fangfei Gou, Zhaoxi Mu, Changhao Zhang, Jian Liu, Weiqiang Wang, Yuntao Wang, Yuanchun Shi, Junxiao Shen
bullets: Challenges the assumption that omni video models must directly hear audio.
Uses a VLM agent that receives speech as text and autonomously investigates video without a predefined workflow.
Achieves 75.0% average accuracy across four omni benchmarks and 77.8% on Video-MME-v2, as reported in the abstract.
With an open-source 27B VLM, outperforms all open-source omni models evaluated.
Concludes that improving agentic reasoning may be more valuable than simply scaling omni data or model size.

papers.abstract: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.
authors: Varun A. Paturkar, Shankar Gangisetty, C. V. Jawahar
bullets: Contains 949 maneuver clips and trajectory annotations for more than 31,000 agents, including over 16,000 motorized two-wheelers.
Supports Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP), with challenge-aware annotations for ego-motion, weak structure, and occlusion.
Video backbones achieve most of their full-observation accuracy early, while zero-shot VLMs generally remain near simple baselines.
LoRA adaptation substantially improves maneuver anticipation but does not close the gap with conventional models for trajectory prediction.
Forecasting is hardest during left turns and under dynamic ego-motion across all evaluated models.

papers.title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic
papers.tldr: MotoVerse introduces a benchmark for predicting MTW rider maneuvers and surrounding-agent trajectories in dense, unstructured traffic from an ego-centric viewpoint.

papers.abstract: Video editors often work with large collections of fragmented footage and must select and organize relevant clips into a coherent story. However, many existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and aim to preserve its original narrative and temporal structure. In this paper, we introduce Clips2Story, a training-free, LLM-based pipeline that enables users to create keyword-specified short videos from a pool of video clips. Given a pool of clips and a user-specified keyword, we first extract text-based multimodal descriptors for each clip and retrieve the clips most relevant to the keyword. We then provide the textual descriptors of these candidate clips to an LLM, which selects and arranges them into an editable storyboard with connective narrations. Finally, we assemble the selected clips and retrieve accompanying visuals for the narrations to compose the output video. To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.
authors: Junnuo Wang, Weihan Xu, Hao-Wen Dong
bullets: Targets editing fragmented, unordered footage into user-specified short videos.
Extracts textual multimodal descriptors, retrieves keyword-relevant clips, and supplies them to an LLM.
The LLM selects and orders clips into an editable storyboard with connective narration.
The system assembles the clips and retrieves visuals to accompany the generated narrations.

papers.abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.
authors: Rohit Mohan, Maximilian Luz, Swarnava Chowdhury, Yao Lu, Florian Drews, Thomas N\"urnberg, Yakov Miron, Federico Tombari, Stefano Gasperini, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses the gap between image-level open-set benchmarks and closed-set panoramic tracking benchmarks.
Builds on real Waymo sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets and temporally cross-view consistent annotations.
Provides unknown-object tracks, camera masks, and auxiliary LiDAR observations for evaluation.
Defines tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking.
Benchmark results show current methods struggle with unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views.

papers.abstract: Many temporal approaches for video recognition rely on explicit cross-channel aggregation projections, which have quadratic complexity in the number of channels, introducing significant computational overhead. In addition, the spatio-temporal representation used for video recognition is biased either toward local order interactions (for CNNs) or toward global order interactions (for transformers). Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, our method introduces two complementary contributions to tackle these problems. First, for the temporal modelling, we introduce parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation, which is linear in the number of channels, inducing a considerable computational reduction. Second, we propose a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions, which allows a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing the computational cost. By combining these two contributions, our proposed VideoMogaNet achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches across multiple video benchmarks (UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, Diving48), while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.
authors: Kevin D. Nguetche, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli
bullets: Targets the quadratic channel cost of explicit cross-channel aggregation in temporal video models.
Uses parallel multi-order depthwise-only convolutions with implicit gating-based aggregation for linear channel complexity.
Introduces dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions to improve representation without added computational cost.
Matches or exceeds state-of-the-art action-recognition performance across UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, and Diving48.
Scope: focuses on reducing temporal modeling overhead while balancing local and global order interactions.

The architecture demonstrates precise focus on discriminative spatial regions where fine-grained object transformations occur (e.g., hand movements, object manipulations), while maintaining temporal consistency through multi-order temporal modulation (MOTM). Highlighted regions show the model’s ability to capture both spatial part-whole compositions via SMixer (SMOGA) and temporal dynamics via MOTM, validating the synergistic coordination between spatial and temporal modalities for fine-grained action understanding.

papers.abstract: Existing multimodal video highlight detectors typically assume that visual, audio, and textual streams are continuously available. In practice, however, inputs may suffer from localized frame missingness or complete-stream outage. We formulate this robustness challenge along two dimensions: temporal missingness, where frames are missing independently in each modality, and stream-level missingness, where one modality is unavailable throughout a video. Moreover, we find that the mean squared error (MSE) loss is misaligned with both the evaluation metrics and the peak-driven nature of highlights. Therefore, we propose Temporal-Stream Modality Dropout (TSMD), which combines structured missingness simulation with a joint objective comprising pointwise MSE, per-video Pearson correlation, and peak-oriented RankNet loss terms. TSMD has three variants: temporal, stream-level, and mixed dropout. On the MoSu and Mr. HiSum datasets, TSMD-Temporal improves mAP@15 by 7.06 and 3.41 points over TripleSumm under 50% independent temporal removal, whereas TSMD-Stream performs the best under complete-stream removal. TSMD-Mix retains most of these complementary benefits and ranks the best or the second-best across the evaluated temporal and stream-level conditions.
bullets: Addresses two missing-input settings: independent temporal frame loss and complete stream outage.
Uses Temporal-Stream Modality Dropout with temporal, stream-level, and mixed variants.
Combines pointwise MSE, per-video Pearson correlation, and peak-oriented RankNet losses.
On MoSu and Mr. HiSum, TSMD-Temporal improves mAP@15 under 50% temporal removal, while TSMD-Stream performs best for complete-stream removal.
TSMD-Mix ranks among the best across both missingness conditions.

papers.abstract: Tracking-by-propagation (TBP) methods perform end-to-end multi-object tracking by propagating track queries across frames, jointly handling detection and identity association without heuristic post-processing while naturally modeling temporal information. However, as detection and association are tightly coupled, detection queries in TBP are expected to discover currently untracked objects and provide complementary current-frame evidence for challenging tracks whose queries and identities are retained. Existing methods largely inherit detection-query formation from single-frame detection and construct such queries before the decoder with little awareness of trajectory states. Consequently, currently untracked objects may be missed, while challenging tracked objects with reduced visibility under occlusion may lack complementary evidence, causing association failures or duplicate responses. To address these issues, we propose TAQ-MOTR, a tracking-aware detection query formation framework that employs a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator (HQG) to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory. By conditioning detection queries on trajectory states, TAQ-MOTR adapts them to \rev{the discovery of currently untracked objects and tracked-object complementation We further introduce a training-only auxiliary detection branch whose one-to-one label assignment is decoupled from that of the main tracking branch, providing additional detection supervision to strengthen the shared HQG and decoder for the discovery of currently untracked objects. TAQ-MOTR improves performance on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and BFT, achieving 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set. Code is available at https://github.com/Magicmiya/TAQ-MOTR
authors: Hanyang Liu, Hong Zhang, Ding Yuan, Yang Han, Yifan Yang
bullets: Addresses missed untracked objects and association failures for occluded or difficult tracks in tracking-by-propagation methods.
Uses a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory.
Adds a training-only auxiliary detection branch with independently assigned labels to strengthen query and decoder learning.
Reports 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set, with improvements also reported on SportsMOT and BFT.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of TAQ-MOTR. TAQ-MOTR forms tracking-aware detection queries before decoding. In the main tracking branch, HQG uses image-based detection proposals as queries and reads track memory and learnable memory as keys/values. The generated detection queries are concatenated with updated track queries and jointly decoded. During training, an auxiliary detection branch shares the detection proposals and HQG layers but removes track memory, producing a separate detection-query group supervised by all current-frame objects. Attention masks isolate this auxiliary group from the main query groups. The right panel shows an HQG layer.

Figure 3: Prior carriers used in HQG. Learnable memory provides learnable detection priors that are independent of specific trajectories. Track memory encodes existing trajectory states from propagated track queries, including content, position, and disappearance-time information. Detection proposals provide current-frame object evidence and coarse spatial priors.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.
authors: Christian Pipal, Eva-Maria Vogel, Morgan Wack
bullets: The study examines how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement validity in MLLM-based video analysis.
Across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets, no input representation consistently performs best.
Native-video macro-F1 varies little across models (.70–.77), while extracted-text performance varies more widely (.52–.80).
Combining modalities rarely improves classification, and higher accuracy does not reliably yield human-aligned regression or prevalence estimates.
Even with each model’s best deployable representation, 45% of prevalence estimates differed from human-coded benchmarks by more than ten percentage points.

papers.abstract: Clustering faces by identity in long, continuous video streams is a challenging task that serves as a building block for human-centric video analysis. The majority of existing face clustering models are offline, i.e., they assume the entire data to be available altogether. In many practical scenarios, however, the entire data is either unavailable or poses computational challenges to be processed in its entirety. A handful of online methods that exist rely on geometric visual features and simple thresholding techniques, which fail when the faces exhibit significant appearance variations in long, unconstrained videos. To this end, we present VISTA, the first vision language framework for online face clustering in long videos. VISTA leverages semantic reasoning in a controlled, uncertainty aware fashion to maintain both high cluster purity and long range identity continuity. This makes it robust to the variations in illumination, pose, and costume changes that the faces and characters exhibit in long real world videos. Extensive experiments on the VPCD benchmark dataset (with 15 full episodes from The Big Bang Theory [2007-2019], Buffy the Vampire Slayer [1997-2003], and Sherlock [2010-2017]) demonstrate that VISTA achieves a robust precision and recall balance, consistently improving over the strongest matched online unsupervised baseline (COFC) under identical detector, embeddings, and evaluation protocol. Code and supplementary material: https://github.com/SkyJiashu/VISTA.
authors: Jiashu Liao, Joanne Garde-Hansen, Sanjay Sharma, Tanaya Guha
bullets: Addresses the need for online face clustering when complete video streams cannot be processed offline.
Combines visual features with controlled semantic reasoning to maintain cluster purity and long-range identity consistency.
Targets challenging variations in illumination, pose, and costumes across unconstrained videos.
Evaluated on 15 full episodes from three TV series in the VPCD benchmark.
Consistently improves the precision–recall balance over the matched online unsupervised COFC baseline under the same protocol.

papers.abstract: Long instructional videos are increasingly used in medical education, industrial training, and procedural knowledge transfer, yet their evidence is often incomplete or unreliable: subtitles may be missing, ASR noisy, OCR sparse, and decisive actions briefly shown without narration. Existing VideoQA systems typically return labels or free-form text, making answer support difficult to inspect. We study Long Video Moment Question Answering (LVMQA), where a system returns timestamped answer-supporting evidence. We propose EP-LVMQA, an evidence-preserving coarse-to-fine framework comprising an Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Evidence Timeline, a Coarse Evidence Planner, and an Evidence-Conditioned Fine Localizer. An evidence card transfers planner scores, matched cues, source-confidence proxies, modality-specific evidence, neighboring context, and a temporal prior between the latter two modules. On MedVidQA, EP-LVMQA achieves 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, improving the strongest non-ours results by 6.3 and 5.1 points. It raises Suff.@2 and Ver.@2 to 25.4 and 22.6, gains of 9.5 and 8.8 points. Under matched low-quality perturbations, average relative degradation is reduced from the strongest non-ours value of 14.6% to 11.1%. On Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights, EP-LVMQA remains broadly comparable to established task-specific localization methods.
authors: Guoning Chen, Zhexun Hu, Yifan Wei, Yixuan Weng, Bin Li, Yufei Zhao
bullets: Targets LVMQA when subtitles, ASR, OCR, or visual evidence are incomplete and unreliable.

Transfers planner scores, matched cues, source-confidence proxies, modality evidence, context, and temporal priors via an evidence card.
On MedVidQA, reports 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, with improved sufficiency and verifiability scores over the strongest non-ours results.
Under matched low-quality perturbations, degradation decreases to 11.1%; performance remains broadly comparable on Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering. Existing solutions either require costly retraining or introduce inefficient multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time. In this work, we show that temporal evidence is already encoded in Video-LLM hidden representations but is not fully exploited during standard inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), a training-free framework that recovers suppressed temporal evidence through analytical hidden-state manipulation in a single forward pass. SPOD consists of two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis (FDA), which identifies salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace (TDS), which constructs orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. By decomposing final hidden states into temporal, prior, and residual components and rescaling them independently, SPOD enhances dynamic information, suppresses static appearance bias, and preserves complementary information. Experiments on VidHalluc, EventHallusion, and VideoMMMU show that SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures while retaining near-vanilla inference efficiency. These results suggest that improving temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend not only on additional supervision, but also on recovering temporal evidence already present in their internal representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/VioAgnes/SPOD.

papers.abstract: Most video anomaly understanding (VAU) systems still infer anomaly judgments from evidence collected in a feed-forward way under predefined rules, typically sampled frames, or events clustered from such frames. This protocol fails when the collected evidence is incomplete under imperfect predefined rules, because once reasoning begins the model can no longer search for the missing evidence. We address this limitation with SEEK-VAU, which reframes VAU as an agentic search-and-verify interaction protocol under a bounded search budget: instead of passively reasoning over pre-collected evidence, the policy actively gathers evidence across the three stages of an anomaly event chain (precursor, trigger, and aftermath) and verifies its sufficiency before finalization, turning event-chain completeness into an explicit design rather than an outcome of predefined rules. A bounded budget caps the cost of this search, but does not by itself teach the policy where to look or when to stop. To make this behavior learnable, we introduce evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV), which rewards selected evidence that remains supportive, compact, and necessary under counterfactual verification. We further introduce SEEK-Bench, featuring video-level episodes with temporal interval annotations, semantic QA and event-chain stage labels. Together, SEEK-VAU and SEEK-Bench establish a strong foundation for evidence-faithful and actively verifiable VAU.
authors: Minghe Wang, Weijun Zeng, Dapeng Luo, Xinyue Wang, Nong Sang
bullets: Addresses incomplete evidence caused by feed-forward systems that rely on predefined frame or event sampling.
Uses an agentic search-and-verify protocol covering precursor, trigger, and aftermath stages.

Applies a bounded search budget to control search cost.
Introduces SEEK-Bench with temporal intervals, semantic questions and answers, and event-chain stage labels.

papers.abstract: Audio-based piano transcription is hampered by the sustain pedal and by noisy or missing soundtracks, problems that video-only transcription avoids, since a top-view video shows directly when each key is pressed and released. Most visual transcription networks, however, describe the whole keyboard with one global feature vector and must learn where each key is. In this paper, we propose KeyWise, a lightweight per-key architecture that exploits the known geometry of the keyboard instead of learning it. The rectified keyboard is divided into 88 equal tiles that serve as regions of interest (ROIs), and one small recurrent network, shared by all keys, follows each key over time. On PianoVAM, KeyWise reaches the onset accuracy of the state-of-the-art V2N (95.0% vs. 94.7% onset F1 at 50 ms and 97.8% vs. 97.0% at 100 ms) with 1.3 M instead of 28.2 M parameters, and it runs 4.7 times faster on the same GPU. At 100 ms, it is also significantly more accurate when the key releases (97.0% vs. 95.5% F1) or the velocities (89.4% vs. 84.5% F1) must be correct as well. On PianoYT, KeyWise pre-trained on PianoVAM reaches 69.4% onset F1 at 100 ms, comparable to the best published result, although it needs fine-tuning for new recording conditions.
authors: Anastasios Chatzigiannis, Natalia Panagou, Maria Koziri
bullets: Avoids audio issues such as sustain-pedal ambiguity and missing or noisy soundtracks by using top-view video.

Transfers to PianoYT with comparable published onset accuracy, but requires fine-tuning for new recording conditions.

papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) aims to infer and segment target objects specified by reasoning queries in videos. Existing methods typically first infer the target and generate a few segmentation tokens for it, which are then fed into a mask decoder for mask prediction. However, such segmentation tokens tend to be both semantically monotonous and spatially ambiguous, making them largely insufficient to represent the target to guide mask prediction. In this paper, we propose an explicit visual object grounding framework for VRS. Specifically, we first propose a spatial-aware prompt generation and refinement scheme, in which we query a multimodal large language model to generate explicit spatial prompts (i.e., bounding box and point set) for the target and then refine them through multi-step dialogue. Furthermore, we introduce a query diversification and alignment module to generate auxiliary queries that describe the same target from different perspectives. We then enforce cross-query consistency between their predicted spatial prompts to alleviate the training bias caused by query limitations. Finally, we select several reliable frames using a prompt-based keyframe selection strategy to support mask decoding and propagation. Extensive experiments on eight datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/viscom-tongji/EVOG.
authors: Jun Huang, Junyang Zhang, Zijie Yue, Bingkun Wang, Yong Luo, Miaojing Shi

Reports significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across eight datasets.

papers.abstract: Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) detects and separates dynamic objects from the static background in a video, which plays a fundamental role in dynamic-scene understanding. Most MOS methods rely on pure visual motion cues alone, such as optical flow or point tracks, which is inherently ambiguous due to the compounded camera and object motions as well as motion-induced appearance changes, e.g. shadows and reflections. Naive fusion of additional information such as depth and semantics, however, cannot leverage their complementarity to the fullest extent. We therefore propose DynOSeg, a novel MOS approach that takes on a two-stage fusion structure. DynOSeg first combines a geometry-aware residual map and depth encoding into a geometric representation of motion, delineating camera motions and object dynamics. We then further incorporate semantic features to refine object understanding. We have additionally curated a diverse training corpus including CARLA-MOS, a new synthetic urban-driving dataset for MOS training. Our experiments show that DynOSeg consistently outperforms published state-of-the-art MOS methods across a diverse range of datasets. Our code and pretrained models can be found at https://github.com/ACFR-RPG/DynOSeg
authors: Xu Han, Yiduo Wang, Yiran Wang, Viorela Ila
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in visual-motion-only MOS caused by camera motion, object motion, shadows, and reflections.
Uses two-stage fusion: geometry-aware residuals with depth first, followed by semantic features for object refinement.
Introduces CARLA-MOS, a diverse synthetic urban-driving training corpus.
Reports consistent gains over published state-of-the-art MOS methods across diverse datasets.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.

papers.abstract: The advancement of multimodal learning is heavily constrained by the scarcity and high annotation cost of high-quality instruction data. While raw videos offer an abundant and dynamic source of visual knowledge, transforming them into precise instruction data remains highly challenging. To bridge this gap, we present VidUEU-Agent, an automated pipeline that synthesizes instruction data from raw videos for multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks. VidUEU-Agent follows a four-stage pipeline: it performs global perception to filter low-quality shots, mines keyframes and multimodal signals, constructs metadata and routes the metadata to synthesize instruction samples. More importantly, our agent framework can autonomously iterate the data distribution based on downstream training results, thereby optimizing data quality, balance, and training effectiveness. Scaling this pipeline, we construct VidUEU-100K, a large-scale dataset of 100K training samples spanning multiple domains and tasks, providing a robust foundation for developing comprehensive multimodal capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning baseline models on VidUEU-100K yields significant and consistent performance gains across diverse representative benchmarks, validating the effectiveness of our proposed agent framework and dataset.
authors: Tengju Ru, Weitong Lian, Zecong Tang, Lingyi Meng, Haoran Li, Zhejun Cui, Yichen Zhu, Hangshuo Cao, Qi Kang, Yechi Liu, Kaixuan Wang, Yu-Jie Yuan, Chunwei Wang, Yu Zhang, Bo Dai
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and high annotation cost of multimodal instruction data.
Uses a four-stage pipeline: quality filtering, keyframe and multimodal-signal mining, metadata construction, and instruction synthesis.
Autonomously refines the data distribution using downstream training results to improve quality, balance, and effectiveness.
Produces VidUEU-100K, a 100K-sample dataset spanning multiple domains and tasks.
Fine-tuning baseline models on VidUEU-100K brings significant and consistent gains across diverse benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multi-instance partial-label learning (MIPL) addresses inexact supervision in both the instance and label spaces, which can be applied to video classification. However, bag-level labels do not explicitly supervise the correspondence between candidate classes and temporal evidence. We propose {\ours}, which couples label disambiguation with temporal evidence allocation through a joint class--time assignment. Occupancy-regularized spherical matching associates contextualized video features while learning nonuniform temporal mass and discouraging excessive concentration. During training, candidate-restricted inference recomputes the assignment within the candidate label set. A dual-marginal KL projection then constructs a structured teacher that incorporates momentum-refined class beliefs while preserving the proposal's temporal occupancy. A single plan-level KL objective aligns the full-space predictor with this teacher. Our analysis characterizes when candidate re-solving differs from masking and shows that, under the stated construction, the joint objective decomposes into class-marginal and class-conditional temporal supervision. We construct VCMIPL benchmarks from Breakfast, DoTA, and FineAction using model-generated candidate labels and evaluate the method across four feature representations. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that PIVOTMIPL outperforms existing MIPL algorithms in both effectiveness and efficiency.
bullets: Addresses weak supervision where videos have candidate labels but unclear class-to-time correspondence.
Uses occupancy-regularized spherical matching to assign contextualized video features to classes and learn nonuniform temporal importance.
Re-solves assignments within candidate labels and applies dual-marginal KL projection to create structured teaching targets.
Optimizes a plan-level KL objective that decomposes into class-level and class-conditional temporal supervision.
On VCMIPL benchmarks from Breakfast, DoTA, and FineAction across four feature types, it outperforms existing MIPL methods in effectiveness and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Physical parameter estimation from video aims to recover the parameters of a known family of governing dynamical equations from pixel observations. Existing identifiability theory for this setting has focused on linear time-invariant (LTI) second-order systems, leaving open what can be identified for nonlinear scalar dynamics. We develop an identifiability theory for nonlinear scalar second-order ODEs, organized by how their velocity dependence interacts with changes of the learned state coordinate. Under a shared non-collapsed state map and explicit same-state velocity-coverage conditions, we show that parameter identifiability depends on the ODE family: some parameters are uniquely identifiable, while in other families only invariant parameter combinations are identifiable or external physical calibration is required. For laws that are at most linear in velocity, compatibility forces affine coordinate alignment, yielding explicit parameter relations, invariants, and calibration conditions. This affine conclusion extends to broader finite velocity-feature families when coordinate curvature can be separated from the declared velocity dependence. For families admitting a squared-velocity term, nonlinear coordinate ambiguity can remain; a law-derived normalization instead enables affine comparison between canonical laws. Experiments on synthetic systems and real pendulum and free-fall videos support the predicted parameter relations, coverage effects, and calibration requirements.
bullets: Addresses the gap between existing LTI theory and nonlinear scalar dynamics observed through pixels.
Identifiability depends on velocity dependence, state-coordinate transformations, and sufficient same-state velocity coverage.
For laws at most linear in velocity, compatible coordinate maps are affine, giving explicit parameter relations, invariants, and calibration conditions.
Squared-velocity laws can retain nonlinear coordinate ambiguity; a law-derived normalization enables affine comparison.
Synthetic, pendulum, and free-fall experiments support the predicted identifiability and calibration behavior.

papers.abstract: Learning from human data offers a scalable path toward embodied intelligence, yet it requires models to accurately understand fine-grained human actions from egocentric observations. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association. We introduce EgoActionBench, a benchmark that represents continuous human manipulation as temporally localized atomic actions associated with the left hand, right hand, or both hands. EgoActionBench contains 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined action annotations. To evaluate such dense predictions, we propose an evaluation protocol that retrieves temporally eligible candidates, selects a prediction by content agreement, and scores semantic fidelity and temporal overlap alongside action precision and recall, jointly capturing what happens, when it happens, and which hand performs it. We benchmark 20 baseline models and systems on EgoActionBench and further adapt two backbones, Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on automatically annotated training episodes. EgoAction improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two backbones, and both adapted models outperform all open-source baselines. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations of current models in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association, highlighting the gap between general video understanding and the action understanding required for embodied intelligence.
bullets: Introduces 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined annotations of temporally localized atomic actions linked to the left hand, right hand, or both.
Proposes an evaluation protocol measuring semantic fidelity, temporal overlap, action precision, and recall.
Benchmarks 20 models and systems, including adapted Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B backbones.
Supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two adapted backbones.
Finds persistent limitations in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of EgoAction. Continuous egocentric video is represented as temporally localized atomic actions on left-hand, right-hand, and both-hands tracks (top). The bottom-left example highlights the action verb, manipulated object, and tool. Adjacent frames illustrate the start and end boundaries of a joint action (bottom right).

Figure 4 EgoAction evaluation pipeline. For each ground-truth action, temporal overlap and hand-track compatibility determine the eligible candidates. Positive field-level semantic agreement selects one prediction, whose original caption, interval, and hand label are used to compute Semantic and temporal IoU. These scores are averaged separately over ground-truth actions with completed evaluations.

papers.abstract: Multimodal retrieval must integrate complementary evidence from views that may be missing, noisy, or unequally informative. When a sample provides limited reliable evidence, learning from its views alone can hinder the acquisition of useful retrieval representations. Semantically related training samples may provide complementary observations, yet existing volume-based objectives jointly align modalities within each sample without explicitly enabling information exchange across samples. We therefore propose a training-time hypergraph fusion framework that connects observed modalities both within samples and across semantically related samples, allowing representation learning to draw on evidence beyond an individual sample while leaving the retrieval pipeline unchanged at inference. The framework includes HyVol as a special case and introduces two configurations: wHyVol learns view contribution weights and symmetric semantic affinities, whereas wRHG additionally models typed interactions and participant roles through relational propagation. Missing modalities are omitted rather than imputed, and the hypergraph is discarded after training, incurring no additional inference cost. Experiments on eleven zero-shot video-text and audio-text retrieval benchmarks demonstrate broad improvements with both GRAM and HyperGRAM. Across 17 video benchmark-modality settings evaluated in both retrieval directions, wRHG outperforms GRAM in all 34 comparisons and HyperGRAM in 33 of 34. Mean text-to-video R@1 increases from 63.4 to 68.2 with GRAM and from 64.8 to 68.4 with HyperGRAM, while the largest video-to-text gain reaches 13.3 percentage points on ActivityNet. Under missing-modality evaluation, both weighted configurations retain positive text-to-video gains over GRAM across seven benchmarks at every evaluated missingness rate, even when 90% of clips lack one modality.
bullets: Addresses noisy, missing, or unevenly informative modalities and the limits of per-sample alignment.
Connects modalities within samples and across semantically related samples through hypergraph regularization.
wHyVol learns view weights and semantic affinities; wRHG further models typed interactions and participant roles.
Improves retrieval broadly across 11 zero-shot video-text and audio-text benchmarks, with no added inference cost.
Maintains positive gains under missing-modality conditions, including when 90% of clips lack one modality.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) Existing methods score each clip alone: a clip’s score depends only on the caption and the clip’s own views, and every other clip in the batch, even a related one, is pushed apart as a negative. (b) Our training-time hypergraph: observed views form vertices, document hyperedges group the views of each clip, and caption-guided semantic hyperedges connect related clips through same-modality and cross-modality links; missing views have no vertex and are not imputed, and each vertex receives a learned reliability weight. (c) At test time the hypergraph is removed: each clip is encoded and scored independently with the original backbone score, so the inference cost equals that of the backbone.

Figure 2: Overview of training-time hypergraph refinement. Each observed modality becomes a weighted vertex, and stop-gradient captions connect semantically related candidates through mutual top-k neighbors. Information is then exchanged either by weighted additive propagation (WHYVOL) or by typed relational messages (WRHG), and the refined embeddings are scored by the unchanged GRAM/HYPERGRAM objective. The hypergraph is used only during training and is removed at inference.

papers.abstract: Fingerspelling - the sequential signing of letters that compose proper names, technical terms, and out-of-vocabulary words - is an integral component of any sign language. Despite Russian Sign Language (RSL) being used by more than 150,000 native signers, no public fingerspelling dataset for RSL exists, in contrast to American, British, German, and several other sign languages. We introduce Znaki the first open RSL fingerspelling dataset: 37,252 video recordings (35.4 hours) of 1,593 unique sequences - proper names sampled from 16 domain categories - recorded by 68 native RSL signers (37 Deaf, 29 hard-of-hearing, and 2 certified interpreters) through a crowdsourcing pipeline with a two-stage signer qualification procedure and expert validation. The dataset covers all 33 Cyrillic handshapes, and its letter-frequency distribution matches the Russian National Corpus. As reference points for future research, we establish two baselines adapted from American Sign Language fingerspelling recognition: a Squeezeformer-based encoder-decoder, reaching a character-level accuracy ($1-\mathrm{CER}$) of 0.932 and a sequence accuracy of 0.596, and Fingerspelling-PoseNet, reaching 0.886 and 0.545, respectively.
bullets: Addresses the lack of public RSL fingerspelling data despite widespread use of RSL.
Contains 37,252 recordings totaling 35.4 hours, covering 1,593 sequences across 16 proper-name domains.
Includes contributions from 68 native RSL signers and all 33 Cyrillic handshapes.
Uses crowdsourced collection with two-stage signer qualification and expert validation.
Provides two baselines: Squeezeformer achieves 0.932 character-level accuracy and 0.596 sequence accuracy; Fingerspelling-PoseNet achieves 0.886 and 0.545.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.
bullets: Addresses the underrepresentation of South African Sign Language in sign-language processing resources.
Collects SASL videos from public sources such as news broadcasts with minimal human intervention.
Uses ASR transcripts, video cropping, and motion-based sentence-boundary detection to create weakly aligned sign–text pairs.
Benchmarks recurrent neural networks and Transformer models for sign-to-text translation.
Transformers outperform recurrent baselines, though the reported translation scores show the task remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Real-time omnimodal assistants are expected to support people in everyday life, but audiovisual understanding alone does not establish whether they can provide timely and appropriate help. We introduce Omni-Life, a benchmark grounded in real-world user needs, deployment scenarios, and device-dependent observations. It combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. The benchmark contains 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance, with 555 required intervention events, and 110 requiring silence throughout to test whether models can withhold unnecessary responses when no assistance is needed. We evaluate twelve configurations featuring mainstream real-time omnimodal models, jointly assessing event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. To examine practical deployment strategies, we study task reminders and response-latency tolerance. Reminders can improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add approximately 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points. These results show that existing models remain insufficient to deliver reliable assistance in real-life applications, calling for tailored model optimization in instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when assistance is not needed.
bullets: Evaluates assistance quality across event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output.
Combines controlled videos of hazards and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol.
Includes 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance and 110 requiring silence, covering 555 intervention events.
Across 12 model configurations, at most 4.48% of assistance-needed videos are handled completely correctly.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects and their spatial relationships evolve in 3D space over time remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), particularly under changing viewpoints. Recent approaches incorporate geometric information into reasoning, but explicit supervision for temporally ordered 4D state evolution and its use as intermediate evidence remains limited. We introduce \textbf{Trace4D}, which trains VLMs to predict 4D state sequences and reason over their inter-timestep changes alongside temporal visual observations. Its 4D-grounded chain-of-thought (CoT) explicitly represents 4D states, analyzes temporal visual context, and connects both as evidence for the answer. We construct Trace4D-Train from in-the-wild videos with 600K 4D perception examples and approximately 70K grounded QA examples, and train with joint supervised fine-tuning followed by geometry-aware GRPO. At inference, Trace4D predicts 4D states and reasoning directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model. Experiments on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D show improved QA accuracy over the base VLMs and benefits from reasoning over 4D state changes and temporal visual observations.
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty in tracking object states and spatial relationships over time under changing viewpoints.
Predicts temporally ordered 4D states, analyzes their changes, and combines them with temporal visual observations in grounded chain-of-thought reasoning.
Trains on in-the-wild videos with 4D perception and grounded QA supervision, followed by geometry-aware GRPO.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral videos provide rich spectral signatures for robust tracking under challenging conditions such as camouflage and low illumination. However, limited hyperspectral annotations and the large RGB-hyperspectral domain gap hinder the direct use of modern temporally pretrained RGB trackers. We propose SProTrack, a multimodal framework that transfers temporal knowledge from pretrained RGB trackers to the hyperspectral domain through latent spectral prompting. The key idea is to decouple temporal modeling from spectral adaptation, allowing temporal dynamics to be inherited from RGB foundation models while hyperspectral information is learned from unlabeled data in a self-supervised manner. Unlike band-selection methods that discard most spectral information or prompt-based approaches that rely on local-search crops, SProTrack learns a global, scene-level spectral representation from the full hyperspectral frame using an autoencoder. This latent representation is used to guide spectral prompt extraction while a pretrained RGB tracker preserves strong temporal modeling on RGB-compatible inputs. By encoding spectral-spatial structure into compact latent prompts, SProTrack bridges the RGB-hyperspectral modality gap without extensive retraining or dense supervision. Experiments on HOT2020 and HOT2023 demonstrate that SProTrack achieves the best overall performance, with strong results across all spectral domains.
bullets: Addresses limited hyperspectral annotations and the RGB–hyperspectral domain gap in object tracking.
Uses an autoencoder to learn global spectral-spatial representations from full hyperspectral frames.
Decouples temporal modeling from spectral adaptation, retaining RGB tracker dynamics while adapting spectral information.
Avoids discarding bands and reliance on local-search crops by generating compact latent prompts.
Reports the best overall performance on HOT2020 and HOT2023, with strong results across spectral domains.

(c) Spectral-Spatial block: a spectral branch models inter-band dependencies via Mamba and a spatial branch captures local patterns via convolution; their fused outputs, stacked across blocks, form the encoder, with a symmetric decoder for reconstruction. papers.abstract: Surgical video understanding is essential for intraoperative assistance such as workflow monitoring, instrument preparation and procedural documentation. Delivering such assistance in real time requires a model to jointly perceive the ongoing scene, remember past surgical events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass. Existing approaches provide limited support for jointly retaining procedural evidence and deciding when to respond in streaming surgical video. In this work, we propose SurgStream, a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework for real-time surgical video understanding. We first introduce Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) to record structured instrument-action-target observations and fold them into phase-level summaries, providing compact and queryable surgical memory. Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) is then devised to supervise response states within clinical windows, enabling timely responses before procedural deadlines. We further introduce SurgStream-Bench, comprising 11.7K streaming interactions across various tasks covering real-time perception, backward memory queries, forward proactive QA, proactive alerts and caption memory. Experiments on SurgStream-Bench show gains over state-of-the-art methods, especially in memory and forward proactive QA. The source code will be available.
bullets: Targets streaming assistance that must perceive scenes, remember prior events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass.
Workflow-Anchored Memory records instrument–action–target observations and compresses them into phase-level summaries.
Deadline-aware Transition Learning supervises response timing within clinical windows.
Introduces SurgStream-Bench with 11.7K streaming interactions spanning perception, memory queries, proactive QA, alerts, and caption memory.
Experiments report gains over existing methods, particularly for memory and forward proactive QA.

papers.abstract: Stress is a leading contributor to long-term physical and mental health decline. The automatic assessment of stress is a promising approach for continuous monitoring and mitigating human biases. However, the development of automated systems remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of physiological and behavioral signals. This paper presents MUPA${}^2$S, a multimodal framework for automatic stress assessment that combines facial video and ECG signals within a unified perception architecture. Both modalities are mapped into a shared token representation without modality-specific components, and processed through asymmetric attention comprising segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states. Experiments on a newly collected 58-subject stress dataset, evaluated under a stratified subject-level protocol, show that facial video achieves 69.44% test accuracy, while ECG-only performance remains close to chance under the proposed representation. Unified Video-ECG fusion achieves a test accuracy of 69.58% at approximately half the number of parameters of feature-level fusion, with negligible additional computational cost. Feature-level fusion does not exceed the video-only baseline, while unified input-level integration provides a parameter-efficient mechanism for jointly processing the two modalities.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of heterogeneous physiological and behavioral signals in automated stress assessment.
Maps facial video and ECG into a shared token representation without modality-specific components.
Uses segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states.
On a 58-subject dataset, video-only accuracy is 69.44%, while ECG-only performance is near chance.
Unified video–ECG fusion reaches 69.58% accuracy with roughly half the parameters of feature-level fusion and negligible extra computation.

papers.abstract: Event-based optical flow estimation using spatiotemporal planar approximation inherently assumes constant velocity and tends to average out temporal velocity variations. In this paper, we propose a flow estimation method that extends this planar approximation along the temporal axis. The resulting event-based optical flow constraint allows existing variational optical flow formulations to model temporal motion variation. Specifically, we partition the space-time volume into sub-intervals and apply a two-step planar approximation to track object edges consistently. Moreover, a spatial compensation mechanism and a temporal regularization term are incorporated to compensate for edge displacements and temporally stabilize the flow estimation, respectively. The experimental results show that modeling temporal motion variation improves flow estimation accuracy over conventional methods.
bullets: Addresses the constant-velocity assumption in conventional spatiotemporal planar approximation.
Partitions the space-time volume into sub-intervals and applies two-step planar fitting to track object edges.
Adds spatial compensation for edge displacement and temporal regularization for stable flow estimates.
Integrates with existing variational optical-flow formulations.
Experiments show improved accuracy when temporal motion variation is modeled.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents need physical intelligence to understand their surroundings through physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning. These capabilities must work together to interpret events and make quantitative judgments. Existing benchmarks advance physical understanding and general-purpose tool use, yet the coordination of these capabilities in physical scenarios remains insufficiently characterized. Inspired by Popper's Three Worlds, we introduce TriPhysBench, a benchmark of 410 questions from 200 videos that brings physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning into a shared evaluation setting. Its measurement-grounded and knowledge-grounded subtasks impose complementary demands on obtaining observations and acquiring external specifications, then applying them to quantitative problems. Among six representative vision-language models, the best achieves an answer accuracy of only 50.38%, revealing limited performance on tasks that require these capabilities to work together. We further introduce TriPhys, a framework that learns a unified policy for physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and quantitative reasoning from complete tool-integrated trajectories. The policy uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into subsequent physical inference. On 110 questions from videos excluded from training, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations, with a 17.7% relative gain in answer accuracy for TriPhys-27B over its Qwen3.6-27B backbone. This work provides a benchmark and a learning pathway toward embodied agents that move beyond recognizing events to understanding and reasoning about the physical processes behind them.
bullets: Introduces 410 questions from 200 videos covering physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning.
Measurement- and knowledge-grounded subtasks test whether agents can obtain observations or specifications and apply them quantitatively.
The best of six evaluated vision-language models reaches only 50.38% answer accuracy, indicating substantial difficulty with coordinated physical reasoning.
TriPhys learns a unified policy that uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into later inference.
On 110 held-out questions, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations; TriPhys-27B achieves a reported 17.7% relative answer-accuracy gain over its backbone.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about surgical video -- which phase is underway, which instruments act, and when events occur -- underpins operative documentation, workflow analysis, and skill assessment. Yet surgical visual question answering is still largely built on single frames and closed labels that cannot express a duration, an ordering, or a count, and the video models that lift the frame limit typically compress every clip the same way regardless of the question, discarding the temporal evidence the answer needs. Worse, the answers are structurally heterogeneous, spanning five incompatible structures -- binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal -- that no single training signal scores uniformly well. We propose SurgQ-VLM, a two-stage model for surgical video question answering. Stage 1 trains a question-conditioned dual-stream (slow/fast) compressor for a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B: cross-attention conditions both streams on the question, and each clip's visual tokens shrink 49x from the raw ViT patches (11x vs. post-merge backbone tokens). Stage 2 post-trains with GRPO under an answer-type-aware reward that scores each question on the metric matching its answer structure (micro-F1 for label sets, normalised error for counts, a content-timing blend for temporal windows). On a sealed 21,840-question test split over Cholec80 and CholecT50, SurgQ-VLM reaches 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10x BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot; GRPO adds 2.5 pp K-Acc (2.0 pp attributable to the answer-type-aware reward), concentrated in the structurally hard types, with answer format unchanged (ROUGE-L). Code is available at https://github.com/DhruvMakwana/SurgQ-VLM.
bullets: Targets limitations of frame-based and uniformly compressed video QA, especially for duration, ordering, and counting questions.
Uses a two-stage architecture: question-conditioned slow/fast visual compression followed by GRPO post-training.
Applies answer-type-specific rewards for binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal answers.
On a sealed 21,840-question test split from Cholec80 and CholecT50, achieves 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10× BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot.
GRPO improves keyword accuracy by 2.5 percentage points, with gains concentrated in structurally difficult answer types.

papers.abstract: A poor start lowers the ceiling, but does not negate the value of finishing well. In autoregressive video temporal grounding, models systematically exhibit an endpoint performance asymmetry, predicting ends significantly worse than starts. A committed flawed start acts as an immutable physical constraint, irreversibly capping the attainable overlap as a sunk loss. While models should minimize the remaining conditional regret, standard post-training paradigms fail to teach this adaptation. Specifically, teacher-forced SFT suffers from strict prefix exposure bias, and holistic trajectory evaluation in standard GRPO inadvertently penalizes conditionally optimal ends if they follow a poor start. To address this, we introduce FinishStrong, a novel two-stage post-training framework explicitly designed to teach optimal continuations. First, Online-start SFT exposes the end prediction to the model's own generated contexts. Second, Conditional-tree GRPO restructures the sampling topology, centering end rewards exclusively within the same-start branch to mathematically isolate the conditional end quality from the inherited start penalty. FinishStrong-9B achieves a state-of-the-art 61.7\% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench, remarkably outperforming flagship closed-source models like Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-Max. Crucially, when forced to continue from imperfect starts, it reduces the subsequent end prediction error by 36.5\%, proving its exceptional ability to end well after flawed starts. Code will be open.
bullets: Autoregressive models predict temporal segment ends worse than starts, and flawed starts can cap the achievable overlap.
Standard teacher-forced SFT and holistic GRPO do not adequately reward conditionally good continuations after poor starts.
The two-stage framework uses Online-start SFT to expose models to their own generated starts.
Conditional-tree GRPO evaluates end quality within the same-start branch, separating continuation quality from inherited start errors.
FinishStrong-9B reports 61.7% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench and reduces end prediction error by 36.5% after imperfect starts.

papers.abstract: Recently, speech-driven facial and oral animation technologies have been used in various fields such as education, speech therapy, and healthcare. But methods to objectively evaluate the quality of generated results are still limited. Accordingly, we propose the Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD), which uses embeddings from an Oral Motion Encoder (OME) and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution. In experiments, FOD reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based metric, Lip Vertex Error (LVE), and showed trends consistent with user preference. Our framework provides objective and reproducible benchmarking without relying on expensive equipment or subjective evaluation, and it can be extended to compare a variety of 2D/3D models.
bullets: Addresses the limited availability of objective evaluation methods for generated facial and oral animation.
Computes distance between Oral Motion Encoder embeddings and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution.
Reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based Lip Vertex Error metric.
Showed trends consistent with user preference in experiments.
Enables reproducible evaluation without expensive equipment or subjective assessment, with potential use across 2D and 3D models.

These two stages collectively define the framework for both learning and assessing articulatory dynamics.

papers.tldr: Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD) is a coordinate-free metric for objectively benchmarking speech-driven oral animation in alignment with established metrics and user preferences.

papers.abstract: Streaming video question answering (QA) requires real-time reasoning over continuous video streams under strict latency and active-context budgets. Current streaming vision-language models (VLMs) often give confident yet ungrounded answers when queries are ambiguous or have false premises, or when relevant visual evidence is no longer in the active context. Proactive clarification can help, but must satisfy the same latency and memory constraints. We present StreamClarify, a training-free framework for grounded streaming QA that combines a pre-answer uncertainty check with hierarchical memory. The check uses the entropy of a binary pre-answer judgment as a lightweight uncertainty score to decide whether to answer directly or request clarification. To support re-answering, a temporal-pyramid KV cache maintains a bounded active visual context, while a CPU-side semantic retrieval archive provides access to historical frames. We further construct StreamClarify-QA, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,837 QA pairs from StreamBench and OVO-Bench, spanning standard, referential ambiguity, and unanswerable scenarios. Across three VLM backbones, StreamClarify improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points over backbone-matched baselines. At comparable trigger rates, entropy-based selection achieves more than 18 points higher precision than random selection in identifying initially incorrect answers. Under oracle user guidance, clarification improves Macro accuracy by up to 3.5 points. We also report a controlled, oracle-assisted Qwen3-VL simulation on Ambiguous QA with generated questions and referent-only user replies, where the entropy-gated condition improves accuracy by 8.3 points.
bullets: Targets confident but ungrounded answers caused by ambiguous queries, false premises, or missing active-context evidence.
Uses a training-free entropy-based pre-answer uncertainty check to decide between answering and asking for clarification.
Maintains bounded visual memory with a temporal-pyramid KV cache plus CPU-side semantic retrieval of historical frames.
Introduces StreamClarify-QA, a 1,837-pair diagnostic benchmark covering standard, ambiguous, and unanswerable scenarios.
Across three VLM backbones, improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points; oracle clarification adds up to 3.5 points, while entropy selection substantially outperforms random triggering.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of StreamClarify. The framework augments a frozen streaming VLM with a pre-answer uncertainty check in a twostage generation loop and hierarchical memory. (a) When pre-answer entropy does not exceed the trigger threshold, the system answers directly using the active temporal-pyramid KV (TP-KV) cache. (b) TP-KV keeps recent frames at full resolution and compresses older observed frames within a fixed active budget. (c) When entropy exceeds the threshold, the system requests clarification and converts the resulting user guidance into a retrieval query. (d) Semantic search retrieves relevant past clips from the archive and combines them with the active TP-KV context for answering after clarification.
