papers.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can now commentate live gameplay, but they are trained and tested on the same games. We study cross-game streaming commentary, in which a model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and find that current commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, which pairs a trainable commentator with a frozen research agent that reads the wiki of the game being played. When the commentator sees something it cannot name, it sends the current frames, and the research agent returns a few wiki entries two seconds later while the stream continues. We train only the commentator, on a single game, in two stages. Information-gain labels teach it to ask only where an answer would help it say what the human caster said, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy of itself that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data, cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%, and achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.
bullets: Cross-game commentators preserve timing but struggle to recognize and understand unfamiliar game worlds.
The system queries relevant wiki entries when it encounters an unknown entity, while commentary continues with a short delay.
Training uses information-gain labels and on-policy self-distillation, requiring commentator training on only one game.
Trained on Baldur’s Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, it improves entity recall, reduces source-game leakage, and achieves strong timing, liveliness, and overall quality.
Results are scoped to streaming commentary on unseen games and rely on available game-wiki information.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison learned by prior within-instance self-supervised methods.
Pairs two visual instances, mixes their local elements, and trains the model to separate them by origin while restoring spatial, temporal, or geometric order.
Uses diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum to create richer automatically verifiable rewards from unlabeled data.
Applied to cross-image jigsaws, 3D depth, and video temporal ordering, with reported gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding across benchmarks.
Evaluations across model scales and families indicate broad generality, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.

papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in long-form video understanding, current benchmarks mostly focus on short clips or hour-scale videos. This leaves a major gap in evaluating ultra-long video understanding, where videos often last tens of hours. To bridge this gap, we introduce DramaVQA, a large-scale benchmark built upon long-form TV dramas. Containing approximately 20K question-answering (QA) pairs, the scale of DramaVQA exceeds previous long-video datasets, such as Video-MME and LVBench, by an order of magnitude. Our benchmark has two main features that make it stand out from existing datasets. First, we establish a scalable, LLM-assisted annotation pipeline that uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate complex questions, followed by strict human checking to ensure high data quality. Second, DramaVQA introduces a multi-level time structure; queries are designed across different video lengths, with the hardest questions requiring overall understanding across the entire drama. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art MLLMs face major challenges when tested on these very long videos, highlighting the need for agentic AI algorithms capable of managing long-term memory. The project is available at https://github.com/xinyuehuo/DramaVQA
bullets: Targets a gap in video benchmarks: understanding dramas lasting tens of hours rather than short clips or hour-scale videos.
Provides approximately 20K question–answer pairs, exceeding prior long-video datasets by an order of magnitude.
Uses an LLM-assisted pipeline to generate complex questions, followed by strict human verification.
Organizes questions across multiple temporal levels, including whole-drama reasoning.
Evaluations show state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle with ultra-long videos, motivating agentic methods with long-term memory.

papers.abstract: Answering a complex question about a long video is a grounding problem: the answer turns on a few seconds of evidence, and vision-language models remain well below human accuracy at finding them. The standard way to spend extra test-time compute on this kind of video reasoning is best-of-N selection: sample several chain-of-thought answers from a fixed model, then let a second model re-watch the video and pick one. Such pipelines are reported by a single headline number, their margin over a majority vote. That number conflates two effects with opposite deployment consequences: the benefit the second model adds by selecting among candidates, and the benefit it would have supplied by solving the question itself. We separate them, measuring the Selection Increment (SI) -- selection accuracy minus the same verifier's accuracy with the candidates withheld -- alongside the margin over self-consistency, across five long-video benchmarks. The Selection Increment is largest for the weakest verifiers: a verifier that solves poorly on its own leaves the candidates the most room to help. Beating the majority vote follows the opposite profile: where the vote already sits near its ceiling no verifier we test improves on it; below that ceiling only the strongest do. On Video-Holmes, the two come apart on a single pool of candidates -- a weak verifier gains +19.3 points from the candidates yet lands 7.1 points below the vote, while the frontier verifier gains the least and beats the vote. The weakest verifier also shows a failure mode: on EgoSchema it picks by where an option sits in the list rather than by what the video shows. Read as a merit score, SI puts a verifier that fails to beat a majority vote at the top of its ranking; read as an audit, it says which of the two effects a headline number delivers. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/best-n-selection-video-reasoning.
bullets: Introduces Selection Increment (SI): verifier accuracy with candidates minus its accuracy when candidates are withheld.
Across five long-video benchmarks, weaker verifiers gain more from candidate answers, while stronger verifiers are more likely to beat majority vote.
On Video-Holmes, a weak verifier gained 19.3 points from candidates but remained 7.1 points below the vote; the frontier verifier gained less but surpassed it.
The weakest verifier showed positional-choice bias on EgoSchema, selecting based on option order rather than video evidence.
SI is useful as an audit of where gains come from, but is misleading as a standalone merit ranking.

papers.selection_reason: Separates selection versus solving effects in best-of-N video reasoning, directly relevant to video-language understanding and VLM evaluation.
papers.title: Selecting or Solving? What Best-of-N Verification Delivers in Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: Best-of-N video reasoning gains must be split into candidate-selection benefit and the verifier’s own solving ability, because these can point to opposite conclusions.

papers.abstract: Dense action detection requires precisely localising multiple overlapping actions in long untrimmed videos. Transformer-based methods achieve strong accuracy but their $O(T^2)$ self-attention cost limits scalability. We present PAM-Mamba, a linear-time $O(T)$ architecture built on Mamba with a multi-branch temporal encoder. Gated Learnable Positional Encoding (GLPE) controls positional signal injection via a scalar gate initialised to zero, starting training without added positional signal. A Hub-and-Spoke Funnel extends the non-hierarchical multi-scale design of PAT with a direct residual from the original full-resolution input to each coarse branch, providing each coarse branch with a projection of the input features. Bi-TemBa (Bidirectional Temporal Mamba) first extracts local motion cues with a shallow Temporal Convolution Module, then applies a cascaded bidirectional Mamba scan; the backward pass refines the forward-scanned representation from the opposite direction, giving each temporal position access to context from both directions in linear time. Uncertainty-Based Mixup uses prediction entropy to guide the selection of mixup partners. Using the PAT evaluation implementation, we obtain 26.82 (Charades I3D), 34.59 (Charades CLIP), 46.56 (MultiTHUMOS I3D), and 46.92 mAP (MultiTHUMOS CLIP), with 26.1-27.9M parameters, 61-63% fewer than PAT.
bullets: Targets precise localization of multiple overlapping actions in long, untrimmed videos without Transformer self-attention’s quadratic cost.
Uses a multi-branch temporal encoder with GLPE, a Hub-and-Spoke Funnel, and bidirectional Bi-TemBa scanning for local and global temporal context.
Introduces entropy-guided Uncertainty-Based Mixup to select training partners.
Reports 26.82/34.59 mAP on Charades and 46.56/46.92 mAP on MultiTHUMOS with I3D/CLIP features.
Uses 26.1–27.9M parameters, reported as 61–63% fewer than PAT.

figures.caption: Figure 3. PAM-Mamba architecture overview. Pre-extracted I3D or CLIP features receive gated learnable positional encoding (including dropout 0.1) and input dropout 0.5 before entering the three-branch encoder. The full-resolution fine branch supplies a shared representation to two independently downsampled coarse branches. Each coarse branch also receives a strided projection of the encoder input. Projection blocks include LayerNorm. The Bi-TemBa inset follows the implementation: TCM is Conv1d, LayerNorm and GELU; the forward scan feeds the backward scan through temporal reversal. The backward output is reversed back, summed with the forward output and normalised, then added to the original block input. Both Mamba scans use pre-normalisation. SimpleFuser projects branch outputs to 1024 dimensions, linearly upsamples coarse outputs and combines them using learned softmax weights. Separate fine and coarse classifiers produce logits Zfine and Zcoarse, blended with the reported 0.25/0.75 weights; a sigmoid gives per-class probabilities.

Figure 4. PAM-Mamba per-class confidence on Charades (CLIP features), video BW2OT. Each panel shows the sigmoid output for one action class over time. The shaded green region marks the ground-truth active interval; the blue shaded area shows positions where the model fires above threshold τ=0.5. The confidence profiles closely track the annotated intervals. The two concurrent actions Eating a sandwich and Holding a sandwich (bottom row) are detected simultaneously over their shared interval.

Figure 2. Efficiency vs. accuracy on MultiTHUMOS (I3D features). Per-frame mAP versus GFLOPs (log scale). PAM-Mamba achieves the highest mAP among the compared methods. Values for prior methods are taken from their publications; *DualDETR’s GFLOPs are reported on TSU.

Predicted intervals closely follow the annotated actions, with small onset and offset deviations. The concurrent actions Holding food and Holding paper/notebook are detected simultaneously over their shared interval.

Bottom: PAM-Mamba’s predicted confidence for each class over time (white = low, deep indigo = high). White dashed lines mark ground-truth onset and offset boundaries. Five of the seven annotated classes are shown. Confidence concentrates within the ground-truth intervals, including the tightly interleaved refrigerator and cup/glass/bottle actions.

papers.selection_reason: Linear-time Mamba architecture for dense action detection in long untrimmed videos, fitting video understanding.
papers.title: PAM-Mamba - Efficient Dense Action Detection using Mamba
papers.tldr: PAM-Mamba enables efficient dense action detection in long videos with linear-time Mamba processing while retaining strong multi-scale temporal context.

papers.abstract: Tracking points that leave the camera's field of view (FoV) requires reasoning about unobserved scene dynamics, a fundamentally different problem from tracking visible correspondences. We present TAP-Out, an offline method that makes this out-of-view (OOV) reasoning explicit by leveraging generative video outpainting as a world-model prior. Given a narrow-FoV input video, TAP-Out outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, locates target objects within the panoramic scene via video object segmentation, and synthesises object-centred perspective crops on which standard in-frame trackers operate. This decoupled design composes off-the-shelf foundation models without requiring task-specific architectural modifications. On the TAPVid360 benchmark, TAP-Out achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving OOV tracking accuracy by approximately 3x over the best prior method. We demonstrate its flexibility on out-of-frame object segmentation and detection and we provide detailed diagnostic analyses across motion regimes, static versus dynamic content, and hallucination quality, characterising when and why the approach succeeds or fails. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/finlay-hudson/TAP-Out
bullets: Addresses out-of-view tracking, which requires inferring unobserved scene dynamics rather than matching visible correspondences.
Outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, segments target objects panoramically, and generates perspective crops for conventional tracking.
Combines off-the-shelf foundation models without task-specific architectural changes.
Achieves approximately 3× higher out-of-view tracking accuracy than the prior best method on TAPVid360.
Also supports out-of-frame segmentation and detection, with analyses of motion, scene dynamics, and hallucination quality.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Further qualitative comparison on TAPVid360 with significant camera motion.
Figure 6: TAP-Out applied to out-of-frame object tracking on the LaSOT benchmark [14].
Figure 3: Qualitative tracking results on TAPVid360. Each column shows tracked point positions on the equirectangular view across timesteps.

Figure 5: Eliminating re-identification failures on LaSOT [14]. A standard tracker (SAM2, left) tracks a white ball when visible (blue circles) but fails to re-identify it upon return (red circle) after extended absence. TAP-Out (right) maintains continuous localisation in the equirectangular domain.

papers.selection_reason: Leverages generative video outpainting as a world-model prior for out-of-view point tracking, transferable to video world models and video understanding.
papers.title: TAP-Out: Tracking Any Point in 360° via Outpainting
papers.tldr: TAP-Out tracks objects after they leave view by outpainting a narrow-FoV video into a 360° world model and applying standard trackers to synthesized object-centred views.

papers.abstract: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.
bullets: Contains over 6,300 questions covering 94 recent films, with evidence spanning an average of 23 minutes.
Questions require tracking characters’ beliefs and meta-beliefs across multiple scenes rather than retrieving a single moment.
Built automatically from screenplay annotations using LLM-generated and verified question–answer–rubric triples; human studies validate quality.
Evaluations of four open-source VLM families show substantial difficulty: the best non-oracle reaches barely half the oracle’s recall.
Visual video evidence outperforms captions and subtitles, while incomplete recall is the primary failure mode.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dataset Construction on an Example. This figure shows (question, answer, rubric) from Deadpool & Wolverine (2024). Preprocessing: screenplay scenes are time-stamped against the subtitles and decomposed into scene events. Character belief annotation: scene by scene, we extract and verify each character’s first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs. Question generation and verification: for a center character (Wolverine) and an anchor (scene 113), we generate the triple and verify every rubric claim against the screenplay.

Figure 3: A second-order belief (Q6) example from Oppenheimer (2023), whose center character is Strauss’s Senate aide and whose anchor scene is S261. At 00:11:50 Strauss watches Einstein walk past him after a private word with Oppenheimer and concludes that Einstein disapproves of him; by 02:41:48 this has hardened into the false belief that Oppenheimer turned Einstein against him. The aide models that belief (meta-beliefs, bottom lane), suggests a better explanation that Strauss rejects, and the film reveals what was actually said only at the very end. Strauss never revises the belief. The question asks what the aide takes Strauss to believe, a belief about a false belief.

Figure 2: A knowledge-split (Q1) example from Sinners (2025), anchored at S82 with Annie as center character. At 01:18:22 Sammie glimpses Stack and Mary in the back room and tells the others that Stack is busy; Smoke, Delta Slim and Annie adopt the same false belief. Each then revises it at a different moment, depending on what they witness: Smoke when he sees Mary feeding (01:19:22), Delta Slim when she runs past him (01:20:03), Annie and Sammie when Stack dies (01:20:08). Meta-beliefs track who knows that Sammie missed each step. The question asks for this knowledge split at the anchor scene; its rubric separates core claims a correct answer must contain from supporting context claims.

Figure 4: An accepting-a-claim (Q7) example from Barbie (2023), with Sasha as center character and S51, Gloria’s car, as anchor scene. Told that a sad girl is causing her malfunction, Barbie misses the scene where Gloria shows her sad sketches (00:35:36) and wrongly concludes that the girl is Sasha; she revises only when Gloria explains in the car (00:52:19). Sasha hears the same true account and rejects it, while her own meta-belief records that Barbie accepts it. The question asks what Sasha makes of her mother’s explanation: noticing that Sasha rejects a true account, and that she is mistaken, is the task.

papers.selection_reason: Long-video QA dataset with theory-of-mind questions directly targets long-form video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: LF-VideoQA: Evaluating Long-Video Understanding with Long-Form Theory-of-Mind Questions
papers.tldr: LF-VideoQA introduces a challenging benchmark for evaluating whether models can synthesize distributed visual evidence in long videos to answer open-ended theory-of-mind questions.

papers.abstract: Online Temporal Action Localization (OnTAL) aims to detect and localize action instances from untrimmed streaming videos in real time. Unlike offline approaches, OnTAL models have no access to future frames and cannot go back and refine earlier predictions, which makes the task considerably harder given the strict real-time constraints and narrow temporal window available. Most existing OnTAL methods lean on either brief anchor-based context or a single-scale memory of past frames, which limits how well they can capture actions unfolding across multiple time scales or requiring long-range reasoning in Procedural Videos. To address these gaps, we present DUGO (Dual-Scale Encoding and Gaussian Memory Online), a new OnTAL framework that jointly models local motion dynamics and long-range temporal dependencies. At its core, DUGO uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder, pairing depth-wise local representations with global self-attention so it can pick up both fine-grained temporal patterns and broader contextual cues. We also introduce a Gaussian Memory Bank, which represents action memory as stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes, allowing for richer temporal memory through gated cross-attention applied at both the encoder and anchor-query stages. Extensive experiments on procedural egocentric datasets (EGTEA, EPIC-Kitchens-100) demonstrate that DUGO achieves state-of-the-art performance while also providing substantial improvements on non-egocentric benchmarks such as Muses. The project page is available at: https://aman554-eq.github.io/DUGO
bullets: Targets Online Temporal Action Localization without access to future frames or the ability to revise past predictions.
Uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder to capture both fine-grained motion and long-range temporal context.
Introduces an input-conditioned Gaussian Memory Bank with gated cross-attention at encoder and anchor-query stages.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on EGTEA and EPIC-Kitchens-100, with improvements on the non-egocentric Muses benchmark.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: DUGO Architecture. DSE replaces the single-granularity encoder with dual branches consisting of depthwise temporal convolutions for local modeling and self-attention for global temporal reasoning, followed by fusion through a learned projection. GMB replaces deterministic history compression with a stochastic mixture of Gaussian prototypes injected at two stages: encoder memory refinement (Pass 1) and decoded anchor query enhancement (Pass 2) through per-head gated cross-attention.

Fig. 1: Motivation. Egocentric procedural videos require fine-grained motion discrimination, memory of prior steps, and procedure-aware framing. Prior OnTAL methods rely on single-scale encoding with absent or one-shot deterministic memory; DUGO introduces dual-scale encoding and a twice-injected stochastic Gaussian memory that preserves multi-modal procedural ambiguity.
Fig. 3: Gaussian prototypes Kg analysis of DUGO on EGTEA and EPIC-Kitchens-100 datasets across various tIoU thresholds.

TABLE II: mAP (%) comparison on MUSES [28]. ∗Our final configuration.

papers.selection_reason: Online temporal action localization in egocentric procedural videos with a dual-scale encoder and Gaussian memory bank; directly fits video understanding and temporal action reasoning.
papers.title: DUGO: Dual-Scale Gaussian Memory for Online Temporal Action Localization in Egocentric Procedural Videos
papers.tldr: DUGO improves real-time action localization in streaming egocentric videos by combining dual-scale temporal modeling with stochastic Gaussian memory.

papers.abstract: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.
authors: Assaf Singer, Maroun Khriesh, Noam Rotstein, Yoni Kasten, Or Litany
bullets: Addresses correspondence, depth, and occlusion errors inherited from lifting 2D tracks into 3D.
Uses a feed-forward trajectory corrector with attention along and across trajectories.
Trains only on geometric 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, independent of images, trackers, or geometry models.
Improves trajectories across different trackers and geometry providers without retraining.
Achieves state-of-the-art WorldTrack accuracy, with gains of 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 APD on dynamic points; faster variants remain competitive.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Inference pipeline of ReLift. Frozen pretrained models lift video observations (a–b) into corrupted and incomplete 3D trajectories (c). The corrector adds residuals to initialized XYZ coordinates to produce the final trajectories (d–e). Below: ray–point tokens ϕti are grouped into Cframe tracklets and embedded as tokens hni, then processed by alternating temporal and across-track attention. The output head predicts frame-level XYZ residuals, which are added to the initialized trajectories. We train the corrector on simulated lifts from clean trajectory annotations (Sec. 3.4).

Figure 5: Simulated versus provider-generated lifts. APD3D gains on all points, in percentage points over the initialized lift, with AllTracker and DA3 (left) or VGGT-Ω (right). “Real” denotes non-simulated, provider-generated training lifts. All runs use the same architecture and 150,000 training steps. Appendix D.1 reports a control with matched training windows.

Trajectories of the same reference pixels are shown from matched novel viewpoints. Ours uses AllTracker and VGGT-Ω; TrackCraft3R shares this geometry, while 4RC and V-DPM use their own reconstructions. Yellow boxes mark magnified regions.

APD3D gains (%) over the initialized lift (Sec. 3.2), per dataset and averaged, for all six tracker–geometry combinations; hatching denotes CoWTracker. Occluded selects ground-truth-occluded point–frames from All, retaining the Allpoint alignment. This subset may differ from the corrector’s masked inputs.

APD3D gains on all points are reported in percentage points over the initialized lift, with AllTracker and DA3 (left) or VGGT-Ω (right). “Mean” averages the four datasets.

papers.abstract: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.
authors: Lidong Lu, Lidong Zou, Xinyi Mao, Jiaxin Lv, Zhenquan Li, Liangrui Dong, Tong Lu, Guo Chen
bullets: Introduces PanoVideoBench, a manually annotated benchmark with 1,000 questions across five categories and 15 types.
Evaluation of 11 models finds cross-view tracking and integrating evidence across space and time to be the main weaknesses.
Constructs PanoVideoCoT with 13,465 reasoning QA pairs from verified panoramic observations and agentic explorations.
Trains PanoVideoReasoner using Panoramic CoT SFT and evidence-privileged on-policy self-distillation.
Achieves 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving its backbone by 12.5 points and prior state of the art by 2.6 points.

papers.abstract: High accuracy on streaming video benchmarks does not establish whether a model uses visual history. Our review of OVO-Bench and StreamingBench finds that recent frames suffice for 32% of sampled historical questions, while models also answer many questions correctly from the question and options alone. We introduce TwinPast to test whether answers correctly follow changes in history, using 350 human-reviewed video pairs spanning five historical tasks. Each pair holds the recent video context, question, and ordered options fixed while changing critical historical evidence and the correct answer. Each video is evaluated independently, and PairAcc requires correct answers for both histories. We evaluate 34 model and input configurations. For Qwen3-VL-8B and DeepSeek-Flash, historical inputs improve performance on TwinPast, reversing the recent-frame advantage on existing benchmarks. The strongest evaluated streaming system reaches 49.14% PairAcc, compared with 66.57-91.43% for the evaluated general-purpose models. This gap persists across all five tasks. Case studies further show that models select states from the wrong time or contradict recorded event order despite retaining the relevant evidence. These findings highlight the need to connect historical memory and retrieval with reasoning that uses evidence according to the question's temporal references and event relations.
authors: Haotian Yang, Yong Chen, Cheng Peng, Haobo Wang, Zhongle Xie, Xuanru Li, Gang Chen
bullets: Existing benchmarks can be solved using recent frames or the question and options alone in many cases, weakening claims of historical understanding.
TwinPast contains 350 human-reviewed video pairs across five historical tasks, changing critical past evidence while keeping recent context and questions fixed.
Its PairAcc metric requires a model to answer correctly under both histories, testing whether predictions follow historical changes.
Across 34 model/input configurations, the strongest streaming system achieved 49.14% PairAcc, below evaluated general-purpose models at 66.57–91.43%.
Failures include selecting states from the wrong time and contradicting the recorded order of events, motivating better temporal retrieval and evidence-based reasoning.

papers.abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.
authors: Eadom Dessalene, Michael Maynord, Amir-Hossein Shahidzadeh, Botao He, Yasamin Tabatabaee, Ruoshi Liu, Ruohan Gao, Paul Pu Liang, Yiannis Aloimonos
bullets: Pairs egocentric video with bimanual EMG, IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation.
Uses EMG as a dense, occlusion-free alternative to costly and subjective manual action annotation.
Learns shared sensorimotor representations through video–EMG cross-modal pretraining.
Transfers the learned representations to action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction.
Also conditions video diffusion on EMG to generate fine-grained hand-manipulation videos; the approach outperforms evaluated video self-supervised baselines across four tasks and eight datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MOTORSENSE. (A) Sensorimotor Alignment. Windows 1, . . . , N of bimanual EMG (left) and egocentric video (right) are embedded by an EMG encoder and a video encoder and aligned with a symmetric contrastive objective (Section 3.2): the video and EMG embeddings of the same window (Vi, Ei) are pulled together, while embeddings from different windows are pushed apart. (B) Downstream Tasks. The learned representations are used for downstream tasks: 1) video diffusion consisting of a single reference frame as input along with EMG control signals, 2) action recognition, 3) 3D hand-object Reconstruction, 4) 3D hand contact prediction.

Figure 7: Qualitative results for video diffusion. We compare our proposed motor conditioning to a video diffusion model conditioned solely on the video history (unimodal conditioning), for a sequence involving the stirring of tofu in a pan. The video conditioning model misinterprets the action performed, generating a video of a scooping action as opposed to a stirring action, whereas our method correctly generates a video of the stirring of tofu.

Figure 8: Qualitative results for video diffusion. We compare our proposed motor conditioning to a video diffusion model conditioned solely on the video history (unimodal conditioning), for a sequence involving the spreading of mayonnaise with a spoon. The video conditioning model misinterprets the action performed, generating a rotation of the bread as opposed to a spreading action of the spoon, whereas our method correctly generates a video of the spreading of mayonnaise with a spoon.

Figure 9: Qualitative results for video diffusion. We compare our proposed motor conditioning to a video diffusion model conditioned solely on the video history (unimodal conditioning), for a bimanual manipulation sequence involving the peeling of an avocado. The video conditioning model renders the index finger as resting against the thumb, whereas our method correctly positions the index finger against the surface of the avocado for the peeling action.

Figure 4: Self-supervised sensorimotor alignment organizes video and EMG by hand action. (a) t-SNE plot of the joint embedding space for video (green) and EMG (purple) derived from the two towers of our self-supervised contrastive model (Section 3.2). A "modality gap" is observed [37] between video and EMG clusters. (b) The clips associated with each pair: the video query (left) and the clip whose EMG was retrieved (right). Each retrieved clip performs the query’s hand action—cutting, mixing in a bowl, drying—with a different object, scene, and recording. (c) The EMG embeddings of (a), coloured by verb with marker shape denoting the object. Despite the network never being trained over these labels, windows of the same action form compact regions (e.g. mix salad, scrape bowl) and verbs group together (the cut family in red). Best viewed zoomed-in and in colour.

Figure 1: EMG captures both categorical and continuous structure of hand actions. (Top) For three discrete hand configurations repeated twice—fist, point, and flat—each pose produces a distinct and reproducible EMG signature: fist is marked by a suppressed purple channel (#7) with respect to flat and a pronounced red channel (#1) with respect to point; point exhibits lower overall amplitude, with less purple than flat and less red than fist; flat is distinguished by pronounced purple and red activation. Sharp grey rectangles reflect the boundaries between hand gestures and rest states. (Bottom) A pick-and-lift sequence combines gradual and abrupt transitions: the hand moves smoothly from rest through pregrasp into grasp, changes sharply as force is applied at lift, then settles—non-instantaneously—into a steady hold. The EMG mirrors this structure, with channels quiet at rest, building subtly through pregrasp and grasp, peaking sharply as the lift begins, and stabilizing during hold.

Each row shows the RGB input, reconstructions from a vision backbone trained without EMG and with EMG (MOTORSENSE pre-training), and ground truth. Incorporating EMG during pre-training yields 3D hands and objects that more closely match the ground truth.

papers.title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding

papers.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.
authors: Jiahe Wu, Bing Cao, Xingyue Guo, Ruipu Zhao, Beiming Yu, Jiekang Feng, Qinghua Hu, Pengfei Zhu
bullets: Targets incomplete visual observations involving small objects, subtle attributes, changing viewpoints, and multimodal inputs.
Organizes tasks around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration across images, sequences, cross-modal images, and viewpoints.
Contains 175k training and 20k human-reviewed test samples; evaluations cover 22 general-purpose VLMs.
Finds persistent weaknesses in spatial judgment and cross-modal/cross-view reasoning, with stronger perception linked to better reasoning.
UAV-PUR models adapted from Qwen3-VL improve multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points for 4B and 8B variants, respectively.

papers.abstract: Streaming video assistance requires models to answer asynchronous questions from an observed prefix under a fixed context budget. Existing approaches model response timing or compress history, but an online state formed before future questions are known can omit visual details before later questions reveal their relevance; the retained state alone cannot recover them. We introduce Watch-Think-Interact (WTI), a closed-loop framework for multi-question streaming video reasoning. WTI maintains compact natural-language memory entries tagged with source-video time ranges; these entries support direct reasoning when sufficient and otherwise anchor selective recall of finer visual evidence. For each question, WTI answers when current context and memory suffice, continues watching when required evidence has not appeared, or recalls a relevant past interval and decides again after incorporating the returned chunks, without replaying the full observed history. To train this behavior, we construct WTI-82K, comprising 82,335 timed questions across 4,812 causally aligned trajectories, and develop Stream-GDPO to optimize complete multi-question streaming rollouts using trajectory-level feedback for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates. WTI achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance among the compared open-source streaming baselines, reaching 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted overall accuracy on OVO-Bench.
bullets: Addresses the problem that early online summaries may omit visual details needed by later questions under a fixed context budget.
Stores compact natural-language memories linked to source-video time ranges, enabling targeted recall without replaying the full history.
Uses a closed-loop policy that decides whether to answer, continue watching, or retrieve past visual evidence before answering.
Trains with Stream-GDPO on WTI-82K, optimizing response timing, video recall, and memory updates across complete question trajectories.
Reports 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted accuracy on OVO-Bench, achieving state-of-the-art performance among compared open-source baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Watch-Think-Interact. For each arriving chunk, WTI updates a short thinking state and chooses to remain silent, answer, or recall. Recall returns visual evidence and loops back to the decision at the same time step; controller-triggered memory updates separately compress elapsed observations into a bounded temporal index. Stream-GDPO optimizes the resulting complete interaction trajectories.

Figure 3: WTI-82K construction pipeline. WTI-82K converts videos into streaming-causal trajectories by standardizing clips, aligning chunk-level evidence chains, generating QAs from aligned evidence, placing query and answerable times, and checking timestamp bounds, answer availability, action grammar, and evidence-interval fields. The resulting samples cover Real-Time, Backward Tracing, and Proactive interactions under the same visibility constraints as inference.

Figure 1: Motivation for Watch-Think-Interact. In causal streaming video, asynchronous questions may require current, past, or not-yet-observed evidence. WTI uses a bounded active window for current perception, compact time-indexed memory for direct reasoning and temporal localization, and selective recall to reload a past visual interval.

Figure 4: Training-time GSPO/Stream-GDPO diagnostics. Panels report outcome accuracy, BT recall triggering, post-recall outcome accuracy, and memory quality; faint and bold curves show raw and rolling values.
Table 1: Results on OVO-Bench. Scores are grouped by Real-Time, Backward, and Forward tasks; Avg. gives the corresponding group average, and Overall gives the benchmark average.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming video reasoning with memory and RL, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Watch-Think-Interact: Bootstrapping Long-Horizon Multi-Turn Streaming Video Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: WTI enables long-horizon streaming video assistants to answer multi-turn questions by combining compact time-tagged memory, selective visual recall, and reinforcement learning for when to watch, recall, or respond.

papers.abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to localize the spatio-temporal tube in a video corresponding to a natural language query. While recent methods achieve strong performance in fully supervised, weakly supervised, and zero-shot settings, they typically rely on computationally expensive architectures, complex training pipelines, or multimodal large language models. We present Pocket-STVG (P-STVG), a lightweight cascade architecture that addresses STVG by combining efficient pre-trained components instead of large end-to-end models. P-STVG integrates a temporal-aware video encoder based on MobileViCLIP, a spatial encoder-decoder derived from MDETR, and a shared aligned text encoder. Temporal localization is performed through either a lightweight 1D U-Net or a simple thresholding strategy, enabling the same framework to operate in both weakly supervised and zero-shot settings. Furthermore, video representations are precomputed independently of the query, yielding an indexing-friendly pipeline for efficient inference and large-scale video collections. Despite requiring fewer than 90M parameters, P-STVG performs on par with weakly supervised methods and improves on earlier zero-shot approaches at a fraction of their memory and computational cost, establishing a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off for STVG.
bullets: Targets efficient spatio-temporal video grounding without large end-to-end models or multimodal LLMs.
Combines MobileViCLIP-based temporal encoding, an MDETR-derived spatial encoder-decoder, and a shared text encoder.
Supports weakly supervised and zero-shot settings using either a lightweight 1D U-Net or thresholding for temporal localization.
Precomputes query-independent video representations to enable efficient inference over large video collections.
Uses fewer than 90M parameters, matches weakly supervised methods, and improves over earlier zero-shot approaches at lower memory and compute cost.

papers.abstract: Video captioning models are increasingly evaluated with metrics designed for single-sentence image captions. We test whether those metrics recover human judgement on dense, multi-window video description, and find that they do not. Six frontier models captioned 196 short clips. Trained annotators post-edited every caption against a failure taxonomy fixed before annotation, once as a whole-clip overview and once window by window, and a quality-control reviewer checked each annotation, yielding 1,144 overview verdicts and 4,672 window verdicts. Reference-overlap metrics do not separate the captions reviewers accepted from those they rejected: BLEU-4 reaches an AUC of 0.510 and a CIDEr-style tf-idf cosine 0.528, and restricting references to reviewer corrections leaves BLEU-4 at 0.479 (95% CI 0.431-0.529), indistinguishable from chance. Review granularity changes what is detected. The same annotators record camera and shot errors on 2.7% of captions when reading the overview and on 12.8% when reading window by window, a 4.7x gap that holds across every robustness check we ran, on the mode most likely to need a near-total rewrite. Correct-overview rates span 54.1-72.7%, but only 4 of 15 pairwise gaps survive Bonferroni correction (5 after adjusting for reviewer and clip effects), and accuracy and derived severity order the models differently. Models with statistically indistinguishable accuracy have sharply different failure profiles, which no single scalar shows. We argue that caption evaluation should record what was wrong rather than only how often, and we report the taxonomy, the per-model profiles, the corpus properties that predict difficulty, and the code that regenerates every number in the paper.
bullets: Six models captioned 196 short clips, with human corrections assessed for whole-clip overviews and window-by-window descriptions.
BLEU-4 and CIDEr-style scores were essentially chance-level at distinguishing accepted from rejected captions.
Window-by-window review detected camera and shot errors 4.7× more often than overview review.
Models with similar overall accuracy showed sharply different failure types, and accuracy and severity ranked models differently.
The study advocates reporting failure taxonomies and per-model error profiles instead of relying on a single scalar score.

papers.abstract: As robots and intelligent systems increasingly interact with humans, they must anticipate long sequences of future actions from only brief observations. While purely neural models typically require extensive observations to predict future actions and remain difficult to interpret and adjust, symbolic priors offer a structured alternative. To this end, we introduce SymAnt, a novel neuro-symbolic approach that unifies the expressiveness of neural networks with the structured reasoning of scene and knowledge graphs. Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint-search over both graphs to construct a symbolic context, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. This symbolic context serves as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves the sequence of future actions. By grounding predictions in symbolic context, SymAnt anticipates long-horizon actions from short observation windows in a parameter-efficient manner, while enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SymAnt, particularly when only short observation contexts are available, across five diverse datasets: Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101.
authors: Fnu Aryan, Yaqi Xie, Joseph Campbell, Woojun Kim, Kwonjoon Lee, Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub, Ehsan Moradi-Pari, Katia Sycara, Simon Stepputtis
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting long action sequences when only brief observations are available.

Uses the resulting symbolic context as a prior for iterative future-action generation and refinement.
Supports parameter-efficient prediction and direct knowledge editing without retraining.
Demonstrates effectiveness across five diverse action-recognition datasets, especially with short observation windows.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual instance segmentation (AVIS) segments and tracks individual sound-producing objects in videos. Existing benchmarks predominantly use monaural audio, which lacks inter-channel cues for spatially distinguishing concurrent sound sources. We introduce AVPS-360 (Audio-Visual Person Segmentation 360), a spatial audio-visual benchmark bridging AVIS and sound event localisation and detection (SELD). Built upon STARSS23, it pairs first-order Ambisonics audio with synchronised 360{\deg} video across 230 recordings totalling 10.5 hours. Recordings average 164.0 seconds. The dataset captures intermittent sound production in real-world interactions dominated by speech, alongside laughter, clapping, and footsteps. It provides 31,678 manually reviewed instance masks linked to source identities and sound-event labels. We also present a baseline that integrates spatial audio with visual features for frame-level segmentation and identity association across frames. Experiments on AVPS-360 show that existing AVIS methods struggle with detection and identity association in long recordings with intermittent sound production, while our baseline substantially improves performance in both aspects.
authors: Yifu Sun, Parthasaarathy Sudarsanam, Tuomas Virtanen, Archontis Politis
bullets: Addresses the limitations of monaural-audio AVIS benchmarks for distinguishing concurrent sound sources.
Pairs first-order Ambisonics audio with synchronized 360° video in 230 real-world recordings totaling 10.5 hours.
Includes 31,678 manually reviewed instance masks linked to source identities and sound-event labels.
Covers primarily speech, plus laughter, clapping, and footsteps during intermittent sound production.
Shows existing AVIS methods struggle with detection and identity association in long recordings, while the spatial-audio baseline improves both.

papers.abstract: Given a set of procedural steps, Video Step Grounding (VSG) aims to identify which steps occur in a video and localize when they are performed. Existing methods are either offline, requiring access to the full video before making predictions, or online, but relying on fixed-length video segments producing noisy, over-segmented outputs. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Step Decomposition (HSD), a training-free framework for online VSG that leverages the semantic understanding capabilities of Large Multimodal Models. HSD addresses two central challenges in online grounding: constructing semantically coherent temporal segments from a streaming video, and bridging the semantic gap between coarse procedural step descriptions and visual observations. To construct elementary temporal units, HSD incrementally groups incoming segments into semantically consistent events, using an anchor caption that is continuously validated against the visual stream. Based on these events, we perform zero-shot procedural step classification and selectively refine uncertain predictions by decomposing candidate steps into finegrained substeps that capture more nuanced visual evidence. By operating on semantically coherent events rather than every fixed-length segment, HSD reduces redundant computation and produces more stable predictions. Experiments on HT-Step, Ego4D Goal-Step, and CrossTask show that HSD substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, overall achieving better step recognition, more accurate temporal localization, and faster inference.
authors: Long Zhou, Luca Zanella, Paolo Rota, Massimiliano Mancini, Elisa Ricci
bullets: Targets online grounding without requiring the full video in advance.
Incrementally groups incoming segments into semantically consistent events using continuously validated anchor captions.
Performs zero-shot classification of procedural steps with Large Multimodal Models.
Decomposes uncertain candidate steps into fine-grained substeps for better visual alignment.
On HT-Step, Ego4D Goal-Step, and CrossTask, it improves recognition, temporal localization, and inference speed over prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HSD. Given an input video V , the Online Semantic Event Construction module incrementally builds each event Ej from fixed-duration segments using a frozen LMM ΦLMM. The first segment of Ej is captioned as γanc, and each arriving segment is appended to Ej if its continuity score ϵsame exceeds ϵnew ; otherwise, Ej is terminated and a new event is initialized. For each completed event Ej , the Zero-Shot Event-to-Step Grounding module predicts a probability distribution pj over procedural steps. If its entropy Hj falls below threshold η, the most likely step is predicted. Otherwise, Hierarchical Step Refinement decomposes the top-k steps into substeps, re-evaluates Ej , aggregates substep scores into psubj , and outputs the final prediction âj .

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now process hour-long videos, making extended multi-turn dialogue over a single video a natural mode of use. Sustaining such a dialogue requires more than answering each question in isolation: the model must retrieve and reuse information established earlier in the conversation, both what it has seen and what it has said, an ability we term in-context video memory. Existing video QA benchmarks leave this ability unmeasured: their questions are mutually independent, never reference one another, and each is answerable from the video alone, so nothing ever requires carrying information across turns. We introduce VideoMemBench, in which each sample pairs a single video with a long multi-turn dialogue, whose turns are connected by typed cross-turn dependencies: an Episodic Dependency refers back to a visual episode described in an earlier turn, probing memory of what the model has seen, while an Answer Dependency builds on the model's own earlier answer, probing memory of what the model has said. Every dependency is verified considering two properties: 1) necessity, meaning the question cannot be answered without its earlier turns, and 2) non-leakage, meaning the question does not restate the information from its earlier turns. To enforce these properties, we design a construction pipeline with three LLM roles: a planner, a generator, and a judger, with each dialogue reviewed by human experts. VideoMemBench comprises 326 videos with 2,476 turns, of which 1,387 depend on earlier turns, including multi-parent dependencies and long-range call-back. Among over 20 evaluated open- and closed-source MLLMs, Claude Opus 5 performs the best with an overall score of only 45.7\%, highlighting the challenge of in-context video memory. Our dataset and evaluation are released.
authors: Zhengdong Hu, Chao Wang, Kaituo Feng, Huanjin Yao, Mingfei Lu, Hehe Fan, Yi Yang
bullets: Evaluates in-context video memory rather than independent video question answering.
Tests two dependency types: recall of earlier visual episodes and reuse of the model’s own prior answers.
Ensures dependencies are necessary and non-leaking, using planner, generator, and judger roles plus human review.
Contains 326 videos and 2,476 dialogue turns, with 1,387 turns dependent on earlier turns.
Across 20+ open- and closed-source MLLMs, the best reported overall score is only 45.7%, underscoring the difficulty.

figures.caption: Figure 2 The VideoMemBench construction pipeline. Starting from a curated video pool, a planner specifies turn intents and a typed dependency graph. A generator constructs the dialogue turn by turn, while a judger checks necessity, non-leakage, and visual grounding, returning failed turns for regeneration. Completed dialogues are checked against the plan and reviewed by human experts.

Figure 1 Example of VideoMemBench with cross-turn dependencies: Independent turns (e.g., T1, T8) establish visually grounded facts; dependent turns refer back to earlier turns through expressions such as “the scene from T1” or “the target from T1”, without restating earlier content. An Episodic Dependency (e.g., T2) requires recalling what the model has seen: the model must recover which scene T1 described before answering the question. An Answer Dependency (e.g., T3, T4) requires recalling what the model has said : each builds on the answer produced at an earlier turn.

Figure 4 Analysis of factors affecting in-context video memory. (a) Accuracy on dependent turns by dependency distance, measured from the current turn to its earliest parent; the dashed line shows the mean across all evaluated models. (b) Accuracy on dependent turns by the number of parents. (c) Independent- and dependent-turn accuracy by dialogue position for two models: the light segment shows dependent-turn accuracy, the full bar height shows independent-turn accuracy, and the dark segment represents their difference. (d) Accuracy on answer-dependent turns under self-rollout and oracle histories. Oracle histories replace previous model responses with ground-truth answers.

Figure 3 Dataset statistics of VideoMemBench. (a) Category distribution across four major domains and their finegrained subcategories. (b) Distribution of videos by duration. (c) Distribution of the number of dialogue turns per video. (d) Distribution of question dependencies, including independent questions, episodic dependencies, and answer dependencies. (e) Text-length statistics for questions, answers, and answer choices, reported as mean ± standard deviation.

papers.abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.
authors: Subhashini Venugopalan, Jenny Tan, Taylor Roper, Jimmy Tobin, Anton Kast, Alicia Martin, Sam Sepah, Amy Pavel
bullets: Targets inline audio descriptions that must fit naturally into existing video silences, including diverse user-generated content.
MTG-AD contains 36 hours of professionally annotated video and more than 8,000 descriptions created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals.
MTG-AD-Eval provides fine-grained, actionable metrics, including rendered-audio assessment of speech overlap and timing.
Frontier MLLMs describe visual events well and reduce overlaps, but still show weaknesses in narrative pacing and flow.
Automated metrics correlate significantly with human ratings; users narrowly prefer human descriptions but find MLLM outputs highly beneficial for comprehension.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) lacks event-stream datasets and models. We introduce Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event conversion of the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus and all additional SAMA training data: 30,650 video clips and 392,162 images. Optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator preserves all mask, referring-expression and dialogue annotations. We also introduce Event-SAMA, adapting SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter. End-to-end training yields 24.37 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on the converted ReVOS valid subset, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline (RGB SAMA-4B: 55.4 on MeViS). Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions of the same events scores 13.23 and 15.94 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$. Without retraining, Event-SAMA works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches their event density. A seed-controlled ablation with a measured noise floor of 0.47 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ finds gains from diverse training sources over MeViS alone (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33), and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity are within noise at this budget. An earlier, partially converted corpus snapshot trained with the identical recipe scores 1.38 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ higher on MeViS and 1.12 higher on ReVOS. Both are single runs that also differ in schedule length, so we draw no conclusion about corpus scale.
authors: Sergei Fedorchenko, Max Zehnder, Nikola Zubi\'c, Rong Zou, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Builds Event-SAMA-239K by converting 30,650 videos and 392,162 images from SAMA data into synthetic event streams while preserving masks, referring expressions, and dialogue annotations.
Adapts SAMA-4B with two-channel event-polarity input embeddings and an event adapter for end-to-end RVOS training.
Achieves 24.37 J&F on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 J&F on converted ReVOS, compared with 55.4 for RGB SAMA-4B on MeViS.
Pseudo-RGB and E2VID reconstructions score lower at 13.23 and 15.94 J&F, supporting direct event-stream processing.

Performance transfers to real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches event density; ablations identify data diversity, initialization, and decoder training as useful under the tested budget.

papers.abstract: Colonoscopy is inherently comparative: reliable visual assessment of polyps often depends on complementary views acquired under different viewpoints and imaging conditions. Retrieving such views requires polyp tracklet representations, which recent contrastive methods learn from temporal cues but still build from manually annotated bounding boxes. We propose an annotation-free framework that constructs tracklet views directly from raw colonoscopy videos, enabling temporal self-supervised learning on full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps. On REAL-Colon, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on tracklet retrieval and re-identification, outperforming both self-supervised and supervised baselines. We then introduce few-shot polyp retrieval, a task closer to clinical use, where a few observations of a target polyp are used to retrieve its remaining tracklets: with only two examples, our method surpasses most competing methods given ten. Finally, we show that a modest number of unlabeled procedures suffices for competitive performance, making on-site model development more practical. Code is available at https://github.com/lparolari/freerep.
authors: Luca Parolari, Lamberto Ballan, Carlo Biffi, Loic Le Folgoc
bullets: Addresses the need to retrieve complementary polyp views across viewpoints and imaging conditions without manual bounding-box annotations.
Builds tracklet views directly from full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps, for temporal self-supervised learning.
Achieves state-of-the-art tracklet retrieval and re-identification on REAL-Colon against supervised and self-supervised baselines.
In few-shot retrieval, two target-polyp examples outperform most competing methods using ten examples.
Competitive performance requires only a modest number of unlabeled procedures, supporting more practical on-site development.

papers.abstract: In segmentation-based continuous sign language recognition, an untrimmed video is first partitioned into lexical units; segmentation is therefore a means to an end---downstream recognition. However, segmenters are usually judged by local boundary detection rather than by the quality of the lexical segments and the recognition they enable. We present BEACON, a begin/end-aware segmenter that combines four-class Outside/Begin/Inside/End (BIOE) labeling, constrained Viterbi decoding over eight legal transitions, and boundary knowledge distilled from a binary teacher into a shared student. Under strict no-cut evaluation with validation-based model selection, BEACON improves segment-F1 by 14.58/14.59 points and boundary-F1 by 2.17/1.22 points, and reduces the downstream word error rate (WER) by 9.10/4.15 points relative to the state-of-the-art in the PHOENIX-14/BSL Corpus. To examine which segmentation metric better reflects downstream recognition, we evaluated five distinct architecture families. Segment-F1 aligns more consistently with lower WER than boundary-F1 in both corpora (Spearman $\rho=-1.0/-0.9$ versus $-0.9/-0.8$). These results support evaluating sign language segmentation in terms of segment quality and downstream recognition utility rather than local boundary accuracy alone.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between local boundary metrics and the quality of lexical segments used for recognition.
Uses four-class BIOE labeling, constrained Viterbi decoding with eight legal transitions, and boundary knowledge distillation from a binary teacher.
Under strict no-cut evaluation, improves segment-F1 and boundary-F1 while reducing downstream WER on PHOENIX-14 and the BSL Corpus.
Across five architecture families, segment-F1 correlates more consistently with lower WER than boundary-F1.
Supports evaluating segmentation by segment quality and downstream recognition utility, not boundary accuracy alone.

figures.caption: Figure 3. The BEACON pipeline. A frozen I3D [3] backbone supplies frame features to a shared temporal encoder (Stage 1, standard). BIOE and soft Begin/End predictions are fused and decoded over the eight legal BIOE transitions (inset), producing a preliminary segment path that satisfies the declared grammar (Stage 2, ours). A binary IO branch reads the same shared hidden states H (no extra encoder) and refines endpoints within a validation-selected radius of at most ±3 frames (Stage 3, ours). During training only, a separately trained, frozen binary teacher (shown dashed, with its own encoder, and discarded after training) distills boundary evidence into this student IO branch via a KL loss; inference uses a single 5M-parameter model with one encoder. The lower strip visualizes the per-frame BIOE labels collapsing into the final segment spans.

Figure 2. Constrained Viterbi decoding [24] over the BIOE grammar. Emission totals are illustrative.

Figure 1. BEACON replaces Renz et al. papers.title: BEACON: Distilled Begin/End-Aware Structured Decoding for Continuous Sign Language Segmentation
papers.tldr: BEACON improves continuous sign language segmentation and downstream recognition by combining begin/end-aware decoding with distilled boundary knowledge, showing that segment quality better predicts recognition performance than boundary accuracy alone.

papers.abstract: 4D perception models, which classify 3D point-cloud videos, are being built into robots, assistive monitoring and AR, yet before deploying one a practitioner cannot check which cue it relies on: how a body part moves, or what shape it has. 3D attribution is single-frame, video attribution is confined to RGB pixels, gradient maps need white-box access, attention is absent from state-space backbones, and point-level perturbations assume a point correspondence across frames that real depth and LiDAR data lack. We present Kinematic Causal Attribution (KCA), a black-box, interventional attribution method that queries only the model's outputs. Its freeze operator removes a region's motion while keeping its shape, and a shape-free proxy removes the shape while keeping the motion. Together they span a motion$\times$geometry cube for every tracked region, whose order-symmetric Shapley decomposition is complete and whose interaction is measured rather than assumed away. The operators rewrite per-frame point sets, so they need no correspondences, and a context-averaged estimator handles structures that span several regions. We validate KCA on the official PSTNet, P4Transformer and Mamba4D trained on MSR-Action3D. The decisive test is an audit: two binary tasks are built from real clips whose classes differ only in the motion or only in the shape of the same arm, and the motion share of the arm's importance follows the defining cue on all three backbones (0.83 vs. 0.60 on P4Transformer, 0.86 vs. 0.30 on PSTNet, 0.92 vs. 0.61 on Mamba4D), a distinction no single attribution map can make. The split costs no faithfulness: the necessity maps have the lowest deletion AUC on P4Transformer and PSTNet, tie with the best baseline on Mamba4D, and lose their correlation with the trained model's once the weights are randomised. Skeleton ground truth, re-sampling stability and cost complete the validation.
bullets: Uses interventional operators to freeze a region’s motion while preserving shape, or remove shape while preserving motion.
Combines these interventions in a motion×geometry cube with an order-symmetric Shapley decomposition that captures interactions.
A context-averaged estimator supports structures spanning multiple tracked regions, and the operators rewrite per-frame point sets without requiring correspondences.
On MSR-Action3D audits across PSTNet, P4Transformer, and Mamba4D, motion attribution tracks whether the defining cue is motion or shape.
Necessity maps show strong faithfulness under deletion tests and lose correlation after model-weight randomization, supporting model-specific attribution.

A local or a context-averaged estimator turns the cube’s outputs into order-symmetric motion and geometry importance whose interaction is measured. Only outputs of f are used, so the same pipeline explains convolutional, attention and state-space backbones.

papers.title: Kinematic Causal Attribution: Black-Box Explanations of Motion versus Geometry for 4D Point-Cloud Video Models
papers.tldr: Kinematic Causal Attribution (KCA) is a black-box method that separates whether 4D point-cloud video models rely on motion or geometry, without point correspondences or internal model access.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.
authors: Lu Wang, Zhuoran Jin, Longxiang Wang, Junhong Chen, Yupu Hao, Yao Xu, Daojian Zeng, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu, Guang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Existing systems often assume complete information, risking endless waiting or hallucinated answers when video or user intent is unclear.
The benchmark evaluates multi-turn interaction across video and user uncertainty with four categories and eight subtasks.
It includes 438 videos and 2,714 manually annotated frame-level windows labeled wait, ask, or answer.
Models remain substantially challenged: the strongest reported model reaches 52.18% on the Ask-F1 metric.
The benchmark covers both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, emphasizing proactive information seeking.
