papers.abstract: Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) requires localizing multiple objects and maintaining their identities over time. Recent query-propagation trackers carry target-specific representations across frames and update them with current-frame image features, yet identity association remains difficult when visually similar targets overlap or cross. During such interactions, current-frame query updates may contain components directed toward nearby active tracks, which may affect identity association in later frames. To investigate this issue, we analyze track-query updates preceding identity switches (IDSWs), where the same target is assigned a different track ID. Our analysis shows that (i) propagated track-query representations change more abruptly before IDSWs, (ii) current-frame updates have larger positive projections along directions toward other active tracks, and (iii) bounding-box intersection over union (IoU) retrieves the counterpart track involved in a subsequent IDSW with high recall when that track remains active before the switch. Motivated by these findings, we propose Test-time Track-Query Calibration (TQC), a training-free and gradient-free method for query-propagation trackers. TQC calibrates the tracker output before propagation using a bounded correction estimated from update components directed toward nearby active tracks. It requires only track-query representations and bounding boxes available during inference, without retraining or architectural modification. Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited inference overhead. Controlled variants on six validation settings further show that TQC's correction direction yields more consistent HOTA improvements than alternative directions with matched correction norms.
authors: Riku Inoue, Shogo Sato, Yu Mitsuzumi, Kazuhiko Murasaki, Tomoyasu Shimada, Takashi Sano
bullets: Problem: Similar targets that overlap or cross can cause track-query updates to absorb information from neighboring tracks, leading to identity switches.

Analysis: Track-query representations change more abruptly before ID switches, with updates showing stronger directional alignment toward other active tracks; IoU often identifies the counterpart track.
Method: TQC applies a bounded, training- and gradient-free correction to tracker outputs before propagation using track-query representations and bounding boxes available at inference.
Results: Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited overhead.
Scope: The method targets query-propagation trackers and relies on nearby active tracks remaining available for calibration.

papers.abstract: Few-shot action recognition (FSAR) requires representations that expose discriminative motion dynamics from only a few labeled videos. Recent trajectory-based methods leverage long-term point tracks for explicit temporal correspondence, but often treat trajectories as carriers of sampled visual features or summarize their motion with compact 2D displacement-based descriptors. We instead view an action as the ordered evolution of 2.5D trajectory states and their local geometric interactions. Based on this view, we introduce GeoTRAM, a geometry-aware trajectory state modeling framework for FSAR. GeoTRAM lifts sparse tracks into 2.5D trajectories, where StateMotion models ordered intra-trajectory state evolution and RelMotion captures state-conditioned local interactions through time-varying relative geometry and motion. Quality-filtered spectral sampling provides more reliable trajectory initialization; complementary semantic, motion, and depth cues are separately refined and preserved for joint spatio-temporal modeling; action-guided reweighting and top-$\rho$ trajectory selection support complementary frame- and trajectory-level matching. Experiments on five FSAR benchmarks demonstrate strong gains on the motion-centric Something-Something benchmarks while maintaining competitive performance on more appearance-driven benchmarks and a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off.
authors: Zhiqi Miao, Marko Haralovi\'{c}, Stanislav Levendeev, Sarvesh Angadi, Jannatul Ferdous, Dan-Cristian Ploesteanu, Jiapan Guo, Estefan\'{i}a Talavera
bullets: Targets the challenge of recognizing actions from only a few labeled videos, especially when motion dynamics are discriminative.
Lifts sparse point tracks into 2.5D trajectories and models both ordered intra-trajectory evolution and time-varying inter-trajectory geometry.
Uses quality-filtered spectral sampling, separate semantic/motion/depth refinement, and action-guided trajectory selection for matching.
Shows strong gains on motion-centric Something-Something benchmarks and competitive results on appearance-driven benchmarks.
Reports a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off, with scope spanning five FSAR benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of GeoTRAM. Reliable tracking seeds are obtained through quality-filtered spectral sampling over DINOv2 [20] patch features and tracked across frames by CoTracker [11]. Relative monocular depth augments the image-plane tracks into 2.5D trajectories, on which StateMotion models the ordered evolution of explicit 2.5D intra-trajectory motion states, while RelMotion captures state-conditioned local interactions among neighboring trajectories. Semantic, depth, and motion cues undergo cue-specific temporal refinement before concatenation and joint spatio-temporal modeling. Finally, dual-CLS-guided reweighting suppresses less action-relevant trajectories, followed by the complementary frame-level prototype matching and top-ρ trajectory-level instance matching.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison between Trokens’ semanticaware point sampling and our quality-filtered spectral point sampling strategies. For each video, the semantic clusters and sampled point locations are visualized on the frame. Semantic-aware sampling often produces fragmented or redundant samples across multiple semantic regions, whereas our quality-filtered spectral sampling suppresses isolated and scattered regions and allocates more seeds to spatially coherent hand–object interaction regions.

papers.abstract: Walking offers a window into physical function that may support interpretable video-based frailty assessment. We developed silhouette-based "gaitomics" to connect frailty predictions with measurable patterns of body configuration and movement. In 66 older adults assessed using the Fried Frailty Phenotype, standardized silhouettes and gait energy images yielded 90 descriptors of shape, temporal variation, motion, and texture. Minimum redundancy maximum relevance selection using the mutual information difference criterion prioritized informative features while limiting redundancy. Each classifier was evaluated using nested stratified cross-validation with five outer and three inner folds at the participant level, with feature ranking and feature-count selection confined to training partitions. Shapley additive explanations examined contributions to held-out predictions. Bilateral silhouette difference led the aggregate feature-selection rankings for three-class classification and both comparisons involving frail participants. Attribution profiles differed across tasks, with texture and consecutive-frame silhouette differences prominent in three-class classification. Among classifier-specific evaluations, CatBoost achieved the highest mean three-class micro-AUC of 0.647 \pm 0.085. Leading pairwise mean micro-AUCs were 0.833 \pm 0.249 for frail versus nonfrail, 0.765 \pm 0.168 for frail versus prefrail, and 0.554 \pm 0.129 for prefrail versus nonfrail classification. These findings connect model predictions to explicit gait characteristics while revealing task-dependent feature priorities and limited separation of prefrail and nonfrail participants. The framework provides an interpretable basis for further investigation, with larger independent studies needed to establish reliability and clinical relevance.
authors: Laura McDaniel, Ryan Roemmich, Crystal Szczesny, Peter Abadir, Rama Chellappa, Basudha Pal

CatBoost achieved a mean three-class micro-AUC of 0.647; frail-versus-nonfrail classification was stronger than prefrail-versus-nonfrail classification.
The study is limited by small sample size and weak prefrail/nonfrail separation; larger independent studies are needed to assess reliability and clinical relevance.

papers.abstract: Video understanding keeps moving toward longer recordings, and the longer a recording is, the more questions can be asked about it. But processing it again for every question does not scale, so many systems watch the video once, build a memory, and answer later questions from it. Yet what to remember is decided before anyone knows what will be asked, and whatever is left out cannot be recovered later. Moreover, whether the savings pay off is judged by token counts, which fall when the input gets shorter but not when the model reuses what it has already computed. We present REEL, an evaluation framework that compares three saved representations built from exactly the same observed frames, so that a change in answers can come only from what the system remembered. Text writes a short record of what happened, Visual keeps the encoder outputs, and Prefix State also keeps the language-model prefix. Each is compared with full reprocessing (Frames) by paired correctness changes, cumulative GPU time, and storage size. Across six vision-language models and two benchmarks, Text and Frames differ in correctness on 20\% to 29\% of questions, even when their mean accuracy is almost the same. By contrast, Visual and Prefix State stay much closer to Frames. With unlimited storage, Prefix State is the cheapest in total GPU time among memories that keep almost all of the answers Frames gets right, for every model on both benchmarks. The trade-off is storage: Prefix State keeps up to about 21 GiB per video, whereas Text needs only kilobytes. Reusing computation and discarding information both look like efficiency, but only the second removes evidence that later questions may need, and neither mean accuracy nor token count tells them apart. REEL makes that difference measurable for any system that answers many questions from one saved memory.
bullets: Compares Text, Visual, and Prefix State memories using the same observed frames, isolating the effect of what is retained.
Evaluates each memory against full frame reprocessing using paired correctness, cumulative GPU time, and storage size.
Text changes answers on 20–29% of questions despite nearly matching mean accuracy; Visual and Prefix State stay closer to full reprocessing.
Prefix State is the cheapest high-retention option in total GPU time, but can require up to about 21 GiB per video versus kilobytes for Text.
REEL applies to systems answering many questions from a shared saved video representation.

papers.abstract: We introduce The Prestige, a video understanding benchmark that probes cognitive visual reasoning through professional magic performances, where deliberate misdirection challenges models to track events and explain unexpected outcomes. The benchmark comprises open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary VLMs reveals a substantial gap between even the strongest model and human performance. We also find systematic discrepancies between human and automated grading and identify recurring model failure modes. Ablations further show that models can select correct multiple-choice answers even when they fail to generate correct explanations independently, motivating further investigations into question formats. Together, these findings highlight limitations in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, underscoring the need for more reliable video understanding models and more rigorous benchmarks.
authors: Shuo Wen, Beixi Du, Edwin Meriaux, Junming Shi, Chloe Si, David Meger, Doina Precup, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Uses professional magic performances and deliberate misdirection to test event tracking and unexpected-outcome explanation.
Covers temporal, causal, and adversarial open-ended questions.
Leading open-source and proprietary VLMs perform well below humans and exhibit recurring reasoning failures.
Models may choose correct multiple-choice answers while failing to generate correct explanations.
Findings expose discrepancies between automated and human grading and motivate more rigorous benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Ball bounces and racket hits are the events from which tennis statistics are derived, and on monocular video the two are easy to confuse. We release a benchmark of 345 bounce and hit annotations at frame level on eight clips that mix broadcast, fixed elevated, phone and court-level viewpoints, with a frozen development and test split, a confusion-aware matcher, clip-level bootstrap intervals and a blind second annotation of three clips. On it we score supervised precise spotters with published broadcast weights, two zero-shot vision-language models, and RallyArb, an arbitration layer over a ball track and player poses that fits no parameter on event labels. The supervised spotters score near-perfectly on broadcast footage and almost nothing on phone and court-level footage, where the pooled bounce F1 of E2E-Spot is 0.130. RallyArb keeps a bounce F1 above 0.8 on the three phone and court-level clips, two of which were used to tune it, and finds 8 of 11 bounces on the held-out one, but it places hits too far from the contact frame to match human timing. The vision-language models detect events on every viewpoint and miss the contact frame by about 0.1 s. Fine-tuned leave-one-clip-out from its broadcast weights, the spotter reaches about 0.8 bounce F1 on two phone and court-level clips and stays at 0.2 on a grazing phone angle. The annotations, the evaluator and the frozen predictions of every scored row are released.
bullets: The benchmark contains 345 frame-level bounce and hit annotations across eight clips and four viewpoint types.
Supervised broadcast spotters perform near-perfectly on broadcast footage but fail on unfamiliar views; E2E-Spot’s pooled bounce F1 is 0.130 on phone and court-level clips.
RallyArb combines ball tracking and player poses without fitting event labels, maintaining bounce F1 above 0.8 on three phone/court-level clips, though tuning included two of them.
Vision-language models detect events across viewpoints but miss the contact frame by roughly 0.1 seconds.
The annotations, evaluator, and frozen predictions are released; cross-view generalization remains limited, especially for grazing phone angles and hit timing.

papers.abstract: Event cameras, spiking cochleas and similar sensors emit asynchronous events, yet most learning systems first bin them into frames or packets, so the output depends on how the stream was sliced. Networks whose state is updated exactly at every event and evolves in closed form between events are invariant to this slicing. We ask what more makes the output (i) independent of the processing order of simultaneous events and (ii) continuous in the time stamps, even when two events cross in time, while (iii) staying sensitive to temporal order. For arbitrary nonlinear event models we prove that (i) and (ii) are each equivalent to pairwise commutation of the event updates, and that once updates commute, all order dependence comes from their non-commutation with the inter-event dynamics and vanishes linearly in the time lag. This identifies a class of time-mediated non-commutative (TM) models and yields a resolution-robustness bound for any model. We construct the minimal TM layer, a learnable, provably Lipschitz generalization of the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator; prove that no single additive layer can uniformly represent ordered pair interactions, whereas a three-dimensional TM state can; show that each TM layer adds two levels of temporal nesting versus one for additive layers; and give a single-layer higher-order construction (TM-k) and a stacking rule preserving all three properties. We instantiate these results as the Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer, linear in the number of events, give a topology-free variant for temporal point processes with closed-form likelihoods, and specify a preregistered clock-robustness protocol with a physical-time threat model for spike-retiming attacks. In preliminary development-set experiments, the TM state beats an otherwise identical additive state by 3.5-9.1 points on DVS128 Gesture and by 24.5 and 30.6 points on SHD and Speech Commands.
authors: Han Wang, Jingyuan Bao, Juntao Wu, Saiao Zhou, Yuman Nie
bullets: Event updates that commute are necessary and sufficient for invariance to simultaneous-event order and continuity under timestamp crossings.
The proposed time-mediated non-commutative (TM) models retain temporal-order sensitivity through interactions with inter-event dynamics.
The minimal TM layer is learnable, provably Lipschitz, and can represent ordered pair interactions that a single additive layer cannot.
The Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer scales linearly with event count; a topology-free variant supports temporal point processes with closed-form likelihoods.
Preliminary development-set results report gains over an otherwise identical additive state on DVS128 Gesture, SHD, and Speech Commands.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Clocked versus clock-free processing. Top: binned pipelines slice the event stream into frames of width ∆; the input tensor depends on ∆ and on the phase of the grid, and moving one event across a bin edge by an arbitrarily small ε changes a count (Theorem 11). Bottom: a CFE network updates its state exactly at every event (jumps, coloured by event type) and evolves it in closed form between events (blue); queries (♦) can be placed at arbitrary times, and the result does not depend on how the stream is cut into packets (Theorem 3). Right: output of a single site as two events of types a and b cross in time, computed from the model equations with illustrative parameters. A gated update (SEL) jumps at the crossing and returns two different values at an exact tie, depending on the processing order; the TM layer is continuous and still distinguishes the two orders. Tie invariance and crossing continuity are each equivalent to commuting jumps (Theorem 5), and order information then enters only through the non-commutation of the jumps with the drift (Theorem 8).

Figure 2: The CFE network. An event stream (top left; ON and OFF events of a schematic rotating gesture), or a sampled signal converted into events by a send-on-delta encoder (bottom left, Theorem 22), drives the CFE layer. The sensor is tiled into sites; an event (red pixel) applies a jump to the state of every site in its 3×3 neighbourhood, with a letter given by its polarity and relative offset, and every site state drifts in closed form between events. TM site: events write the fast trace u and, through the mark-dependent gate gc(m)Rc, read the delayed trace s into the accumulator v; no event writes a coordinate that events read, so all jumps commute (Theorem 7). Exact parallel scan: each event acts as an affine map, so the states are computed exactly by a segmented parallel scan, and tie groups may be processed in any order. Queries read the site states x(Tq) at arbitrary times; a readout shared by all arms (signed-log normalization with raw features, convolution over the site grid, anchor-based pooling, a memory across queries and a linear layer) gives a prediction at every query. For event sequences without topology, an intensity head with a closed-form compensator gives the exact likelihood (Theorem 23). Bar heights are schematic.

Figure 3: State difference when two events of different types swap places at lag δ (FP64). TM and NS change linearly in δ , below the Lipschitz bound of Theorem 14. Selective updates jump by a constant amount at every lag, as Theorem 6 predicts.
Figure 4: DVS128 Gesture, folds 0 and 2 (198 calibration clips): accuracy against observation window for TM, NS and the stateless arm (ZERO). The benefit of the ordered state is largest early.

papers.selection_reason: A partition-invariant temporal neural network for asynchronous event streams, relevant to event-based visual understanding.
papers.title: Learning Without Clocks: Partition-Invariant Neural Network
papers.tldr: A theory and neural architecture for processing asynchronous events without clock-dependent binning while preserving temporal order and robustness to timing changes.

papers.abstract: Cross-view object correspondence identifies the same object across views. However, existing methods often rely on frame-wise matching or sequential tracking, which can propagate correspondence errors under appearance changes or occlusions. Therefore, we introduce cross-view temporal object correspondence, which requires preserving object identity across both views and time from a query mask. To address this, we propose XTrack, a unified framework which repurposes a pretrained video DiT with semantic and spatiotemporal priors for RGB-to-mask latent transport, jointly modeling cross-view matching and temporal tracking. However, naive video DiTs do not guarantee accurate cross-view grounding and often attend to semantically similar yet incorrect objects across views. Thus, we introduce focal cross-view attention alignment, hard negative conditioning, and local context crop strategies to ensure reliable grounding. Finally, beyond these architectural enhancements, we also tackle the lack of dense annotation by introducing a pseudo-label curation pipeline that converts sparse Ego-Exo4D annotations into dense supervision to enable effective video-level training. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of XTrack as a unified framework, ensuring robust temporal consistency and identity preservation.
bullets: Addresses error propagation from frame-wise matching and sequential tracking in cross-view correspondence.
Uses RGB-to-mask latent transport with semantic and spatiotemporal priors to jointly model cross-view matching and temporal tracking.
Improves cross-view grounding through focal attention alignment, hard-negative conditioning, and local context crops.
Introduces a pseudo-label curation pipeline to create dense supervision from sparse Ego-Exo4D annotations.
Reports robust temporal consistency and identity preservation, without specific quantitative results in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of XTrack.

Figure 8: Difference between noise-to-mask and RGB-to-mask design. (a) Our RGB-to-mask architecture directly predicts mask flow from RGB latents, allowing the transport trajectory to focus entirely on mask prediction. (b) In contrast, the noise-to-mask design predicts masks by denoising from noise while conditioning on RGB latents, following the standard diffusion formulation. As a result, the model implicitly undergoes an intermediate noise-to-RGB transport before mask prediction. Implicit noise-to-RGB transition is further visualized through PCA analysis in Fig. 9.

Figure 4: Pseudo-label curation pipeline. (a) performs bidirectional propagation from anchor frames and identifies unreliable regions, which are refined by (b) cross-view geometric verification and further filtered by (c) within-view semantic verification.

Figure 11: Additional qualitative results of comparison with V2-SAM. Results are shown in the exo-query, ego-target setting. As a match-then-track pipeline, V2-SAM heavily depends on the initial cross-view match, making it difficult to refine incorrect or incomplete matches during tracking. In contrast, our method more reliably localizes the target object’s presence across frames, producing temporally stable masks under challenging cross-view appearance changes.

Figure 1: Comparison of cross-view temporal object correspondence paradigms. (Top) (a) propagates the mask in the query view and matches it per frame. (b) starts with initial match, then tracks in each view independently. (c) XTrack jointly models cross-view correspondence and temporal dynamics. (Bottom) Comparison of different cross-view correspondence paradigms.

Figure 6: Motivation for temporal reasoning in cross-view object correspondence. Conventional frame-wise matching methods suffer from several failure modes, including empty predictions when the query object is absent and incorrect correspondences under ambiguous appearances. Since predictions are made independently for each frame, the resulting target correspondences often become temporally inconsistent.
Figure 5: Qualitative results on Ego-Exo4D [16]. Results are shown for the Exo2Ego setting. Additional Exo2Ego results are provided in Fig. 12, and the opposite setting is shown in Fig. 13.

Figure 16: Qualitative results of dataset curation pipeline. (a) Forward-only propagation produces temporally inconsistent results, including missing masks and inaccurate object localization. (b) Backward propagation still exhibits similar failure cases, including incorrect propagations and ambiguous predictions. (c) Our cross-view geometric verification stage selects geometrically consistent correspondences from bidirectional propagation results. (d) Our within-view semantic verification stage further refines the selected masks by removing semantically incorrect predictions that cannot be resolved through geometry alone. These results demonstrate that both cross-view geometric verification and within-view semantic verification are necessary for constructing reliable dense correspondence annotations.

Figure 10: Visualization of cross-view attention. (a) shows the exocentric query frame and query mask used as input. (b) visualizes the cross-view attention map Aego→exo, indicating which exocentric regions the ego-side target attends to when establishing correspondence. (c) visualizes the reverse attention map Aexo→ego. (d) shows the resulting ego-side prediction mask. The first and third rows correspond to the baseline without attention alignment, while the second and fourth rows show the results after applying focal attention alignment. Without alignment, attention is broadly dispersed across irrelevant regions, resulting in inaccurate or missing predictions. In contrast, focal attention alignment produces compact and localized attention patterns that better align with the target object, leading to more accurate cross-view correspondence predictions.

papers.selection_reason: Unified cross-view temporal object correspondence using video DiT priors; fits video understanding and temporal identity tracking.
papers.title: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Cross-View Temporal Object Correspondence
papers.tldr: XTrack repurposes a pretrained video diffusion Transformer to track the same object across views and time from a query mask, maintaining identity despite appearance changes and occlusions.

papers.abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.
bullets: Introduces an annotated egocentric tennis dataset synchronized with five allocentric views, global positions, contact times, and stroke labels.
Evaluates seven tasks, including player/ball localization, trajectory forecasting, stroke anticipation, contact-time prediction, and contact-position estimation.
Best models reach 0.14 m ego-player and 0.54 m ball localization error, 0.34 m and 0.91 m forecasting error over 1.1 s, and 0.14 s contact-time error.
Auxiliary depth improves 3D ball localization; longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, suggesting reliance on scene context over motion alone.
A conditional diffusion model generates adaptive whole-body tennis motion from vision predictions at real-time rates.
papers.selection_reason: Egocentric video spatiotemporal reasoning and action anticipation for robots; evaluates vision and VLMs.
papers.title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video
papers.tldr: The study evaluates vision models for perceiving and predicting tennis dynamics from egocentric video, finding strong localization and contact-time prediction while revealing challenges in metric depth and ball forecasting.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon camera-controlled video generation relies on persistent memory to maintain scene consistency. Existing systems follow two strategies to achieve this consistency. Full-history approaches retain all generated observations, causing unbounded storage and retrieval costs. Selective-construction approaches reduce redundancy, but make one-time retention decisions that are never revisited, even as an observation's value changes with the evolving memory bank. Both strategies leave a shared question unresolved: as the generated history evolves, which stored observations should still remain in memory? Our key insight is that the value of a stored observation is not fixed, but relational: it depends on the alternatives currently available in the memory bank. A view supported by many geometrically and visually similar substitutes can be relinquished with little loss of coverage, whereas an observation with few viable alternatives should remain regardless of age. We introduce Keepsake, an online, training-free controller for fixed-capacity spatial memory. At each update, Keepsake constructs a pose-appearance graph over retained and newly generated observations, combining camera-pose proximity with visual similarity. A retention priority jointly captures the number of strong substitutes and the similarity of the closest alternative, allowing Keepsake to continually reassess memory value, preserve observations with little alternative support, and evict highly replaceable ones under a fixed budget. The controller modifies only the persistent-memory update; the host generator, denoising schedule, and retrieval rule remain unchanged. Across MemCam and WorldMem, Keepsake improves FVD and LPIPS under a fixed memory budget. On 180-second MemCam trajectories, it retains only 32 of 5,397 frames while reducing FVD by 35.1%.
bullets: Full-history memory has unbounded costs, while one-time selective retention cannot adapt as the memory bank evolves.
Keepsake is an online, training-free controller that builds a pose-appearance graph over retained and new observations.
It prioritizes observations with few strong geometric and visual substitutes and evicts highly replaceable ones.
The controller changes only persistent-memory updates, leaving the host generator, denoising schedule, and retrieval rule unchanged.
Across MemCam and WorldMem, it improves FVD and LPIPS; on 180-second MemCam trajectories, it keeps 32 of 5,397 frames and reduces FVD by 35.1%.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Keepsake, a training-free controller for selective spatial memory in long-horizon video generation, addressing scene consistency through relational value assessment of stored frames.
papers.title: Keepsake: Selective Spatial Memory for Long-Horizon Video Generation
papers.tldr: Keepsake continually retains the most irreplaceable observations in a fixed-capacity video memory, improving long-horizon consistency while storing far fewer frames.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
authors: Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng, Qiangpeng Yang, Shilei Wen
bullets: Addresses the weakness of language-only reasoning traces, which can lose access to relevant video evidence.
Constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments instead of relying only on coordinates or pasted crops and frames.
Uses visual token prediction over an input-video-derived vocabulary to unify visual reconstruction and text generation.
Supports interleaved text and visual latent states, with a reinforcement-learning extension that jointly optimizes visual and text token actions.
Improves performance across multiple video benchmarks, particularly on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Improves video reasoning in multimodal LLMs via latent visual evidence generation, directly relevant to video understanding and multimodal large language models.
papers.title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
papers.tldr: VideoLVR lets multimodal models revisit compact latent visual evidence during video reasoning, reducing visual forgetting without greatly expanding context.

papers.abstract: Automatic soccer event spotting supports highlight generation, video indexing, and sports analytics, but existing methods depend on large annotated datasets and soccer-specific training. We present a zero-shot framework that detects, classifies, and temporally localizes events in full-length soccer broadcasts without task-specific parameter training. Each match is segmented into overlapping clips represented by a compact visual storyboard and the aligned commentary transcript, which a general-purpose multimodal model processes jointly. On three manually annotated matches containing 130 events, the best configuration achieves 72.0% F1@5s and outperforms SoccerNet-trained CALF and NetVLAD++ in a cross-dataset setting, while the storyboard representation reduces inference cost by 72% compared with individual frames. We further analyze the effects of model family, input representation, and prompt optimization, and introduce an evidence-grounded excitement-scoring stage that ranks detected events with natural-language explanations for highlight selection.
authors: Sadia Kamal, Mahmudul Hasan, Tony Braskich
bullets: Addresses the need for soccer event detection without large annotated, soccer-specific training datasets.
Processes overlapping clips using compact visual storyboards aligned with commentary transcripts.
Achieves 72.0% F1@5s on 130 events across three manually annotated matches and compares favorably in a cross-dataset evaluation.
Storyboards reduce inference cost by 72% versus using individual frames.
Adds evidence-grounded excitement scoring with natural-language explanations for highlight selection.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot event spotting in soccer broadcasts with multimodal storyboard; relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Zero-Shot Multimodal Event Spotting in Soccer Broadcasts
papers.tldr: A zero-shot multimodal framework spots, classifies, localizes, and ranks soccer events in full-match broadcasts using visual storyboards and commentary, without task-specific training.

papers.abstract: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.
authors: Zhongrui Gui, Junyu Xie, Tengda Han, Weidi Xie, Andrew Zisserman
bullets: Studies identifying principal characters without cast lists, actor photos, or pre-built character banks.
Defines character naming: linking a dialogue-mentioned name to the corresponding visible character.
Uses cinematic cues including shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, references, gaze, and temporal continuity.
Provides a dataset and annotations for character naming and first appearances, plus a video-and-dialogue model.
Introduces progressive character-bank construction and compares the model with proprietary multimodal language models.
papers.selection_reason: Character identification in films using video and dialogue; relevant to video-language understanding.
papers.title: As the Story Unfolds: Watching a Film and Identifying Characters as a Human Does
papers.tldr: This work introduces online character naming in films, using video and dialogue to identify who a mentioned name refers to as the story unfolds.

papers.abstract: Video captioning aims to preserve visual information through compact descriptions, predominantly using natural language. However, precisely expressing fine-grained spatial structures and temporal dynamics in natural language often leads to lengthy and potentially ambiguous descriptions. In this work, we explore Code as Video Caption, a paradigm where executable programs serve as a complementary representation of visual content through graphical primitives, layout rules, and functions of time. To examine whether code captions effectively preserve video information, we compare them with natural language captions on downstream question answering and video reconstruction tasks. Our results show that code captions achieve superior reasoning accuracy and reconstruction fidelity. Despite these advantages, realizing the potential of code captioning depends on whether current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate faithful code captions. To systematically assess this capability, we introduce CodeCap-Bench, which comprises 323 videos spanning five categories of structured 2D content, along with fine-grained annotations and a multi-level evaluation framework. Extensive experiments reveal that while leading proprietary MLLMs demonstrate promising code captioning capabilities, they still struggle to faithfully capture complex temporal dynamics, with open-source models lagging substantially behind.
authors: Jiafu Tang, Yifan Xu, Eric Tang, Junjie Zhao, Shipeng Luo, Te Sun, Haoxuan Hu, Yiyan Ji, Xinlong Chen, Zihao Wang, Yang Shi, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Jiaheng Liu
bullets: Natural language often poorly captures fine-grained spatial structure and temporal change in compact, unambiguous descriptions.
The proposed paradigm represents videos with executable programs using graphical primitives, layout rules, and time-dependent functions.
Code captions outperform natural-language captions on downstream video question answering and reconstruction tasks.
CodeCap-Bench contains 323 videos across five structured 2D-content categories, with fine-grained annotations and multi-level evaluation.
Proprietary MLLMs show promise, while open-source models lag substantially; complex temporal dynamics remain a key limitation.
papers.selection_reason: Explores code-based video captions and evaluates MLLM captioning capability, relevant to video understanding and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: CodeCap-Bench: Can Code Serve as a Good Video Caption?
papers.tldr: Code can preserve structured video information better than natural-language captions, but current multimodal models still struggle to generate faithful code for complex temporal dynamics.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for enhancing the video reasoning capability of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). Despite its empirical effectiveness, we show that outcome-level optimization can introduce an undesirable shortcut amplification effect, whereby models increasingly favor text-prior answers even when they are not supported by the visual evidence. To characterize this behavior, we investigate the training dynamics of video RLVR through the lens of perceptual uncertainty, analyzing how predictive uncertainty evolves under video-conditioned and text-only contexts. Our analysis identifies a perceptual uncertainty collapse phenomenon, in which RL training continuously sharpens the model's answer distribution while the uncertainty reduction attributable to visual evidence progressively diminishes. A further gradient-direction analysis reveals that such confidence enhancement becomes increasingly less aligned with visually grounded uncertainty reduction and is instead dominated by text-prior compression. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bifocal Self-distillation Policy Optimization (BSPO), a self-distillation framework that regulates policy updates with two complementary distributional signals. Specifically, BSPO derives empirical reasoning principles from intra-group correct and incorrect rollouts to identify reasoning-sensitive tokens, and introduces shortcut-aware visual perturbation to penalize predictions that remain invariant when task-relevant visual evidence is weakened. By adaptively reweighting the original RL advantage, BSPO preserves the task-solving benefits of RLVR while promoting updates that are both reasoning-sensitive and visually grounded. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of BSPO in improving video reasoning performance and strengthening visual faithfulness.
authors: Jiafeng Liang, Xianhao Ou, Tao Ren, Rongchuan Mu, Runxuan Liu, Dandan Tu, Ming Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Bing Qin
bullets: RLVR may make models increasingly confident in text-prior answers unsupported by video evidence.
Perceptual uncertainty collapse occurs as visual evidence contributes less to uncertainty reduction during training.
Gradient analysis links this confidence growth more to text-prior compression than to visual grounding.
BSPO combines self-distillation from correct/incorrect rollouts with shortcut-aware visual perturbations to guide policy updates.
Experiments show improved video reasoning performance and stronger visual faithfulness.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes shortcut amplification in video RLVR and proposes visually grounded policy optimization; relevant to video understanding and large multimodal models.
papers.title: Uncovering Shortcut Amplification in Video RLVR through the Lens of Perceptual Uncertainty Collapse
papers.tldr: The paper finds that video RLVR can amplify text-based shortcuts by collapsing visually grounded uncertainty, and proposes BSPO to preserve reasoning gains while improving visual faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Despite significant progress, current models struggle to generate comprehensive video captions, constrained primarily by coarse-grained supervision, which often fails to capture spatial-temporal dynamics and the underlying logical intent. To address this issue, we introduce MVRCap, a novel framework that reformulates video captioning as a reinforcement learning task steered by structured verification. Central to our approach is a Fine-Grained Verifiable Reward mechanism, serving as dense supervision to enforce rigorous visual-semantic alignment. Specifically, we construct this reward system anchored by three complementary pillars: a Hierarchical Concept Coverage Reward utilizing our newly constructed MVRCap-QA dataset to ensure multi-dimensional completeness and semantic depth, a Factuality Verification Reward to enhance factual consistency, and a Conciseness Constraint to maximize semantic density. Furthermore, we curate the high-quality MVRCap-SFT dataset, providing structured annotations across six key dimensions, to serve as a robust foundational initialization for the RL policy in this training pipeline. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MVRCap achieves state-of-the-art performance on authoritative benchmarks including VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG.
authors: Weihuang Lin, Xianing Chen, Zhibin Wang, Congzhi Zhang, Yiwei Ma, Jiayi Ji, Miao Chen, Jun Song, YuCheng, Bo Zheng, Xiaoshuai Sun, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses coarse-grained supervision that misses videos’ spatial-temporal dynamics and logical intent.
Recasts video captioning as reinforcement learning guided by fine-grained visual-semantic verification.
Combines hierarchical concept coverage, factuality verification, and conciseness rewards.
Uses the MVRCap-QA dataset for coverage evaluation and MVRCap-SFT for structured policy initialization.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on the VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Video captioning reformulated with RL and fine-grained verifiable rewards; directly fits video understanding and video-language understanding.
papers.title: MVRCap: Towards Comprehensive Video Captioning via Hierarchical Multi-Dimensional Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: MVRCap improves comprehensive video captioning by training with hierarchical, verifiable rewards that promote coverage, factuality, and conciseness.

papers.abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), which route predictions through a layer of human-interpretable concepts, have substantially improved the interpretability of visual classification by exposing an explicit, language-based rationale for each prediction. Most existing work focuses on static images, and temporal dynamics in videos have been underexplored in conceptual representation. We propose a framework that extends concept-based image recognition to procedural video understanding. It represents a multi-step video as a temporal sequence of segment-level concept score vectors and feeds this sequence into a Transformer encoder to predict the class label. We also explore a way to estimate the contribution of each concept for further interpretability. We evaluated three concept sets of different granularities on cooking and household-activity videos and found that coarser-grained concepts are sufficient for classifying these videos, which implies that fine-grained textual descriptions may be unnecessary.
authors: Ryoya Yoshiyama, Bowen Wang, Yuta Nakashima
bullets: Extends Concept Bottleneck Models from static images to multi-step video understanding.
Represents videos as temporal sequences of segment-level concept score vectors.
Uses a Transformer encoder to predict video classes.
Estimates each concept’s contribution to improve interpretability.
Evaluation on cooking and household-activity videos suggests coarse-grained concepts are sufficient.
papers.selection_reason: Concept bottleneck representation for procedural video recognition; relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Drop the Details, Get the Gist: Dynamic Conceptual Representation for Video Recognition
papers.tldr: A concept-based Transformer recognizes procedural videos from temporal sequences of segment-level concepts, showing that coarse concepts can suffice without fine-grained descriptions.

papers.abstract: Video models answer from sampled frames and may miss the decisive moment. A common remedy is to commit to an answer, re-examine the video, and confirm or revise it, a loop now mainly learned with reinforcement learning (RL). We find that RL erodes the initial answer, a phenomenon we term confidence erosion, where confidence means the label-verified reliability of the initial answer instead of self-reported certainty: because errors can be repaired later, a correct initial answer earns less reward, and the initial answer stalls even as the final answer's gain over it rises. We propose the principle confident first, reflective second: the initial answer must stay reliable on its own, above a floor set by a reference policy, and reflection may only add to it. Our method, CoFire, implements this principle with one mechanism for each erosion channel: reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference. CoFire reaches 67.0% mean accuracy on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method, and improves initial-answer and final accuracy over outcome-reward RL by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average: a stronger initial answer carries through to a stronger final one.
authors: Zihao Lin, Jingyuan Liu, Yucheng Zhang, Yuguang Yao, Lifu Huang
bullets: RL-based reflection can cause confidence erosion: correct initial answers are undervalued because later correction is rewarded.
CoFire enforces a reference-policy reliability floor for the initial answer and allows reflection to add, not replace, its value.
It addresses reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference as sources of erosion.
CoFire achieves 67.0% mean accuracy across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method.
Compared with outcome-reward RL, it improves initial and final accuracy by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses video understanding by using reinforcement learning to refine answers through reflection, specifically tackling confidence erosion in video models.
papers.title: Confident First, Reflective Second: Reinforcement Learning of Confidence-Preserving Reflection for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: CoFire trains video models to answer reliably before reflection, preserving initial-answer quality while still improving final answers through re-examination.

papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.
Evaluates 37 closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, alongside human evaluation.
Humans achieve 68.5% video-only accuracy, compared with 50.0% for the strongest evaluated MLLM, Qwen3.6-27B, in zero-shot evaluation.
Finds recurring errors in interpreting the wearer’s body, temporal events, repetition counts, and hand-side biases.
Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and training data for egocentric body-motion and temporal reasoning in MLLMs; directly relevant to egocentric video learning and video understanding.
papers.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
papers.tldr: SOMA benchmarks fine-grained body-motion understanding in egocentric video and reveals substantial gaps between current MLLMs and human performance.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.
authors: Yuqi Li, Chuanyue Yan, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Xiaoqin Feng, Junming Liu, Xi Xiao, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen, Yingli Tian
bullets: Video VLMs face high computation, latency, and memory costs on long visual sequences.
Methods are categorized by intervention stage: input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding.
Post-training quantization is treated as a cross-stage approach with different calibration requirements.
The survey examines how intervention location affects preservation of task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence.
Prior results and shared-setting experiments assess accuracy–latency trade-offs and highlight that local gains may not yield end-to-end speedups.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of training-free inference acceleration for video LLMs, organizing token pruning and memory-efficient techniques for long-video understanding.
papers.title: Training-Free Inference Acceleration for Video Large Language Models: Methods, Trade-offs, and Evaluation
papers.tldr: This survey organizes training-free methods for accelerating video VLM inference, analyzing their efficiency–evidence-preservation trade-offs across the pipeline.

papers.abstract: Dyadic relationship recognition aims to identify the latent social relationship between two individuals from their multimodal interactions. Existing methods typically project heterogeneous cues into a shared representation and optimise a flat classification objective, overlooking that relationships may rely on different interaction patterns. For instance, distant relationships can often be inferred from direct behavioural correspondence, whereas close relationships are better reflected by coordinated affective, behavioural, and multimodal responses. To address this limitation, we propose HiRe-DRR, a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning framework that organises relationship evidence from three complementary perspectives: feature level, interaction type, and relationship hierarchy. HiRe-DRR decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations and constructs homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions. We further introduce the Mixture-of-Interaction Transformer (MoI-Former), which treats diverse interactions as specialised experts and employs relation-aware sparse routing to identify relationship-relevant evidence while preserving contextual interaction information. The proposed Hierarchical Conditional Loss (HC-Loss) exploits the hierarchical nature of social relationships through coarse-to-fine supervision, enabling structured relationship reasoning. Extensive experiments on three dyadic relationship benchmarks demonstrate that HiRe-DRR outperforms recent representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods. Our routing analysis further reveals that distant relationships tend to rely on low-level homogeneous interactions, whereas closer relationships focus on high-level heterogeneous interactions. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tw-repository/HiRe-DRR.
authors: Wang Tang, Fethiye Irmak Dogan, Linbo Qing, Ce Zhu, Hatice Gunes
bullets: Addresses the limitation that different social relationships depend on different interaction patterns.
Decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations with homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions.
Uses MoI-Former with relation-aware sparse routing to select relevant interaction evidence while retaining context.
Applies HC-Loss for coarse-to-fine supervision aligned with relationship hierarchies.

Experiments on three benchmarks show improvements over representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods; routing analysis links distant relationships to low-level homogeneous interactions and closer relationships to high-level heterogeneous interactions.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical multimodal interaction reasoning for dyadic relationship recognition in video; directly a video understanding task with transferable interaction reasoning.
papers.title: Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning for Dyadic Relationship Recognition
papers.tldr: HiRe-DRR improves dyadic relationship recognition by hierarchically reasoning over multimodal cues and interaction types rather than using flat classification.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
authors: Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma
bullets: Long-video QA is difficult because sparse frame sampling can miss decisive evidence, while spurious cues can still mislead models.
S-MME benchmarks shortcut-biased behavior from misleading language correlations and salient but irrelevant visual content.
CLEAR estimates bias using question-only and locally salient-clip views, then intervenes on hidden states at inference.
Experiments across five benchmarks show consistent gains in prediction and robustness across different MLLMs.
CLEAR is presented as a complementary test-time scaling approach; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free counterfactual hidden-state intervention to mitigate bias in MLLM long-video QA; relevant to video understanding, multimodal LLMs, and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Diagnosing and Correcting Bias in MLLM for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: The paper diagnoses shortcut biases in MLLMs for long-video QA and introduces training-free CLEAR to reduce misleading linguistic and visual cues during inference.

papers.abstract: Uniform frame sampling can miss brief evidence in sparse-event videos when the VLM sees only K frames. We propose EARS (Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and motion), a training-free, query-free front-end that ranks frames using optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity. The evidence score alone has frame-level AP 0.39; used only to select frames for the VLM, EARS with temporal diversity reaches localization AP 0.94, compared with 0.88 under Uniform sampling. In the updated matched study, at K = 1 EARS reaches XD-subset F1 0.660 versus 0.614 for centered Uniform (the paired interval includes zero); earlier backbone studies use separate protocols. On mostly-silent UCF-Crime, however, EARS slightly trails Uniform. A single configuration is used across both benchmarks; the new controls do not repeat the original held-out search. EARS therefore targets low-budget videos whose salient evidence aligns with motion or audio; on dense narratives or stealthy events, uniform or semantic selection remains preferable, and cheap modality statistics cannot reliably route between them. Code: https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/EARS
bullets: Targets sparse-event videos where uniform sampling may miss brief evidence under a frame budget.
Training-free, query-free retrieval ranks frames by optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity.
With temporal diversity, EARS achieves localization AP 0.94 versus 0.88 for uniform sampling; at K=1, XD-subset F1 is 0.660 versus 0.614, with an interval including zero.
Performance slightly trails uniform sampling on mostly-silent UCF-Crime videos.
Scope is limited: uniform or semantic selection may be better for dense narratives or stealthy events, and modality statistics cannot reliably choose the strategy.
papers.selection_reason: Evidence-aware frame retrieval for budgeted video reasoning; fits video understanding and efficiency.
papers.title: EARS: Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and Motion for Budgeted Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: EARS improves low-budget video reasoning by selecting diverse frames using motion and audio cues, outperforming uniform sampling when salient events align with these signals.

papers.abstract: Point-supervised temporal action localization (PTAL) aims to recognize and localize action instances in untrimmed videos using only point-level annotations. Existing pseudo-label-based methods have made substantial progress in PTAL. However, confidence-based initialization can overlook well-localized proposals. Meanwhile, existing methods either keep pseudo-labels fixed during detector training or update them without fully exploiting alternative boundary evidence from the original proposal pool. These limitations constrain supervision quality, thereby hindering detection performance. To learn high-quality pseudo-labels, we propose a framework that integrates prior-guided initialization with consensus-guided refinement during detector training. Our framework comprises two modules: Prior-Guided Initialization (PGI) and Consensus-Guided Refinement (CGR). PGI combines proposal confidence with point-derived priors to establish instance-specific reliability for initial pseudo-label selection and candidate retention. CGR continually uses the retained original candidates to construct boundary targets, combining their consensus with evolving detector predictions to refine pseudo-labels throughout training. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves competitive detection performance compared with existing methods. In particular, our method achieves 68.5\% average mAP over tIoU thresholds 0.1--0.7 on THUMOS14, surpassing PseR by 3.7 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/zhenyingfang/LHQP
bullets: Addresses missed well-localized proposals and weak pseudo-label updates in existing PTAL methods.
Prior-Guided Initialization combines proposal confidence with point-derived priors to select reliable initial pseudo-labels and retain candidates.
Consensus-Guided Refinement uses retained original proposals and evolving detector predictions to refine action boundaries throughout training.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, achieving 68.5% average mAP across tIoU 0.1–0.7 on THUMOS14, 3.7 points above PseR.
papers.selection_reason: Pseudo-label refinement for point-supervised temporal action localization; fits video understanding.
papers.title: Learning High-Quality Pseudo-Labels for Point-Supervised Temporal Action Localization
papers.tldr: A pseudo-labeling framework improves point-supervised temporal action localization by combining point-guided initialization with consensus-based refinement during detector training.

papers.abstract: Effective video agents must learn not only how to answer, but also where to look next. Transferring this capability to smaller models is challenging because each observation serves two purposes: supporting an answer and guiding the search for further evidence. Textual descriptions may capture what is currently visible while omitting cues needed for subsequent acquisition. We introduce Latent Agentic Reasoning for Video Analysis (LARVA), a framework that distills multi-round video agents through jointly learned latent reasoning and visual observations. Rather than communicating through captions, an observer passes compact continuous representations to a reasoner that selects the next acquisition action or produces the final answer. Crucially, action and answer supervision propagate through this interface, training the observer to communicate information useful for downstream decisions. Observation reconstruction and reasoning-distribution alignment provide auxiliary supervision from textual teacher trajectories. Across five video-understanding benchmarks, LARVA achieves strong performance with 4B and 7B backbones. On VideoHolmes, Video-MME, and LVBench, the 7B model outperforms a textual CoT student trained on the same teacher trajectories by 5.1, 2.5, and 3.7 percentage points, respectively. These results highlight the value of jointly learning how agents represent evidence and act on it when distilling video-understanding capabilities.
authors: Junzhang Liu, Hao Yuan, Qi Zhang, Yiming Wu, Long Chen, Zhecan Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring agentic video understanding when observations must both support answers and guide future evidence acquisition.
Uses compact continuous latent representations between an observer and a reasoner instead of textual captions.
Jointly trains observation and reasoning through action/answer supervision, with reconstruction and reasoning-distribution alignment as auxiliary signals.
Evaluated with 4B and 7B backbones across five video-understanding benchmarks.
The 7B model surpasses a same-trajectory textual CoT student by 5.1, 2.5, and 3.7 percentage points on VideoHolmes, Video-MME, and LVBench, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Joint latent reasoning and observation for agentic video understanding fits video-language understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Joint Latent Reasoning and Observation for Agentic Video Understanding
papers.tldr: LARVA distills multi-round video-agent capabilities into smaller models by jointly learning what visual evidence to represent and how to act on it.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative video models have improved visual realism, making detection increasingly dependent on subtle temporal inconsistencies. However, these signals are weak and spatially localized, while most of the video content is redundant. This creates a fundamental mismatch: existing detectors rely on heavy backbones to model full videos, which leads to high computational cost and limited scalability. In this work, we rethink AI-generated video detection from a representation perspective. Instead of modeling entire videos, we restructure them into compact temporal slice representations that isolate informative temporal evolution. We introduce a lightweight framework using frequency-aware temporal slice consistency learning, where informative spatial rows and columns are aggregated over time to form slice-domain inputs. This reparameterization suppresses redundant appearance while preserving discriminative temporal dynamics, enabling efficient and targeted detection. By constructing slices from both high- and low-frequency regions, our method exposes complementary temporal artifacts, including unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness. We instantiate this idea in a Temporal Slice Consistency Network, which integrates task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer to model cross-slice and cross-frequency dependencies. We further introduce AI-Artist, a new benchmark with artist-curated videos from recent high-fidelity generators, including Seedance and Kling. Experiments on GenVideo and AI-Artist show that our method achieves strong performance while requiring over 400$\times$ fewer model-forward FLOPs and 3.6$\times$ faster model inference than the strong video-based baseline ReStraV (2.9$\times$ faster end to end, including preprocessing), enabling scalable and practical deployment.
authors: Wei Shang, Zhiyuan Li, Shengfeng He
bullets: Targets the redundancy and high computational cost of full-video detectors, where generation artifacts are weak and spatially localized.
Aggregates informative spatial rows and columns over time into compact slices, suppressing appearance redundancy while preserving temporal dynamics.
Uses high- and low-frequency slices to capture complementary artifacts such as unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness.
Implements Temporal Slice Consistency Network with task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer.
Evaluated on GenVideo and the new AI-Artist benchmark; reports strong performance, 3.6× faster model inference, and 2.9× faster end-to-end processing than ReStraV.
papers.selection_reason: Temporal-slice representation learning for AI-generated video detection fits video understanding and drastically reduces compute.
papers.title: Temporal Slice Learning for AI-Generated Video Detection with 400$\times$ Fewer FLOPs
papers.tldr: A lightweight temporal-slice representation detects AI-generated videos by focusing on subtle temporal artifacts, reducing model-forward computation by over 400× while accelerating inference.

papers.abstract: Intelligent operating rooms require accurate awareness of surgical workflow for better intra-operative decisions, teamwork, and surgical documentation. Therefore, accurately recognizing surgical phase during surgery is crucial. However, previous artificial intelligence-based methods provide fluctuating predictions for the transitions, restricting their clinical use. To address this challenge, we propose a clinically meaningful framework that integrates a Swin Transformer and Temporal Transformer Encoder (TTE) for effective surgical phase recognition and a parallel YOLOv11s network for real-time surgical instrument localization. To avoid phase flickering and to produce stable workflow predictions, a causal temporal smoothing is applied. The proposed framework is tested on the Cholec80 dataset for the simultaneous recognition of the surgical phases and instruments. The overall phase recognition accuracy of this model was 92%, and the macro average F1-score was 0.86. This performance surpasses CNN based methods such as EndoNet (81.7%) and SV-RCNet (85.3%), as well as temporal convolutional and transformer-based approaches including TeCNO (88.6%), Trans-SVNet (90.9%), and LoViT (91.5%). Besides, the module of instrument detection achieved mAP@0.5 = 0.863. The reliability of the results is confirmed, obtaining a high recognition rate of the workflows, and a high accuracy of the localization of the instruments. The proposed framework can serve as a foundation for intelligent surgical assistance, enriching situation awareness, and potential robotic surgery applications. Code will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/ac005sheekar/LapChol-Surgery-Swin-Cholec80
authors: Sheekar Banerjee, Md. Shahabuddin, Md. Mahbub Hasan Akash, Nabilah, Mohammad Arafat Hussain
bullets: Addresses fluctuating phase predictions, especially during workflow transitions, which limit clinical use.
Combines a Swin Transformer, Temporal Transformer Encoder, and causal temporal smoothing for phase recognition.
Uses a parallel YOLOv11s network for simultaneous surgical instrument localization.
On Cholec80, achieves 92% phase accuracy, 0.86 macro-F1, and instrument-detection mAP@0.5 of 0.863.
Supports potential intelligent surgical assistance, situation awareness, and robotic surgery applications.
papers.selection_reason: Temporal transformer for surgical phase recognition in laparoscopic video.
papers.title: Shifted Window Temporal Transformer for YOLO-Guided Phase Recognition in Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Surgery
papers.tldr: A Swin–Temporal Transformer with causal smoothing recognizes laparoscopic surgical phases more stably while YOLOv11s localizes instruments in real time.

papers.abstract: Road anomalies such as collisions, violations, and sudden hazards demand more from video understanding than detection: a practical system must verify what happened, describe the scene, and explain the cause. We find these competences pull in opposite directions for vision-language models: closed-form questions reward precise, evidence-grounded reasoning, while open-ended answers are scored by similarity to reference text, where matching the annotation style matters as much as reasoning correctly. We present Reason-or-Recite (RoR), a two-specialist framework for the Traffic Anomaly Reasoning track of the 2026 AI City Challenge. RoR (1) rewrites the official chain-of-thought annotations into a structured, temporally grounded schema and LoRA-tunes a 9B vision-language model on the enhanced traces; (2) fine-tunes a 4-bit-quantized 27B model on answers alone, absorbing the annotation style; and (3) selects between the two candidates per question with a training-free LLM judge. RoR ranks first on the in-domain leaderboard with mean score 0.6788.
bullets: Traffic anomaly video understanding requires verifying events, describing scenes, and explaining causes.
Closed-form questions favor precise, evidence-grounded reasoning, while open-ended scoring also rewards matching annotation style.
RoR LoRA-tunes a 9B model on structured, temporally grounded reasoning traces and fine-tunes a 4-bit 27B model on answer text.
A training-free LLM judge selects the better specialist response for each question.
RoR ranks first on the in-domain 2026 AI City Challenge leaderboard, scoring 0.6788.
papers.selection_reason: Video-language reasoning for traffic anomalies using specialist VLMs and an LLM judge.
papers.title: Reason or Recite: Complementary Specialists with an LLM Judge for Traffic Anomaly Reasoning
papers.tldr: RoR combines reasoning- and style-specialized vision-language models with an LLM judge to improve traffic anomaly understanding, ranking first in-domain with a mean score of 0.6788.

papers.abstract: An action seen once and the same action seen three times receive the same action-recognition label, so that supervision does not require a model to count. Answers shared across histories that differ in event order, accumulation, or relations leave those distinctions unconstrained; we call this state under-specification. Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) addresses it by training on source-grounded probes of event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency; under the same recent-frame interface it improves OVO-Bench over a strict-matched generic temporal supervision baseline while remaining comparable on StreamingBench, with the largest gain in hallucination detection.
