papers.selection_reason: Evidence-grounded benchmark for audio-visual reasoning in Omni LLMs, spanning multimodal understanding and video-language temporal reasoning.
papers.title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: EvaOmni evaluates whether audio-visual models can both answer questions correctly and identify the supporting evidence, revealing persistent weaknesses in grounded reasoning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language trackers (VLTs) accept descriptions intended to assist tracking, but accepting text does not establish that its content changes tracking decisions, particularly as visual evidence deteriorates. We introduce DISTRACT, a matched-intervention benchmark that holds video, target, and distractor fixed while crossing four text priors with four image degradations along a controlled severity axis. We evaluate five VLTs on four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise representation probes, and activation patching. Molmo2 and JointNLT exhibit directed text use. Some effects contract under degradation, whereas others show no significant endpoint change after multiplicity correction. UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack respond only weakly to changes in text semantics, with no directed behavioral effect surviving FDR correction in the tested settings. Model-internal analyses reveal that at decision-near states, correct-versus-conflicting text is decodable in Molmo2 and JointNLT but not in the other three systems. In the responsive models, decodability peaks at late states where replacement produces little behavioral change, whereas replacing selected earlier states redirects conflict-associated trajectories toward the target. Because matched-correct donors do not significantly outperform unrelated donors, these interventions identify earlier intervention-sensitive states without establishing target-specific semantic rescue. DISTRACT thus exposes when and where text affects tracking under degraded visual evidence.
bullets: Uses matched interventions crossing four text priors with four controlled image-degradation levels while holding video, target, and distractor fixed.
Evaluates five trackers across four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise probes, and activation patching.
Molmo2 and JointNLT show directed text use; UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack show no significant directed behavioral effects after FDR correction.
In responsive models, text is decodable near decisions, but earlier-state interventions more effectively redirect conflict-associated trajectories.
The benchmark identifies intervention-sensitive states, but does not establish target-specific semantic rescue because matched-correct donors did not outperform unrelated donors.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes text use in vision-language trackers under degradation; relevant to multimodal and video-language understanding.
papers.title: DISTRACT: Degradation-Indexed Study of Textual Reference Across Competing Targets
papers.tldr: DISTRACT tests whether and where textual references actually influence vision-language tracking as visual evidence degrades.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.
authors: Yuhang Chen, Guangyue Liu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Targets a gap in streaming benchmarks that focus mainly on timestamped question answering rather than deciding whether, when, and how to respond.
Defines six tasks across proactive intervention, continuous engagement, and coordination during overlapping or multi-party interaction.
Provides 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and temporal metadata.
Separately evaluates response quality, participation decisions, and timing using response quality, window response rate, and reaction latency.
Leading models respond in under a second on average, but window response rates reach at most 53.77%; adapting responses to new information remains difficult.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for real-time multimodal interaction with visual engagement evaluates video understanding and MLLM capabilities.
papers.title: DIVE: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Interaction with Visual Engagement in Continuous Streams
papers.tldr: DIVE benchmarks whether multimodal models can sustain timely, context-aware full-duplex interaction throughout continuous audio-visual streams.

papers.abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.
authors: Marc Chapus, Carlos Crispim-Junior, V\'eronique Eglin, Atilla Baskurt
bullets: Existing VideoQA benchmarks are dominated by small ground-truth counts, masking errors at rarer cardinalities.
The benchmark contains 2,600 synthetic videos with 26 balanced counts from 5 to 50, controlled camera motion, and single-class static objects.
Sixteen video-language models are evaluated zero-shot; none exceeds 27.6% exact-match accuracy.
Accuracy varies unpredictably with cardinality, including monotonic declines and peak-and-collapse patterns.
Models favor particular integers, with performance dropping sharply at neighboring counts, motivating balanced diagnostic benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic benchmark for object counting by video-language models; directly targets video understanding and multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models
papers.tldr: CountVideoBench reveals strong, model-specific biases in video object counting that standard, small-count-skewed benchmarks often hide.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Siqi Guo, Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets premature responses and other timing errors in streaming video understanding.
Uses a question-specific plan to identify observations and completion signals.
Checks draft answers at informative moments for stability, frame grounding, and event completion.
Maintains verified observations in an event ledger while the video stream unfolds.
Improves official protocols by up to 5.9 PAUC points and 6.2 accuracy points across evaluated benchmarks and backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free framework for streaming video understanding and temporal response timing, directly relevant to video-language understanding.
papers.title: PACE: Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit for Training-Free Response Timing in Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: PACE is a training-free framework that helps video LLMs decide both what to answer and when to emit it by checking answer stability, evidence grounding, and event completion.

papers.abstract: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.
authors: Yuheng Zhang, Jie Zhang, Yuecong Min, Yunwei Zhao, Meichen Liu, Qiankun Li, Shiguang Shan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of analyzing emotions in videos with few explicit semantic cues but strong sensory effects.
Introduces OSVD, a dataset of 12,000 annotated 5-second clips with video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual emotion labels and sensory-grounded explanations.
Uses Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment to align representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics.
Uses Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution with Shapley values to identify dominant modalities and audiovisual synergy or conflict.
Experiments report improved emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality.
papers.selection_reason: Psychophysics-inspired MLLM for video emotion analysis with modality dynamics alignment and audio-visual attribution.
papers.title: PI-MLLM: Psychophysics-Inspired Multimodal Large Language Model for Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis
papers.tldr: PI-MLLM models visual motion and acoustic dynamics to better predict and explain emotions elicited by oddly satisfying videos.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic video contains state transitions induced by camera displacement, deformable tissue, and instrument interaction, yet existing pre-training methods treat dynamics implicitly. Inspired by action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive world models and by the observation that endoscopic optical flow contains both shared image-plane displacement and localized residual motion, we reformulate passive endoscopic video pre-training as causal motion-guided latent-state prediction. We present EndoWorld-JEPA, to our knowledge the first latent world-model pre-training framework designed for general-purpose endoscopic video representation learning. In place of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics, the model conditions prediction of the next latent state on motion observed up to the current state. Its Optical Motion-guided module separates dominant displacement from residual motion and converts the resulting evidence into an ordered temporal motion condition and spatial local-motion weights. Complementary global and motion-local predictors use these outputs: the temporal condition modulates both latent transitions, whereas the local weights define an auxiliary motion-local state that extends prediction from scene-level evolution to spatially selective dynamics. Patch-wise motion weighting emphasizes localized change while retaining anatomical context, and past-motion-window dropout randomly withholds the complete motion condition to reduce dependence on unreliable motion. This global--local formulation learns predictable visual--motion dynamics in representation space without reconstructing stochastic appearance artifacts. Evaluation shows that a common pre-trained checkpoint achieves strong transfer across four downstream benchmarks, supporting motion-guided global--local latent prediction as an effective pre-training paradigm for endoscopic video.
authors: Jie Wang, Shilong Yang, Tao Zhou, Juan Yu, Rong Qu, Jianfeng Ren, Zhicheng Zhang, Linlin Shen
bullets: Addresses the implicit treatment of camera, tissue, and instrument-induced dynamics in existing endoscopic pre-training methods.
Uses observed motion instead of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics to condition next-state latent prediction.
Separates dominant image-plane displacement from localized residual motion to form temporal motion conditions and spatial motion weights.
Combines global and motion-local predictors, with motion-window dropout to reduce reliance on unreliable motion cues.
A shared pre-trained checkpoint transfers effectively across four downstream benchmarks, supporting the proposed paradigm.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world-model pre-training for endoscopic video with motion-guided prediction fits world-model and video representation learning interests.
papers.title: EndoWorld-JEPA: Motion-Guided Global-Local Latent World Modeling for Endoscopic Video Representation Learning
papers.tldr: EndoWorld-JEPA learns endoscopic video representations by predicting global and localized latent-state dynamics guided by observed optical motion.

papers.abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.
authors: Chuanyang Ma, Chenye Wang, Yixuan Wang, Huiling Zhou, Xingqun Qi, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Caifeng Shan, Zhenan Sun
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in predicting semantically and geometrically distinct futures from similar egocentric observation histories.
Uses fixation strength and recency to modulate a vision-language model via Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation for intention inference.
Maps intentions to contact, support, and placement fields with Anticipatory Contact Grounding.
Generates 6-DoF object trajectories and articulated motion for both hands using a diffusion-based model.
Introduces the phase-aware EgoAIM benchmark with fine-grained intention annotations; reports state-of-the-art intention and motion forecasting, with near-oracle performance in some phases.
papers.selection_reason: Egocentric hand-object interaction forecasting with gaze-based intention disambiguation fits embodied video learning and video understanding.
papers.title: Gaze2HOI: Gaze-Aware Intention Disambiguation for Egocentric Hand-Object Interaction Forecasting
papers.tldr: Gaze2HOI uses gaze cues to disambiguate intent and forecast future hand-object interactions, including contact geometry and coordinated hand-object motion.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen
bullets: RoboJudge-Bench evaluates MLLM judges on Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment using 800 human-annotated videos from 8 corpora, 10 generators, and varied hand embodiments.
Existing general-purpose and general-domain video judges show limited or inconsistent agreement with human judgments in embodied scenarios, especially for physical adherence.
RoboJudge-Train contains 12K videos with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales.
RoboJudge-9B is fine-tuned with supervised learning and reinforcement learning, achieving the highest reported agreement on the benchmark with a Pearson correlation of 0.719.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and model for evaluating embodied video generation using MLLMs, directly addressing the evaluation of embodied world models and video generation.
papers.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
papers.tldr: RoboJudge introduces a benchmark and trained 9B multimodal judge that better aligns with humans when evaluating the physical validity and instruction following of embodied video generations.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding with multimodal LLMs is fundamentally constrained by the mismatch between video length and the model's limited visual context budget, making frame selection essential for practical reasoning. Existing query-aware methods typically rely on heuristic pipelines: they assign one-dimensional query-conditioned scores to frames and then apply sampling, ranking, or extraction rules to form the final subset. While effective in practice, such methods are generally not derived from an explicit optimization objective and struggle to capture the heterogeneous evidence required for complex reasoning. In this paper, we revisit long-video frame selection from a principled optimization perspective. We formulate it as a structured evidence-allocation problem and propose OTFS, an optimal transport framework that maps multiple evidence sources onto video frames. To reflect the asymmetry of this problem---important evidence should be preserved, whereas redundant frames need not absorb mass---we instantiate this view with a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective and an efficient solver, OTFS-Sinkhorn. Combined with an exact dynamic program for coverage-aware subset extraction, OTFS yields a practical two-stage training-free pipeline. We further show that, in the single-source case, our formulation induces a Gibbs-type distribution over frames, making Q-Frame's temperature-scaled distribution a special case of our framework while also providing a broader perspective for understanding related prior methods. Experiments on three long-video understanding benchmarks show that OTFS consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines. Codes are available at https://github.com/barry664/OTFS.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between long videos and multimodal LLM context limits, where heuristic query-aware selection may miss heterogeneous evidence.
Maps multiple evidence sources to video frames using a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective.
Uses an efficient OTFS-Sinkhorn solver followed by exact dynamic programming for coverage-aware subset extraction.
Provides a training-free two-stage pipeline and shows that Q-Frame’s temperature-scaled distribution is a special single-source case.
Outperforms strong training-free baselines across three long-video understanding benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the critical bottleneck of long-video understanding by formulating frame selection as an optimal transport problem, directly relevant to video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: A Principled Optimal Transport Framework for Frame Selection in Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: OTFS formulates long-video frame selection as semi-unbalanced optimal transport to allocate diverse evidence under limited visual context.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to understand user-generated videos by integrating multiple modalities. Existing methods often treat modalities as symmetric, overlooking the fact that language provides a dominant semantic prior while nonverbal signals are complementary and noise-prone. To address this, we propose a Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing, termed TAME, that reformulates MSA as an uncertainty-guided refinement paradigm, where the language prior is calibrated and enhanced by selectively trusted nonverbal evidence. Specifically, TAME adopts an asymmetric Mixture-of-Modality-Experts framework, in which textual features act as a fixed and always-activated shared expert, while audio-textual and video-textual cross-modal branches serve as dynamically routed auxiliary experts. Furthermore, we introduce lightweight Prophet Heads to quantify the sample-level predictive uncertainty of each individual modality, and this uncertainty metric is further incorporated into the modality router to realize reliability-aware expert aggregation and fusion. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS datasets demonstrate that TAME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the majority of metrics while reducing parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2% over the mixture-of-expert baseline. %These results confirm that asymmetric expert construction with uncertainty-guided routing is an effective paradigm for MSA.
authors: Xiaohua Huang, Bingrui Lei, Xiuyan hao, Ling Zhou, Yuan Zong, Wenming Zheng, Guoying Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating text, audio, and video as equally reliable, despite language providing a stronger semantic prior.
Uses an asymmetric mixture-of-modality-experts design with an always-active text expert and dynamically routed audio-textual and video-textual experts.
Introduces lightweight Prophet Heads to estimate modality-specific, sample-level uncertainty for reliability-aware expert routing and fusion.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance on most metrics.
Compared with a mixture-of-experts baseline, reduces parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal sentiment analysis with uncertainty-guided MoE routing; transferable to video-language understanding and efficient expert routing.
papers.title: Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.tldr: TAME improves multimodal sentiment analysis by anchoring fusion on language and routing complementary audio/video evidence according to predictive uncertainty.

papers.abstract: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.
authors: Sanghyeok Lee, Juyeon Ko, Joonmyung Choi, Jongha Kim, Dohwan Ko, Ji Soo Lee, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Targets moment retrieval and highlight detection in long, variable-length videos.
Builds a multi-scale SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments.
Uses a temporally adaptive kernel to aggregate SuperClips with location- and duration-aware weights.
Introduces relative saliency losses to learn the importance of different clips.
Achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks, with promising gains.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-scale temporal pyramid for video moment retrieval and highlight detection.
papers.title: SuperClip Pyramid for Video Temporal Grounding
papers.tldr: SCVTG improves video temporal grounding by modeling events at multiple temporal granularities with semantically grouped SuperClips and adaptive aggregation.

papers.abstract: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos. Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.
authors: Zepeng Sun, Naichuan Zheng, Hailun Xia, Junjie Wu
bullets: Optical-flow extraction is a major OAD bottleneck; codec motion vectors are available directly during video decoding.
The method retains existing temporal detector architectures and uses two-stage feature alignment and teacher-guided RGB+MV training.
On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, it reaches 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow.
Decoder-to-prediction processing is 11.48× faster on CPU and 2.04× faster on GPU.
Scope: evaluated on THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD; performance remains below the optical-flow counterpart.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient online action detection using codec motion vectors instead of optical flow.
papers.title: CodecMotion-OAD: Efficient Online Action Detection with Compressed-Domain Motion
papers.tldr: CodecMotion-OAD replaces costly optical flow with decoder-provided motion vectors for efficient online action detection, achieving near-flow accuracy with substantially faster processing.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.
authors: Haonan Zhao, Jiaxuan Chen, Qingyang Liu, Shuochen Chang, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of re-encoding or retrieving video evidence for every question.
Uses causal tracing to identify video-specific model layers for memory adaptation.
Distills the representation changes caused by visual clips into a text-only memory under compact multi-scale supervision.
Evaluated on LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, achieving data-efficient video-free QA with fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods.
Scope: memory is adapted separately for each video, so it is not a universal video memory.
papers.selection_reason: Test-time training internalizes long-video memory into parameters for video-free QA.
papers.title: Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training for Long-Video Understanding
papers.tldr: MIT^3 adapts a model per video to store visual knowledge in compact parameters, enabling text-only long-video question answering without repeatedly processing frames.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video supports diverse applications, including robot learning, augmented reality, and human activity understanding. Recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from such video requires estimating both hand motion and camera egomotion to express the hands in a consistent reference frame. Many existing pipelines recover hand and camera motion in separate stages, combining hand detection, hand reconstruction, camera tracking, and trajectory refinement. We present V-JEPA Hand, a simple feed-forward video model that jointly reconstructs bilateral hand motion and camera motion from egocentric clips. It uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to extract spatio-temporal features from full-frame video and a query-based predictor to decode these features into per-frame hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion. We use the predicted camera motion to express the hand trajectories in a common world frame. The model accepts known focal lengths or predicts them when unavailable. It reconstructs each clip in a single forward pass. We train both components end to end in a single stage on a mixture of diverse pseudo-labelled videos and high-precision 3D annotations. A single model achieves the lowest coverage-aware mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard. It also yields lower world-frame trajectory errors than the compared SLAM-based pipelines. Ablations support the benefits of video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision. V-JEPA Hand achieves a forward-pass throughput of 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000. Project page: https://qft-333.github.io/V-JEPA-Hand-Page/.
authors: Ruicheng Li, Qixiu Li, Yu Deng, Sicheng Xu, Jiaolong Yang, Baining Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating hand motion and camera egomotion together for metric, consistent 3D trajectories.
Uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 video encoder and query-based predictor to estimate hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion.
Trains end to end with pseudo-labelled videos and high-precision 3D annotations; focal lengths can be provided or predicted.
Achieves the lowest coverage-aware MPJPE among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard, with lower world-frame trajectory errors than compared SLAM pipelines.
Runs at 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000; ablations indicate benefits from video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Joint 3D hand and camera trajectory recovery from egocentric video; fits embodied egocentric video learning and video understanding.
papers.title: V-JEPA Hand: Simple, Accurate and Fast 3D Hand and Camera Trajectory Recovery from Egocentric Videos
papers.tldr: V-JEPA Hand is a fast, single-pass model that jointly recovers 3D hand and camera trajectories from egocentric video in a common world frame.

papers.abstract: We investigate how frozen pretrained visual and depth representations support dense optical flow when coupled with a supervised matching network. Building on TTSFlow, this paper studies Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) feature decoding and one coarse-to-fine refinement stage. Our method fuses features from frozen DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 models and estimates optical flow through a trainable transformer-based matching pipeline. After optical-flow training on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D, it achieves 2.37 endpoint error (EPE) on the Sintel training split, Final pass, compared with 2.52 for the FlowSeek (T) configuration reported here. Our RoCo-Spring 2026 entry, RoCo-29.VSAI, obtains a robustness-balanced score of 1.1038, Spring EPE of 1.411, and RobustSpring proxy EPE of 4.739, with a lower balanced score than seven of the twelve listed reference baselines. These results characterize the complete pipeline, which reuses frozen foundation backbones and performs one refinement stage. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/Visual-and-Spatial-AI-Lab/FFlow}
bullets: Addresses dense optical-flow estimation using frozen pretrained visual and depth representations.
Fuses DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 features in a trainable transformer-based matching network.
Uses DPT feature decoding and a single coarse-to-fine refinement stage, trained on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D.
Achieves 2.37 EPE on the Sintel training split, Final pass, versus 2.52 for the reported FlowSeek (T) configuration.
The reported RoCo entry scores 1.1038 balanced robustness, with Spring EPE 1.411 and RobustSpring proxy EPE 4.739.
papers.selection_reason: Dense optical flow from frozen visual and depth foundation features; transferable to embodied perception and video motion understanding.
papers.title: Foundation Model Driven Optical Flow
papers.tldr: Frozen DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 features, decoded with DPT and refined once, enable a supervised transformer pipeline for optical flow with competitive Sintel performance.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.
authors: Xinhao Ji, Hui En Pang, Hao Li, Kairui Hu, Jiner Wang, Mingze Sun, Ziang Cao, Yalun Dai, Thang Luu, Qin Ma, Hongyi Chen, Yukang Cao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly reconstructing observer motion, scene geometry, and hand-object interactions in a shared world frame.
Introduces EgoX-Engine, which combines geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment for automatic annotations.
Provides EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset, and EgoX-Bench, a one-hour benchmark spanning indoor/outdoor manipulation and locomotion.
EgoX performs joint metric reconstruction in a single forward pass given video and first-frame object masks.
Reports improvements over evaluated baselines in camera, hand, depth, and object pose metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Joint world-grounded reconstruction of camera, scene, hands, and objects from egocentric video; learns embodied knowledge from human experience.
papers.title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience
papers.tldr: EgoXperience enables coherent world-grounded reconstruction of cameras, scenes, hands, and objects from monocular egocentric video using aligned supervision and a unified model.

papers.abstract: Human egocentric experience offers a rich foundation for learning how the world is organized and how it changes through interaction. Realizing this potential at scale requires turning growing volumes of recordings into learning resources that connect scene structure, object semantics, and interaction histories across viewpoints and time, while reducing dependence on costly manual annotation. We introduce HOLI-WORLD, an integrated ecosystem connecting experience capture, world representation, automated data construction, model learning, and independent evaluation. To sup- port learning at scale, HOLIWORLD-Foundry combines complementary static and dynamic perception to automatically construct world records that connect persistent scene structure and evolving object states with interaction histories and supporting observations. HOLIWORLD-Data organizes these records from approximately 100 self-collected scenes into grounded learning resources, including approximately 80K QA pairs used to train HOLIWORLD-VL-4B. Independent human annotations of heldout recordings form HOLIWORLD-Bench, supporting evaluation of both annotation quality and learned spatial and temporal understanding. Experiments on ScanNet, ScanNet++, Aria Digital Twin, and HOLIWORLD-Bench demonstrate strong performance in static perception and dynamic tracking, while training on HOLIWORLD-Data substantially improves HOLIWORLD-VL-4B's spatial and temporal reasoning on HOLI- WORLD-Bench and EgoDynamic4D. HOLIWORLD provides a practical foundation for expanding learning resources from the continuous flow of human experience and advancing machine understanding of the dynamic world.
authors: Hao Li, Xiyuan Zheng, Yuanyuan Gao, Yalun Dai, Xinhao Ji, Xuan-Li Chen, Jing Zhao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting large-scale human-egocentric experience into richly connected, low-annotation learning resources.
HOLIWORLD-Foundry combines static and dynamic perception to build records linking persistent scenes, changing object states, interactions, and observations.
HOLIWORLD-Data organizes approximately 100 self-collected scenes into resources including approximately 80K QA pairs for training HOLIWORLD-VL-4B.
HOLIWORLD-Bench uses independent annotations of held-out recordings to evaluate annotation quality and spatial-temporal understanding.
Experiments report strong static perception and dynamic tracking, with training data improving spatial and temporal reasoning on HOLIWORLD-Bench and EgoDynamic4D.
papers.selection_reason: Builds world intelligence from egocentric human experience, learning spatial/temporal understanding and interaction histories from human videos.
papers.title: Holi-World: Building Holistic World Intelligence from Human-Ego Experience
papers.tldr: HOLI-WORLD turns egocentric recordings into scalable resources for learning static scene structure, object dynamics, and interaction-aware spatial-temporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: While VideoLLMs have made significant progress in understanding short video benchmarks, they often struggle to summarize long-form ones. This is mainly due to performance degradation caused by long-context prompts, the inherent difficulty of preserving temporal continuity and a lack of semantically rich concepts in event descriptions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces the first recursive Video Language Summarization Model (RVLSM) designed for video processing and tailored to long-form video-to-text summarization. RVLSM recursively decomposes videos into semantically coherent segments and delegates chunk-level reasoning to VideoLLM sub-models and external tools. It employs (1) Semantic Temporal Decomposition (STD), which preserves temporal coherence and continuity through a scene-aware chunking strategy that dynamically partitions videos according to semantic boundaries, and (2) Adaptive Multimodal Tool Calling (AMTC), which ensures semantic richness of the summary via a routing mechanism that selectively invokes auxiliary modules such as action recognition, optical character recognition, automatic speech recognition, and object detection. Experiments on the VideoXum and MixTyVSum benchmarks show that RVLSM consistently improves over zero-shot VideoLLM baselines across multiple model settings and performance metrics, and is competitive with a state-of-the-art fine-tuned model for video-to-text summarization. Importantly, the named entities in the RVLSM's summaries align more closely with those detected in the ground-truth summaries than those detected by baseline and state-of-the-art methods, confirming the saliency of the event descriptions it generates.
authors: Alessia Intini, Lorenzo Vaiani, Enrico Chen, Luca Cagliero
bullets: Addresses VideoLLMs’ difficulties with long contexts, temporal continuity, and sparse event descriptions.
Uses Semantic Temporal Decomposition to split videos at meaningful scene boundaries while preserving continuity.
Uses Adaptive Multimodal Tool Calling to selectively invoke action recognition, OCR, ASR, and object detection.
Outperforms zero-shot VideoLLM baselines across VideoXum and MixTyVSum settings and metrics.
Generates summaries with named entities more closely aligned to ground-truth summaries and is competitive with a fine-tuned state-of-the-art model.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a recursive Video Language Summarization Model (RVLSM) designed for long-form video-to-text summarization. It employs semantic temporal decomposition and adaptive multimodal tool calling, improving long-video understanding.
papers.title: Long-form Video-to-Text Summarization using Recursive Language Models
papers.tldr: RVLSM improves long-form video summarization by recursively segmenting videos and selectively using multimodal tools to produce temporally coherent, semantically rich summaries.

papers.abstract: Bringing legacy video back to contemporary screens does not necessarily make it look contemporary. Earlier imaging pipelines often leave color casts, muted chroma, weak con- trast, and tonal imbalance, while correcting these character- istics still relies heavily on expert colorists and scales poorly to long, multi-shot videos. We formulate long video color modernization, a task that updates the chromatic and tonal appearance of legacy color footage while preserving scene content and coherence across frames and shots. We introduce a scalable, training-free framework that jointly modernizes grids of temporally adjacent keyframes using a pretrained text-guided image editing model, producing coherent con- temporary references without paired supervision. Compact shot-specific color transforms then propagate these adjust- ments throughout each shot, preserving spatial structure and temporal stability. We conduct a multidimensional evaluation on diverse legacy videos spanning five decades. We combine a human evaluation of perceived modernness with quantita- tive measures of content fidelity, temporal stability, percep- tual quality, and efficiency, and introduce Source-Weighted Inter-shot Grade Consistency (SW-IGC) to assess grade co- herence across shots. On our evaluation set, our frame- work achieves the highest perceived modernness while re- maining competitive across complementary measures, open- ing a path toward the systematic study of long video color modernization. Code is available at https://github.com/jiwoomood/ Video_Color_Modernization.git
authors: Dongyun Kim, Jiwoo Choi, Jaeseong Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Targets color casts, muted chroma, weak contrast, and tonal imbalance in legacy footage without relying on expert colorists.
Uses a pretrained text-guided image editor to modernize grids of temporally adjacent keyframes without paired training data.
Propagates keyframe adjustments through each shot with compact, shot-specific color transforms for spatial and temporal stability.
Evaluated diverse legacy videos spanning five decades using human modernness judgments and measures of fidelity, stability, quality, efficiency, and cross-shot consistency.
Achieves the highest perceived modernness while remaining competitive on complementary evaluation measures.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses long video color modernization, focusing on temporal coherence and using tools for video understanding. The method involves semantic temporal decomposition and adaptive tool calling, which are relevant to long-form video understanding.
papers.title: From Legacy to Contemporary: Scalable Color Modernization for Long Video
papers.tldr: A training-free framework modernizes the color and tone of long legacy videos while preserving content and maintaining consistency across frames and shots.

papers.abstract: Video-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual recognition but struggle with causal reasoning. Current evaluations are flawed: multiple-choice QA allows shortcuts, and open-ended QA lacks robust automatic evaluation. We introduce Causal Chain Generation (CCG), a novel task where models have to generate the sequence of intermediate events connecting a cause and an effect. This structured setup demands genuine reasoning and enables reliable automatic scoring. We accompany this task with two complementary metrics: SODA-Embedding, which measures the semantic matching of a generated chain against a reference, and Causal-QA, which probes the chain's causal coherence by asking whether it contains the specific causal facts needed to reconstruct the narrative. We provide two test sets: SF20K-CC, a manually annotated diagnostic on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, a movie clip benchmark derived from audio descriptions. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with narrative causality understanding, frequently hallucinating or omitting key events. To address this, we fine-tune VLMs with GRPO using a composite reward that combines a format reward, SODA-Embedding, and Causal-QA accuracy, demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines.
authors: Ridouane Ghermi, Vicky Kalogeiton, Ivan Laptev
bullets: Existing multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations can enable shortcuts or lack reliable automatic scoring for causal reasoning.
Causal Chain Generation (CCG) requires models to produce intermediate events connecting a video’s cause and effect.
SODA-Embedding evaluates semantic similarity to reference chains, while Causal-QA tests whether generated chains contain essential causal facts.
Two benchmarks are presented: SF20K-CC, based on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, derived from movie audio descriptions.
State-of-the-art VLMs often hallucinate or omit key events; GRPO fine-tuning with a composite reward substantially improves performance over strong baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses video-language causal reasoning and VLM fine-tuning, fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM interests.
papers.title: From Cause to Effect: Generating Intermediate Event Chains in Videos
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a structured task and evaluation framework for testing and improving video-language models’ ability to generate causally coherent event chains between causes and effects.

papers.abstract: Dense temporal audio-visual captioning is important for multimodal video understanding and generation. However, prior work is constrained by three main limitations: (1) the lack of a dataset combining high temporal resolution, longer videos, and bidirectional alignment between time and events; (2) the reliance of most existing RL methods on checklists; and (3) the lack of a benchmark that bidirectionally evaluates event semantic correctness and temporal accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose: (1) AVTime-50K, a high-quality 50K-scale dataset with temporally precise, semantically accurate captions and longer videos; (2) AVTime, a state-of-the-art model optimized with a novel Bidirectional Temporal-Semantic Alignment (BiTSA) reward that imposes explicit bidirectional constraints between time and events; and (3) AVTime-Bench, a specialized benchmark that introduces a novel bidirectional evaluation of temporal accuracy and semantic correctness. Our code, models, and datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Apryle/avtime.
authors: Mingyang Wu, Kaituo Feng, Bohao Li, Kaixiong Gong, Zihao Yin, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Addresses limitations in temporal resolution, video length, bidirectional time–event alignment, and checklist-based reinforcement learning.
Introduces AVTime-50K, a 50K-scale dataset containing longer videos with temporally precise and semantically accurate captions.
Proposes the Bidirectional Temporal-Semantic Alignment (BiTSA) reward to explicitly constrain alignment between event timing and semantics.
Introduces AVTime-Bench for joint evaluation of temporal accuracy and semantic correctness.
Code, models, and datasets are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes AVTime dataset and model for dense audio-visual captioning with bidirectional temporal-semantic alignment. Relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: AVTime: Reinforcing Dense Audio-Visual Captions with Bidirectional Alignment
papers.tldr: AVTime advances dense audio-visual video captioning with a large temporally precise dataset, bidirectional reward optimization, and a matching evaluation benchmark.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.
authors: Jiaxuan Sun, Biao Wang, Shuai Li
bullets: Standard video GRPO gives every rollout the same frames, which can cause homogeneous rewards and weak group-relative learning.
Multi-Frame Rollouts create aligned, temporally subsampled views from one maximal-frame decode to diversify visual evidence without architectural changes.
Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit rewards a correct lower-frame-ratio trajectory only when all full-ratio reference rollouts fail.
Experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks show robust improvements over standard GRPO.
The method uses no auxiliary networks or model-architecture modifications.
papers.selection_reason: RL framework for video reasoning in MLLMs with multi-frame rollouts; fits video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: FrameGRPO: Incentivizing Video Reasoning via Multi-Frame Rollouts and Temporal Credit
papers.tldr: FrameGRPO improves video reasoning by diversifying sampled temporal views during GRPO training and selectively rewarding efficient correct solutions.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models can jointly understand video, audio, and text, yet they remain weak at temporal grounding, a capability essential for real-world audio-visual applications. To understand this limitation, we look beyond final predictions and examine the model's internal temporal evidence. We identify a temporal generation gap: the internal attention of the model localizes the target moment more accurately than the timestamps it generates. To close this gap, we propose TACG (Temporal Attention-Consistency Grounding), a post-training method that treats internal attention as a reliable temporal pivot and aligns it with both the model prediction and the ground-truth annotation through attention-consistency training. We further build a 580K-sample training dataset by reconstructing temporal QA from dense audio-visual annotations and organizing general omni-modal instruction data. Using TACG and this training dataset, we train OmniGround, a general-purpose omni-modal model with stronger temporal grounding capability, without injecting any additional temporal cues. OmniGround reaches state-of-the-art omni-modal temporal grounding, including 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while staying competitive on both general audio-visual understanding and vision-only grounding.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Depeng Wang, Hao Lin, Ke Xu, Ya Guo, Huijia Zhu, Tanfeng Sun, Xinghao Jiang
bullets: Identifies a temporal generation gap: internal attention localizes target moments more accurately than generated timestamps.
Introduces TACG, a post-training attention-consistency method using internal attention as a temporal pivot.
Builds a 580K-sample dataset from dense audio-visual annotations and general omni-modal instructions.
Achieves 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while remaining competitive in broader audio-visual and vision-only tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves temporal grounding in omni-modal LLMs using attention-consistency training. This advances multimodal temporal reasoning and video understanding.
papers.title: OmniGround: Strengthening Omni-Modal Temporal Grounding via Attention-Consistency Training
papers.tldr: OmniGround improves omni-modal video-audio-text temporal grounding by aligning internal attention with predicted and ground-truth timestamps.

papers.abstract: Video vision-language models (VLMs) have strong semantic understanding, yet remain unreliable at precise temporal grounding. Existing gains from explicitly aligning video frames with absolute time suggest that VLMs may already encode accurate temporal locations internally but lose precision when expressing them as timestamps. Our analysis across four VLMs and two grounding datasets confirms this hypothesis: attention intervals outperform predicted intervals on approximately 66% of valid examples. We term this discrepancy the temporal generation gap. Because precise temporal annotations are expensive, this finding motivates closing the gap to improve temporal grounding using only unlabeled video-query pairs. We propose Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses internal temporal attention as self-supervision for Group Relative Policy Optimization and applies a ground-truth-free criterion to select high-value samples. SAPO consistently improves temporal grounding across multiple datasets and models spanning weak to strong initial grounding ability. Relative mIoU gains reach 33.7% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 5.4% on the strong Time-R1-7B. The improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Depeng Wang, Wei Chen, Ke Xu, Ya Guo, Huijia Zhu, Tanfeng Sun, Xinghao Jiang
bullets: Identifies a temporal generation gap: attention-based intervals outperform model-predicted timestamps on about 66% of valid examples.
Trains with Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization, combining attention-derived supervision with Group Relative Policy Optimization.
Uses a ground-truth-free criterion to select high-value unlabeled video-query pairs.
Improves temporal grounding across datasets and VLMs, with relative mIoU gains of up to 33.7%.
Improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.
papers.selection_reason: Improves temporal grounding in VLMs using self-supervised attention policy optimization (SAPO). This addresses temporal reasoning and video-language understanding.
papers.title: SAPO: Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization for Improving Temporal Video Grounding in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: SAPO uses a VLM’s internal temporal attention as self-supervision to improve precise video moment localization without labeled temporal annotations.

papers.abstract: Video Question Grounding (VideoQG) requires both accurate question answering and precise temporal localization. Existing supervised methods rely on costly temporal annotations, while existing zero-shot approaches are primarily designed for Video Question Answering (VQA) and are not optimized for temporal grounding. We propose DiffGround, an action-driven zero-shot framework built upon frozen Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Our framework first predicts an answer-relevant action cue that transforms the input question into an explicit semantic target for grounding. Action Cue converts a reasoningoriented question into an action-centric retrieval query. Guided by the action cue, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) efficiently selects informative keyframes for reasoning. Finally, we introduce Semantic Diff Refinement, a training-free temporal refinement method that exploits semantic differences between neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings to recover complete action segments from sparse predictions. Extensive experiments on NExT-GQA and STAR show that DiffGround consistently outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods, establishing a new state of the art for Video Question Grounding.
authors: Cheng-Han Lee, Amir Salimi, Hsiang-Wei Huang, Che-Chun Su, Min Sun, Cheng-Hao Kuo
bullets: Targets Video Question Grounding without costly temporal annotations.
Uses frozen multimodal models to predict answer-relevant action cues and select informative keyframes.
Applies training-free Semantic Diff Refinement to recover complete action segments from neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings.
Evaluated on NExT-GQA and STAR, where it outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods.
Scope: relies on frozen MLLMs/VLMs and is designed for action-centric temporal grounding.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot video question grounding with MLLMs; relevant to video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: DiffGround: Semantic Difference-Guided Zero-Shot Video Question Grounding
papers.tldr: DiffGround enables zero-shot video question grounding by converting questions into action cues and refining sparse temporal predictions with semantic differences.

papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.
authors: Haoyang Fan, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
bullets: Targets streaming video QA, where queries can arrive at any time and only a few preceding frames are typically relevant.
Encodes segments independently at varying representation levels, from inexpensive visual features to full KV caches.
Dynamically completes retrieved segments and pipelines computation across CPU and GPU resources using offline cost profiles.
Reports competitive accuracy with up to 10.4× lower time-to-first-token than prior methods and up to 5.9× lower than streaming systems.
Sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT below 0.5 s, or up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT below 2 s.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces StreamAhead for real-time streaming video QA, addressing video understanding and optimizing KV cache computation for efficiency.
papers.title: StreamAhead: Real-Time Streaming Video Question Answering via Adaptive Precomputation
papers.tldr: StreamAhead adaptively precomputes video representations to balance continuous processing with low-latency question answering.

papers.abstract: Video large multimodal models have improved at identifying cross-frame visual evidence and conducting open-web retrieval, as reflected in recent video deep research (VDR) benchmarks. However, existing VDR benchmarks primarily evaluate tool-use trajectories and final responses without verifying whether a model actually uses the temporal video information or the retrieved web evidence. To fill this gap, we introduce \method{}, an evidence-grounded benchmark with three features. First, it combines human review with restricted-access probing across multiple models to exclude questions answerable from parametric knowledge or a single information source. Second, each question carries structured video-to-web evidence annotations that link the relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence. Third, its evaluation protocol separately scores video grounding, web evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness. Across eight multimodal agent systems, the best reaches 76.0\% answer accuracy, yet none recovers the complete required web evidence for more than 8\% of questions. Our benchmark is publicly available at \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hh721/vdr_temp}.
authors: Xiyuan Liang, Yu Wang, Zuhao Yang, Ziting Wang, Duo Li, Sudong Wang, Zhongyu Yang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets a gap in existing VDR benchmarks, which assess trajectories and answers without verifying evidence use.
Filters questions through human review and restricted-access probing to require both video and web information.
Provides structured annotations linking relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence.
Separately evaluates video grounding, web-evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness.
Across eight multimodal agents, the best answer accuracy is 76.0%, while no system recovers complete web evidence for over 8% of questions.
papers.selection_reason: Evidence-grounded benchmark for video deep research; relevant to video understanding and multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: GroundedVDR: Grounding Video-to-Web Evidence Dependencies in Video Deep Research
papers.tldr: GroundedVDR benchmarks whether video deep-research agents genuinely ground answers in both temporal video evidence and supporting web sources.

papers.abstract: Recognizing fine-grained bodily behaviors, such as self-grooming, postural shifts, and backchanneling, is a useful intermediate step for computational social signal analysis. But the behaviors that matter vary across social contexts, and retraining a model for each new taxonomy is expensive. Vision-language models (VLMs) can adapt to new categories through text prompts, yet they lack sensitivity to body structure and often confuse subtle postural distinctions. We propose PRIMA (Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter), a lightweight module that injects a body-structure prior into frozen VLMs using human pose as a training-time supervisory signal, requiring no pose input at inference. PRIMA separates a model-specific projection head from a shared core that encodes transferable body-configuration knowledge; adapting to a new VLM requires retraining only the head. We train PRIMA on a micro-action dataset and evaluate entirely through zero-shot prompting. The adapter improves recognition on its training domain, transfers to additional VLM backbones at different scales with the core frozen, and generalizes to two unseen target datasets from social psychology and daily activity recognition. In a supporting downstream study, the improved behavior predictions also yield higher correlations with human ratings of rapport and dominance in a collaboration context. Within the scope of the tested models and indoor datasets, the results indicate that pose-guided training can produce body-structure priors that generalize across unseen behavior vocabularies and can be partially reused across VLM backbones while preserving RGB-only inference.
authors: Mingcong Ding, Babette B\"uhler, Tim F\"utterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Enkelejda Kasneci
bullets: Addresses the cost of retraining models for changing social-behavior taxonomies and VLMs’ weak sensitivity to fine-grained posture.
Uses human pose only during training to guide a lightweight adapter, while inference relies on RGB and text prompts without pose input.
Separates a shared transferable core from a VLM-specific projection head, enabling adaptation to new backbones by retraining only the head.
Reports improved recognition on the training domain, transfer across VLM backbones, and generalization to two unseen datasets.
Improved behavior predictions also correlate more strongly with human ratings of rapport and dominance; scope is limited to tested models and indoor datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot bodily behavior recognition in video via pose-guided VLM adapter, directly relevant to video understanding and action recognition.
papers.title: PRIMA: Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter for Zero Shot Social Bodily Behavior Recognition
papers.tldr: PRIMA equips frozen vision-language models with transferable pose-informed body-structure knowledge for zero-shot recognition of subtle social behaviors using only RGB at inference.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. Code is available at \url{github.com/Miraclecsc/Frame_Selection_GRPO}.
authors: Shuochen Chang, Bingjie Gao, Qingyang Liu, Qianli Ma, Yibo Miao, Haonan Zhao, Zhaohe Liao, Xiaofeng Zhang, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static keyframe-label supervision and the evidence needed for complex downstream reasoning.
Initializes a lightweight saliency policy with supervised learning, then refines it against a frozen MLLM environment.
Uses answer-token negative log-likelihood as a dense reward and a KL term to preserve consistency with the learned prior.
Achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based frame scorers while retaining lightweight inference efficiency on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.
The selector is trained once and transfers across multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient long-video frame selection for MLLMs; fits video understanding and token selection efficiency.
papers.title: From Label Priors to Task Evidence: Efficient Long-Video Frame Selection via Bayesian GRPO
papers.tldr: A Bayesian GRPO frame selector uses downstream MLLM answer likelihoods as task evidence to efficiently select informative frames from long videos.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.
authors: Jaehong Myung, Seunghun Oh, Unsang Park
bullets: Full-video speech-vision decisions can fail despite useful evidence being available in nearby visual windows.
Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED) is a training-free diagnostic that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation.
TED uses ASR transcripts and utterance intervals to query audio-free windows for temporal forecasting, alignment, or cross-modal binding.
Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, temporal forecasting accuracy improves from 29.3–33.7% to 79.3–82.2% with TED.
Controls indicate that the observed temporal anchor—not merely query replacement or region availability—drives recovery.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses temporal composition in audio-visual LLMs, relevant to multimodal and video understanding.
papers.title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
papers.tldr: TED shows that AV-LLMs often possess locally recoverable visual evidence but fail to aggregate it correctly relative to spoken utterance timing.
