papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}
authors: Junwei Wen, Deshui Miao, Guangming Lu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xin Li, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the video reference gap between language-based reasoning and visual evidence across frames.
Builds a chronological chain of video primitives linking entity references with temporal support and spatial evidence.
Uses selected primitives to generate box prompts and temporal guidance for video mask prediction.
Trains the representation with supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning.
Shows strong performance across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Spatiotemporally grounded video reasoning segmentation with video CoT; relevant to video understanding, multimodal LLMs, and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: Think Visually Across Space and Time: Grounded Reasoning for Video Segmentation
papers.tldr: TCoVP grounds video reasoning in timestamped spatial and temporal evidence to improve segmentation of implicitly described targets.

papers.abstract: Understanding when during a video a model makes its critical observations is essential for interpreting video-understanding systems. However, existing attribution methods often spread evidence diffusely across near-duplicate frames. We introduce Sufficient Frame Subsets: compact sets of frames in which all other frames are masked, yet each subset independently preserves the model's prediction. We evaluate our method on two complementary benchmarks, UCF101 and Something-Something v2, using both CNN- and transformer-based architectures. Our results show that the proposed algorithm identifies highly compact and effective frame subsets for explaining model decisions. We also find that models capable of relying on a greater number of sufficient frame subsets tend to perform better, possibly because they are more robust, consistent with prior research. Finally, the extracted frame subsets help us analyze model failure cases, reveal which aspects of a video the model has learned to emphasize, and identify opportunities for improving future training procedures.
bullets: Addresses diffuse attribution across near-duplicate frames in video understanding.
Masks all frames outside each candidate subset and tests whether the prediction is preserved.
Evaluated on UCF101 and Something-Something v2 with CNN- and transformer-based models.
Finds highly compact, effective subsets and links reliance on more sufficient subsets with better model performance.
Supports failure analysis, inspection of learned visual emphasis, and future training improvements.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies compact sufficient frame subsets for video model decisions; relevant to video understanding and frame/token selection.
papers.title: Sufficient Frame Subsets for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Sufficient Frame Subsets identifies compact groups of video frames that independently preserve a model’s prediction, enabling more focused explanations of video decisions.

papers.abstract: We show that a video can be represented with just a few keyframes without sacrificing a given model's belief about the video. Our method is the first of its kind that extracts these keyframes conditioned on the model's prediction, which is massively helpful for building explainable video models. We then fairly distribute the importance of the video to the model among the keyframes with game theoretically fair Shapley values. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that keyframe attribution is superior to the traditional frame attribution. Further, we conduct preliminary exploration on highlighting the important changes among the frames by looking at the differences between adjacent keyframes.
bullets: Extracts keyframes conditioned on the model’s prediction.
Represents videos with few keyframes without changing the model’s belief.
Uses game-theoretic Shapley values to distribute importance fairly across keyframes.
Experiments show keyframe attribution outperforms traditional frame attribution.
Also explores highlighting important changes between adjacent keyframes.
papers.selection_reason: Keyframe extraction for video model explanation; relevant to video understanding and frame/token selection.
papers.title: MoCKEFA: Model-Conditioned Keyframe Extraction and Fair Attribution for Video Model Explanation
papers.tldr: MoCKEFA explains video models by selecting a few prediction-preserving keyframes and fairly attributing the model’s decision among them.

papers.abstract: Comparing videos to assess their semantic similarity remains a challenging task for current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which are primarily trained with single-video objectives. While most prior works have focused on computing global similarity, recent studies have introduced the more challenging problem of concept-based similarity, which measures how similar two videos are with respect to specific concepts (e.g., activity, location). However, no dedicated approaches have yet leveraged LMMs to explicitly address this task. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap introducing Video Caption Entailment for video similarity estimation (VICE): a dual-branch design that leverages LMMs for cross-video reasoning. Each branch jointly processes one video and the caption of the other, measuring their alignment for a specific concept via video-language entailment. The outputs from both branches are fused to produce a final similarity score, along with a textual explanation of the model reasoning. This approach leverages the model's native single-video understanding while enabling fine-grained comparative reasoning between video and text. Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show that VICE outperforms models that process both videos simultaneously, highlighting the promise of single-video reasoning for concept-based similarity estimation.
authors: Benedetta Liberatori, Lorenzo Vaquero, Elisa Ricci, Paolo Rota
bullets: Addresses the challenge of concept-based video similarity, such as comparing activity or location, which is not directly handled by most LMMs.
Uses two branches, each processing one video with a caption of the other to assess concept-specific video–language alignment.
Fuses both entailment outputs into a similarity score and an explanation of the model’s reasoning.
Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show improved performance over models that process both videos simultaneously.
The approach is scoped to leveraging single-video understanding for cross-video comparative reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Uses video-language entailment for concept-based video similarity, fitting video-language understanding.
papers.title: Video-Language Entailment for Video Similarity Estimation
papers.tldr: VICE uses bidirectional video–caption entailment to enable LMMs to estimate concept-specific similarity between videos with textual explanations.

papers.abstract: Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to localize and segment objects referred to by natural-language expressions throughout a video. Although large vision-language models (LVLMs) implicitly encode localization cues in their attention maps, these attentions are often noisy, diffuse, and scattered across layers, heads, and modalities, limiting their direct use for segmentation. Existing methods typically rely on handcrafted attention-selection heuristics or computationally expensive attention refinement. We propose ATLAS, an attention adaptation framework that learns to transform raw LVLM attentions into object-centric localization cues. ATLAS treats attentions from all layers, heads, and modalities as structured features, combining high-resolution frame-level attentions that capture spatial information with low-resolution video-level attentions that encode temporal context. A lightweight U-Net equipped with temporal attention and FiLM-based modulation fuses these complementary representations to generate coarse segmentation heatmaps, which are propagated across the video using SAM2. Extensive experiments on challenging referring and reasoning video segmentation benchmarks show that ATLAS outperforms existing frozen-backbone methods. Code and models are available at \url{https://hamidreza-136.github.io/atlas/}.
authors: Hamidreza Dastmalchi, Ali Cheraghian, Aijun An, Abdelwahed Khamis, Lars Petersson
bullets: Addresses diffuse, scattered, and cross-layer attention that limits LVLM-based video segmentation.
Treats attention from all layers, heads, and modalities as structured features.
Fuses high-resolution spatial attention with low-resolution temporal context using a lightweight U-Net, temporal attention, and FiLM modulation.
Generates coarse segmentation heatmaps and propagates them through videos with SAM2.
Reports outperforming existing frozen-backbone methods on challenging referring and reasoning video segmentation benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts LVLM attention for reasoning video object segmentation, directly fitting video-language understanding.
papers.title: ATLAS: Learning to Adapt LVLM Attention for Reasoning Video Segmentation
papers.tldr: ATLAS learns to convert noisy LVLM attention maps into object-centric cues for reasoning video object segmentation.

papers.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.
authors: Kerui Chen, Jinglu Wang, Yun Wang, Xinjiang Wang, Yan Lu
bullets: Addresses long-video context limits and the cost of reprocessing videos for each query.
Represents videos with time-anchored text and sparse images across multiple temporal scales.
Uses separate Writer and Reader workflows, optimized respectively for source fidelity/coverage and evidence localization/utilization.
Evolving the workflows improves average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness.
Reduces storage by about 99.86% while improving QA accuracy over direct frame input and a comparable agentic method.
papers.selection_reason: Long-video QA with reusable memory for MLLMs; fits video understanding.
papers.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
papers.tldr: Video-EMem creates compact, reusable long-video memories that reduce repeated processing while improving question answering and lowering query latency.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
authors: Haonan Hu, Shuhao Chen, Weisen Jiang, Lizhao Gao, James Kwok, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets the excessive visual-token cost of videos lasting tens of minutes to hours.
Uses a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to encode frames with temporal context.
Trains frame and query embeddings with a contrastive objective to distinguish relevant from irrelevant frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs.
Scope: focuses on query-guided frame selection for long-video question answering.
papers.selection_reason: Query-relevant frame selection for long-video VideoLLMs with streaming KV cache; fits video understanding and token/frame efficiency.
papers.title: FrameScout: Scouting Query-Relevant Frames for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameScout selects query-relevant frames from long videos using temporally contextualized streaming representations and contrastive frame-query alignment, improving VideoLLM long-video understanding.

papers.abstract: Sparse-frame video-language models can change their answers when only the sampling timestamps shift. Raw agreement exposes this problem, but it need not rank errors better than token confidence or identify which additional observation will repair an answer. We argue that answer risk and action value must be estimated separately. PhaseGuard+ probes a frozen VLM at controlled temporal offsets, predicts the reliability of the phase-vote answer, and predicts the example-wise correctness gain of a specific rescue action. The second score routes only examples expected to benefit from denser frames or a stronger VLM. Both predictors use lightweight models trained on public data; the VLMs remain frozen. We use 256 Perception Test videos for method development and evaluate on a disjoint 256-video test set comprising 554 Physics questions. For Qwen3-VL-8B, reliability AUROC rises from 68.0% with token softmax to 74.8% (+6.8 pp, 95% CI [2.6, 10.7] pp). Routing 30% of questions to Qwen3-VL-32B reaches 67.87% accuracy, compared with 63.66% for budget-matched random routing (+4.21 percentage points, CI [1.89, 6.40]). All four tested rescue pairs significantly outperform random routing. Temporal sensitivity becomes actionable when the system learns both whether an answer is unreliable and whether an available action is likely to fix it.
bullets: Sparse-frame video-language models can change answers when sampling timestamps shift.
The method probes a frozen VLM at controlled temporal offsets and forms a phase-vote answer.
Separate lightweight predictors estimate answer reliability and the correctness gain from denser frames or a stronger VLM.
On Qwen3-VL-8B, reliability AUROC improves from 68.0% to 74.8% over token softmax.
Routing 30% of questions to Qwen3-VL-32B achieves 67.87% accuracy versus 63.66% for random routing; all four rescue pairs outperform random routing.
papers.selection_reason: VideoQA reliability and rescue-action routing based on temporal sampling perturbations; fits video-language understanding.
papers.title: Learning When to Trust and Reobserve Sparse-Frame VideoQA from Temporal Sampling Perturbations
papers.tldr: PhaseGuard+ uses temporal perturbations to estimate both VideoQA answer reliability and which rescue action is likely to improve it.

papers.abstract: Recognizing micro-expressions in real-world conversations is challenging, as these facial movements are brief and faint, and their interpretations are strongly dependent on the contextual circumstances of their occurrence. Most existing methods are de-contextualized, as they analyze isolated video clips while disregarding the semantic and acoustic cues in the surrounding dialogue that help explain the emergence of an expression. Decades of psychological studies have shown that social context exerts influences on facial behavior over two key dimensions: how an expression is interpreted and how strongly it is generated to begin with. However, existing micro-expression research rarely incorporates such contextual factors into its models. As an example, provocative utterances from an interlocutor may elicit suppressed negative affective reactions, which isolated silent clips are unable to account for. We propose TriCoME, a trimodal dataset consisting of visual, audio and text data sourced from real-world conversations. In this dataset, each micro-expression is paired with its concurrent utterance and preceding context. We further annotate the context based on conversational role to denote two categories: external stimuli from an interlocutor's utterance and internal background from the subject's own utterance. On this basis, we propose the Hierarchical Focusing Fusion Network (HFFNet), which aligns acoustic and semantic streams at fine granularity, compresses long dialogue sequences, modulates attention toward conversational roles via a context-type embedding, and routes each sample between visual-only and multimodal decisions based on visual confidence to prevent noisy context from degrading recognition performance.
authors: Junbo Wang, Yan Zhao, Shigang Wang, Jian Wei, Qiming Zhang, Yu Wu
bullets: Micro-expressions are brief, subtle, and difficult to interpret without surrounding conversational context.
TriCoME pairs each expression with concurrent utterances and preceding context across visual, audio, and text modalities.
Context is annotated by conversational role, distinguishing interlocutor-generated stimuli from the subject’s own internal background.
HFFNet hierarchically fuses aligned acoustic and semantic cues, models long dialogue context, and focuses on conversational roles.
A confidence-based routing mechanism falls back to visual-only recognition when contextual signals may introduce noise.
papers.selection_reason: Micro-expression recognition in conversational video with multimodal context is a video understanding task.
papers.title: Trimodal Context-Aware Micro-Expression Recognition in Real-World Conversations: A Dataset and a Hierarchical Fusion Network
papers.tldr: TriCoME and HFFNet enable context-aware micro-expression recognition by combining visual, acoustic, and semantic cues from real-world conversations.

papers.abstract: Characters, locations, and actions recur throughout a movie, so many of its moments differ only in fine-grained details. Grounding such a moment in a full-length movie requires resolving that detail rather than matching the attributes it shares with other moments, yet existing temporal movie grounding benchmarks rarely test this. We introduce CoM$^2$-Bench, a benchmark of confusable query pairs, where the two queries in each pair share most attributes but differ in a single distinguishing detail within a full movie, posing a challenge for recent temporal grounding approaches. To locate where grounding breaks down, we analyze a retrieve-then-localize pipeline, in which a retriever first selects a short candidate chunk and a localizer then performs temporal grounding within it. Separating the two stages lets us attribute each failure to either retrieval or localization. We find that retrieval is the major bottleneck: state-of-the-art retrievers often select a moment's confusable counterpart, because their choices follow the content the two moments share rather than the detail that tells them apart. To address these failures, we propose a simple, training-free remedy, Agentic Window Search (AWS): an MLLM agent $\textit{Decomposes}$ the query into attribute-level sub-queries, then $\textit{Inspects}$ each candidate window against them and $\textit{Expands}$ the window when evidence is cut off at its edge. AWS works with existing retrievers and localizers without additional training, raising mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8.
authors: Dong-Hee Kim, Seonwoo Choi, Changbeen Kim, Juyeon Ko, Youngju Choi, Il Hyeon Mun, Hyunwoo J. Kim, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Introduces paired queries that share most attributes but differ in one distinguishing detail.
Evaluates retrieve-then-localize pipelines on full-length movies and separates retrieval from localization failures.
Finds retrieval is the main bottleneck: systems often select a confusable counterpart based on shared content.
Proposes training-free Agentic Window Search, which decomposes queries, inspects candidate windows, and expands truncated windows.
Improves mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8 when used with existing retrievers and localizers.
papers.selection_reason: Temporal grounding benchmark and MLLM agent for confusable movie moments, relevant to video-language understanding.
papers.title: Grounding Confusable Movie Moments
papers.tldr: CoM²-Bench exposes fine-grained confusions in movie moment grounding, while Agentic Window Search improves retrieval and localization without training.

papers.abstract: AI-generated video (AIGV) detection is increasingly important for mitigating misinformation, impersonation, and other malicious uses of synthetic media, yet existing detectors often generalize poorly to unseen generators in open-world settings. To better understand this challenge, we analyze the failure modes of AIGV detectors under cross-generator out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts and observe that detector representations strongly encode generator-specific cues, which are associated with substantial ID-OOD performance drops. Further analysis shows that naively perturbing generator-sensitive tokens can even reduce OOD performance, indicating that generator-related cues and detection-relevant evidence are only partially separable. Motivated by these findings, we propose Forensic Obfuscation of geneRator-specific cues via Gradient-guided Embedding perturbation (FORGE), a token-aware adversarial training framework for open-world AIGV detection. FORGE identifies tokens that are strongly associated with generator-specific shortcuts yet less critical to real/fake discrimination, and selectively perturbs them during training to suppress generator-dependent patterns while preserving useful forensic evidence. Through synchronized adversarial training between an attacker and a detector, FORGE encourages the detector to learn more transferable generator-invariant forensic representations. Experiments on 29 held-out benchmark entries show that FORGE achieves an average F1 of 92.62, outperforming eight strong baselines by 5.31 points, while also remaining robust under four common post-processing attacks. We will release our code and datasets upon acceptance.
authors: Qi Zhou, Yuanfan Li, Huiqi Deng, Hongbin Pei, Yazhe Tang
bullets: Existing detectors often overfit to generator-specific cues, causing substantial performance drops on unseen generators.
Naively perturbing these cues can hurt detection because generator signals and real/fake evidence are only partly separable.
FORGE uses token-aware, gradient-guided adversarial embedding perturbations to reduce reliance on generator-dependent patterns.
Synchronized attacker–detector training encourages generator-invariant forensic representations.
On 29 held-out benchmark entries, FORGE reaches 92.62 average F1, surpasses eight baselines by 5.31 points, and remains robust to four post-processing attacks.
papers.selection_reason: Adversarial training for open-world AI-generated video detection, relevant to video understanding and forensics.
papers.title: Beyond Generator-Specific Shortcuts: Open-World AI-Generated Video Detection via Adversarial Training
papers.tldr: FORGE improves open-world AI-generated video detection by suppressing generator-specific shortcuts while preserving transferable forensic evidence.

papers.abstract: Long-video agents must map hours or days of multimodal evidence into a bounded context while respecting token and latency budgets, making memory design a context-management challenge. Existing memory systems largely rely on hand-designed policies, leaving open how to jointly optimize memory design for performance and efficiency. We propose Long Video Meta-memory Harness (LVMH), an automated multi-agent framework that formulates memory-policy development as multi-objective code search around a fixed answer model. To guard against self-certification and development-set overfitting, LVMH separates implementation from independent review and enforces protected observation boundaries. Persistent meta-memory records past proposals, traces, costs, and failures to guide subsequent policy revisions. Through this harness, we discover Self-Evolving Evidence Memory (SEEM), a "text-first, vision-second" policy that answers from compact structured event memory and evidence specialists, consulting localized frames through a selective visual gate. The policy evolved on EgoLifeQA generalizes to unseen benchmarks, outperforming Meta-Harness on both Ego-R1 Bench and Video-MME (L) with GPT-5 mini. Across the three benchmarks, SEEM with GPT-5 achieves 65.7% average accuracy, surpassing the previous state of the art by 7.7 percentage points with approximately 32x lower average evaluation token use and 91x shorter average response time.
authors: Liwei Che, Benlin Liu, Dai Li, Xiangyan Li, Zijian Wu, Changjiang Li, Minghao Guo, Chengzhi Mao, Vladimir Pavlovic, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Addresses the challenge of compressing hours or days of multimodal video into bounded context under token and latency budgets.
Uses multi-objective, multi-agent code search around a fixed answer model, with independent review, protected observations, and persistent meta-memory.
Discovers SEEM, a text-first, vision-second policy that uses structured event memory and selectively retrieves localized frames.
SEEM generalizes from EgoLifeQA to unseen benchmarks, outperforming Meta-Harness on Ego-R1 Bench and Video-MME (L).
Across three benchmarks, SEEM with GPT-5 reaches 65.7% average accuracy, with approximately 32× lower token use and 91× shorter response time than prior state of the art.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes memory policies for long-video agents, advancing long-video understanding and efficiency.
papers.title: LVMH: A Meta-Optimization Harness for Long-Video Agent Memory
papers.tldr: LVMH automatically searches for efficient long-video memory policies and discovers SEEM, which improves accuracy while greatly reducing token use and response time.

papers.abstract: Central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) remain a major source of preventable morbidity and mortality in healthcare settings. Proper execution of the central line dressing change (CLDC) procedure is essential for infection prevention, yet current approaches to competency assessment rely primarily on manual ob- servation by clinical educators, making evaluation time-intensive, difficult to scale, and limited in consistency and granularity. These challenges highlight the need for AI-assisted skill evaluation methods that can support more objective, reproducible, and scalable assessment of clinical performance. However, progress in this area has been constrained by the lack of broad-scale, clinically grounded datasets for developing and evaluating such methods. In this work, we present the collection process of a large-scale video dataset for CLDC skill evaluation, comprising 365 recordings of registered nurses collected during the 2026 annual competency exam at Houston Methodist Hospital. Each video is paired with subtask-level temporal annotations and clinical performance assessments spanning 17 subtasks of the procedure. We describe the data collection and curation pipeline, including pilot testing of record- ing configurations, annotation protocol design, and post-collection processing. We further establish the feasibility of video-based skill assessment through benchmark experiments with spatiotemporal deep learning models. This dataset provides a foundation for future research on automated clinical skill assessment, feedback generation, and AI-assisted training in nursing education.
authors: Ummey Tanin (Pam), Shannan K. Hamlin (Pam), Hsin-Mei Chen (Pam), Peizhu (Pam), Qian
bullets: Addresses the scalability, consistency, and granularity limits of manual clinical competency assessment.
Contains 365 recordings of registered nurses performing central line dressing changes during an annual competency exam.
Pairs videos with temporal annotations and clinical performance assessments across 17 procedure subtasks.
Describes a collection, curation, and annotation pipeline, including recording pilots and post-collection processing.
Benchmark experiments with spatiotemporal deep-learning models demonstrate the feasibility of video-based skill assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a large-scale video dataset for automated clinical skill evaluation and benchmarks spatiotemporal models, relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: The Collection of a Real-World, Large-Scale Dataset for Automated Skill Evaluation in Central Line Dressing Change
papers.tldr: This work introduces a large, clinically grounded video dataset for AI-based evaluation of central line dressing change skills.

papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of pedestrian crossing intentions plays a critical role in enhancing the safety of pedestrian-vehicle interactions in autonomous driving. However, effectively capturing subtle spatiotemporal patterns in pedestrian pose sequences and integrating complementary visual and ego-vehicle motion information remain challenging. This paper proposes a spatial-temporal-channel attention-enhanced multimodal graph network (STC-MGNet) for pedestrian crossing intention prediction. STC-MGNet introduces a spatial-temporal-channel (STC) attention-enhanced pose graph encoder to learn discriminative representations from pedestrian pose sequences. Three parallel attention branches selectively emphasize informative skeletal joints, observation frames, and feature channels, with their outputs integrated through learnable fusion weights. To leverage complementary visual and ego-vehicle motion information, a multi-stage cross-modal channel modulation mechanism is introduced to adaptively refine pose representations through modality-specific channel gating at successive graph encoding stages. Experimental results demonstrate that STC-MGNet achieves accuracy rates of 70%, 87%, and 88% on the JAADbeh, JAADall, and PIE datasets, respectively, outperforming several representative baseline methods. Ablation experiments further highlight the complementary contributions of visual and ego-vehicle motion information to prediction performance.
bullets: Targets safer pedestrian–vehicle interaction by modeling subtle spatiotemporal cues in pedestrian pose sequences.
Uses parallel spatial, temporal, and channel attention to emphasize informative joints, frames, and feature channels.
Applies multi-stage cross-modal channel modulation to refine pose features using visual and ego-vehicle motion cues.
Reports accuracies of 70%, 87%, and 88% on JAADbeh, JAADall, and PIE, respectively.
Ablations indicate that visual and ego-vehicle motion information make complementary contributions.
papers.selection_reason: Spatiotemporal pose graph with multimodal attention for pedestrian action/intention prediction; fits video action understanding.
papers.title: STC-MGNet: Spatial-Temporal-Channel Attention-Enhanced Multimodal Graph Network for Pedestrian Intention Prediction
papers.tldr: STC-MGNet improves pedestrian crossing-intention prediction by combining attention-enhanced pose graphs with visual and ego-vehicle motion information.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the overview of the runs related to the Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) and Video Question Answering (VQA) tracks of TRECVID 2025 on behalf of the CERTH-ITI team. For the AVS track, we introduce a two-stage framework built on foundation models. In the first stage, multiple vision-language models (VLMs) encode both the input query, augmented through LLM-generated rephrasings, and the candidate video shots, producing weighted similarity scores for initial retrieval. In the second stage, we utilize a Multimodal-LLM(MLLM)-based reranking module that evaluates the semantic alignment between each shot among the top-N highest-ranked ones and the original query, generating updated relevance scores for reordering these shots. This MLLM-driven reranking significantly improves contextual matching and produces more accurate final rankings without requiring any model training. Regarding the VQA track, we fine-tune an audio-visual MLLM model on the provided TRECVID training dataset and we implement an inference-time scaling technique to enhance the multimodal understanding capabilities of the MLLM. For the open-ended Answer Generation (AG) task, we aggregate multiple model responses per question via a majority vote. The responses are generated with greedy sampling from different random frame subsets of the video and they are ranked based on the number of votes. For the Multiple-Choice (MC) task, instead of voting, we use mean pooling on the logits assigned by the fine-tuned model to each candidate response. Through the combination of fine-tuning and frame subset ensembling we achieve the highest score across 3 metrics in the VQA AG task and the second highest in the VQA MC task.
authors: Andreas Goulas, Damianos Galanopoulos, Ioannis Patras, Vasileios Mezaris
bullets: AVS uses LLM-generated query rephrasings and multiple VLMs for initial video-shot retrieval, followed by MLLM-based reranking of the top-N shots.
The AVS reranker assesses semantic alignment with the original query and requires no additional model training.
VQA fine-tunes an audio-visual MLLM on TRECVID training data and applies inference-time scaling over different random frame subsets.
For answer generation, responses are aggregated by majority vote; for multiple choice, candidate logits are averaged.
The approach achieves the highest score on three VQA answer-generation metrics and the second-highest score on the multiple-choice task.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM-based video QA and reranking for video search; relevant to video understanding and multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: MLLM Frame Subset Ensembling for Audio-Visual Video QA and MLLM-based Reranking for Ad-hoc Video Search in TRECVID 2025
papers.tldr: The CERTH-ITI team combines foundation-model retrieval and MLLM reranking for AVS with frame-subset ensembling for VQA, achieving top performance in several TRECVID 2025 tasks.

papers.abstract: In real-world videos, sound events are often associated with localized and fine-grained visual cues, such as object motion, object-part dynamics, contact events, and interactions between objects. Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods employ implicit conditioning based on global visual representations or explicit control derived from temporal and spatial cues. However, subtle sound-producing and sound-indicative interactions remain insufficiently captured, leaving room for more precise visual conditioning of sound-event semantics and temporal dynamics. Motivated by this observation, we refer to regions containing such sound-relevant visual evidence as Semantic-Critical Regions (SCRs) and introduce SCR-V2A, a V2A generation framework that explicitly localizes and encodes SCRs as fine-grained visual guidance for audio generation. Specifically, we first identify SCRs through sound-related visual localization. We then transform the localized regions into a control representation through adapter-based dual visual encoding, which jointly captures global visual context and fine-grained sound-relevant evidence. The representation is used to condition a downstream audio generation model. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that SCR-V2A achieves strong performance in distribution matching and audio quality while remaining competitive in cross-modal alignment and requiring few trainable parameters. These results highlight the value of prioritizing fine-grained, sound-relevant visual regions for V2A generation.
authors: Yun Fang, Wei Guo, Zhuonan Liang, Heng Wang, Weidong Cai
bullets: Targets subtle cues such as object motion, contact events, object-part dynamics, and inter-object interactions that global video representations may miss.
Localizes Semantic-Critical Regions (SCRs) using sound-related visual localization.
Uses adapter-based dual visual encoding to combine global context with fine-grained SCR guidance.
Conditions a downstream audio generation model on the resulting visual representation.
Shows strong distribution matching and audio quality across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, with competitive cross-modal alignment and few trainable parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Video-to-audio generation with fine-grained visual localization; relevant to video understanding and cross-modal conditioning.
papers.title: Semantic-Critical Regions for Video-to-Audio Generation
papers.tldr: SCR-V2A improves video-to-audio generation by explicitly focusing on fine-grained visual regions that contain sound-relevant evidence.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on audio-visual question answering, but correct answers do not necessarily imply that their stated reasoning is grounded in relevant perceptual evidence. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate final-answer accuracy, offering limited insight into whether model-generated rationales correctly identify visual regions, temporal intervals, and audio events supporting predictions. We introduce ANCHOR, a benchmark and evaluation framework for measuring grounded-rationale alignment in multimodal reasoning, comprising 2,319 videos and 8,272 question-answer pairs with structured reasoning traces, temporal evidence, spatial bounding boxes, and salient audio cues, including a human-refined test set of 224 videos and 975 question-answer pairs. We separately measure answer correctness, hallucination, logical divergence, and conciseness, with direct spatial and temporal grounding measurements on a focused subset. Across the full benchmark, twelve contemporary MLLMs show a substantial alignment gap: models with comparable answer performance can differ markedly in whether their explanations are supported by annotated evidence. On a matched subset of 100 videos and 446 question-answer pairs, rankings remain highly stable across human-refined, Gemini-generated, and GPT-generated references (mean Pearson r=0.99), providing evidence against model-reference circularity within this subset. Grounding-cue ablations of three MLLMs on the full human-refined test set reveal a consistent modality hierarchy: removing video reduces accuracy by 38.4-41.8 points, while removing bounding boxes (3.2-7.7 points) and audio (4.2-5.6 points) causes smaller, complementary, model-dependent drops. These findings show answer-only evaluation obscures important grounding failures and position ANCHOR as a testbed for evaluating accurate and evidence-aligned audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Joel Julin, Souraja Kundu, Liza Dahiya, George Z. Wei, Liuyue Xie, Jingru Yi, Xu Zhang, Hao Yang, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Introduces a benchmark with 2,319 videos and 8,272 question-answer pairs, including structured reasoning traces and annotated evidence.
Measures answer correctness, hallucination, logical divergence, conciseness, and direct spatial-temporal grounding.
Finds a substantial alignment gap: models with similar answer accuracy can differ greatly in evidence-supported explanations.
Reference rankings are highly stable across human- and model-generated rationales on a matched subset (mean Pearson r=0.99).
Ablations show video removal causes the largest accuracy drop, while bounding boxes and audio provide smaller, complementary benefits.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for grounded audio-visual reasoning and evaluation of rationales.
papers.title: ANCHOR: Audio-Visually Grounded Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Benchmark
papers.tldr: ANCHOR evaluates whether multimodal models’ reasoning is grounded in the relevant visual, temporal, and audio evidence—not just whether their answers are correct.

papers.abstract: Physical reasoning about humans in videos has largely focused on everyday interactions, where contact, pressure, pose, and motion support embodied perception and contact-aware applications. Still, short and forceful properties like impact events remain relatively underexplored, despite their relevance to broader understanding of how abrupt physical events affect the human body. To fill this gap, we introduce human-centric impact localization, a new task that localizes target physical impacts temporally within a video and spatially on the human body. We further present HAPACT, a HumAn-centric imPACT dataset and benchmark built from movie clips, containing over 2.8K video-query pairs with more than 20K fine-grained human-annotated frames. We built HAPACT around viewer-grounded annotation, text-conditioned localization, and supervision at frame-level temporal and SMPL-X-based spatial granularity. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our benchmark, we conduct extensive evaluations of existing methods, employing video moment retrieval models for temporal localization and human-scene contact models for spatial localization. For the spatial task, we propose a text-conditioned baseline by reformulating localization as query-guided body-region selection. Benchmark results show that physical impact localization remains challenging for existing methods, motivating HAPACT as a dedicated benchmark to support physical impact reasoning in videos.
authors: Youngrae Kim, Yejin Jang, Eunho Kim, Youjin Sung, Kun-Woo Song, Sangpil Kim, Sang Ho Yoon
bullets: Defines human-centric impact localization as joint temporal and spatial localization of abrupt physical impacts.
Provides over 2.8K video-query pairs and more than 20K fine-grained, human-annotated frames from movie clips.
Uses viewer-grounded, text-conditioned annotations with frame-level timing and SMPL-X-based body-region supervision.
Evaluates video moment retrieval and human-scene contact models, and introduces a text-conditioned body-region selection baseline.
Results indicate that existing methods face substantial challenges in physical impact reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces HAPACT, a benchmark for human-centric physical impact localization in movies, relevant to Video Understanding and Embodied AI.
papers.title: HAPACT: A Benchmark For Human-Centric Physical Impact Localization in Movies
papers.tldr: HAPACT introduces a benchmark for locating physical impacts in movies both in time and on the human body, revealing that current methods still struggle with this task.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained alignment between text and video object trajectories is a core challenge in multimodal understanding. Existing embedding models excel at global retrieval, yet their single global representation entangles multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics, limiting direct object-level grounding. To address this issue, we propose VTrajEmbed, an embedding model that decomposes a video into object trajectories and aligns each trajectory embedding with text for object-level grounding through retrieval. Our main contributions: (1)Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding, a dual-branch architecture that establishes trajectory representations by densely sampling low-resolution frames for high-frequency motion cues and sparsely selecting high-resolution frames for scene context, aggregated by a shared LLM backbone; (2)Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning, a training objective built upon these representations that couples an intra-group loss and a batch-level bidirectional loss under a relation mask, excluding unverified relations and preventing confirmed matches from becoming false negatives; (3)Text2Traj-Bench, a trajectory-level text-video benchmark with model-assisted construction and human-verified query--trajectory relations. Experimental results show that VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively, and achieves 49.48% average R@1 across five global retrieval benchmarks, compared with 42.86% for Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B.
authors: Ruizhi Chen, Zining Fan, Yudi Guo, Jiang Liu, Zhiyu Lin, Zhongjiang He, Shouqian Shi, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses global embeddings’ tendency to entangle multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics.
Uses Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding to combine dense low-resolution motion cues with sparse high-resolution scene context.
Introduces Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning with relation masking to handle verified matches and unknown relationships.
Provides Text2Traj-Bench, a human-verified trajectory-level text–video benchmark.
VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes VTrajEmbed for aligning text with video object trajectories, a relevant technical contribution to Video Understanding and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: VTrajEmbed: Aligning Text with Video Object Trajectories via Spatiotemporal Embeddings
papers.tldr: VTrajEmbed enables object-level text–video grounding by aligning text with individual video trajectories rather than a single global video representation.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
authors: Lieqi Liu, Rui gao, Jia-Chen Gu, Wenbo Hu, Zhaobin Mo, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Targets long-tail, safety-critical scenarios that existing perception and simple temporal benchmarks underrepresent.
Covers six task families, including spatial reasoning, temporal memory and extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness.
Combines multiple-choice judgments with free-form VQA requiring scene explanations and driving-decision justifications.
Across 12 models, the best reported average multiple-choice accuracy is 43.4%, compared with an approximately 20% random-choice baseline.
Finds that descriptive scene understanding does not guarantee accurate safety judgments, with motion reconstruction especially challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces STRIDE, a benchmark for spatiotemporal reasoning in driving edge cases, highly relevant to VLMs and Video Understanding.
papers.title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases
papers.tldr: STRIDE benchmarks whether vision-language models can reason about object motion, interactions, and future consequences in complex driving edge cases.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: BEV tokenization compresses video MLLM visual tokens while improving embodied spatial reasoning, combining spatial intelligence, token merging, and video understanding.
papers.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens
papers.tldr: Cambrian-BEV improves embodied spatial reasoning by aggregating multi-view video features into a compact, persistent bird’s-eye-view representation.

papers.abstract: Answering complex spatial reasoning questions from egocentric video requires determining what evidence is needed, acquiring targeted observations, and combining them through multiple reasoning steps. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to perform this process reliably. Agentic systems address this challenge by querying external vision and geometry tools, but training their reasoning leaves these tools unchanged, so inaccurate observations can still lead to incorrect answers. We introduce EgoP$^{2}$C, a framework that internalizes a plan-perceive-compose process within a single VLM. To this end, we first train specialized Planner and Perception teachers using separate adapters (Dual-LoRA), then fine-tune the corresponding experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) student under their supervision. We subsequently train the student on trajectories generated by its current policy using a segment-level extension of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), assigning different trajectory segments to different supervisors. The Planner teacher supervises which evidence-seeking questions to ask, when to stop gathering evidence, and how to compose the final answer. The Perception teacher supervises the video-grounded answers to those questions. At inference, the student executes this adaptive workflow end-to-end, without external spatial tools. Across three spatial reasoning benchmarks, EgoP$^{2}$C students built from Qwen3-VL-8B and SenseNova-SI-1.3-8B outperform their base models by an average of 9.2 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Across both backbones, EgoP$^{2}$C reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8-66.3% and achieves $1.29$-$1.49\times$ speedups over their shared Dual-LoRA teacher.
authors: Chaoyu Li, Arka Sadhu, Yuliang Li, Hyo Jin Kim, Yuning Chai, Pooyan Fazli
bullets: Addresses unreliable multi-step spatial reasoning caused by inaccurate external tool observations.
Uses Planner and Perception teachers with Dual-LoRA to supervise a mixture-of-experts student.
Applies segment-level multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train the student on its own trajectories.
The resulting workflow adaptively asks evidence-seeking questions, stops gathering evidence, and composes final answers.
Across three benchmarks, it improves base-model accuracy by 9.2 and 7.5 points, reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8–66.3%, and achieves 1.29–1.49× speedups over the teachers.
papers.selection_reason: Internalizes plan-perceive-compose reasoning for egocentric video spatial understanding, fitting spatial intelligence and video-language reasoning.
papers.title: EgoP$^{2}$C: Internalizing Plan-Perceive-Compose for Spatial Reasoning in Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: EgoP²C teaches a single VLM to plan, selectively perceive, and compose answers for spatial reasoning in egocentric video without external tools.

papers.abstract: Manual annotation of synchronized video and EEG recordings is a bottleneck in preclinical seizure research. We present an empirical study of seizure detection and behavioral severity grading using 24,131 paired clips from 601 sessions across 20 rats in a soman-induced epilepsy model. Ten video architectures and seven single-channel EEG models are evaluated independently on binary detection and three- and five-class severity tasks. In the session-exclusive reference comparison, R(2+1)D-18 and GRU achieve detection macro-F1 scores of 0.968 and 0.974, respectively; for five-class grading, the corresponding scores are 0.657 and 0.560. Subject-exclusive evaluation reduces five-class macro-F1 to 0.475 for video and 0.404 for EEG, highlighting the difficulty of grading unseen animals. Temporal-sampling experiments demonstrate the value of multiple frames, while detection performance varies relatively little across the evaluated video architectures. A separate video-only binary-detection evaluation on RodEpil achieves a mean seizure-class F1 of 0.979 after uniform re-encoding to reduce identified class-correlated encoding cues. The study characterizes existing models for behavior-defined severity labels under the evaluated protocol, motivating further investigation of expert-assisted annotation workflows. Our code and github page is available here.
authors: Alloy Das, Shreyan Ganguly, Nyzil Massey, Hung Phi Doan, Zhanhong Jiang, Thimmasettappa Thippeswamy, Soumik Sarkar
bullets: Evaluates 10 video architectures and 7 EEG models on 24,131 synchronized clips from 601 sessions involving 20 rats.
Detection is strong under session-exclusive evaluation, with best reported macro-F1 of 0.968 for video and 0.974 for EEG.
Five-class severity grading is more difficult, reaching 0.657 for video and 0.560 for EEG in session-exclusive evaluation.
Subject-exclusive testing lowers five-class macro-F1 to 0.475 for video and 0.404 for EEG, emphasizing limited generalization to unseen rats.
Multiple-frame temporal sampling helps; detection varies little across video architectures, and a re-encoded RodEpil evaluation reports seizure-class F1 of 0.979.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of video and EEG models for seizure detection and severity grading, fitting video understanding and temporal representation learning.
papers.title: Seeing Seizures: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Video and EEG Deep Learning for Automated Rodent Seizure Detection and Severity Grading
papers.tldr: This study benchmarks video and single-channel EEG deep-learning models for automated rodent seizure detection and behavioral severity grading, finding strong detection but substantially harder generalization to unseen animals and severity classes.

papers.abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to jointly localize a target in space and time given a natural-language query. Despite continued advances, existing STVG benchmarks remain largely centered on localizing targets through instance-specific descriptions, leaving them largely decoupled from long-form reasoning increasingly emphasized in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this paper, we introduce Event-STVG, a task that shifts STVG from locating what is described toward event-level reasoning by unifying long-form context, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding. To facilitate research on Event-STVG, we construct a large-scale benchmark comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal substantial difficulty, with the strongest model achieving only 5.4% m-vIoU at the 10-minute horizon. Across domains, we consistently observe confusion among repeated same-type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. Event-STVG establishes a new challenge for visual understanding in MLLMs, calling for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time. Code and annotations are available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/EventSTVG
authors: Yizhe Zhang, Xujia Wang, Songqi Tang, Xujie Tang, Leo Jiahao Jiang, Jiacheng Wang, Bowen Qu, JinBo Li, Qin Wang, Ji Qi, Lei Hou, Bin Xu, Juanzi Li
bullets: Targets limitations of existing STVG benchmarks, which focus mainly on instance-specific descriptions rather than long-form event reasoning.
Unifies long-context understanding, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding.
Contains 4,016 annotated event occurrences spanning soccer and seven additional domains.
State-of-the-art MLLMs perform poorly, with the strongest model reaching 5.4% m-vIoU at a 10-minute horizon.
Models commonly confuse repeated same-type events, struggle with spatial grounding, and rarely ground all required roles jointly.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a new spatio-temporal video grounding task with long-form event reasoning, directly relevant to video-language understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning
papers.tldr: Event-STVG introduces a challenging benchmark for grounding complex, repeated events and their roles across long videos in both space and time.

papers.abstract: Video models commonly use uniform grids even though visual complexity varies substantially across space and time. We introduce OctVideo, which approximates a video clip with an octree. This hierarchy recursively partitions a spatio-temporal volume into eight subvolumes, so that smooth regions remain coarse while detailed regions receive finer cells. Each leaf stores local RGB values and spatio-temporal gradients, supplemented by a lightweight learned residual. For reconstruction, a Conv1D VAE maps the serialized cells to a regular latent grid and selectively refines details during decoding. Our VAE achieves 36.12 dB PSNR with 38.2M parameters and 189.4 GFLOPs per clip on Kinetics-400 (K400). It also generalizes zero-shot to the high-resolution Densely Annotated VIdeo Segmentation (DAVIS) 2016 dataset with reconstruction quality comparable to the best evaluated models. On both datasets, it requires the fewest model FLOPs and achieves the fastest encoding and decoding among the evaluated models. OctVideo also supports video understanding, achieving competitive recognition performance with few input tokens when trained from scratch. By exploiting the redundancy already present in video signals and efficiently processing sparse structures, OctVideo provides an efficient representation for video.
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of uniform spatio-temporal grids for videos with uneven visual complexity.
Recursively partitions clips into eight-way subvolumes, storing RGB values, gradients, and learned residuals at leaves.
Uses a Conv1D VAE to serialize octree cells into a regular latent grid and selectively refine details during decoding.
Achieves 36.12 dB PSNR on Kinetics-400 and generalizes zero-shot to DAVIS 2016 with comparable reconstruction quality.
Reports the fewest model FLOPs and fastest encoding/decoding among evaluated models, while retaining competitive recognition with few input tokens.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces OctVideo, an octree-based video representation that efficiently encodes spatio-temporal volumes, offering a novel approach to video representation learning.
papers.title: Octree-based Video Representation
papers.tldr: OctVideo represents videos with an adaptive octree that allocates computation to detailed regions, enabling efficient reconstruction and competitive understanding.

papers.abstract: Sparse video understanding often requires selecting a small set of visual evidence under a fixed frame budget. Most sparse selectors allocate this budget globally, allowing all frames to compete with one another. For temporally localized events, this can be a poor inductive bias: useful evidence is often distributed across pre-event context, the event itself, and post-event consequences. We study fixed-budget evidence allocation for localized event videos and show that globally competitive Top-$K$ selectors can preserve recognition and grounding while producing unstable event evidence. On DoTA Video Anomaly Recognition, Global Top-$K$ obtains competitive recognition and temporal grounding, but low selector-event alignment at $K=12$ (Frame AUC $51.5 \pm 10.8$). We propose dKFD, a phase-structured differentiable selector that reserves evidence capacity across pre-event, event, and post-event phases after full-sequence temporal encoding. Under matched-budget multi-seed evaluation, dKFD improves Frame AUC by $+30.97$ over a matched Global Top-$K$ selector at $K=12$ ($p<0.01$), while yielding modest but statistically significant recognition gains and comparable temporal grounding. Mechanism ablations show that phase supervision is load-bearing: removing it reduces Frame AUC to $41.1 \pm 12.0$ even when phase-partitioned budgets are retained. Downstream diagnostics on VRU-Accident show consistent gains over learned Global Top-$K$ across VLM families, while dense captioning reveals a boundary condition where uniform sampling remains competitive. These results support phase-structured allocation as a controlled fixed-budget approach for event-centric sparse evidence selection, not as a universal video summarization strategy.
bullets: Global Top-K selection can recognize and temporally ground events while selecting unstable, poorly aligned evidence.
dKFD uses full-sequence temporal encoding and a differentiable phase-structured selector with reserved capacity for three event phases.
On DoTA at K=12, dKFD improves Frame AUC by 30.97 points over matched Global Top-K, with modest recognition gains and comparable grounding.
Removing phase supervision substantially reduces selector-event alignment, indicating it is central to the method.
Gains extend across VLM families on VRU-Accident, but uniform sampling remains competitive for dense captioning; the method is not presented as universal video summarization.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a phase-structured selector for localized event understanding in video, improving evidence selection for temporally localized events.
papers.title: dKFD: Phase-Structured Evidence Allocation for Fixed-Budget Localized Event Understanding
papers.tldr: dKFD improves fixed-budget evidence selection for localized events by allocating frames across pre-event, event, and post-event phases.

papers.abstract: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.
authors: Yitong Xia, Zeren Jiang, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Processes clean video latents in one encoder pass, avoiding iterative denoising.
Uses on-demand spatial queries and continuous-time queries for flexible spatial and temporal prediction.
Adds a frozen video-depth LoRA as a geometry prior without introducing trainable parameters.
Performs strongly on 3D point tracking, video depth, and camera pose estimation, including complex in-the-wild motion.
Demonstrates the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception.
papers.selection_reason: Video generator repurposed for 4D perception; fits 3D vision and video understanding.
papers.title: Gen4P: Video Generators are 4D Perceivers
papers.tldr: Gen4P repurposes a pretrained video generator as a fast, unified feed-forward model for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video.

papers.abstract: Understanding characteristics and activities of individuals in complex multi-person environments is crucial for real-world applications. However, existing datasets often simplify this problem to grounded group activity recognition, single-person activity recognition, or close-set activity recognition, thus limiting the generalizability of models trained on these datasets. In this work, we introduce the task of Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition (GHADAR), which involves describing the characteristics and activity descriptions of \textbf{every} person in a video, provided the location of the person in the video, which is more practical for real-world applications. To facilitate this, we introduce a new dataset derived from AVA-Actions by generating open-set captions for the person description and activity. In addition, we propose a novel method to effectively utilize the information contained in grounding during training by constraining the cross-attention masks during training in VLMs to improve performance for this task. Our experiments show that our method outperforms SOTA VLMs on this task. Finally, we demonstrate the limitations of existing evaluation metrics, which are overly reliant on human-annotations and exact text-text matching. As an added video-based evaluation, we propose a holistic VLM-based evaluation schema that compares concepts {\em directly} between the video and the generated predictions. Thus, in this work, we develop a complete framework for GHADAR, including a dataset, a novel method and an evaluation schema, thereby establishing a strong foundation for future research in this domain.
authors: Jay N. Paranjape, Jurijs Nazarovs, Rohan Sarkar, Yue Guo, Lipeng Ke, Sankar Venkataraman, Vishal M. Patel, Nataraj Jammalamadaka
bullets: Addresses the limitations of datasets focused on group activities, single-person actions, or closed activity sets.
Introduces GHADAR, requiring grounded, open-set descriptions of each person in a multi-person video.
Creates a dataset from AVA-Actions with generated captions for personal characteristics and activities.
Constrains VLM cross-attention masks during training to better exploit person grounding.
Reports better performance than existing VLMs and proposes holistic video-to-text concept evaluation beyond exact text matching.
papers.selection_reason: Grounded per-person activity recognition in video with VLM cross-attention masking and new evaluation schema.
papers.title: Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition in Videos
papers.tldr: GHADAR enables video models to describe every person’s characteristics and activities using their locations, supported by a new dataset, grounding-aware training, and video-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).
authors: Jiapeng Shi, Qiuxia Hou, Jiaqi Leng, Junke Wang, Yanhao Zhang, Haonan Lu, Ziyi Ye, Zuxuan Wu
bullets: Addresses the weak fine-grained alignment of methods that treat captions as unstructured text.
Uses event-centric supervision through the self-curated EVA-Data dataset.
Combines supervised fine-tuning with GRPO optimization.
Optimizes global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization.
Reports gains of 9.0% on ChronusAV and 3.3% on WorldSense.
papers.selection_reason: Event-centric audiovisual video captioning and alignment; directly fits video-language understanding and temporal event reasoning.
papers.title: EVA-Cap: Optimizing Audiovisual Video Captioning via Event-Centric Alignment
papers.tldr: EVA-Cap improves audiovisual video captioning by decomposing captions into atomic events and optimizing their audiovisual alignment.

papers.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
authors: Zhuoming Liu, Jinhong Lin, Lin Zhang, Yiwu Zhong, Yin Li
bullets: Addresses the context bottleneck caused by memory methods that retrieve or append historical video observations to current inputs.
Uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to consolidate incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA parameter updates while keeping current observations as input.
Introduces MaLoW-Instruct, a streaming-video instruction dataset with 381K question-answer pairs across 56K videos.
Achieves 3.9%–11.8% higher performance than prior memory approaches on OVO-Bench’s backward split, with modest latency overhead.
Also improves action success on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%, suggesting applicability to vision-language-action models.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming VLM memory via LoRA weights; improves video understanding and VLA action success.
papers.title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos
papers.tldr: MaLoW turns long-term video history into evolving LoRA weights, enabling streaming VLMs to retain context without repeatedly reloading past observations.

papers.abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
authors: Agnese Chiatti, Matteo Matteucci, Viola Schiaffonati
bullets: Studied 56 AI-literate participants across 392 video question-answering trials.
After each response, participants rated task-specific trust and chose to reject, verify, or fully delegate to AI.
Higher post-interaction trust strongly predicted delegation, but trust and delegation were not equivalent.
Verification was the most common policy and often occurred alongside high trust.
Delegation increased with task order, motivating enacted delegation traces as a framework for studying human-AI oversight.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates human delegation and trust in interaction with multimodal AI (Video QA), relevant to multimodal model evaluation and user interaction.
papers.title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
papers.tldr: An online study shows that trust predicts how people delegate to multimodal AI, while observed delegation behavior captures experience-related factors that trust ratings miss.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence.
