We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
authors: Dongjie Cheng, Ruifeng Yuan, Ran Wei, Ning Song, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Li
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed visual-imagination pipelines, such as novel-view synthesis, for diverse reasoning tasks.
Uses tools and skills to help the VLM decide whether and how to imagine, formulate generation requests, and interpret visual evidence.
Introduces co-evolution of tools, skills, and execution code from feedback while keeping model weights fixed.
Improves over direct reasoning with the same VLM across seven spatial, temporal, causal, and perceptual benchmarks.
Reports relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA; the strongest variant outperforms five evolving baselines across five benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: VWM-driven agentic reasoning for spatiotemporal and spatial tasks fits world models, video understanding, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
papers.tldr: CoWorld Reasoner equips a VLM with an evolving, tool-based video world-model harness for flexible visual imagination and stronger spatiotemporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Surgical teams could benefit from assistants that watch the video for requested events, such as "tell me when the clip applier appears during Calot triangle dissection", and answer questions about what has already happened. We formalise this task as request-driven event detection with exact semantics and causal alert decisions, and present SurgStreamer. It separates procedure-specific perception, which maps the 1-FPS stream to a structured state over tools, actions and phases, from procedure-agnostic reasoning, which evaluates a formal monitoring condition over this state and an event memory, either with exact rules or with a small controller that addresses entities through pointers rather than names. We evaluate this monitoring core with gold conditions. On a pre-registered, sealed test set of 12 laparoscopic cholecystectomies, SurgStreamer reached a macro event-F1 of 0.598 over full procedures. On identical 75-s windows with only the window available to every method, it scored 0.677. The tested configurations of the streaming vision-language model OneStreamer-4B, including ones fine-tuned on SurgStreamer's state or on video with an adapted vision encoder, scored at most 0.540 (Holm-adjusted p <= 0.012). At three external centres, re-training only perception raised performance on held-out procedures from 0.239 to 0.470. On a new procedure, pituitary surgery, controller weights trained on cholecystectomy matched an in-domain controller on oracle state (0.947 vs 0.938). On predicted state they missed the pre-registered non-inferiority margin (-0.024 [-0.040, -0.008]) unless the alert thresholds were re-calibrated. The results support separating perception from reasoning and point to perception under distribution shift as the main limitation.
authors: Bowen Xiang, Jon S. Heiselman, Michael I. Miga
bullets: Formalizes monitoring with exact event semantics, causal alert decisions, structured state, and event memory.
Maps 1-FPS video to tools, actions, and phases, then evaluates conditions using rules or a pointer-based controller.
Achieved macro event-F1 of 0.598 on full procedures and 0.677 on identical 75-second windows.
Outperformed tested OneStreamer-4B configurations, which reached at most 0.540 under the reported evaluation.
Perception under distribution shift remains the main limitation; retraining helped across centres, while cross-procedure transfer required recalibration.
papers.selection_reason: Request-driven event detection in surgical video, fits video understanding.
papers.title: SurgStreamer: proactive, request-driven monitoring of surgical video streams with structured state and a reusable reasoning layer
papers.tldr: SurgStreamer separates surgical-video perception from reusable request-driven reasoning to detect specified events and answer questions about prior events.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have accelerated video generation technologies. However, AI-generated videos (AIGVs) remain susceptible to various distortions, highlighting the need for dedicated video quality assessment methods. Content semantics play an important role in AIGV quality assessment, with source prompts typically used as textual references. However, these prompts may not accurately reflect the generated video content, resulting in a discrepancy between the intended textual description and the generated result. To address this limitation, this paper proposes VGCap, an AIGV quality assessment framework guided by visually grounded captions that align better with generated content. Specifically, we introduce two forms of captions: a global caption obtained by minimally revising the source prompt based on multi-frame visual evidence, and prompt-independent segment captions that describe localized temporal content. Together, these captions provide complementary textual evidence for assessing spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment. Experimental results on the LGVQ and FETV datasets show that VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions. Further ablation studies on caption sources and temporal components confirm the effectiveness of visually grounded captions for each quality dimension, while highlighting the benefits of segment-level features for temporal quality prediction. The source of VGCap will be available at https://github.com/lolo123-123/VGCap.
authors: Kehao Zhou, Yixuan Li, Yuxuan Jiang, Fan Zhang
bullets: Source prompts can diverge from the actual video, limiting content-aware quality assessment.
VGCap uses a revised global caption based on multi-frame evidence and prompt-independent segment captions for localized temporal content.
These complementary captions assess spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment.
Experiments on LGVQ and FETV show VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions.
Ablations support visually grounded captions and show segment-level features benefit temporal quality prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Visually grounded captioning for AI-generated video quality assessment; relevant to video-language understanding and temporal quality evaluation.
papers.title: Beyond Source Prompts: Towards Visually Grounded AI-Generated Video Quality Assessment
papers.tldr: VGCap improves AI-generated video quality assessment by replacing unreliable source prompts with visually grounded captions that better match generated content.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.
authors: Boyu Cui, Junhao Luo, Zhihao Wang, Linghan Chen, Zejun Li, Jiwen Zhang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei
bullets: Existing video benchmarks focus mainly on interpreting observed content, not anticipating assistance needs or deciding when to respond.
The benchmark measures daily perception, risk prediction, and intervention.
It evaluates 12 open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems.
Current models struggle with well-calibrated response decisions and appropriate restraint.
Training P$^3$I-Assistant-4B with additional proactive data improves several tasks, but gains vary by capability.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for proactive video understanding with video-language models, directly fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM topics.
papers.title: From Perception to Prediction and Intervention: Benchmarking Proactive Video Assistants in Real-Life Scenarios
papers.tldr: P$^3$IBench evaluates whether video assistants can perceive situations, predict risks, and intervene appropriately in real-life streaming scenarios.

papers.abstract: Understanding video content requires reasoning at multiple levels of granularity, from identifying objects to interpreting their interactions and localizing when specific actions occur. This thesis studies three query-guided grounding tasks that answer where key objects are (object-level grounding), how they interact (relationship-level grounding), and when specific moments occur (moment-level grounding). For object-level grounding, we present QDETRv, a query-guided extension of the Detection Transformer for one-shot localization of unseen objects in videos, which combines query-context fusion, a memory module for temporal consistency, and unsupervised pretraining on synthetic object trajectories. We further propose the Temporal Object-Aware Vision Transformer (TOViT) for few-shot video object detection, which builds on a language-aligned open-set vision encoder and propagates high-confidence object features across frames. For relationship-level grounding, we introduce few-shot referring relationships in videos: given a (subject, predicate, object) query and a few support videos sharing the predicate, the entities are localized by optimizing a T-partite random field using a meta-learned relation network with query-conditioned translational embeddings, Global Semantic Aggregation, Local Localization Aggregation, and belief-propagation-based message passing. For moment-level grounding, we propose the Moment Alignment Transformer (MATR) for video-to-video moment retrieval, which uses dual-stage Dynamic Time Warping for pre- and post-fusion alignment, learnable queries for boundary prediction, and self-supervised pretraining with temporal augmentations; MATR also extends to text-to-video moment retrieval with performance comparable to, or better than, the state of the art. These contributions advance query-guided video understanding across spatial, relational, and temporal grounding.
bullets: Addresses where objects are, how entities interact, and when relevant moments occur in videos.
Introduces QDETRv for one-shot unseen-object localization and TOViT for few-shot video object detection.
Models few-shot referring relationships with a meta-learned relation network and T-partite random-field inference.
Proposes MATR for video-to-video moment retrieval, with an extension to text-to-video retrieval.
Reports text-to-video retrieval performance comparable to or better than state of the art; scope centers on few-shot, open-set, and query-guided settings.
papers.selection_reason: Covers query-guided video grounding for objects, relationships, and moments, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Where, How, and When: Query-Guided Grounding for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: This thesis develops query-guided methods to ground video content at the object, relationship, and moment levels.

papers.abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.
authors: Zane Durante, Paul Tang, Keshigeyan Chandrasegaran, Amit Kaushal, Shrinidhi Kowshika Lakshmikanth, Feolu Kolawole, Yu Jun Zheng, Yifan Geng, Shobhit Agarwal, Kevin Schulman, Juan Carlos Niebles, Ehsan Adeli, Arnold Milstein, Li Fei-Fei
bullets: Builds minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical data into hourly reports.
Lets an LLM agent query the hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records.

Achieves up to 84.8% action-detection accuracy and 61.0% QA accuracy, compared with 49.3% for the strongest same-backbone baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Multimodal video-based action detection and behavior understanding fit video understanding.
papers.title: TRACER: A Multimodal Harness for Patient Care in Hospitals
papers.tldr: TRACER is a training-free multimodal system that organizes continuous hospital video and clinical records into queryable timelines for patient-behavior analysis.

papers.abstract: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.
authors: Huachao Zhu, Junjielong Xu, Sicheng Li, Liang Yang, Mingtao Chen, Zhichao Hu, Li Jiang, Pinjia He
bullets: Introduces a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases spanning 14 claim–fact classes and three versions of each video.
Misleading claims reduce mean accuracy from 90.1% to 51.9%; 42.8% of initially correct answers flip to the trap answer.
Evaluates seven open-weight and four proprietary models, finding that strong performance without claims does not imply claim resistance.
Proposes DEAR, a training-free agent that separates evidence arbitration from reading and answers from a fresh context.
Across 500 videos and three proprietary models, DEAR raises misleading-claim accuracy to 81.8–85.2% and reduces trap answers to 11.6–15.0%.

papers.title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing
papers.tldr: VisualTrust shows that multimodal models often let misleading on-screen claims override video evidence, while DEAR substantially improves resistance without reducing no-claim accuracy.

papers.abstract: Identifying individual dogs from barks in real-world videos remains challenging and largely unexplored. Solving this problem would enable long-term behavioral analysis, veterinary monitoring, and animal welfare monitoring by attributing vocalizations and behaviors to the correct individual. Real-world videos are challenging because multiple dogs may bark simultaneously, become occluded, or move in and out of view. Prior studies show that canine vocalizations and visual appearance contain discriminative identity information, but these modalities have largely been studied independently. We present a multimodal dog-fingerprinting framework combining visual identification, multiple-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting to associate bark events with individual dogs while maintaining persistent profiles. The framework synchronizes bark events with tracked dogs and updates profiles using visual appearance and vocal characteristics, enabling identification despite occlusion, overlapping vocalizations, and off-screen barking. We also introduce a benchmark of 46 real-world videos containing 213 manually annotated bark events. Our framework correctly localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU $\geq 0.30$ and achieves a 91.33% F1 score for visible versus off-screen barking detection.
authors: Aryahvishwa Babu, Kingsley Jin, Lillian Wang, Tuan M. Dang, Theron S. Wang, Jeorge Joshi, Annie Cao, Kenny Q. Zhu
bullets: Addresses dog identity attribution during barking despite occlusion, simultaneous vocalizations, and dogs moving off-screen.
Combines visual identification, multi-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting into persistent dog profiles.
Introduces a benchmark of 46 real-world videos with 213 manually annotated bark events.
Localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU ≥ 0.30.
Detects visible versus off-screen barking with a 91.33% F1 score.

papers.title: Audio-Visual Dog Identification and Tracking in Real-World Videos
papers.tldr: A multimodal framework identifies and tracks individual dogs by linking their visual appearances with vocal fingerprints in challenging real-world videos.

papers.abstract: Dementia affects millions of older adults worldwide, yet early detection remains difficult outside clinical settings. Traditional models primarily rely on text or voice-based responses, capturing only a limited view of human cognition despite the inherently multimodal nature of human expression. This work proposes a contactless, multimodal screening framework that leverages video, audio, and text signals collected during structured voice-based interactions with Amazon Alexa. By incorporating these modalities, our approach captures a more holistic representation of human behavior encompassing speech patterns, vocal characteristics, facial expressions, and linguistic structure, which may enable more accurate detection of cognitive decline. Different participants completed three conversational tasks designed to probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall. We pursued three objectives: (1) evaluate which of the three Alexa tasks provides the most informative cognitive signals, (2) compare the effectiveness of unimodal models, and (3) assess the benefits of multimodal fusion models. Task-level analysis shows that the video model achieves its best performance on Command-Reading, with an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69), while the audio model performs best on Question-Answering, reaching an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73). In contrast, the multimodal model demonstrates consistently stable performance across tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.76 (AUC 0.75) on Command-Reading and 0.76 (AUC 0.73) on Question-Answering. These findings demonstrate that multimodal behavioral cues captured through naturalistic interactions can reliably distinguish MCI from healthy aging, highlighting the limitations of traditional diagnostic paradigms and supporting the shift toward multimodal, real-world cognitive assessment frameworks.
authors: Sankalp Vaish, Rishank Singh, Sumukh Veeramalla, Caroline Summerour, John A. Batsis, Xiaohui Liang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of detecting cognitive decline outside clinical settings using richer behavioral signals than text or voice alone.
Analyzes three tasks probing spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall, comparing unimodal and multimodal models.
Video performs best on Command-Reading, while audio performs best on Question-Answering.
Multimodal models show stable performance across tasks, reaching 0.76 accuracy on both Command-Reading and Question-Answering.
Results support multimodal, real-world cognitive assessment, though performance varies by task and modality.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal video/audio/text fusion for behavioral assessment; transferable to video understanding.
papers.title: Task-Centric Multimodal Learning for Cognitive Impairment Detection
papers.tldr: A contactless Alexa-based framework combines video, audio, and text to detect mild cognitive impairment from multimodal behavioral cues during conversational tasks.

papers.abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment remains a critical bottleneck in dementia care, demanding scalable tools capable of capturing subtle behavioral decay. To capture the subtle temporal changes of cognitive decline, we introduce a behavioral dataset collected across seven unscripted multimodal interactions over an 18-month horizon. This dataset formalizes continuous, multi-session interactions into a dense 4D tensor (Batch * Session * Time * Feature) that explicitly preserves concurrent local dynamics alongside long-term changes. To effectively process these complex behavioral patterns, we propose CogDrift-4D: a novel, hierarchical 4D Transformer framework. To capture the complex trajectory of cognitive decline, CogDrift-4D implements a dual-level behavioral fatigue and drift modeling architecture. At the intra-session level, the model computes localized least-squares regression slopes to quantify the acute ``fading'' of frame-level facial action units and acoustic energy. At the inter-session level, a recursive cross-attention feedback encoder acts as a cumulative fatigue accumulator, mapping the patient's continuous behavioral drift across successive sessions. To mitigate environmental noise and track failures across sessions, a localized Quality Gate dynamically filters low-integrity features before final fusion, also an early fusion that integrates semantic insights with raw physical dynamics. Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.
authors: Sankalp Vaish, Sumukh Veeramalla, Rishank Singh, Caroline Summerour, John A. Batsis, Xiaohui Liang
bullets: Introduces a behavioral dataset spanning seven unscripted multimodal interactions over 18 months.
Represents continuous sessions as a dense Batch × Session × Time × Feature 4D tensor.
Uses hierarchical modeling: intra-session regression slopes capture acute behavioral fading, while inter-session cross-attention accumulates longitudinal drift.
A localized Quality Gate filters low-integrity features and fuses semantic information with physical behavioral dynamics.
On structured verbal and linguistic interactions, achieves 0.733 ± 0.13 accuracy and 0.716 ± 0.14 F1; scope is limited to the reported interaction setting.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical 4D Transformer for multimodal temporal behavioral modeling; transferable to video understanding.
papers.title: CogDrift-4D: Hierarchical Multimodal Modeling of Temporal Behavioral Decay for MCI Detection
papers.tldr: CogDrift-4D models short- and long-term behavioral decline across multimodal interactions to support scalable MCI detection.

papers.abstract: Accident anticipation aims to recognize anomalous driving cues before a crash while avoiding false alarms during normal driving. Existing approaches typically formulate this task as binary classification, focusing on whether an accident will occur rather than when it will occur. We propose PRE-ACT, a framework that models accident risk as a continuously evolving signal that increases as the crash approaches. By explicitly enforcing temporal ordering and distance-to-accident awareness, our method progressively raises risk while suppressing premature alarms, leading to significant improvements on MM-AU subsets and Nexar. We further introduce a Separation Score to evaluate the global behavior of predicted risk curves beyond local temporal windows. Code and visualizations are available at https://github.com/giddyyupp/PRE-ACT.
bullets: Accident anticipation must detect danger early without triggering false alarms during normal driving.
PRE-ACT replaces binary accident prediction with continuously evolving, distance-to-accident-aware risk estimation.
Temporal ordering constraints encourage risk scores to rise as a crash approaches.
The method reports significant improvements on MM-AU subsets and Nexar.
A Separation Score evaluates the global quality of predicted risk curves beyond local temporal windows.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes temporal risk estimation for accident anticipation, fitting video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Progressive Risk Estimation for Accident Anticipation
papers.tldr: PRE-ACT estimates accident risk as a progressively increasing signal, improving early-warning behavior while reducing premature alarms.

papers.abstract: Low-light video processing remains an underexplored problem in computer vision, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality ground-truth data. Existing public datasets exhibit several limitations, including restricted motion diversity, limited scene coverage, weak degradations, reliance on auxiliary modalities such as event data, and misalignment between low-light inputs and ground truth. Furthermore, current datasets typically address either low-light enhancement or scene understanding, whereas these tasks should be considered jointly. We introduce \textbf{OLiVES}, a benchmark dataset for outdoor low-light videos with dynamic scenes, designed to support both low-light video enhancement (LLVE) and video object segmentation (VOS). The dataset addresses key content gaps by incorporating a diverse range of natural textures, animals, occlusions, dynamic activities, and close-up scenes. To the best of our knowledge, OLiVES is the first outdoor low-light video dataset captured using professional cinema-grade cameras. It provides over 25,000 aligned normal- and low-light frame pairs, along with over 46,000 VOS annotations. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLVE and VOS methods on OLiVES and show that training on it improves performance on both tasks. The OLiVES project page is available at: https://anonymous-OLiVES.github.io/.
authors: Yini Li, Joanne Lin, David Blackham, David Bull, Nantheera Anantrasirichai
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and misalignment of high-quality ground truth for outdoor low-light video.
Covers diverse dynamic content, including natural textures, animals, occlusions, activities, and close-ups.
Supports both low-light video enhancement and video object segmentation.
Contains over 25,000 aligned frame pairs and over 46,000 VOS annotations captured with cinema-grade cameras.
Benchmarking shows that training on OLiVES improves performance on both tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for low-light video enhancement and video object segmentation, relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: OLiVES: An Outdoor Low-Light Video Benchmark for Enhancement and Segmentation
papers.tldr: OLiVES is an outdoor low-light video benchmark with aligned normal/low-light frames and segmentation annotations for jointly evaluating enhancement and scene understanding.

papers.abstract: In various industries, smoke and fire are two of the most important threats in the workplace. One of the common methods for detecting smoke and fire is the use of infrared thermal and smoke sensors, which cannot be used in outdoor applications. Therefore, the use of vision-based methods seems necessary. The problem of smoke and fire detection is spatiotemporal and requires spatiotemporal solutions. This paper presents a method that uses spatial features along with temporal-based features to detect smoke and fire in the scene. It consists of three main parts; the task of each part is to reduce the error of the previous part so that the final model has a robust performance. This method also uses transformer modules to increase the accuracy of the model. The results of our model show the proper performance of the proposed approach in solving the problem of smoke and fire detection and can be used to increase workplace safety.
authors: Alireza Mirrashid, Mohammad Khoshbin, Ali Atghaei, Hassan Shahbazi
bullets: Addresses the limitations of infrared thermal and smoke sensors in outdoor environments.
Models smoke and fire detection as a spatiotemporal vision problem.
Uses three sequential components, each intended to reduce errors from the preceding stage.
Incorporates transformer modules to improve detection accuracy.
Reports proper performance and potential to improve workplace safety, without specific quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Spatio-temporal transformer for fire and smoke detection in video fits video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Attention-Based Spatio-Temporal Approach for Fire and Smoke Detection
papers.tldr: A transformer-enhanced vision model combines spatial and temporal features for robust outdoor smoke and fire detection.

papers.abstract: Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) aims to capture objects and their evolving relationships in videos. This requires accounting for both the persistence of object identities and abrupt changes in relationships. Existing methods aggregate information across frames to exploit temporal context, but an emphasis on consistency can obscure these changes. As a result, a model may retain its previous prediction even after the underlying relation has changed. We refer to this failure mode as relational semantic inertia. To address this issue, we propose Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer (RTAformer), a one-stage framework that separately models entity persistence and relation changes. It injects calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries to guide predicate updates, while cross-frame instance alignment during training helps reduce cross-frame representational drift. Experiments on Action Genome show improvements in recall and mean recall over existing methods, with ablation studies supporting the contributions of the proposed components and comparisons using matched backbones showing larger gains on relation-transition frames than on non-transition frames.
authors: Jaeyeon Heo, Geuntaek Lim, Yukyung Choi
bullets: Addresses the failure of temporal consistency methods to update predictions when video relationships change.
Uses a one-stage Transformer that separately models entity persistence and relation transitions.
Guides predicate updates with calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries.
Applies cross-frame instance alignment during training to reduce representational drift.
On Action Genome, improves recall and mean recall, with larger gains on relation-transition frames.
papers.selection_reason: Relation-transition-aware transformer for video scene graph generation, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: RTAformer: Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer for Video Scene Graph Generation
papers.tldr: RTAformer improves video scene graph generation by modeling persistent entities separately from changing relationships to reduce relational semantic inertia.

papers.abstract: MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities, but conventional few-step sampling ties the interval queried from the model to the duration of the state update. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, the mean midpoint horizon benefit increases from 0.109 to 1.308 FID, indicating sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution. A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or extra queries, including gains on five checkpoints trained after rule selection. A milder rule also improves mean FID by 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, with fixed-rule FID gains on the evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints. However, matched-budget calibration favors query-start shifting in historical CIFAR tests, and the tested Horizon allocation adds no FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. Thus, prediction horizon is a distinct, position- and state-sensitive inference control, but not a universally preferred one.
authors: Tinglan Wang, Haixu Liu, Shaobo Chen, Nuo Qian, Qi Gao, Kai Wen, Yu Yao
bullets: Longer horizons worsen FID early in sampling but improve it near the midpoint across seven CIFAR-10 checkpoints at CFG 2.
Horizon effects depend on both query position and the states entering the query, not query time alone.
A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or additional queries; a milder rule improves it by 1.041 on a stronger grid.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates inference dynamics in MeanFlow (video generation), specifically decoupling model queries from state updates, which is relevant to video generation and understanding.
papers.title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow
papers.tldr: Decoupling MeanFlow’s model-query horizon from the state-update duration reveals a position- and state-sensitive inference control that can improve FID without retraining or extra queries, but is not universally best.

papers.abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.
authors: Tom\'a\v{s} \v{C}\'i\v{z}ek, Matej Straka, Illia Volkov, Mat\v{e}j Kripner, Ervin Maci\'c, Jiri Matas, Klara Janouskova, Martin Schmid
bullets: Addresses the limitations of FIFO and hand-crafted memory-update rules for handling distractors, occlusions, and object motion.
Adds a lightweight memory controller that treats memory selection as a sequential decision-making problem.
The controller is trained with reinforcement learning to maximize tracking performance.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks.
Applying the same approach to SAM 2 also outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of 12 benchmarks, indicating cross-generation generality.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based memory control for visual object tracking in SAM 3; fits video understanding and tracking.
papers.title: SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking
papers.tldr: SAM3RL uses reinforcement learning to control which frames enter SAM 3’s memory bank, improving visual object tracking without runtime overhead.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised temporal action localization (UTAL) aims to identify action categories and localize their temporal boundaries without annotation supervision. Existing methods typically derive supervision for both tasks solely from RGB and optical-flow representations, often resulting in noisy category assignments and inaccurate temporal boundaries. In this work, we reveal an overlooked property of video codecs: group-of-pictures quantization patterns preserve category-discriminative dynamics, while motion-vector and residual variations exhibit pronounced responses around action transitions. Based on this insight, we propose CoDy, a codec dynamics-guided framework that exploits the codec as complementary information to the visual view for UTAL. CoDy integrates a codec-enhanced view with RGB and flow through confidence-aware consensus clustering, producing reliable soft pseudo-labels. It further converts codec dynamics into a class-agnostic boundary prior, which supervises visual boundary learning and guides proposal initialization and iterative refinement. The codec branches are only used during the training stage and introduce no extra codec-side computation at inference. Extensive experiments on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3 demonstrate that CoDy consistently outperforms existing UTAL methods and achieves state-of-the-art localization performance. These results establish codec signals as effective annotation-free priors for jointly inferring which actions occur and when they occur.
authors: Tianyu Yan, Qingyi Yang, Qin Yang, Xufei Guo, Yuan Tang, Rui Wang, Yixue Hao, Long Hu
bullets: Addresses noisy pseudo-labels and inaccurate boundaries in unsupervised temporal action localization.
Combines RGB, optical flow, and codec-enhanced features with confidence-aware consensus clustering to generate soft pseudo-labels.
Uses motion-vector and residual changes as a class-agnostic boundary prior for proposal initialization and iterative refinement.
Codec branches are used only during training, adding no codec computation at inference.
Achieves state-of-the-art localization performance on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3.
papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised temporal action localization using codec dynamics as priors; fits video understanding.
papers.title: CoDy: Codec Dynamics as Complementary Priors for Unsupervised Temporal Action Localization
papers.tldr: CoDy uses video codec dynamics as complementary, annotation-free priors to improve unsupervised action recognition and temporal boundary localization.

papers.abstract: We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively. Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/
authors: Boyuan Sun, Deshui Miao, Wenzhao Gao, Shaoyong Jia, Shaohui Jiao, Chi Liu, Yan Shu, Derek Li, Bryan Dai, Shengsheng Qian, Qibin Hou
bullets: Continuously records visual changes in structured memory, preserving event transitions and temporal evolution.
Uses query-driven planning to identify needed evidence and guide memory retrieval.
Replays targeted historical frames to recover details omitted during initial observation.
Reports overall scores of 66.07% on OVO-Bench and 59.53% on StreamingBench.
Addresses limitations of compressed video histories that lose details and cannot recover missing evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic streaming video understanding with change-aware memory and query-driven replay; fits video understanding.
papers.title: DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: DeltaStreamer improves streaming video understanding by combining change-aware memory with query-driven replay to preserve and recover evidence for future questions.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce visually realistic videos that nevertheless violate the physical consequences implied by the prompt and scene. Existing benchmarks largely rely on holistic plausibility scores or broad quality dimensions, leaving it unclear which physical behavior is being tested and why a model fails. We introduce PhyMetric, a scene-level diagnostic benchmark that recasts physical plausibility evaluation as verifiable, scene-grounded question answering. PhyMetric contains 1{,}115 scenes spanning 50 physical categories across six domains, paired with 8{,}920 answer-balanced binary questions over 12 evaluation dimensions. Each scene is associated with eight targeted yes/no questions and a structured physical prior specifying the governing law, expected temporal sequence, observable signatures, and common failure modes. At evaluation time, a vision-language model (VLM) judge answers each question from question-aware sampled frames conditioned on the prior, and correctness is hierarchically aggregated into scene, dimension, physical category, and model scores. Experiments on four open-source T2V models and three VLM judges show that scene-specific binary QA is a critical component of the protocol: when each targeted question is replaced by a single generic plausibility query, evaluator accuracy drops to the chance level. Structured physical priors offer a complementary signal that improves human alignment of the resulting scores, with effects that vary across VLM judges of different capacity. These findings establish PhyMetric as a benchmark that turns physical plausibility evaluation from opaque holistic scoring into interpretable, scene-level inspection. Our project page is available at: https://mengsiwei.github.io/PhyMetric/.
authors: Siwei Meng, Xuerou Cai, Rui Hu, Ping Liu
bullets: Benchmarks 1,115 scenes across 50 physical categories and six domains with 8,920 balanced binary questions.
Each scene includes eight targeted questions and a structured prior covering governing laws, temporal sequences, observable signs, and failure modes.
A VLM judge answers questions from sampled frames, with scores aggregated from scene level to model level.
Across four open-source T2V models and three VLM judges, targeted QA is essential; generic plausibility questions perform at chance.
Structured physical priors improve alignment with human judgments, with effects varying by VLM judge capacity.
papers.selection_reason: Scene-level diagnostic benchmark for physical plausibility in text-to-video generation via VLM-based QA; fits video understanding and evaluation.
papers.title: PhyMetric: Diagnosing Physical Plausibility in Text-to-Video Generation via Scene-Level QA
papers.tldr: PhyMetric evaluates whether text-to-video outputs obey scene-specific physical laws using targeted, interpretable visual question answering.

papers.abstract: Crash Moment Localization aims to localize the major physical impact that interrupts controlled flight in an onboard first-person-view (FPV) video recorded by a drone, thereby providing a temporal reference for retrospective crash analysis in aerial robotics. However, existing crash-video datasets predominantly target surveillance or dash-camera footage, and their annotation schemes and task formulations are not designed for temporal localization of the major physical impact in UAV onboard FPV videos. To address this gap, we present FPV-CRASH, a dataset and fixed-protocol reference evaluation for offline Crash Moment Localization in drone FPV videos. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 drone FPV clips (526 Crash and 526 Normal); each Crash clip has a single-frame reference annotation for the Crash Moment, and every clip is paired with four English captions automatically generated from sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal label. Normal clips carry no timestamp target and provide training-time background supervision. The captions support an auxiliary Text-to-Video Retrieval task, whereas localization inference remains video-only. We further provide a heatmap-based reference model that estimates a continuous Crash Moment timestamp from sparsely sampled frames. Under the fixed, non-source-disjoint clip-level protocol, the reference model reduces MAE from 1.12 s for the strongest fixed timing-prior baseline to 0.56 s (a 50% relative reduction) and achieves a median absolute error (MedAE) of 0.33 s; the fraction of clips localized within 0.5 s rises from 37.14% to 65.71%. The release includes annotations, available source video identifiers and URLs, clipping metadata, fixed split lists, and preprocessing code so that the reportable portion can be reconstructed without redistributing source footage. At submission time, all source-compilation URLs remained accessible.
authors: Jifan Zhang, Tingyu Wang, Qian Liu, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Targets offline temporal localization of major physical impacts in UAV onboard FPV footage, a gap in existing crash datasets.
Contains 1,052 clips: 526 Crash and 526 Normal; Crash clips have single-frame crash annotations, while Normal clips provide background supervision.
Includes four automatically generated English captions per clip for auxiliary text-to-video retrieval, though localization is video-only.
A heatmap-based model improves MAE from 1.12 s to 0.56 s and raises localization within 0.5 s from 37.14% to 65.71%.
Provides reproducible metadata, split lists, annotations, and preprocessing code without redistributing source videos.
papers.selection_reason: Dataset and reference model for temporal crash moment localization in drone FPV videos.
papers.title: FPV-CRASH: A Dataset for Offline Crash Moment Localization in Drone First-Person-View Videos
papers.tldr: FPV-CRASH introduces a dataset and benchmark for locating the major crash moment in drone FPV videos, with a reference model achieving 0.56 s MAE.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.
authors: Zhixin Cai, Ruoqi Yuan, Xinchen Yang, Zhuofan Chen, Jun Bai, Chuantao Yin, Wenge Rong
bullets: Targets unsupported video-grounded responses in Video LLMs.

papers.abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.
authors: Zeyang Zhang, Linxiang Gao, Meiqi Gu, Xingyan Chen, Minrui Luo, Kaifeng Lyu, Tianxing He

The theory shows that self-conditioned constant-depth backbones can match the expressive power of space-bounded Turing machines.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes self-conditioning in flow matching for visual reasoning, providing a transferable technical insight for deep sequential reasoning in generative models.
papers.title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Self-conditioning allows flow-matching samplers to use additional steps for genuinely deeper visual reasoning, overcoming a limitation of vanilla flow matching.

papers.abstract: Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross-modal distillation and joint face-lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random-projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual-stream architecture that jointly processes lip region-of-interest (ROI) and full-face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross-modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual-only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM-based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out-of-domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face-lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme-discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.
authors: Jing-Xuan Zhang, Genshun Wan, Jianqing Gao, Jia Pan, Yumei Zhang, Lichen Zhang

Supports Transformer or LLM-based decoders and reports 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3% WER on LRS2, LRS3, and WildVSR.

papers.tldr: FLARE improves visual speech recognition by distilling speech knowledge from Whisper while jointly modeling lip and full-face video cues.

papers.abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.
authors: Rui Chen, Xingyu Chen, Pengxin Xu, Kai Chen, Junzhi Yu

Uses complementary video representations and treats dense query predictions as an over-complete set of temporal event hypotheses.

papers.title: HyrCap: Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals for Temporal Event Understanding

papers.abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
authors: Zihao Lin, Haoyu Dong, Haobo Xu, Chi-Chih Chang, Xuying Ning, Yinglong Xia, Shuang Yang, Zhuokai Zhao, Xinying Song, Dongfang Liu, Lifu Huang, Yang Song, Qifan Wang
bullets: Recursive harness evolution is studied for agentic video understanding with a frozen vision-language model.
Analysis of over 4,000 candidates identifies validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap.

Across four benchmarks, it raises the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to BRSI and reduces the validation-test gap by 37.9%.

papers.title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness

papers.abstract: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks
authors: Georgios Angelidis, Aggelos Psiris, Maria Vakalopoulou, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos, Giorgos Sfikas, Iraklis Varlamis
bullets: A convergent meta-analysis synthesizes published aerial and remote-sensing video results across four evidence tiers.

papers.title: The Gap Is in the Geometry: A Convergent Meta-Analysis of Multi-Facet Aerial and Remote Sensing Video Understanding

papers.abstract: Repetition counting requires identifying and enumerating action cycles over time. While state-of-the-art video language models describe actions fluently, they fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats. To investigate this limitation, we introduce RepProbe, a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions, with controls for clip position, temporal coverage, and duration. These controls allow us to study the counting failure directly and locate where in the model it arises. Counting accuracy collapses at high counts across the video language models we evaluate, and controlled experiments show this collapse is not explained by frame sampling alone. We compare model outputs with linear probes trained on the final-layer representations used to generate those outputs. We find a consistent representation-to-output dissociation: substantial count information remains linearly decodable even when models fail to report the correct count. Further analysis shows this failure arises primarily at the output stage, where answers concentrate on a small set of preferred numbers rather than the available count information. The dissociation holds on both real and synthetic videos and is not explained by clip duration, position, or scene content. These results indicate that models encode repetition structure but do not reliably report it in their outputs. Project page: https://arenaa.github.io/RepProbe-webpage/
bullets: Introduces a 42K-clip benchmark with 1–20 controlled repetitions in real and synthetic videos.
Counting accuracy collapses at high counts, and the failure is not explained by frame sampling, clip duration, position, or scene content.
Linear probes recover count information from final-layer representations even when model outputs are incorrect.
The main bottleneck occurs at the output stage, where predictions favor a small set of preferred numbers.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic benchmark for repetition counting in video language models, targeting temporal and action understanding.
papers.title: RepProbe: Can Video Language Models Count Repeated Actions? A Diagnostic Benchmark
papers.tldr: RepProbe shows that video language models often encode how many times an action repeats but fail to report the correct count, especially for high repetition counts.

papers.abstract: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.

Includes manually verified annotations spanning varied domains and video durations.

papers.title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding
papers.tldr: OmniCompass is a holistic benchmark diagnosing MLLM performance on temporal, spatial, and question-answering tasks using visual and joint audio-visual evidence.

papers.abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
authors: Yuhan Zhu, Xiangyu Zeng, Qingyi Si, Chenxu Yang, Yifei Li, Luozheng Qin, Junhao Zhou, Dingyu Yao, Jun Zhang, Chuanyu Qin, Zhiqiu Zhang, Yuandong Yang, Yuqi Xu, Tianyu Zhang, Hongcheng Guo, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, Limin Wang

Adapts pretrained multimodal language models with a shared scoring head instead of autoregressive answer generation.
Supports cached inference for sequential queries and joint inference for multiple queries over the same video history.

papers.title: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction
papers.tldr: VideoJev turns video understanding into efficient, reusable scoring decisions for temporal grounding and multiple-choice QA, enabling fast interactive visual agents.

papers.abstract: Video understanding benchmarks are the primary yardstick for measuring progress in video-language modeling, and a growing body of work relies on them to claim improvements. The reported benchmark scores in these works, however, are almost always produced by frameworks (e.g., lmms eval) used as black boxes: certain evaluation choices like frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting are inherited from preset defaults and seldom inspected carefully. We show these unexamined choices are a major source of variance. Even for the same model checkpoint, evaluation configuration alone can shift accuracy by up to 19.5pp. Hence, it is unclear whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements in capability or differences in evaluation setup. Moreover, many benchmark samples offer little evidence of visual capability, since they can be answered without the video, and the full suites are expensive to evaluate. We address these issues in two parts. First, we curate existing suites for discriminability and efficiency, producing Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark over 791 videos spanning diverse tasks and durations, which largely preserves model rankings, at 5 times inference speedup for a full-frame count sweep experiment (4-128 frames). Second, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol by sweeping the configuration space to isolate choices that measurably affect results, distill them into best practices and reporting standards, and release reproducible reference scores across five models and seven benchmarks. We hope that the proposed evaluation framework and the Meta-Video benchmark will support video understanding research by providing a reproducible and efficient foundation to measure progress in a reliable way.
authors: Soumya Shamarao Jahagirdar, Anna Kukleva, Vishaal Udandarao, Samuel Thomas, Brian Kingsbury, Rogerio Feris, James R. Glass. Ameya Prabhu, Hilde Kuehne
bullets: Evaluation settings such as frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting can change accuracy by up to 19.5 percentage points for the same model.
The authors curate Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark covering 791 videos, diverse tasks, and varied durations.
Meta-Video largely preserves model rankings while enabling a 5× speedup for a full-frame-count sweep experiment.
The work proposes best practices and reporting standards based on a systematic evaluation-configuration sweep.
Reproducible reference scores are released for five models across seven benchmarks.

papers.title: Meta-Video: Efficient Standardized Evaluation for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Meta-Video makes video-understanding evaluation faster, more discriminative, and reproducible by standardizing configuration choices that can substantially alter benchmark results.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in generative models has made talking-head deepfakes highly realistic and easy to create, jeopardizing public trust. However, most audio-visual deepfake detectors rely on lip-speech synchronization and are designed for static, frontal videos, limiting their reliability in dynamic, in-the-wild recordings where the speaker moves and lip cues are degraded or missing. As an alternative, we propose a physics-aware detector for dynamic speaking videos that leverages an acoustic constraint: in real recordings, speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance, whereas deepfake generation can break this coupling. Our method combines distance estimates from video with distance-dependent acoustic measures from speech to detect deepfakes. Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show that the proposed physical cue is effective in dynamic scenarios, and that it complements lip-sync-based detectors, with a simple ensemble achieving consistent gains across datasets. Codes are available at https://byulharang.github.io/PADD/.
authors: Kyeongrae Kim, Kim Sung-Bin, Oh Hyun-Bin, Tae-Hyun Oh
bullets: Targets realistic deepfakes in dynamic, in-the-wild videos where lip-sync cues may be unreliable or missing.
Estimates speaker-to-camera distance from video and compares it with distance-dependent acoustic properties of speech.
Uses a physical consistency cue that deepfake generation may disrupt.
Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show effectiveness in dynamic scenarios.
The cue complements lip-sync detectors, with a simple ensemble providing consistent gains across datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Audio-visual deepfake detection in talking-head videos fits video understanding and temporal analysis.
papers.title: Physics-Aware Deepfake Detection via Distance-Speech Consistency
papers.tldr: A physics-aware detector identifies dynamic talking-head deepfakes by checking whether speech energy changes consistently with the speaker’s distance from the camera.

papers.abstract: Cross-domain few-shot action recognition (CD-FSAR) aims to recognise unseen action classes in a target domain from a handful of labelled videos. Despite advances in representation learning, CD-FSAR inference still relies on prototypes estimated from extremely limited support examples. To assess this bottleneck, we perform an oracle analysis with the representation fixed. Constructing oracle prototypes and decision boundaries from ground-truth query labels improves 5-way 1-shot accuracy by 7--20 percentage points across five target datasets. This reveals a substantial estimation gap: the representation contains useful discriminative information, but prototypes and boundaries estimated from scarce supports fail to capture each episode's true class structure. Motivated by this, we propose TRACE, a training-free transductive inference framework that improves episode-level estimation without modifying the backbone. TRACE comprises two complementary stages. Confidence-Thresholded Transductive Prototype Refinement (CTPR) refines support-based prototypes using confidently predicted queries. The refined prototypes initialise a lightweight per-episode classifier, which Transductive Classifier Refinement (TCR) further adapts by encouraging confident, class-balanced predictions over all queries. Together, the two stages improve prototype and boundary estimation, enabling better use of information in the unlabelled queries. Across five target datasets (HMDB51, UCF101, SSv2, Diving48, and RareAct) in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong CD-FSAR baseline, including gains of more than six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot, while recovering much of the oracle-estimated gap. These results suggest that improving test-time estimation is a powerful, broadly applicable complement to representation learning for CD-FSAR under extreme support scarcity.
authors: Changyi Li, Zeyu Yang, Yu Xiao
bullets: An oracle analysis shows that scarce-support prototype and decision-boundary estimation is a major bottleneck, despite useful learned representations.
TRACE uses two training-free transductive stages: confidence-based prototype refinement (CTPR) and class-balanced classifier refinement (TCR).
The method leverages confidently predicted unlabelled queries to better estimate each episode’s class structure.
Across five target datasets and both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong baseline, with gains exceeding six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot.
The approach recovers much of the oracle-estimated gap, but its scope is limited to test-time transductive settings with available unlabelled queries.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses few-shot action recognition in video and improves episode-level estimation through training-free transductive test-time refinement.
papers.title: Closing the Estimation Gap: Training-Free Transductive Inference for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition
papers.tldr: TRACE improves cross-domain few-shot action recognition without retraining by refining prototypes and episode-specific classifiers using unlabelled queries.

papers.abstract: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.
authors: Anubhav Kataria, Shreya Ghosh, Jingwen Ye, Abhinav Dhall
bullets: Targets faithful explanations for small, evolving facial movements that existing MLLMs often describe without causal grounding.

Uses H-TCC to identify key moments, relevant facial regions, and causal necessity through targeted occlusion.
Fine-tuning improves appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87%, with additional gains for actions, temporal emotion, and deepfake detection.
