papers.title: When, Where, and Why: Hierarchical Causal Explainability for Video Face Understanding with MLLMs
papers.tldr: VideoFace-X-LLM combines weakly supervised data and hierarchical causal analysis to explain when, where, and why facial behaviours occur in video.

papers.abstract: Reliable video reasoning requires models to produce correct answers and expose supporting visual evidence. Open-o3-Video enables verifiable reasoning by embedding timestamps and object-level bounding boxes into reasoning traces, but is restricted to frames from an initial sparse sampler. We introduce Open-o3-Video-v2, which formulates video reasoning as a unified agentic evidencegrounded process. The model identifies missing information, acquires additional observations, grounds the moments and objects supporting its reasoning, and writes this evidence into the trajectory before continuing or answering. To support this behavior, we construct STGR-v2-CoT135K, including 52K multi-turn agentic grounded reasoning trajectories, and STGR-v2-RL-13K for reinforcement learning. We further propose Clue-Seek GRPO (CS-GRPO), which tracks how tool calls change accumulated evidence, rewards clue coverage and step-wise gains, and penalizes excessive, repetitive, or uninformative retrieval. On V-STaR, Open-o3-Video-v2-4B achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone by 8.5% and 12.6%, respectively. It also delivers consistent gains across general video understanding, long-video reasoning, and temporal grounding benchmarks. These results show that active evidence acquisition and verifiable object-level grounding are complementary for reliable video reasoning. The code and models are released at https://msalab-pku.github.io/projects/Open-o3-Video-v2.
authors: Jiahao Meng, Zhongyuan Bao, Yue Tan, Haiquan Wen, Renrui Zhang, Anna Wang, Jason Li, Yanwei Fu, Yunhai Tong, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Frames video reasoning as an agentic process: identify gaps, retrieve additional observations, ground relevant moments and objects, then answer.
Introduces STGR-v2-CoT135K and STGR-v2-RL-13K datasets for multi-turn grounded reasoning and reinforcement learning.
Proposes Clue-Seek GRPO, rewarding evidence coverage and useful retrieval while penalizing repetitive or uninformative tool calls.
The 4B model achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM on V-STaR, with gains over its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone and across multiple video benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic video reasoning with verifiable spatio-temporal evidence; fits video understanding and multimodal LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Open-o3-Video-v2: Seek, Ground, and Reason with Verifiable Spatio-Temporal Evidence
papers.tldr: Open-o3-Video-v2 improves reliable video reasoning by actively seeking missing visual evidence and grounding answers in verifiable timestamps and object regions.

papers.abstract: Video reward models are trained and evaluated on human preferences between videos that often differ simultaneously on properties such as prompt alignment, visual fidelity, motion, and generator identity. As a result, aggregate accuracy does not reveal which video properties a reward model can reliably distinguish. We construct preference pairs by controlled interventions that change one property of a generated video while holding the rest fixed. The resulting pairs, by construction, provide preferences for how the videos differ along a specific dimension, without requiring any human annotation. We propose IsoVRBench, a video generation reward modeling benchmark of 8,000 such pairs across eight interventions, and show that state-of-the-art models separate broad quality differences between generators but miss important features such as temporal order. The best reward model reaches only 60.8% on reordered frames against 100% for humans, and rankings on existing benchmarks do not predict this failure. Using the synthetic isolated intervation pairs as training data leads to 1) IsoVRM, a reward model outperforming its counterpart trained with a larger human labeled preference dataset by 3.8 points on VBench-2.0, 2) IsoWan, the video generator post-trained with IsoVRM, outperforming its human-data counterpart in human preferences, and 3) gains that stack when combined with human data. Because intervention pairs are automatically generated rather than collected, the benchmark and training data can be easily extended as generators evolve.
authors: Shuyue Stella Li, Jacqueline He, Jiahui Chen, Sreya Dutta Roy, Yulia Tsvetkov, Luke Zettlemoyer, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Xiaochuang Han
bullets: Existing aggregate preference accuracy can hide failures on specific video properties such as temporal order.
The benchmark contains 8,000 pairs across eight controlled interventions, changing one property while holding others fixed.
State-of-the-art models distinguish broad generator-quality differences but perform poorly on reordered frames, with the best reaching 60.8% versus 100% for humans.
Training on these synthetic pairs produces IsoVRM, which improves VBench-2.0 performance by 3.8 points over a counterpart trained on a larger human-labeled dataset.
IsoVRM also improves post-trained video generation, with gains stacking when combined with human data; the approach can be extended as generators evolve.
papers.selection_reason: Video reward modeling benchmark for generated video properties, directly relevant to video understanding and evaluation.
papers.title: IsoVRBench: Video Reward Modeling Without Human Feedback
papers.tldr: IsoVRBench uses automatically generated, property-isolated video pairs to expose and improve weaknesses in video reward models without human feedback.

papers.abstract: Agentic video reasoning systems gather and assess video evidence across stages, selecting relevant spans as visual evidence for answering questions. New candidates and observations prompt reassessment of the current span, but revisions can correct localization errors or discard useful evidence already present in the adopted span. Systems therefore need to connect evidence organization across stages with temporal state control, allowing accumulated information to jointly inform revision assessment while explicit adoption decisions govern how assessment outcomes affect downstream visual evidence. We introduce VideoSlate, a stateful commit-control framework built around shared evidence. A typed evidence blackboard links candidate spans, provenance, construction, and verifier observations, enabling an incumbent-relative certifier to assess revision support from the candidate, current span, and related proposals. Based on certification, the controller authorizes a revision or retains the current span, separating evidence accumulation from state updates and recording each decision and its evidence on the blackboard. Extensive evaluations across video grounding and grounded question-answering benchmarks show that VideoSlate can improve temporal localization through selective revision.
authors: Shuo Zheng, Yuanjie Dang, Peng Chen, Jianjun Xiang, Ronghua Liang, Mohammed Bennamoun, Qiuhong Ke
bullets: Addresses the risk that iterative evidence gathering either retains localization errors or discards useful existing evidence.
Uses a typed evidence blackboard to track candidate spans, provenance, construction, verifier observations, and related proposals.
An incumbent-relative certifier evaluates whether a proposed revision is supported by accumulated evidence.
A controller explicitly commits to revising the span or retaining it, while recording each decision and its evidence.
Evaluations on video grounding and grounded question-answering benchmarks show improved temporal localization through selective revision.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses temporally grounded video reasoning and evidence selection, fitting video understanding.
papers.title: VideoSlate: Stateful Commit Control for Temporally Grounded Agentic Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: VideoSlate improves agentic video reasoning by controlling when new temporal evidence should replace or preserve the current video span.

papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in joint audio--visual generation. However, audio--visual synchronization remains a challenge, as generated speech and sound often temporally misalign with visual events. A key bottleneck is the lack of human-annotated data, reliable evaluation benchmarks, and synchronization-aware evaluation models for generated audio--visual outputs. To address these limitations, we conduct a comprehensive study spanning data, benchmarking, and reward modeling. We first introduce SyncReward-Data-80K, a dataset containing 80K professional synchronization ratings for clips from eight audio--visual generators. A taxonomy-guided construction pipeline covers four sound-event families: Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient. We further construct \textbf{SyncReward-Bench}, a held-out benchmark of 1K clips, each independently rated by multiple professionals. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate specialized synchronization metrics and omni-modal models, revealing their substantial misalignment with human judgments. Finally, we develop SyncReward, a reward model that combines semantic--temporal contrastive pretraining on real clips with human supervision on generated clips. As an evaluation metric, SyncReward achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among the evaluated methods. As a reward, it improves synchronization through inference-time best-of-$N$ selection and reinforcement learning based post-training. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and code at https://github.com/WeChatCV/SyncReward.
authors: Kaisi Guan, Ying Ba, Wenjing Wang, Xihua Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Ruihau Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of human-aligned data and reliable synchronization evaluation for audio–visual generation.
Releases SyncReward-Data-80K with professional ratings spanning Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient sound events.
Introduces SyncReward-Bench, a 1K-clip held-out benchmark with multiple independent professional ratings.
Finds that existing synchronization metrics and omni-modal models often misalign with human judgments.

Combines semantic–temporal contrastive pretraining with human supervision; it achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among evaluated methods and improves synchronization via best-of-N selection and reinforcement-learning post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Reward model for audio-visual synchronization; relevant to temporal alignment in video generation and understanding.
papers.title: SyncReward: Human-Aligned Synchronization Reward for Audio-Visual Generation
papers.tldr: SyncReward introduces human-rated data, a benchmark, and a reward model to evaluate and improve audio–visual synchronization in generated clips.

papers.abstract: Training-free language-based video anomaly detection (VAD) uses frozen vision--language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) to localize abnormal events without task-specific model-weight optimization. Existing approaches increasingly exploit broader temporal and semantic context, yet generic context does not necessarily foreground abnormal events or specify how video-level semantics should modify local anomaly scores. We introduce a training-free semantic feedback framework that uses VAD-guided active observation for video anomaly understanding (VAU) and returns the resulting anomaly-focused description to refine temporal detection. Starting from an upstream anomaly-score curve, we adapt reasoning-based iterative frame selection: high-score regions seed the observations, and anomaly scores together with VLM relevance assessments guide subsequent temporal exploration. A frozen video-language model generates a single open-ended anomaly description from the selected frames. The description is returned through two complementary feedback levels: video-level feedback determines whether the score distribution should be suppressed, preserved, or sharpened, with selective visual rechecking, while local feedback retrieves event-related windows and promotes scores only after target-local visual verification. All model weights remain frozen, and feedback is applied once without regenerating the description. On the HIVAU video-summary evaluations of UCF-Crime and XD-Violence, VAD-guided observation improves GPT-rated reasonability, detail, and consistency over the matched CLIP-guided variant. For VAD, semantic feedback improves the re-evaluated upstream detector from 84.36% to 86.25% AUC on UCF-Crime and from 68.07% to 72.58% AP on XD-Violence, where the final AUC is 91.74%.
authors: Hangil Park, Seungheon Kim, Tae-Kyun Kim
bullets: Addresses the gap between generic temporal context and anomaly-focused semantic refinement in language-based VAD.
Selects frames iteratively from high anomaly-score regions, using anomaly scores and VLM relevance to guide exploration.
Generates one open-ended anomaly description, then applies video-level and local feedback to refine temporal scores.
Video-level feedback suppresses, preserves, or sharpens score distributions; local feedback verifies event-related windows before promotion.
Improves upstream detection from 84.36% to 86.25% AUC on UCF-Crime and from 68.07% to 72.58% AP on XD-Violence; final XD-Violence AUC is 91.74%.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free video anomaly analysis with semantic feedback; fits video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Anomaly-Guided Observation and Two-Level Semantic Feedback for Training-Free Video Anomaly Analysis
papers.tldr: A training-free framework uses anomaly-guided frame observation and two-level semantic feedback to improve video anomaly localization and explanation with frozen VLMs and LLMs.

papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
authors: Yike Wu, Keyan Chen, Qixiong Wang, Xi Xiang, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses redundant, noisy, or disruptive computation in MLLMs during video spatial reasoning.
Uses a training-free multiagent framework that plans steps to gather missing spatial evidence and combines it with native evidence.
Applies stage-aligned verification to identify whether failures arise from planning, perception, or reasoning.
Uses dependency-based recovery to recompute affected states while preserving valid intermediate results.
Achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three MLLMs and two benchmarks, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Residual test-time agentic computation for video spatial reasoning; fits spatial intelligence and test-time learning.
papers.title: ReTAC: Residual Test-Time Agentic Computation for Video Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: ReTAC improves video spatial reasoning by directing test-time agentic computation only toward unresolved requirements and localized failures.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) aims to generate language-level interpretations of anomalous events in long videos, requiring visual evidence that supports explanation beyond anomaly detection alone. Existing VAU pipelines commonly rely on anomaly-centric or predefined temporal sampling strategies, which efficiently emphasize suspicious moments but overlook contextual cues, object interactions, and temporally distributed evidence needed for reasoning. Motivated by recent progress in learnable temporal selection for long-video question answering, we revisit VAU temporal sampling as a downstream-aligned evidence selection problem. We introduce the semantic-conditioned Temporal Sampling Q-Former that learns to select temporal visual evidence through the VAU generation objective. Since generic VAU prompts provide weak video-specific guidance, we condition the sampler on CLIP-embedded object tags automatically extracted from the input video. These tags are used only for temporal evidence selection and are not appended to the LLM generation prompt, separating sampler conditioning from prompt augmentation. The proposed sampler operates in visual-token space, computes soft temporal selection weights from frame-level representations, and merges duplicated selections before response generation. Experiments on HIVAU-70K show that our model achieves the best performance among the compared fine-tuned models, while ablations demonstrate that learnable temporal sampling improves over fixed anomaly-focused sampling and that CLIP-embedded object-tag conditioning further improves over generic-prompt conditioning. Our results suggest that temporal sampling in VAU should be aligned with explanation-oriented evidence utility rather than anomaly saliency alone.
authors: Hangil Park, Seungheon Kim, Tae-Kyun Kim
bullets: Targets video anomaly understanding, where explanations require contextual cues, object interactions, and evidence spread across long videos.
Introduces a Temporal Sampling Q-Former that learns soft temporal evidence selection from the VAU generation objective.
Conditions selection on automatically extracted CLIP-embedded object tags without adding them to the LLM prompt.
Operates in visual-token space and merges duplicate selections before response generation.
On HIVAU-70K, it performs best among compared fine-tuned models; ablations show gains over fixed anomaly-focused and generic-prompt sampling.
papers.selection_reason: Learnable temporal evidence selection for video anomaly understanding; fits video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Learning Temporal Evidence Selection for Video Anomaly Understanding
papers.tldr: A semantic-conditioned learnable sampler selects temporally distributed video evidence to improve language-based anomaly explanations beyond anomaly-focused sampling.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong results on video question answering, yet often fail to recover the temporal structure that makes a video coherent. They may merge neighboring events, miss single-event progression, or infer implausible relations across events. We study structured temporal understanding as the ability to recover event structure from visual evidence, including event boundaries, single-event progression, and multi-event relations. We argue that this gap arises from a mismatch between current post-training objectives and temporal reasoning, where caption-style supervision allows models to rely on language shortcuts rather than visual temporal grounding. To address this, we propose EventLens, a vision-centric reinforcement learning framework that learns video understanding through event-structure recovery. Instead of reconstructing captions, EventLens trains models to recover temporal structure under controlled perturbations, such as altered temporal granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order. We instantiate this framework with a three-level temporal ontology and derive three verifiable task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning. These tasks admit deterministic rewards, enabling task-specialized GRPO training without human preference labels or learned reward models. We further introduce multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MT-OPD) to consolidate specialized policies into a unified model. Experiments on Qwen3-VL backbones show consistent improvements on temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning benchmarks, while preserving general video-QA performance. Learning curves further demonstrate that EventLens achieves comparable downstream transfer with significantly reduced training cost compared to direct mixed RL optimization.
authors: Guowen Zhang, Boshen Xu, Zihao Yue, Ziheng Wang, Xiaokun Liu, Xin Tao, Wenyu Qin, Pengfei Wan, Qin Jin
bullets: Targets temporal-structure failures such as merged events, missed progression, and implausible cross-event relations.
Uses vision-centric reinforcement learning with controlled temporal perturbations, including altered granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order.
Trains three task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning, with deterministic rewards and task-specialized GRPO.
Uses multi-teacher on-policy distillation to combine specialized policies into one unified model.
Reports improved temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning while preserving general video-QA performance and reducing training cost versus direct mixed RL.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses temporal structure recovery in video understanding using reinforcement learning. It tackles the temporal grounding gap in MLLMs, which is a core problem in video understanding.
papers.title: EventLens: Event-Structure Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: EventLens improves video understanding by training multimodal models to recover event boundaries, progression, and relations rather than merely reconstruct captions.

papers.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.
authors: Shuo Gao, Chenhao Zheng, Zhongzheng Ren
bullets: Addresses the linear memory and latency growth caused by encoding every video frame as visual tokens.
Uses a training-free, inference-only strategy that ranks frames by prompt relevance and diversity, then packs them at varying resolutions.
Works with off-the-shelf VLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
Experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME report consistent improvements over full-resolution, token-reduction, and keyframe-selection baselines.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, gains are 12.9%, 10.6%, and 9.7% on the three benchmarks, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Constant-memory frame packing for long-video understanding; efficient token/frame selection.
papers.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FramePack-U enables VLMs to understand arbitrarily long videos with constant memory by packing prompt-relevant, diverse frames into a fixed-size visual representation.

papers.abstract: Detailed video captioning has become an essential semantic interface for multi-modal understanding and generation. While existing methods mainly target short videos, extending them to long videos remains challenging, primarily due to limited context windows of current video understanding models. A naive solution is to adopt segment-wise captioning followed by concatenation, yet this paradigm often suffers from inconsistent subject references and fragmented long-range narratives. To mitigate these issues, we introduce PIGEONS, an incremental long-video captioning model built upon a Persistent Identity Gallery and an Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary. Before caption generation, PIGEONS scans the entire video to construct an identity gallery that captures key subjects along with their visual references, thereby providing a stable referential anchor. The model then performs clip-by-clip captioning conditioned on the persistent gallery and an evolving overarching narrative summary, which compactly maintains and updates essential long-range contextual information after each captioning step. To enable these capabilities, we develop a three-stage training strategy that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PIGEONS markedly improves long-video captioning performance, achieving superior accuracy, completeness, and subject referential consistency over existing methods, while maintaining competitive performance on short-video captioning.
authors: Xinlong Chen, Weihong Lin, Yuanxing Zhang, Xinyu Liu, Yue Ding, Bozhou Li, Bohan Zeng, Yang Shi, Qiang Liu, Pengfei Wan, Liang Wang, Tieniu Tan
bullets: Addresses fragmented narratives and inconsistent subject references caused by segment-wise captioning and limited context windows.
Builds a Persistent Identity Gallery from the full video to maintain stable visual references for key subjects.
Generates captions clip by clip while updating an Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary for long-range context.
Uses a three-stage training strategy combining supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Experiments report improved long-video captioning accuracy, completeness, and referential consistency, with competitive short-video performance.
papers.selection_reason: Incremental long-video captioning with identity and narrative memory; fits video-language understanding.
papers.title: PIGEONS: Incremental Long-Video Captioning with Persistent Identity Gallery and Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary
papers.tldr: PIGEONS improves long-video captioning by preserving subject identities and updating a compact narrative across video clips.

papers.abstract: Not every moment in a video is equally useful for recognizing an action. A few decisive moments often carry the evidence: the instant an object moves, the peak of a dive, or one object placed on another. Existing video datasets rarely provide large-scale, action-conditioned labels for which short segments carry that evidence. This work asks whether vision-language models can identify meaningful moments at scale and whether those labels improve action recognition.We introduce Meaningful Moments (MM), a corpus of about 4.58 million VLM-generated per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 class-labeled videos spanning Something-Something v2 (SSv2), Kinetics-400 (K400), and Diving-48 across 622 action classes. We freeze the action classifier and vary only temporal sampling. An alpha-parameterized comparison of importance-led selection against an importance-inverted control separates gains from the VLM signal from gains caused by variable-density sampling alone. Across all three datasets, VLM-derived importance is informative: at the hard-cut endpoint, keeping VLM-important segments outperforms keeping VLM-designated filler. Usefulness depends on class structure. On Diving-48, importance-led fast-forwarding preserves full-video recognition while the inverted control collapses by roughly 30 percentage points. On K400, hard-cut selection beats uniform sampling by 1.45 percentage points, rising to 2.05 under threshold selection. On SSv2, the labels carry signal but do not recover full-video performance. Direct scoring matches greedy removal within its noise floor at roughly 25 times fewer oracle calls, and a four-VLM cross-oracle study shows consistent downstream trends. We release the importance labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0; SSv2 class strings remain under CC-BY-NC-4.0.
bullets: Introduces about 4.58 million per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 videos across SSv2, Kinetics-400, and Diving-48, covering 622 action classes.
Uses frozen action classifiers and controlled temporal sampling, including importance-inverted selection, to distinguish VLM signal from variable-density sampling effects.
VLM-important segments preserve full-video performance on Diving-48, improve Kinetics-400 accuracy over uniform sampling, and provide signal but not full recovery on SSv2.
Direct scoring achieves results comparable to greedy removal with roughly 25× fewer oracle calls; trends are consistent across four VLMs.
Releases the labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0, with SSv2 class strings separately licensed under CC-BY-NC-4.0.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-derived temporal importance labels for video action recognition; fits video understanding.
papers.title: Meaningful Moments: A Corpus of VLM-Derived Temporal Importance Labels for Video Action Recognition
papers.tldr: Meaningful Moments is a large corpus of VLM-generated temporal importance labels showing that selecting action-critical video segments can improve or preserve recognition, depending on the dataset.

papers.abstract: Recent trackers built on foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) achieve strong performance by propagating object masks through memory. However, this strength is also a key source of failure: under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors, an incorrect prediction can enter the tracking loop and be propagated over time, resulting in persistent identity drift. Existing approaches seek to prevent such failures through improved memory and temporal modeling, but once a failure occurs, the tracker has no explicit mechanism to recognize or correct it. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. A vision-language verification agent first reasons over spatio-temporal context to determine whether the tracker is still following the target. When a failure is detected, a correction agent uses temporal context to recover the target before tracking continues. The correction agent is trained on real SAM3 failures, augmented with targeted identity-switch and distractor perturbations that expose it to challenging ambiguities during recovery. On LVOS-v2 and SecVOS, Dual-Agent improves SAM3 by 1.2 and 2.7 $J\&F$, respectively. Importantly, the proposed framework transfers without retraining to SAM2.1, SeC, and Cutie, as well as to long-term video object tracking benchmarks including LaSOT-ext, TNL2K, and VOT-LT2022. Our results show that explicitly reasoning about when tracking fails and how to recover provides a complementary path to robust tracking beyond improving propagation alone. Project page: valaybundele.github.io/Dual-Agent.
authors: Valay Bundele, Susmit Agrawal, Mehran Hosseinzadeh, The Nam Nguyen, Hendrik P. A. Lensch
bullets: Targets persistent identity drift caused by incorrect masks being propagated through tracker memory under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors.
Uses a verification agent to reason over spatio-temporal context and identify whether tracking has failed.
Uses a correction agent trained on real SAM3 failures plus identity-switch and distractor perturbations to recover the target.
Improves SAM3 by 1.2 J&F on LVOS-v2 and 2.7 J&F on SecVOS.
Transfers without retraining to multiple trackers and long-term video tracking benchmarks, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-guided failure verification and recovery for video object tracking/segmentation; fits video understanding.
papers.title: When Trackers Fail: VLM-Guided Verification and Recovery for Robust Video Object Segmentation
papers.tldr: Dual-Agent improves video object segmentation by detecting tracker failures with a vision-language agent and recovering the target before identity drift persists.

papers.abstract: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. We transfer frozen V-JEPA2 features to a set of heterogeneous sensors comprised by RGB video, depth video, and radar time series. A shared fusion model uses modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of subset supervision, pooling capacity, and representation transfer on 39 OMuSense-23 subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds. With matched downstream parameter counts, the final model reaches recording-level activity macro-F1 of $75.23%\pm0.60$ averaged across seven subsets. Supervising all subsets in each batch improves the matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points (conditional 95% subject-bootstrap interval [0.647, 3.209]), while query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision. Radar probes support transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels, 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance, and the tested Consensus-JEPA loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.
authors: Yunxiang Luo, Constantino \'Alvarez Casado, Xiaoting Wu, Nhi Nguyen, Le Nguyen, Manuel Lage Ca\~nellas, Miguel Bordallo L\'opez
bullets: Evaluates all seven non-empty sensor subsets using modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit sensor availability.
On 39 OMuSense-23 subjects, achieves 75.23% ± 0.60 recording-level activity macro-F1 averaged across subsets.
Supervising every sensor subset improves performance over a matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points.
Query pooling shows no clear benefit over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision.
Radar probes support representation transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels; 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance.
papers.selection_reason: Transfers video representations to multimodal sensor fusion for activity and pose recognition.
papers.title: Learning Multimodal Sensor Fusion with JEPA Representations for Breathing Activity and Pose Recognition
papers.tldr: A multimodal fusion model transfers frozen V-JEPA2 features across RGB, depth, and radar sensors to recognize breathing activity and pose despite missing modalities.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are good at video understanding and code generation, but it remains unclear whether they can recover the physical laws underlying videos, a capability essential for converting videos into executable simulations and for providing structured physical supervision in robotics. Captioning motion video does not imply that a model has inferred its governing dynamics, estimated quantitative parameters, or can regenerate the observed scene from code. Existing video-physics benchmarks evaluate plausibility, property estimation, or future-state prediction, but offer limited insight into whether models can translate visual dynamics into runnable simulation code. We introduce PhySimCode, a benchmark for physics video-to-code generation: given only a raw video, a model must infer the relevant physics, recover parameter values, and generate runnable Python that reproduces the input video. The dataset contains 160.6K procedurally generated samples spanning 162 physics phenomena across analytic SciPy simulations and PyBullet-rendered rigid-body, articulated, fluid, and contact-rich scenes; each sample bundles the simulation code, physical parameters, rendered video, and a structured chain-of-thought covering observations, laws, ODEs, numerical methods, and validation checks. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art closed- and open-source MLLMs along physical-law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery. Models reliably state physics laws (4.27-4.93/5) yet score only 1.51-2.47/5 on inferring them from video, and the best system (Claude Sonnet 4.6) recovers just 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within $\pm 20\%$, exposing a substantial video-to-simulation gap. The 2,430-video evaluation set is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SourajaKundu123/PhySimCode and the evaluation code at https://github.com/SourajaKundu/PhySimCode
authors: Souraja Kundu, Aditya Gupta, Joel Julin, Yizhou Zhao, Liuyue Xie, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Targets video-to-code generation requiring physical-law inference, parameter recovery, and runnable simulation reproduction.
Includes 160.6K procedurally generated samples covering 162 phenomena across analytic and PyBullet-based simulations.
Evaluates law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery across 10 MLLMs.
Models state physics laws well (4.27–4.93/5) but infer them from video poorly (1.51–2.47/5).
The best system recovers only 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within ±20%, highlighting the benchmark’s challenging scope.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLM physics video-to-code generation fits video understanding and multimodal large language model evaluation.
papers.title: PhySimCode: A Benchmark and Evaluation Method for Physics Video to Code Generation
papers.tldr: PhySimCode benchmarks whether multimodal models can turn physics videos into executable, quantitatively accurate simulations, revealing a large gap between describing laws and recovering them from visual dynamics.

papers.abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. In the L3 stage, we propose an agentic annotation workflow, and equip the agent with several key tools, which empower the agent to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases, significantly reducing the need for human intervention. We conduct extensive experiments across various content issues, and results demonstrate that each stage of the autopilot labeling framework progressively improves labeling accuracy, and has significantly reduced manual labor costs in real-world applications by up to 85%.
authors: Junwen Chen, Hongwei Wang, Zixuan Wang, Jingbing Wang, Gorden Liu, Sheng Siong Ong, Xiaojiao Zang, JuChin Chao, Ze Jin, Kaiwen Men, Yin Li, Jeremy Li, Zhuolin Hao, Hongyu Xiong, Yang Song
bullets: Targets the inefficiency, slow iteration, and expense of manual short-video annotation.
L1 uses a supervised fine-tuned discriminative multimodal large language model (MLLM) for direct label prediction.
L2 applies a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short-video data for zero-shot, flexible labeling.
L3 introduces an agentic workflow with tools to address complex, unfamiliar, or ambiguous cases.
Experiments across content issues show progressive accuracy gains and substantial real-world reductions in manual effort.
papers.selection_reason: Develops MLLM-based autopilot labeling for short video content, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Towards Autopilot Labeling for Short Video Content Governance
papers.tldr: A multi-stage autopilot framework progressively automates short-video content labeling, achieving higher accuracy while reducing manual labor costs by up to 85%.

papers.abstract: Video understanding agents rely on a harness to acquire evidence, use tools, and reason, but improving it requires substantial effort. Recent self evolution methods seek to optimize harnesses through execution feedback to reduce human intervention. However, existing methods often rely on annotated video questions and answers or focus on updating model parameters, leaving harness evolution from unlabeled videos underexplored. VideoEvoHarness jointly evolves a Questioner and a Solver harness from unlabeled videos with frozen model parameters. The Questioner constructs questions and computes reference answers directly from video memory records. Question quality assessments and Solver execution trajectories guide question generation policy revisions. The Solver supports evolving skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools using execution feedback. Executable strategies define workflows in code, reducing repeated interpretation of natural language instructions. Each round, candidate harnesses are compared on identical validation questions, with validated improvements retained for later use. Experiments on benchmarks and a dedicated benchmark question set, using videos disjoint from evolution videos, show higher overall accuracy than initially and transfer gains across backbones. Overall accuracy on this set also improves progressively across rounds. This supports our foundational framework for harness evolution from unlabeled videos, opening a promising direction for self evolving video agents. Code is available at https://github.com/Wei-Xin-Xu/VideoEvoHarness.
authors: Weixin Xu, Yifan Liu, Yi Wang, Mingfei Rong, Zhenyu Yang, Zhisheng Zhong, Shengsheng Qian, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving agent harnesses without annotated video question–answer data or parameter updates.
The Questioner generates questions and reference answers from video memory, using quality assessments and Solver trajectories to revise its question-generation policy.
The Solver evolves skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools; executable code-based workflows reduce repeated interpretation of natural-language instructions.
Candidate harnesses are evaluated on identical validation questions, retaining validated improvements across rounds.
Experiments report higher accuracy than the initial harness, transfer gains across backbones, and progressive improvement across evolution rounds on disjoint videos.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving agent harness for video understanding is relevant to video understanding systems.
papers.title: VideoEvoHarness: Self Evolving Agent Harness from Unlabeled Videos for Video Understanding
papers.tldr: VideoEvoHarness self-evolves video-understanding Questioner and Solver harnesses from unlabeled videos while keeping model parameters frozen.

papers.abstract: Sexual harassment represents a pervasive societal challenge, with a substantial proportion of incidents remaining unreported due to insufficient evidence and delayed intervention mechanisms. Smart surveillance systems capable of detecting such incidents in real-time could assist law enforcement and serve as a deterrent. However, video-based harassment detection poses significant challenges, including variations in clothing, illumina- tion, partial occlusions, low resolution, and diverse camera view- points. Despite its social importance, this problem has received limited research attention, primarily due to the scarcity of large- scale annotated video datasets. To address this gap, we extend the Sexual Harassment Video (SHV) dataset to 600 short video clips sourced from YouTube and annotated into harassment and non-harassment categories using consistent labeling guidelines. We fine-tune three state-of-the-art video transformer models, VideoMAE, ViViT, and TimeSformer, pretrained on Kinetics- 400, for binary harassment classification. Experimental results show that all three models achieve competitive classification performance, with TimeSformer attaining the highest test accu- racy of 92.27%, outperforming VideoMAE 91.71% and ViViT 91.16% on the extended SHV test set. Our analysis reveals that performance is notably influenced by dataset size, video quality, frame sampling strategy, and model architecture. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of modern video transformers for this sensitive real-world task.
authors: Jubayer- Al- Mahmud, Md Shamimul Islam, Md Nur Hossain
bullets: Addresses real-time video-based harassment detection despite visual challenges and limited annotated data.
Expands the Sexual Harassment Video dataset to 600 YouTube clips labeled as harassment or non-harassment.
Fine-tunes VideoMAE, ViViT, and TimeSformer pretrained on Kinetics-400 for binary classification.
TimeSformer achieves 92.27% test accuracy, compared with 91.71% for VideoMAE and 91.16% for ViViT.
Performance is influenced by dataset size, video quality, frame sampling, and model architecture.
papers.selection_reason: Fine-tuning video transformers for harassment classification is a video understanding application.
papers.title: Video-Based Sexual Harassment Detection Using Fine-Tuned Video Transformers
papers.tldr: The study evaluates fine-tuned video transformers for sexual-harassment detection, with TimeSformer achieving the best reported test accuracy on an expanded dataset.

papers.abstract: Reliable individual monitoring is essential for dairy cattle welfare and early heat stress detection in Precision Livestock Farming (PLF). However, translating raw multi-camera videos into automated diagnostics remains challenging due to disconnected tracking and recognition pipelines and complex physical environments. Dense mutual occlusions and cross-camera viewpoint variations fragment identities, while environmental noise, including camera vibrations, and limited agricultural data obscure subtle heat stress cues such as rapid breathing and flank undulations. To bridge low-level visual features and high-level behavioral diagnostics, we propose CowCare, a unified framework combining viewpoint-robust tracking with spatiotemporal heat stress recognition. Its tracking module, CowTrack, maintains cross-camera identity consistency through a View-Decoupled Aggregation Network (VDA-Net). Instead of relying on static global representations, VDA-Net aggregates localized textures under heavy occlusion and uses a Viewpoint Decoupling Transformer (VDT) to suppress transient viewpoint variations. CowTrack further incorporates a causal online self-supervision mechanism for continuous adaptation to dynamic farm scenes. The resulting tracklets are subsequently processed by TSDF-Net, a fine-grained video understanding network. Its Temporal Stabilization and Aggregation Module (TSAM) suppresses high-frequency jitter, while a Diffusion Semantic Prior (DSP) uses frozen pre-trained diffusion semantics to enhance subtle behavioral signals and mitigate overfitting. Extensive evaluations on two real-world farm benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness: CowTrack achieves 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 for global multi-object tracking on MVCow, and TSDF-Net achieves 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow. These results establish CowCare as a robust end-to-end framework for automated livestock health monitoring.
authors: Xin Liu, Weiran Li, Minghao Zhu, Mina Han, Zhenbo Li
bullets: Addresses identity fragmentation from occlusion and cross-camera viewpoint changes, plus subtle and noisy heat-stress cues.
CowTrack uses localized feature aggregation, viewpoint decoupling, and causal online self-supervision for adaptive cross-camera identity consistency.
TSDF-Net stabilizes temporal signals and uses frozen diffusion-model semantics to improve recognition of subtle behaviors.
On two real-world farm benchmarks, CowTrack reports 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 on MVCow, while TSDF-Net reaches 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow.
The framework targets robust automated monitoring in dynamic agricultural environments, though its scope is limited to the evaluated farm benchmarks and visual cues.
papers.selection_reason: Spatiotemporal heat-stress recognition from multi-camera video fits video understanding.
papers.title: CowCare: A Unified Visual Framework for Viewpoint-Robust Cattle Tracking and Spatiotemporal Heat-Stress Analysis
papers.tldr: CowCare unifies viewpoint-robust multi-camera cattle tracking with fine-grained video analysis to support automated heat-stress monitoring in complex farm environments.

papers.abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.
authors: Pushp Garg, Himangshu Sarma, Mrinmoy Ghorai
bullets: Addresses variable signing speeds, complex spatial structure, and limited large-vocabulary ISL benchmarks.
Uses entropy-driven SVD sampling to retain informative keyframes and reduce computational redundancy.
Models irregular temporal gaps with Continuous Dual Positional Encoding and a distance-aware Elastic Transformer.
Captures bimanual geometry through a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN with unified bone-joint features.
Introduces a 9,453-video, 120-class native ISL dataset and reports 89.8% accuracy, with scope focused on gloss recognition.
papers.selection_reason: Sign language recognition from video with temporal and kinematic modeling fits video understanding.
papers.title: A Hybrid Kinematic GCN and Elastic Transformer for Efficient Indian Sign Language Recognition
papers.tldr: A structurally aware hybrid model efficiently recognizes 120-class Indian Sign Language by combining informative keyframe sampling, irregular-time modeling, and bimanual kinematic graph reasoning.

papers.abstract: We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Enzhi Zhou, Junan Lin, Dulan Zhou, Weiqiang Wang, Yuge Huang, Jian Liu
bullets: Covers six dimensions: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose.
Questions target quantities such as depth, interpersonal distance, gaze angle, velocity, trajectories, blink count, and contact-deformation strength.
Labels are generated programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state rather than human annotation or model estimation.
The benchmark includes a training corpus produced by the same pipeline and evaluates both open- and closed-source MLLMs.
Results indicate that all six dimensions remain challenging and are only partially dissociable for current MLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for human-centric physical and spatial perception in MLLMs; fits spatial intelligence and video understanding.
papers.title: HumanPhys: A Human-Centric Physical-World Perception Benchmark for Real-World Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: HumanPhys benchmarks whether multimodal models can infer physically grounded human- and camera-related quantities from real-world visual inputs.

papers.abstract: We present CAST-ASD (Causal Attention over Speakers and Time), a causal joint model for active speaker detection (ASD). Recent ASD models improve performance by jointly processing all faces in a scene, but operate offline, with the full clip available before any frame is labelled. Low-latency causal detectors instead process each face independently. CAST-ASD combines joint face reasoning with fully causal inference. It applies scene-level attention across faces within the current frame and causal temporal attention over each face's history, enabling information sharing across speakers with zero lookahead. Its parameter count does not grow with the number of faces. On MSDWild, where most negative face-frames contain a visible competing speaker, CAST-ASD reduces competing-speaker false alarms by 32% relative to the causal per-face detector it extends, with larger gains as scene occupancy increases. It outperforms all causal baselines on both validation splits while using only one-tenth the inter-speaker parameters of a three-block fixed-roster convolution. Code and models are available at https://github.com/prathamg007/CAST-ASD.
authors: Pratham Gupta, Haotian Qi, Tushar Sandhan, Gabriel Skantze
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between offline joint models and causal per-face detectors.
Uses scene-level attention across faces in the current frame and causal temporal attention for each face.
Keeps parameter count independent of the number of faces.
On MSDWild, reduces competing-speaker false alarms by 32% versus its causal per-face baseline, with larger gains in more crowded scenes.
Outperforms causal baselines on both validation splits while using one-tenth the inter-speaker parameters of a fixed-roster convolution model.
papers.selection_reason: Causal joint attention for online active speaker detection; fits video understanding.
papers.title: CAST-ASD: Causal Attention over Speakers and Time for Online Active Speaker Detection
papers.tldr: CAST-ASD enables low-latency active speaker detection by jointly reasoning across faces and causal temporal histories without looking ahead.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions from the observed video, with evidence drawn from recent observations or earlier events. Historical context can improve recall but may interfere with judgments based on recent frames. Its usefulness depends on both when it is introduced and which clips are selected, while relevance alone does not guarantee sufficient evidence for an answer. We propose SPARE, a framework that combines adaptive historical retrieval with visual encoder sharing. A lightweight gate predicts whether recent observations provide sufficient evidence to answer the question. When additional evidence is predicted to be necessary, a multimodal embedding model retrieves relevant historical clips to supplement the current context. LoRA instruction tuning trains the understanding model to use recent observations and retrieved history jointly and abstain when the evidence remains insufficient. To reduce redundant visual parameters, the understanding and retrieval branches share a visual encoder while retaining separate language backbones. Four linear adapters align the shared features with the retrieval model through distillation at the visual token and final retrieval embedding levels. With visual-only inputs, SPARE achieves 77.78% on the evaluated Real-time and Backward task groups of OVO-Bench and 73.31% on StreamingBench. Compared with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluated at 2 fps, SPARE improves accuracy by 20.68 percentage points on OVO-Bench and 14.15 percentage points on StreamingBench.
authors: Senbin Xu, Zijun Zhang, Xinhua Wu, Li He, Jubo Feng, Li Qiao, Zhen Gao, Yan Zhang, Jixiang Luo, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses the challenge of balancing recent observations with potentially useful—but distracting—historical context.
Uses a lightweight gate to determine whether additional evidence is needed, then retrieves relevant past clips with a multimodal embedding model.
Trains the model to jointly use current and retrieved evidence and abstain when evidence remains insufficient.
Shares a visual encoder across understanding and retrieval branches, with separate language backbones and distillation-based adapters.
With visual-only inputs, reaches 77.78% on evaluated OVO-Bench tasks and 73.31% on StreamingBench; the abstract reports gains over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 2 fps.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video QA with adaptive historical retrieval; fits video understanding.
papers.title: SPARE: Shared Perception and Adaptive Retrieval of Evidence for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: SPARE improves streaming video question answering by adaptively retrieving historical clips only when recent frames are insufficient, while sharing visual features between perception and retrieval.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.
authors: Chaoyue Li, Shoudong Han, Haoyang Wu, Boxue Yang, Sijia Chen, Yufan Chen, Ruping Zhang
bullets: Defines Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU): tracking entity continuity, forecasting future trajectories and events, and grounding predictions in observed visual evidence.
SceneForesee provides paired observed/future scenes with shared identities, including 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K evidence-linked events.
EvoSee jointly reasons over future geometry and event semantics using shared candidate states and entity assignment.
EvoSee improves over Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1.
It also improves Dyn-Bench question answering and grounding, supporting predicted entity changes as dynamic representations for spatiotemporal reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and framework for scene evolution and spatiotemporal reasoning in video with LMMs.
papers.title: SceneForesee: Learning Scene Evolution for Spatiotemporal Reasoning
papers.tldr: SceneForesee introduces a benchmark and EvoSee framework for predicting and explaining how entities and scenes evolve over time from video.

papers.abstract: Understanding and tracking a dynamic world are fundamental to visual intelligence. Existing video benchmarks provide limited insight into whether models can maintain a coherent understanding of evolving world state. Building such a benchmark from real-world videos is challenging because the underlying world state is partially observable, making annotations hard to obtain. To close this gap, we introduce Video-Arena, a benchmark that turns competitive games into scalable, verifiable tests of how well models understand evolving world states from videos. Specifically, inspired by how humans understand dynamic events, we evaluate spatiotemporal world state understanding and tracking through three task categories: perceiving critical events, interpreting state updates, and tracking the resulting states. Our pipeline can generate videos and aligned reference labels from game records at scale. To keep evaluation affordable and reproducible, we curate a golden set of 180 tasks across 9 games and run evaluations under two protocols: native visual understanding and tool-assisted agentic analysis. The best-performing systems achieve F1 scores of and under the two protocols, respectively. The result highlights that native models struggle to perceive events reliably, while tool-assisted systems improve event recovery but still struggle to interpret state updates and track the resulting states consistently over time. Our project page is in https://videoarena-bench.github.io
authors: Kuan Zhang, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yue Su, Xiangnan Wu, Zirong Chen, Run Luo, Tao Tan, Yinhe Zheng, Yiming Li
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating coherent understanding of partially observable, dynamic world states in real-world videos.
Generates videos and aligned reference labels from competitive game records at scale.
Covers three capabilities: critical-event perception, state-update interpretation, and resulting-state tracking.
Includes 180 tasks across 9 games under native visual-understanding and tool-assisted agentic protocols.
Finds that tools improve event recovery, but systems still struggle with state interpretation and consistent temporal tracking; the abstract omits the reported F1 values.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for spatiotemporal video understanding and world-state tracking; directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Video-Arena: A Scalable Agentic Video Benchmark for Spatiotemporal Capability
papers.tldr: Video-Arena benchmarks whether models can perceive events, interpret updates, and track evolving world states in videos using scalable, verifiable game-based tasks.

papers.abstract: Accurate artery extraction from X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) is essential for coronary artery disease diagnosis and intervention. However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra-arterial contrast information. We propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model (TDBM) that formulates vessel extraction as image translation and learns from physics-informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics-based XCA synthesis engine generates diverse, perfectly aligned pairs of contrast-enhanced and contrast-free images. Using these pairs, TDBM learns cross-domain mappings to recover high-fidelity vessel information. Temporal conditioning incorporates adjacent frames to improve consistency, while a vessel-aware contrastive loss exploits background-invariant synthetic pairs to enhance vascular discrimination. We evaluate TDBM on two XCA vessel segmentation datasets and conduct a reader study using two real-patient XCA sequence datasets. Zero-shot segmentation is further assessed on retinal imaging and fluorescence microscopy datasets. Results demonstrate that TDBM consistently outperforms existing methods and generalizes effectively across imaging modalities. Code and trained weights will be available at: https://github.com/Advanced-AI-in-Medicine-and-Physics-Lab/TDBM
authors: Jinkui Hao, Donald R. Cantrell, Ramez Abdalla, Sameer A. Ansari, Bo Zhou
bullets: Addresses poor vessel visibility, cardiac and respiratory motion, and limited annotated XCA data.
Generates aligned contrast-enhanced/contrast-free image pairs with a physics-based synthesis engine.
Uses temporal conditioning and vessel-aware contrastive learning to improve consistency and vascular discrimination.
Evaluated on XCA segmentation, real-patient sequence reader studies, and zero-shot retinal and fluorescence microscopy tasks.
Reports consistent improvements over existing methods and effective cross-modality generalization, without specifying numeric results.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model for vessel extraction that uses physics-informed synthetic data and temporal conditioning, bridging video generation and understanding.
papers.title: Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model for Vessel Extraction Using Physics-informed Synthetic Data
papers.tldr: TDBM uses physics-informed synthetic XCA pairs and temporal diffusion modeling to extract vessels while preserving intra-arterial contrast information without manual annotations.

papers.abstract: Video segmentation models recognize and track objects over time, but they do not indicate whether each segmented region moves independently of the observing camera. This dynamicity attribute cannot be inferred from semantics alone and is confounded by camera ego-motion. We introduce \method, an online framework that augments query-based video segmentation with region-level dynamicity prediction. It jointly produces the original segmentation outputs and a dynamic or static state for each predicted region. At inference, DynEoMT uses only the current frame and propagated queries, without optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps. Because established video segmentation benchmarks do not annotate this attribute, we also introduce a class-agnostic offline supervision pipeline using camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, DynEoMT achieves balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance. These results show that segmentation-region dynamicity can be learned from propagated queries, enabling its online prediction without a dedicated motion-processing pipeline at inference. The complete code will be released as open source to enable full reproduction of the method and experiments.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of distinguishing independently moving objects from camera-induced motion, which semantics alone cannot resolve.
Jointly predicts segmentation masks and region-level dynamicity without optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps at inference.
Introduces an offline supervision pipeline based on camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering.
Evaluated on VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, achieving balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6 while largely preserving segmentation performance.
papers.selection_reason: Online video segmentation with region-level dynamicity prediction; temporal video understanding.
papers.title: DynEoMT: Learning Object Dynamicity from Online Segmentation Queries
papers.tldr: DynEoMT augments online video segmentation with per-region dynamic/static predictions using only current-frame inputs and propagated queries.

papers.abstract: Modern video-language models are increasingly treated as general-purpose video reasoners, yet it remains unclear whether they robustly capture temporal dynamics in safety-critical settings such as driving. We study this question through controlled ego-motion tasks that require identifying actions from driving videos. Across video-language models, we find that standard prompting, visual prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought prompting remain unreliable and highly task- and model-dependent, with persistent class biases, although newer models show substantial task-specific few-shot gains. In contrast, lightweight LoRA finetuning and simple probes trained on intermediate visual features recover strong motion-discriminative performance, indicating that motion-relevant cues are often present inside the models but are not reliably used by the final video-to-language pathway. These results suggest that, in driving, current video-language models remain unreliable temporal reasoners and often behave more like frame-level, bias-driven recognizers than dependable temporal world models.
authors: Shiva Sreeram, Erfan Aasi, Tsun-Hsuan Wang, Alaa Maalouf, Daniela Rus
bullets: The study evaluates temporal understanding through controlled ego-motion action-identification tasks in driving videos.
Standard, visual, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting are unreliable and strongly dependent on the task and model.
Models exhibit persistent class biases, though newer systems can gain substantially from task-specific few-shot examples.
Lightweight LoRA finetuning and probes on intermediate visual features achieve strong motion discrimination.
Findings suggest final video-to-language pathways underuse temporal cues, causing models to act more like frame-level recognizers than temporal world models.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluation of temporal reasoning in video-language models for driving.
papers.title: Mind the Temporal Gap: Evaluating Video Models for Temporal Understanding in Driving
papers.tldr: Current video-language models often fail to reliably understand temporal dynamics in driving videos, despite containing motion-relevant information that lightweight adaptation can unlock.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively unmasking multiple tokens in parallel using a learned mask predictor. Their output carries two errors: parallelization error due to parallel sampling, and estimation error from the mask predictor learned with finite samples. Existing theory treats these errors separately, and the available statistical bounds typically scale with the number $V^L$ of length-$L$ sequences over a vocabulary of size $V$, suffering from the curse of dimensionality. In this work, we establish end-to-end statistical guarantees showing that transformer-based MDMs learn structured distributions with a sample complexity governed by their latent structure. Specifically, we model this structure through mixtures of hidden Markov trees, which capture latent dependencies within components and heterogeneity across components. When the data distribution is well approximated by such a mixture, a transformer-based MDM with parallel unmasking schedules achieves $\varepsilon$-accurate sampling in KL divergence with $\widetilde{O}(LK_{\mathrm{par}}/\varepsilon)$ training samples, where $K_{\mathrm{par}}$ is polynomial in $L$, $V$, the number of hidden states, and the number of mixture components. The transformer network and sampling procedure require no knowledge of the tree topologies or component parameters, thereby adapting to the unknown latent structure automatically. Overall, our results provide theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of MDMs on real-world data.
bullets: Addresses both parallelization and finite-sample estimation errors in masked diffusion models.
Models structured data as mixtures of hidden Markov trees, capturing latent dependencies and component heterogeneity.
Proves end-to-end ε-accurate sampling in KL divergence with approximately O(LK_par/ε) training samples.
The polynomial factor K_par depends on sequence length, vocabulary size, hidden states, and mixture components.
The method adapts to unknown tree topologies and component parameters without requiring them as input.
papers.selection_reason: Provides theoretical guarantees for transformer-based Masked Diffusion Models learning structured distributions, bridging video understanding and latent dynamics prediction.
papers.title: Transformer-Based Masked Diffusion Models Provably Learn Distributions with Latent Structure
papers.tldr: Transformer-based masked diffusion models can learn discrete distributions with latent structure using sample complexity that depends on the structure rather than the full sequence space.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models learn mostly from paired image-text data or annotated video, and raw web video is rarely used to further train an existing language model. We study whether raw video, with no captions and no text loss, can serve as mid-training data for a pretrained language model. Frames are encoded into continuous visual tokens, and the language model learns to predict the next visual token. We mid-train Qwen3-1.7B on raw clips from YT-Temporal-1B and then apply the same image-text instruction tuning to it and to the model without mid-training, so that the two differ only in mid-training. The mid-trained model scores 2.9 points higher on average across four video benchmarks and 5.1 points higher across ten image benchmarks, spanning perception, document, and chart tasks. Text performance is preserved even though mid-training includes no text, with an average of 48.9 across 14 text benchmarks compared with 48.0 for the model without mid-training. Analyses across training show that the image and video gains emerge within 30% of training and plateau thereafter, varying by less than 0.5 points. Predicting captions fails to outperform next-visual-token prediction, demonstrating that video mid-training can remain purely self-supervised without the computational overhead or labeling noise of automated captioning.
authors: Jaedong Hwang, Xiaoqian Shen, Ernie Chang, Changsheng Zhao, Chong Zhou, Saksham Suri, Qi Qian, Zechun Liu, Lemeng Wu, Qinsi Wang, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Wei Wen
bullets: Raw, uncaptained web video can be used to mid-train a pretrained language model.
The method encodes frames as continuous visual tokens and trains the model to predict the next visual token.
After identical image-text instruction tuning, mid-training yields +2.9 average points on four video benchmarks and +5.1 on ten image benchmarks.
Text performance is preserved: 48.9 average across 14 text benchmarks versus 48.0 without mid-training.
Gains appear early and plateau; caption prediction does not outperform next-visual-token prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Self-supervised raw-video mid-training of MLLMs via next visual token prediction improves video and image understanding.
papers.title: Mid-Training Language Models on Raw Video
papers.tldr: Mid-training a language model on raw video by predicting visual tokens improves downstream video and image understanding while preserving text performance, without captions or text supervision.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly evolving toward continuous audio--visual reasoning, creating an urgent need for evaluations that expose their capability limits. Audio--visual captioning is an ideal diagnostic task, yet current benchmarks face a coupled trade-off: whole-caption scores provide coverage without localization, local probes provide localization without coverage, and unconstrained LLM judges introduce instability. We introduce OmniCapBench (Omni-Video Caption Benchmark), a benchmark that reframes audio--visual caption evaluation as a deep-structured diagnostic framework. OmniCapBench shifts the prediction target from free-form text to sets of atomic, verifiable evaluation units across three tracks: entity references, visual shots, and audio events, enabling reliable scoring with deterministic constraint checks and localized LLM-based semantic comparisons. With 786 densely annotated videos, OmniCapBench effectively distinguishes MLLM perception errors, including temporal grounding failures, identity drift, cross-modal misalignment, and hallucinated descriptions. Evaluating frontier MLLMs reveals strong local perception but weak long-horizon audio--visual reasoning, particularly in identity drift and cross-modal misalignment, providing a fine-grained roadmap for omnimodal development.
authors: Zhongyu Yang, Jiale Tao, Ruitao Chen, Zuhao Yang, Yingfang Yuan, Xueliang Zhao, Auden, Kai Wang, Shuai Shao, Biao Wang, Steve Yves, Qinglin Lu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between broad whole-caption coverage, localized evaluation, and unstable unconstrained LLM judging.
Decomposes captions into three tracks: entity references, visual shots, and audio events.
Combines deterministic constraint checks with localized LLM-based semantic comparisons for reliable scoring.
